chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: You are the victim of a cognizable offence and need to report it to the police.
chunks.text:
Situation: You are the victim of a cognizable offence and need to report it to the police.
Applicable Law: Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1898.
Immediate Action: Visit the local Police Station that has territorial jurisdiction over the area where the crime occurred.
Authority: Station House Officer (SHO) or the Officer-in-Charge of the Police Station.
Procedure:
1. Inform the SHO orally or in writing about the incident.
2. If given orally, the police officer is legally bound to reduce it to writing.
3. The recorded statement will be read over to you.
4. You must sign the statement after verifying its accuracy.
5. The SHO will enter the substance in the Daily Diary (Roznamcha) and register the FIR.
6. A free copy of the FIR must be provided to you.
Required Documents:
- Original CNIC and copies.
- Written application detailing the offence (optional but recommended).
- Any available evidence (medical report, CCTV, witnesses).
Application/Petition Type: Written Application to SHO.
Filing Route: Direct submission at the Police Station front desk.
Next Step: Police begin investigation under Chapter XIV of CrPC.
Possible Remedy: Initiation of criminal investigation and arrest of accused.
Relevant Court/Forum: Area Magistrate (for monitoring police progress).
Case-Study Reference: State vs. Accused (Standard FIR Procedure).
Source: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, Section 154.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: The police (SHO) refuse to register an FIR for a cognizable offence.
chunks.text:
Situation: The police (SHO) refuse to register an FIR for a cognizable offence.
Applicable Law: Section 22-A and 22-B of CrPC; Article 199 of the Constitution.
Immediate Action: Submit a written complaint to the Superintendent of Police (SP) or DSP (Complaint Cell).
Authority: Ex-Officio Justice of Peace (Sessions Judge) / SP Complaints.
Procedure:
1. File a written application to the SP Complaints via post or by hand, retaining a receipt.
2. If the SP does not act, file a petition under Section 22-A(6) CrPC before the Sessions Judge (Ex-Officio Justice of Peace).
3. The court will call for a report and parawise comments from the SHO.
4. After hearing arguments, if a cognizable offence is made out, the court will issue directions to the SHO to register the FIR.
5. Alternatively, file a direct/private complaint to the Magistrate under Section 200 CrPC.
Required Documents:
- Copy of the written application given to the SHO and SP.
- Postal receipts (TCS/Registry) proving the application was sent to SP.
- CNIC copy and affidavit.
Application/Petition Type: Petition under Section 22-A/22-B CrPC.
Filing Route: Through a lawyer in the District & Sessions Court.
Next Step: Hearing before the Justice of Peace.
Possible Remedy: Court order binding the police to register the FIR.
Relevant Court/Forum: District & Sessions Court (Ex-Officio Justice of Peace).
Case-Study Reference: Your situation may be similar to reported case PLD 2016 SC 581 (FIR Registration Guidelines).
Source: CrPC Sections 22-A, 22-B, 154, 200.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: You wish to bypass the police or the police refused FIR, and you want to directly prosecute the accused in court.
chunks.text:
Situation: You wish to bypass the police or the police refused FIR, and you want to directly prosecute the accused in court.
Applicable Law: Section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
Immediate Action: Draft a private criminal complaint (Istighasa).
Authority: Judicial Magistrate of the First Class / Area Magistrate.
Procedure:
1. File the complaint directly before the Magistrate having jurisdiction.
2. The Magistrate examines the complainant on oath and any witnesses present (Section 200).
3. If the Magistrate finds sufficient ground, they issue summons or a warrant against the accused (Section 204).
4. The Magistrate may also direct a police inquiry under Section 202 before issuing process.
Required Documents: Written complaint (Istighasa), CNIC, list of witnesses, documentary evidence.
Application/Petition Type: Private Criminal Complaint under Sec 200 CrPC.
Filing Route: Filing branch of the Magistrate Court.
Possible Remedy: Direct trial of the accused without police challan.
Relevant Court/Forum: Court of Judicial Magistrate.
Case-Study Reference: Private prosecution cases bypass police investigation.
Source: CrPC Section 200.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: A person has been arrested by the police.
chunks.text:
Situation: A person has been arrested by the police.
Applicable Law: Article 10 of the Constitution; Sections 54, 61, 167 of CrPC.
Immediate Action: Ascertain the location of the police station and the FIR details. Contact a lawyer immediately.
Authority: Police (Arresting Authority) and Judicial Magistrate.
Procedure:
1. The police can arrest without warrant only in cognizable offences (Section 54 CrPC).
2. The arrested person has a fundamental right to be informed of the grounds of arrest and consult a lawyer (Article 10).
3. The police cannot detain a person for more than 24 hours without court permission.
4. Within 24 hours, the police must produce the accused before a Magistrate to seek physical remand (Section 61 & 167 CrPC).
Required Documents: Copy of FIR, CNIC of accused (for bail bonds later).
Possible Remedy: Bail application or Habeas Corpus petition if detention is illegal/unrecorded.
Relevant Court/Forum: Area Magistrate.
Case-Study Reference: Your situation may be similar to reported cases on illegal detention and Article 10 rights.
Source: Constitution of Pakistan (Art 10), CrPC Sections 54, 61, 167.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: Police have presented the accused before a Magistrate and are asking for physical custody (remand) to investigate.
chunks.text:
Situation: Police have presented the accused before a Magistrate and are asking for physical custody (remand) to investigate.
Applicable Law: Section 167 of CrPC.
Immediate Action: The defense lawyer must oppose physical remand and request judicial remand (sending accused to jail, not police custody).
Authority: Judicial Magistrate.
Procedure:
1. Police produce the accused before the Magistrate within 24 hours of arrest.
2. Police request physical remand for a specific number of days, providing reasons (e.g., weapon recovery).
3. Magistrate examines the police diaries (Zimnies) to see if physical custody is justified.
4. Maximum aggregate physical remand cannot exceed 15 days (except in ATA/NAB cases).
5. After physical remand ends, accused is sent on judicial remand to prison.
Required Documents: Police diaries, FIR copy.
Application/Petition Type: Oral arguments by defense counsel opposing remand.
Next Step: Apply for post-arrest bail once judicial remand is granted.
Relevant Court/Forum: Court of Judicial Magistrate.
Source: CrPC Section 167.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: The accused is already in police or judicial custody and seeks release on bail pending trial.
chunks.text:
Situation: The accused is already in police or judicial custody and seeks release on bail pending trial.
Applicable Law: Sections 496 (Bailable) and 497 (Non-bailable) of CrPC.
Immediate Action: Draft and file a Post-Arrest Bail Application.
Authority: Judicial Magistrate, Sessions Court, or High Court.
Procedure:
1. Bailable Offence: File application under Sec 496. Bail is a matter of right. Court grants it upon submission of surety bonds.
2. Non-Bailable Offence: File under Sec 497. Bail is a matter of discretion.
3. General Rule for Non-bailable: "Bail not jail", but typically refused for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or 10+ years (Prohibitory Clause).
4. Exceptions for Prohibitory Clause: Women, minors under 16, sick/infirm, or if there are "further inquiry" grounds.
Required Documents: Bail application, copy of FIR, Vakalatnama, CNIC of accused and surety.
Filing Route: Filed first in the trial court (Magistrate or Sessions). If rejected, filed in the next higher court.
Possible Remedy: Release from custody upon furnishing surety bonds.
Relevant Court/Forum: Trial Court -> Sessions Court -> High Court.
Source: CrPC Sections 496, 497.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: You have not been arrested but apprehend imminent arrest by police due to an FIR or complaint motivated by malice or ulterior motives.
chunks.text:
Situation: You have not been arrested but apprehend imminent arrest by police due to an FIR or complaint motivated by malice or ulterior motives.
Applicable Law: Section 498 and 498-A of CrPC.
Immediate Action: File for Pre-Arrest (Anticipatory) Bail before arrest takes place.
Authority: Court of Session or High Court.
Procedure:
1. Must be filed in the Sessions Court first (or High Court in exceptional circumstances).
2. The accused MUST surrender physically before the court during the hearing.
3. Court may grant interim pre-arrest bail and issue notice to the State/Police for a final hearing.
4. At the final hearing, if the court finds the FIR is maliciously motivated (ulterior motives), it will confirm the bail. Otherwise, it recalls the bail, and police can arrest the accused outside the courtroom.
Required Documents: Bail application, copy of FIR, Vakalatnama, affidavit, surety bonds.
Application/Petition Type: Pre-Arrest Bail Petition.
Relevant Court/Forum: Sessions Court.
Case-Study Reference: Your situation may be similar to PLD 1983 SC 82 (Hidayat Ullah Khan case) regarding malice requirements.
Source: CrPC Sections 498, 498-A.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: Understanding the complete lifecycle of a criminal trial.
chunks.text:
Situation: Understanding the complete lifecycle of a criminal trial.
Applicable Law: Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
Procedure:
1. FIR Registration (Sec 154) / Private Complaint (Sec 200).
2. Investigation by Police (Sec 156-173).
3. Submission of Challan / Police Report under Section 173 to the Magistrate (within 14+3 days).
4. Supply of statements and documents to the accused (Sec 241-A / 265-C).
5. Framing of Charge by the Court (Sec 242 / 265-D).
6. Plea of Accused (Guilty / Not Guilty).
7. Prosecution Evidence (Examination-in-chief by prosecutor, cross-examination by defense).
8. Statement of the Accused under Section 342 CrPC (Accused explains circumstances).
9. Defense Evidence (if accused opts to present witnesses under Sec 340(2)).
10. Final Arguments by both sides.
11. Judgment (Acquittal or Conviction).
12. Sentencing and Appeal.
Source: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
Note on Time: Actual time varies heavily by court, jurisdiction, case type, and circumstances.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: You need to resolve a civil dispute (property, contract, damages, declaration).
chunks.text:
Situation: You need to resolve a civil dispute (property, contract, damages, declaration).
Applicable Law: Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), 1908.
Immediate Action: Send a legal notice (optional but recommended), then file a Plaint.
Authority: Civil Judge / Senior Civil Judge.
Procedure:
1. Institution of Suit: File a written Plaint detailing the facts, cause of action, and relief sought (Order VII CPC).
2. Issuance of Summons to the Defendant (Order V).
3. Written Statement: Defendant files a reply within 30 days (Order VIII).
4. Framing of Issues: Court identifies the points of factual and legal dispute (Order XIV).
5. Evidence: Plaintiff submits documentary and oral evidence; Defendant cross-examines. Then Defendant submits evidence.
6. Final Arguments.
7. Judgment and Decree (Order XX).
8. Execution: Filing an execution petition to enforce the decree (Order XXI).
Required Documents: Plaint, Vakalatnama, CNIC, lists of witnesses, documentary evidence, court fee (as per Court Fees Act, varies by province/claim value).
Filing Route: Institution branch of the Civil Courts.
Possible Remedy: Court decree granting injunction, declaration, damages, or specific performance.
Relevant Court/Forum: Civil Court.
Source: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: Resolving family matters such as Khula, Divorce, Dower (Mehr), Dowry Articles (Jahez), Restitution of Conjugal Rights.
chunks.text:
Situation: Resolving family matters such as Khula, Divorce, Dower (Mehr), Dowry Articles (Jahez), Restitution of Conjugal Rights.
Applicable Law: West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964; Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961.
Immediate Action: File a family suit in the Family Court.
Authority: Judge Family Court.
Procedure:
1. Wife or Husband files a plaint in the Family Court (jurisdiction usually where the wife resides).
2. Court issues notice/summons to the defendant.
3. Defendant files a Written Statement.
4. Pre-Trial Reconciliation: Mandatory stage where the judge attempts to reconcile the parties.
5. If reconciliation fails, court proceeds (if it's a Khula case, Khula is usually granted immediately upon failure of reconciliation, subject to return of dower).
6. Recording of Evidence for other claims (maintenance, dowry).
7. Post-Trial Reconciliation.
8. Final Judgment and Decree.
Required Documents: Plaint, Nikah Nama (Marriage Certificate), CNIC, list of dowry articles with receipts (if claiming), birth certificates of children.
Costs: Court fee for family suits is nominal (usually Rs. 15).
Relevant Court/Forum: Family Court.
Source: West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: Dispute over the custody of minor children (Hizanat) after separation or divorce.
chunks.text:
Situation: Dispute over the custody of minor children (Hizanat) after separation or divorce.
Applicable Law: Guardians and Wards Act, 1890; West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964.
Immediate Action: File an application for custody or guardianship.
Authority: Guardian Judge (Family Court).
Procedure:
1. File petition under Section 9 or 25 of the Guardians and Wards Act before the Guardian Judge.
2. Notice is issued to the other parent.
3. The court's paramount consideration is the "Welfare of the Minor" (not strict rights of parents).
4. Interim Custody / Visitation: The court establishes a schedule for the non-custodial parent to meet the child during the pendency of the case.
5. Evidence is recorded regarding the financial, moral, and emotional capacity of both parents.
6. Final order awarding permanent custody.
Required Documents: Petition, minor's birth certificate/B-Form, CNIC of applicant.
Possible Remedy: Custody of the child, or court-mandated visitation rights.
Relevant Court/Forum: Guardian Judge / Family Court.
Case-Study Reference: Your situation may be similar to reported cases on "welfare of the minor" paramountcy.
Source: Guardians and Wards Act, 1890.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: A wife or children are not being financially supported by the husband/father.
chunks.text:
Situation: A wife or children are not being financially supported by the husband/father.
Applicable Law: Muslim Family Laws Ordinance (MFLO) 1961; West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964.
Immediate Action: File a maintenance suit in the Family Court or apply to the Arbitration Council.
Authority: Judge Family Court or Union Council Chairman.
Procedure (Family Court):
1. Wife files a suit for past and future maintenance for herself and/or children.
2. Notice to husband.
3. Court may fix Interim Maintenance during the trial.
4. Evidence regarding husband's income/assets is presented.
5. Final decree fixing monthly maintenance amount.
Required Documents: Nikah Nama, children's birth certificates, evidence of husband's income/salary slips.
Possible Remedy: Monthly financial allowance; recovery of past unpaid maintenance.
Relevant Court/Forum: Family Court.
Source: West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: Dispute between landlord and tenant (e.g., eviction, unpaid rent).
chunks.text:
Situation: Dispute between landlord and tenant (e.g., eviction, unpaid rent).
Applicable Law: Provincial Rent Restriction Acts (e.g., Punjab Rented Premises Act 2009, Sindh Rented Premises Ordinance 1979).
Jurisdiction: Note that tenancy laws are strictly provincial. Punjab, Sindh, KPK, Balochistan, and ICT have their own specific rent laws.
Immediate Action: Ensure a registered tenancy agreement exists. Send a legal notice.
Authority: Rent Registrar / Rent Controller (usually a Civil Judge acting as Rent Controller).
Procedure (e.g., Punjab):
1. Tenancy agreement MUST be registered with the Rent Registrar.
2. To evict a tenant or recover rent, landlord files an Eviction Petition before the Rent Controller.
3. Notice is issued to the tenant.
4. Tenant must seek "leave to defend" (permission to contest the case).
5. If leave is granted, evidence is recorded.
6. Final order of eviction or rent recovery.
Required Documents: Registered Tenancy Agreement, legal notices sent, proof of default.
Application/Petition Type: Eviction Petition.
Relevant Court/Forum: Rent Controller.
Source: Provincial Rented Premises Acts.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: Dispute over ownership, possession, or illegal occupation of immovable property.
chunks.text:
Situation: Dispute over ownership, possession, or illegal occupation of immovable property.
Applicable Law: Transfer of Property Act 1882; Specific Relief Act 1877; Illegal Dispossession Act 2005.
Immediate Action: File a civil suit for declaration/possession, or a criminal complaint if illegally dispossessed by land grabbers.
Authority: Civil Court or Sessions Court (for Illegal Dispossession Act).
Procedure (Civil Suit for Declaration/Injunction):
1. File a suit for declaration of title and permanent injunction under the Specific Relief Act.
2. File an application for a stay order (Temporary Injunction under Order 39 Rules 1 & 2 CPC) to prevent the property from being sold or altered during the trial.
3. Civil trial stages follow (Plaint, Written Statement, Issues, Evidence, Decree).
Procedure (Illegal Dispossession Act):
1. If dispossessed by the "Qabza Mafia", file a direct complaint in the Sessions Court.
2. Court directs police/revenue officer to investigate and report.
3. Fast-track trial for restoration of possession.
Required Documents: Title documents (Registry, Fard, Allotment Letter), CNIC.
Possible Remedy: Declaration of ownership, recovery of possession, or stay order.
Relevant Court/Forum: Civil Court or District & Sessions Court.
Source: Specific Relief Act, 1877; Illegal Dispossession Act, 2005.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: You purchased a defective product or received faulty/deficient services.
chunks.text:
Situation: You purchased a defective product or received faulty/deficient services.
Applicable Law: Provincial Consumer Protection Acts (Punjab, Sindh, KPK, Balochistan, ICT).
Jurisdiction: Procedures and strict timelines vary by province.
Immediate Action: Send a mandatory legal notice to the seller/service provider.
Authority: District Consumer Court.
Procedure:
1. Send a written Legal Notice giving the seller 15 days to resolve the issue (refund, replace, or repair).
2. If unresolved, file a claim in the Consumer Court within 30 days of the cause of action.
3. No court fee is required to file a consumer claim.
4. Court issues notice to the respondent.
5. Trial proceeds.
Required Documents: Receipt/Proof of purchase, copy of the Legal Notice sent and its postal receipt, CNIC.
Application/Petition Type: Consumer Claim for Damages/Refund.
Filing Route: Filed with the Registrar of the Consumer Court.
Possible Remedy: Refund, replacement, and damages for mental agony.
Relevant Court/Forum: District Consumer Court.
Source: Provincial Consumer Protection Acts.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: Unfair dismissal, unpaid wages, or workplace rights violation.
chunks.text:
Situation: Unfair dismissal, unpaid wages, or workplace rights violation.
Applicable Law: Provincial Industrial and Commercial Employment (Standing Orders) Ordinances; Industrial Relations Acts (IRA).
Immediate Action: Serve a grievance notice to the employer.
Authority: Labour Court / NIRC (National Industrial Relations Commission).
Procedure:
1. Grievance Notice: The worker must send a grievance notice to the employer within 3 months of the incident (e.g., termination).
2. The employer has 15 days to reply.
3. If unsatisfied or no reply, file a Grievance Petition in the Labour Court within 2 months.
4. The Labour Court adjudicates the matter, takes evidence, and passes an award.
Required Documents: Appointment letter, termination letter, salary slips, copy of grievance notice with postal receipt.
Application/Petition Type: Grievance Petition under IRA.
Possible Remedy: Reinstatement with back benefits, or recovery of unpaid dues.
Relevant Court/Forum: Labour Court.
Source: Industrial Relations Acts.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: You are a victim of online fraud, hacking, cyberbullying, or unauthorized use of identity.
chunks.text:
Situation: You are a victim of online fraud, hacking, cyberbullying, or unauthorized use of identity.
Applicable Law: Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), 2016.
Immediate Action: Secure all digital evidence (screenshots, URLs, emails) and do not delete them.
Authority: Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) Cybercrime Wing.
Procedure:
1. Online Complaint: Register the initial complaint via https://complaint.fia.gov.pk/ or email.
2. Physical Visit: Visit the nearest FIA Cybercrime Reporting Center.
3. Submit a written application addressed to the Additional Director FIA, detailing the crime and attaching evidence.
4. FIA conducts a preliminary verification/inquiry.
5. If an offence under PECA is made out, FIA registers an FIR.
6. The accused is investigated, arrested, and a challan is submitted to the Cybercrime Court.
Required Documents: CNIC, detailed application, USB/CD with screenshots, links, IP addresses, transaction receipts (for fraud).
Filing Route: FIA Cybercrime Reporting Centers.
Possible Remedy: Takedown of content, arrest of cybercriminals, recovery of defrauded money.
Relevant Court/Forum: FIA (Investigation) -> Designated Cybercrime Court (Trial).
Source: PECA 2016.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: Harassment at the workplace by a colleague, boss, or employer.
chunks.text:
Situation: Harassment at the workplace by a colleague, boss, or employer.
Applicable Law: Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010.
Immediate Action: File a complaint internally or directly to the Ombudsperson.
Authority: Internal Inquiry Committee OR Federal/Provincial Ombudsperson for Protection against Harassment.
Procedure:
1. You can submit a written complaint to the organization's Internal Inquiry Committee, which must decide within 30 days.
2. Alternatively, you can directly file a complaint with the Provincial or Federal Ombudsperson.
3. The Ombudsperson issues a notice to the accused and management.
4. Hearings are conducted.
5. The Ombudsperson can award major or minor penalties (warning, demotion, dismissal, fine).
Required Documents: Written complaint, evidence of harassment (emails, messages, witnesses).
Application/Petition Type: Harassment Complaint.
Possible Remedy: Disciplinary action against the harasser, compensation.
Relevant Court/Forum: Ombudsperson for Harassment.
Source: Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act, 2010.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: You cannot afford a lawyer and need free legal representation.
chunks.text:
Situation: You cannot afford a lawyer and need free legal representation.
Applicable Law: Legal Aid and Justice Authority Act, 2020; District Legal Empowerment Committees (DLEC).
Immediate Action: Apply to the relevant legal aid authority or bar council.
Authority: Legal Aid and Justice Authority, DLECs, or Provincial Bar Councils.
Procedure:
1. Identify the forum: For criminal cases (especially women/children), approach the Legal Aid and Justice Authority. For civil/general, approach DLEC (through the Deputy Commissioner or District Judge).
2. Submit a formal application proving indigency (inability to pay), usually requiring a Zakat certificate or income affidavit.
3. The committee reviews the application.
4. If approved, a lawyer is appointed from their panel, and their fee is paid by the state/committee.
Required Documents: CNIC, poverty/income certificate, details of the legal case.
Filing Route: Office of the District & Sessions Judge (for DLEC) or Bar Council office.
Possible Remedy: Free legal representation and coverage of court fees.
Source: Legal Aid and Justice Authority Act, 2020.

chunks.title: Comprehensive Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Situation: You are dissatisfied with the final judgment or an interim order of a lower court.
chunks.text:
Situation: You are dissatisfied with the final judgment or an interim order of a lower court.
Applicable Law: CrPC (Criminal) or CPC (Civil).
Immediate Action: Obtain certified copies of the impugned judgment/order immediately.
Authority: Appellate Court (Sessions Court, High Court, or Supreme Court).
Procedure (Civil/Criminal Appeal):
1. Obtain certified copies of the trial court's judgment and decree/order.
2. Draft a Memorandum of Appeal citing the grounds (errors in law or fact).
3. File the appeal in the higher court strictly within the limitation period (usually 30 days, but varies).
4. For interim orders where no appeal lies, file a Revision Petition (Section 115 CPC or Section 439 CrPC) to correct jurisdictional errors.
Required Documents: Memorandum of Appeal, certified copies of the impugned judgment, Vakalatnama.
Next Step: The appellate court will hear arguments on admission and issue notice to the respondent.
Relevant Court/Forum: District/Sessions Court (if trial was Magistrate/Civil Judge) or High Court.
Note on Time: The limitation period is strictly enforced; delays must be justified by an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
Source: CrPC, CPC, Limitation Act.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872) — Short title, extent and commencement. This Act may be called the Contract Act, 1872. It extends to the whole of Pakistan and applies to all contracts made on or after 1 September 1872. Source: The Pakistan Code (pakistancode.gov.pk). Status: CURRENT. Provisions: Sections 1–238.
chunks.text: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872) — Short title, extent and commencement. This Act may be called the Contract Act, 1872. It extends to the whole of Pakistan and applies to all contracts made on or after 1 September 1872. Source: The Pakistan Code (pakistancode.gov.pk). Status: CURRENT. Provisions: Sections 1–238.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Contract Act — Interpretation Clause. (a) Proposal (offer): when one person signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything with a view to obtaining the assent of that other; (b) Promise: proposal when accepted becomes a promise; (c) Promisor/promisee: person making / accepting the proposal; (d) Consideration: when at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing something; (e) Agreement: every promise and every set of promises forming consideration for each other; (f) Contract: agreement enforceable by law; (g) Void agreement: not enforceable by law; (h) Voidable contract: enforceable at option of one party; (i) Contingent contract: to do or not to do upon happening of uncertain event.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Communication, acceptance and revocation of proposals — Section 3: Communication of proposal, acceptance and revocation are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party proposing, accepting or revoking by which he intends to communicate or which has the effect of communicating.
chunks.text: Communication, acceptance and revocation of proposals — Section 3: Communication of proposal, acceptance and revocation are deemed to be made by any act or omission of the party proposing, accepting or revoking by which he intends to communicate or which has the effect of communicating.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Communication when complete — Communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. Communication of acceptance is complete as against the proposer when put in course of transmission to him; as against the acceptor when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer. Revocation is complete against the person who makes it when it is put in course of transmission; against the person to whom it is made when it comes to his knowledge.
chunks.text: Communication when complete — Communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made. Communication of acceptance is complete as against the proposer when put in course of transmission to him; as against the acceptor when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer. Revocation is complete against the person who makes it when it is put in course of transmission; against the person to whom it is made when it comes to his knowledge.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Revocation of proposals and acceptances — A proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer. An acceptance may be revoked at any time before the communication of the acceptance is complete as against the acceptor, but not afterwards.
chunks.text: Revocation of proposals and acceptances — A proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer. An acceptance may be revoked at any time before the communication of the acceptance is complete as against the acceptor, but not afterwards.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: How revocation is made — A proposal is revoked by: (1) notice of revocation by the proposer; (2) lapse of time prescribed or if no time prescribed, by lapse of reasonable time; (3) failure of condition precedent; (4) death or insanity of the proposer, if the fact of death or insanity comes to the knowledge of the acceptor before acceptance.
chunks.text: How revocation is made — A proposal is revoked by: (1) notice of revocation by the proposer; (2) lapse of time prescribed or if no time prescribed, by lapse of reasonable time; (3) failure of condition precedent; (4) death or insanity of the proposer, if the fact of death or insanity comes to the knowledge of the acceptor before acceptance.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Acceptance must be absolute — In order to convert a proposal into a promise, the acceptance must be absolute and unqualified, and must be expressed in some usual and reasonable manner unless the proposal prescribes the manner of acceptance.
chunks.text: Acceptance must be absolute — In order to convert a proposal into a promise, the acceptance must be absolute and unqualified, and must be expressed in some usual and reasonable manner unless the proposal prescribes the manner of acceptance.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Acceptance by performing condition — Performance of the conditions of a proposal, or the acceptance of any consideration for a reciprocal promise which may be offered with a proposal, is an acceptance.
chunks.text: Acceptance by performing condition — Performance of the conditions of a proposal, or the acceptance of any consideration for a reciprocal promise which may be offered with a proposal, is an acceptance.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Express and implied promises — Promises may be express (made by words spoken or written) or implied (inferred from the conduct of the parties or from circumstances).
chunks.text: Express and implied promises — Promises may be express (made by words spoken or written) or implied (inferred from the conduct of the parties or from circumstances).

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: What agreements are contracts — All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not expressly declared to be void.
chunks.text: What agreements are contracts — All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not expressly declared to be void.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Who are competent to contract — Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority (18 years in Pakistan), who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.
chunks.text: Who are competent to contract — Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority (18 years in Pakistan), who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Sound mind — A person is said to be of sound mind if at the time of making the contract he is capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests.
chunks.text: Sound mind — A person is said to be of sound mind if at the time of making the contract he is capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Free consent — Two or more persons are said to consent when they agree upon the same thing in the same sense.
chunks.text: Free consent — Two or more persons are said to consent when they agree upon the same thing in the same sense.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Free consent defined — Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by: (1) coercion, (2) undue influence, (3) fraud, (4) misrepresentation, or (5) mistake.
chunks.text: Free consent defined — Consent is said to be free when it is not caused by: (1) coercion, (2) undue influence, (3) fraud, (4) misrepresentation, or (5) mistake.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Coercion — Coercion is the committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the Pakistan Penal Code, or the unlawful detaining or threatening to detain any property, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement.
chunks.text: Coercion — Coercion is the committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the Pakistan Penal Code, or the unlawful detaining or threatening to detain any property, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Undue influence — A contract is said to be induced by undue influence where the relations subsisting between the parties are such that one of the parties is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other.
chunks.text: Undue influence — A contract is said to be induced by undue influence where the relations subsisting between the parties are such that one of the parties is in a position to dominate the will of the other and uses that position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Fraud — Fraud means and includes any of the following acts by a party to a contract or with his connivance: (a) suggestion of a fact which is not true; (b) active concealment of a fact; (c) promise made without intention of performing it; (d) any other act fitted to deceive; (e) any such act or omission as the law specially declares to be fraudulent.
chunks.text: Fraud — Fraud means and includes any of the following acts by a party to a contract or with his connivance: (a) suggestion of a fact which is not true; (b) active concealment of a fact; (c) promise made without intention of performing it; (d) any other act fitted to deceive; (e) any such act or omission as the law specially declares to be fraudulent.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Misrepresentation — Misrepresentation means: (a) a positive assertion of a fact not true but believed to be true; (b) any breach of duty which gives an advantage to the person committing it by misleading the other; (c) causing a party to make a mistake as to the substance of the thing which is the subject of the agreement.
chunks.text: Misrepresentation — Misrepresentation means: (a) a positive assertion of a fact not true but believed to be true; (b) any breach of duty which gives an advantage to the person committing it by misleading the other; (c) causing a party to make a mistake as to the substance of the thing which is the subject of the agreement.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Voidability of agreements without free consent — When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.
chunks.text: Voidability of agreements without free consent — When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion, fraud or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Void agreements due to mistake — Where both parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void.
chunks.text: Void agreements due to mistake — Where both parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement, the agreement is void.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Lawful consideration and object — The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful unless it is: forbidden by law, or would defeat the provisions of any law, or is fraudulent, or involves injury to the person or property of another, or the court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy.
chunks.text: Lawful consideration and object — The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful unless it is: forbidden by law, or would defeat the provisions of any law, or is fraudulent, or involves injury to the person or property of another, or the court regards it as immoral or opposed to public policy.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Agreement without consideration void — An agreement made without consideration is void, unless: (1) it is expressed in writing and registered under the Registration Act and is made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in near relation; (2) it is a promise to compensate for something voluntarily done; (3) it is a promise to pay a debt barred by limitation law.
chunks.text: Agreement without consideration void — An agreement made without consideration is void, unless: (1) it is expressed in writing and registered under the Registration Act and is made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in near relation; (2) it is a promise to compensate for something voluntarily done; (3) it is a promise to pay a debt barred by limitation law.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Agreement in restraint of marriage void — Every agreement in restraint of the marriage of any person, other than a minor, is void.
chunks.text: Agreement in restraint of marriage void — Every agreement in restraint of the marriage of any person, other than a minor, is void.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Agreement in restraint of trade void — Every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind is void to that extent. Exceptions: sale of goodwill, partnership non-compete during term.
chunks.text: Agreement in restraint of trade void — Every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind is void to that extent. Exceptions: sale of goodwill, partnership non-compete during term.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Agreements in restraint of legal proceedings void — Agreements limiting time to enforce rights, restricting parties from enforcing rights through courts, or discharging parties from liability for breach, are void.
chunks.text: Agreements in restraint of legal proceedings void — Agreements limiting time to enforce rights, restricting parties from enforcing rights through courts, or discharging parties from liability for breach, are void.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Agreements void for uncertainty — Agreements, the meaning of which is not certain or capable of being made certain, are void.
chunks.text: Agreements void for uncertainty — Agreements, the meaning of which is not certain or capable of being made certain, are void.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Wagering agreements void — Agreements by way of wager are void. No suit shall be brought for recovering anything alleged to be won on a wager.
chunks.text: Wagering agreements void — Agreements by way of wager are void. No suit shall be brought for recovering anything alleged to be won on a wager.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Contingent contracts — A contingent contract is a contract to do or not to do something if some event collateral to the contract does or does not happen.
chunks.text: Contingent contracts — A contingent contract is a contract to do or not to do something if some event collateral to the contract does or does not happen.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Enforcement of contingent contracts — Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event happens cannot be enforced unless the event has happened. If the event becomes impossible, such contracts become void.
chunks.text: Enforcement of contingent contracts — Contingent contracts to do or not to do anything if an uncertain future event happens cannot be enforced unless the event has happened. If the event becomes impossible, such contracts become void.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Obligation of parties — Parties to a contract must either perform or offer to perform their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act or of any other law.
chunks.text: Obligation of parties — Parties to a contract must either perform or offer to perform their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act or of any other law.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Effect of refusal to accept offer — Where a promisor has made an offer of performance and the promisee does not accept it within a reasonable time, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance nor loses his rights under the contract.
chunks.text: Effect of refusal to accept offer — Where a promisor has made an offer of performance and the promisee does not accept it within a reasonable time, the promisor is not responsible for non-performance nor loses his rights under the contract.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Effect of refusal of party to perform — When a party to a contract has refused to perform or disabled himself from performing his promise in its entirety, the other party may put an end to the contract.
chunks.text: Effect of refusal of party to perform — When a party to a contract has refused to perform or disabled himself from performing his promise in its entirety, the other party may put an end to the contract.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Personal performance — A contract involving personal skill or confidence must be performed by the promisor personally unless the contract allows delegation.
chunks.text: Personal performance — A contract involving personal skill or confidence must be performed by the promisor personally unless the contract allows delegation.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Time for performance — Where no time is specified for performance, the promise must be performed within a reasonable time.
chunks.text: Time for performance — Where no time is specified for performance, the promise must be performed within a reasonable time.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Reciprocal promises — When a contract consists of reciprocal promises to be simultaneously performed, no promisor need perform his promise unless the promisee is ready and willing to perform his reciprocal promise.
chunks.text: Reciprocal promises — When a contract consists of reciprocal promises to be simultaneously performed, no promisor need perform his promise unless the promisee is ready and willing to perform his reciprocal promise.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Effect of failure to perform at fixed time — When a party fails to perform at the stipulated time and the contract is not void due to time being essential, the contract is voidable at the option of the other party if the intention was that time should be essential.
chunks.text: Effect of failure to perform at fixed time — When a party fails to perform at the stipulated time and the contract is not void due to time being essential, the contract is voidable at the option of the other party if the intention was that time should be essential.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Doctrine of frustration — An agreement to do an impossible act is void. A contract to do an act which becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made becomes void when the impossibility or unlawfulness occurs.
chunks.text: Doctrine of frustration — An agreement to do an impossible act is void. A contract to do an act which becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made becomes void when the impossibility or unlawfulness occurs.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Effect of novation, rescission and alteration — If the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract or to rescind or alter it, the original contract need not be performed.
chunks.text: Effect of novation, rescission and alteration — If the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract or to rescind or alter it, the original contract need not be performed.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Promisee may dispense with performance — Every promisee may dispense with or remit wholly or in part the performance of the promise made to him, or may extend the time for such performance, or may accept instead of it any satisfaction which he thinks fit.
chunks.text: Promisee may dispense with performance — Every promisee may dispense with or remit wholly or in part the performance of the promise made to him, or may extend the time for such performance, or may accept instead of it any satisfaction which he thinks fit.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Consequences of rescission of voidable contract — When a person at whose option a contract is voidable rescinds it, the other party need not perform his promise. The party rescinding must restore any benefit received from the other party.
chunks.text: Consequences of rescission of voidable contract — When a person at whose option a contract is voidable rescinds it, the other party need not perform his promise. The party rescinding must restore any benefit received from the other party.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement — When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract must restore it or make compensation for it.
chunks.text: Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement — When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract must restore it or make compensation for it.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Indemnity — A contract of indemnity is a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself or by the conduct of any other person.
chunks.text: Indemnity — A contract of indemnity is a contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor himself or by the conduct of any other person.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Indemnity defined — A contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor or any other person is called a contract of indemnity.
chunks.text: Indemnity defined — A contract by which one party promises to save the other from loss caused to him by the conduct of the promisor or any other person is called a contract of indemnity.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Guarantee defined — A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default. The person who gives the guarantee is called the surety, the person for whom the guarantee is given is called the principal debtor, and the person to whom the guarantee is given is called the creditor.
chunks.text: Guarantee defined — A contract of guarantee is a contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default. The person who gives the guarantee is called the surety, the person for whom the guarantee is given is called the principal debtor, and the person to whom the guarantee is given is called the creditor.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Consideration for guarantee — Anything done or any promise made for the benefit of the principal debtor may be a sufficient consideration to the surety for giving the guarantee.
chunks.text: Consideration for guarantee — Anything done or any promise made for the benefit of the principal debtor may be a sufficient consideration to the surety for giving the guarantee.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Surety's liability — The liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract.
chunks.text: Surety's liability — The liability of the surety is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, unless it is otherwise provided by the contract.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Discharge of surety — Any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance.
chunks.text: Discharge of surety — Any variance made without the surety's consent in the terms of the contract between the principal debtor and the creditor discharges the surety as to transactions subsequent to the variance.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Discharge by release of principal debtor — The surety is discharged if the creditor releases the principal debtor, or does any act inconsistent with the rights of the surety, or omits to do any act which his duty to the surety requires.
chunks.text: Discharge by release of principal debtor — The surety is discharged if the creditor releases the principal debtor, or does any act inconsistent with the rights of the surety, or omits to do any act which his duty to the surety requires.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Discharge by creditor's act or omission — The surety is discharged if the creditor loses or parts with any security given to him by the principal debtor without the surety's consent.
chunks.text: Discharge by creditor's act or omission — The surety is discharged if the creditor loses or parts with any security given to him by the principal debtor without the surety's consent.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Bailment defined — A bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall be returned or disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them when the purpose is accomplished.
chunks.text: Bailment defined — A bailment is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall be returned or disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them when the purpose is accomplished.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Delivery to bailee — The delivery to the bailee may be actual or constructive.
chunks.text: Delivery to bailee — The delivery to the bailee may be actual or constructive.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Bailor's duty — The bailor is bound to disclose to the bailee faults in the goods bailed of which the bailor is aware and which materially interfere with their use or expose the bailee to extraordinary risks.
chunks.text: Bailor's duty — The bailor is bound to disclose to the bailee faults in the goods bailed of which the bailor is aware and which materially interfere with their use or expose the bailee to extraordinary risks.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Care to be taken by bailee — In all cases of bailment, the bailee must take as much care of the goods bailed as a man of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods of similar quality and value.
chunks.text: Care to be taken by bailee — In all cases of bailment, the bailee must take as much care of the goods bailed as a man of ordinary prudence would take of his own goods of similar quality and value.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Bailee when not liable — If the bailee has taken the amount of care required by Section 151, he is not responsible for the loss, destruction or deterioration of the thing bailed.
chunks.text: Bailee when not liable — If the bailee has taken the amount of care required by Section 151, he is not responsible for the loss, destruction or deterioration of the thing bailed.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Liability for unauthorized use — If the bailee makes any unauthorized use of the goods bailed, he is liable to make compensation to the bailor for any damage arising from such use.
chunks.text: Liability for unauthorized use — If the bailee makes any unauthorized use of the goods bailed, he is liable to make compensation to the bailor for any damage arising from such use.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Pledge defined — The bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise is called pledge. The bailor is called the pawnor and the bailee is called the pawnee.
chunks.text: Pledge defined — The bailment of goods as security for payment of a debt or performance of a promise is called pledge. The bailor is called the pawnor and the bailee is called the pawnee.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Pawnee's right of retainer — The pawnee may retain the goods pledged as security for the payment of the debt or the performance of the promise.
chunks.text: Pawnee's right of retainer — The pawnee may retain the goods pledged as security for the payment of the debt or the performance of the promise.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Pawnee's right where pawnor defaults — If the pawnor makes default in payment of the debt or performance of the promise, the pawnee may sell the goods pledged after giving reasonable notice to the pawnor.
chunks.text: Pawnee's right where pawnor defaults — If the pawnor makes default in payment of the debt or performance of the promise, the pawnee may sell the goods pledged after giving reasonable notice to the pawnor.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Agent defined — An agent is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done or who is so represented is called the principal.
chunks.text: Agent defined — An agent is a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done or who is so represented is called the principal.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Who may employ agent — Any person who is of the age of majority and of sound mind may employ an agent.
chunks.text: Who may employ agent — Any person who is of the age of majority and of sound mind may employ an agent.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Who may be agent — As between the principal and third persons, any person may become an agent.
chunks.text: Who may be agent — As between the principal and third persons, any person may become an agent.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: No consideration for agency — No consideration is necessary to create an agency.
chunks.text: No consideration for agency — No consideration is necessary to create an agency.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Agent's authority — The authority of an agent may be express or implied.
chunks.text: Agent's authority — The authority of an agent may be express or implied.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Implied authority — Authority is said to be implied when it is inferred from the circumstances of the case, and things spoken or written, or the ordinary course of dealing.
chunks.text: Implied authority — Authority is said to be implied when it is inferred from the circumstances of the case, and things spoken or written, or the ordinary course of dealing.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Extent of agent's authority — An agent having authority to do an act has authority to do every lawful thing which is necessary in order to do such act.
chunks.text: Extent of agent's authority — An agent having authority to do an act has authority to do every lawful thing which is necessary in order to do such act.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Agency for sale — An agent having authority to carry on a business has authority to do all things usual in the course of such business.
chunks.text: Agency for sale — An agent having authority to carry on a business has authority to do all things usual in the course of such business.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Ratification — Where acts are done by one person on behalf of another but without his knowledge or authority, the other may elect to ratify such acts. The effect of ratification is the same as if the acts had been performed by authority.
chunks.text: Ratification — Where acts are done by one person on behalf of another but without his knowledge or authority, the other may elect to ratify such acts. The effect of ratification is the same as if the acts had been performed by authority.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Termination of agency — An agency is terminated: by the principal revoking the authority; by the agent renouncing the business; by completion of business; by death or insanity of principal or agent; by insolvency of principal.
chunks.text: Termination of agency — An agency is terminated: by the principal revoking the authority; by the agent renouncing the business; by completion of business; by death or insanity of principal or agent; by insolvency of principal.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Agent's duty — An agent must conduct the business of his principal according to the directions given by the principal. In the absence of directions, according to the custom which prevails in doing business of the same kind.
chunks.text: Agent's duty — An agent must conduct the business of his principal according to the directions given by the principal. In the absence of directions, according to the custom which prevails in doing business of the same kind.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Skill and diligence — An agent must act with reasonable diligence and use such skill as he possesses.
chunks.text: Skill and diligence — An agent must act with reasonable diligence and use such skill as he possesses.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Agent's duty to communicate — An agent must communicate with his principal and take instructions from him in cases of difficulty.
chunks.text: Agent's duty to communicate — An agent must communicate with his principal and take instructions from him in cases of difficulty.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Principal's liability for agent's acts — The employer of an agent is bound to indemnify him against the consequences of all lawful acts done by the agent in exercise of his authority.
chunks.text: Principal's liability for agent's acts — The employer of an agent is bound to indemnify him against the consequences of all lawful acts done by the agent in exercise of his authority.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Principal bound by agent's acts — Contracts entered into through an agent and obligations arising from acts done by an agent in the exercise of his authority have the same legal consequences as if the contracts had been entered into and the acts done by the principal personally.
chunks.text: Principal bound by agent's acts — Contracts entered into through an agent and obligations arising from acts done by an agent in the exercise of his authority have the same legal consequences as if the contracts had been entered into and the acts done by the principal personally.

chunks.title: The Contract Act, 1872 (Act IX of 1872)
chunks.chunkTitle: Notice to agent — Any notice given to or information obtained by the agent in the course of business conducted by him for the principal shall, as between the principal and third parties, have the same legal consequences as if it had been given to or obtained by the principal.
chunks.text: Notice to agent — Any notice given to or information obtained by the agent in the course of business conducted by him for the principal shall, as between the principal and third parties, have the same legal consequences as if it had been given to or obtained by the principal.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984) — The law of evidence applicable to all judicial proceedings in Pakistan. Repeals and replaces the Evidence Act 1872. Source: Pakistan Code (pakistancode.gov.pk). Status: CURRENT.
chunks.text: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984) — The law of evidence applicable to all judicial proceedings in Pakistan. Repeals and replaces the Evidence Act 1872. Source: Pakistan Code (pakistancode.gov.pk). Status: CURRENT.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Interpretation — In this Order, 'court' includes all judges, magistrates, arbitrators and all persons legally authorized to take evidence. 'Facts' include physical/mental states and conditions. 'Relevant fact' means one fact connected with another in any of the ways referred to in the provisions of this Order.
chunks.text: Interpretation — In this Order, 'court' includes all judges, magistrates, arbitrators and all persons legally authorized to take evidence. 'Facts' include physical/mental states and conditions. 'Relevant fact' means one fact connected with another in any of the ways referred to in the provisions of this Order.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Definition of evidence — Evidence means and includes: (1) all statements which the court permits or requires to be made before it by witnesses in relation to matters of fact under inquiry (oral evidence); (2) all documents produced for the inspection of the court (documentary evidence).
chunks.text: Definition of evidence — Evidence means and includes: (1) all statements which the court permits or requires to be made before it by witnesses in relation to matters of fact under inquiry (oral evidence); (2) all documents produced for the inspection of the court (documentary evidence).

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Res gestae — Facts which, though not in issue, are so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction are relevant, whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places.
chunks.text: Res gestae — Facts which, though not in issue, are so connected with a fact in issue as to form part of the same transaction are relevant, whether they occurred at the same time and place or at different times and places.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue — Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect, immediate or otherwise, of relevant facts or facts in issue, or which constitute the state of things under which they happened, or which afforded an opportunity for their occurrence or transaction, are relevant.
chunks.text: Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue — Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect, immediate or otherwise, of relevant facts or facts in issue, or which constitute the state of things under which they happened, or which afforded an opportunity for their occurrence or transaction, are relevant.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Motive, preparation and conduct — Any fact which shows motive for any fact in issue or relevant fact, or any fact which constitutes preparation for or previous or subsequent conduct with reference to any fact in issue or relevant fact, is relevant.
chunks.text: Motive, preparation and conduct — Any fact which shows motive for any fact in issue or relevant fact, or any fact which constitutes preparation for or previous or subsequent conduct with reference to any fact in issue or relevant fact, is relevant.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Facts necessary to explain or introduce relevant facts — Facts necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or relevant fact, or which support or rebut an inference suggested by such fact, or which establish the identity of any person or thing, are relevant.
chunks.text: Facts necessary to explain or introduce relevant facts — Facts necessary to explain or introduce a fact in issue or relevant fact, or which support or rebut an inference suggested by such fact, or which establish the identity of any person or thing, are relevant.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Admissions defined — An admission is a statement, oral or documentary, which suggests any inference as to any fact in issue or relevant fact, and which is made by any person under the circumstances hereinafter mentioned.
chunks.text: Admissions defined — An admission is a statement, oral or documentary, which suggests any inference as to any fact in issue or relevant fact, and which is made by any person under the circumstances hereinafter mentioned.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Admission by party to proceeding — Statements made by a party to the proceeding, or by an agent authorized to make them, are admissions. Also statements by persons who have a proprietary or pecuniary interest in the subject-matter of the proceeding.
chunks.text: Admission by party to proceeding — Statements made by a party to the proceeding, or by an agent authorized to make them, are admissions. Also statements by persons who have a proprietary or pecuniary interest in the subject-matter of the proceeding.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Confessions defined — A confession is an admission made at any time by a person accused of an offence stating or suggesting the inference that he committed that offence.
chunks.text: Confessions defined — A confession is an admission made at any time by a person accused of an offence stating or suggesting the inference that he committed that offence.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Confession caused by inducement, threat or promise — A confession made by an accused person is irrelevant if it appears to the court to have been caused by any inducement, threat or promise proceeding from a person in authority, sufficient to give the accused grounds for supposing that he would gain any advantage or avoid any evil in reference to the proceedings.
chunks.text: Confession caused by inducement, threat or promise — A confession made by an accused person is irrelevant if it appears to the court to have been caused by any inducement, threat or promise proceeding from a person in authority, sufficient to give the accused grounds for supposing that he would gain any advantage or avoid any evil in reference to the proceedings.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Confession to police officer — No confession made to a police officer shall be proved against a person accused of any offence.
chunks.text: Confession to police officer — No confession made to a police officer shall be proved against a person accused of any offence.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Confession in custody — No confession made by any person while in custody of a police officer, unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved.
chunks.text: Confession in custody — No confession made by any person while in custody of a police officer, unless made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, shall be proved.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Information leading to discovery — When any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, so much of such information as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved.
chunks.text: Information leading to discovery — When any fact is deposed to as discovered in consequence of information received from a person accused of any offence, so much of such information as relates distinctly to the fact discovered may be proved.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Confession by co-accused — A confession made by one accused person against another accused person, when they are tried jointly for the same offence, may be taken into consideration against the other accused.
chunks.text: Confession by co-accused — A confession made by one accused person against another accused person, when they are tried jointly for the same offence, may be taken into consideration against the other accused.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Burden of proof — Whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts must prove that those facts exist. The burden of proof lies on the person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side.
chunks.text: Burden of proof — Whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts must prove that those facts exist. The burden of proof lies on the person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Burden of proof in criminal cases — In criminal proceedings, the burden of proving the guilt of the accused lies on the prosecution. This is the principle of presumption of innocence until proven guilty.
chunks.text: Burden of proof in criminal cases — In criminal proceedings, the burden of proving the guilt of the accused lies on the prosecution. This is the principle of presumption of innocence until proven guilty.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Presumptions — The court may presume the existence of certain facts. Presumptions may be rebuttable or irrebuttable. Illustrations: Certified copies of public documents are presumed genuine; a person in possession of stolen goods soon after theft may be presumed to have stolen them.
chunks.text: Presumptions — The court may presume the existence of certain facts. Presumptions may be rebuttable or irrebuttable. Illustrations: Certified copies of public documents are presumed genuine; a person in possession of stolen goods soon after theft may be presumed to have stolen them.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Estoppel — When one person has by his declaration, act or omission intentionally caused or permitted another person to believe a thing to be true and to act upon such belief, neither he nor his representative shall be allowed to deny the truth of that thing in any suit or proceeding.
chunks.text: Estoppel — When one person has by his declaration, act or omission intentionally caused or permitted another person to believe a thing to be true and to act upon such belief, neither he nor his representative shall be allowed to deny the truth of that thing in any suit or proceeding.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Estoppel of tenant — No tenant of immovable property, or person claiming through such tenant, shall be permitted to deny that the landlord had title to the property at the beginning of the tenancy.
chunks.text: Estoppel of tenant — No tenant of immovable property, or person claiming through such tenant, shall be permitted to deny that the landlord had title to the property at the beginning of the tenancy.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Witness competence — All persons shall be competent to testify unless the court considers they are prevented from understanding the questions put to them or from giving rational answers due to tender years, extreme old age, disease of mind or body, or any other similar cause.
chunks.text: Witness competence — All persons shall be competent to testify unless the court considers they are prevented from understanding the questions put to them or from giving rational answers due to tender years, extreme old age, disease of mind or body, or any other similar cause.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Dumb witnesses — A witness who is unable to speak may give his evidence in writing or by signs, which must be interpreted.
chunks.text: Dumb witnesses — A witness who is unable to speak may give his evidence in writing or by signs, which must be interpreted.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Number of witnesses — No particular number of witnesses is required for proof of any fact, unless otherwise provided by any law.
chunks.text: Number of witnesses — No particular number of witnesses is required for proof of any fact, unless otherwise provided by any law.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Examination of witnesses — Witnesses shall be first examined-in-chief, then cross-examined, and then re-examined. Leading questions may not be put in examination-in-chief or re-examination without the court's permission, but may be put in cross-examination.
chunks.text: Examination of witnesses — Witnesses shall be first examined-in-chief, then cross-examined, and then re-examined. Leading questions may not be put in examination-in-chief or re-examination without the court's permission, but may be put in cross-examination.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Hostile witness — A party may, with the permission of the court, cross-examine his own witness if the witness appears hostile, adverse or interested in the outcome.
chunks.text: Hostile witness — A party may, with the permission of the court, cross-examine his own witness if the witness appears hostile, adverse or interested in the outcome.

chunks.title: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984)
chunks.chunkTitle: Impeaching credit of witness — The credit of a witness may be impeached by: (1) evidence of persons that they do not believe the witness on oath; (2) proof that the witness has been bribed or accepted offers; (3) former inconsistent statements; (4) evidence of general reputation for untruthfulness.
