chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Muslim Personal Law of Succession and Inheritance — Governed by Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1962 and classical Islamic jurisprudence. Source: Pakistan Code. Status: CURRENT.
chunks.text: Muslim Personal Law of Succession and Inheritance — Governed by Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1962 and classical Islamic jurisprudence. Source: Pakistan Code. Status: CURRENT.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Quranic Heirs — Fixed-share heirs (Quranic heirs) include: husband, wife, daughter, son's daughter (how low soever), father, mother, grandfather (how high soever), grandmother (how high soever), full sister, consanguine sister, uterine brother, and uterine sister.
chunks.text: Quranic Heirs — Fixed-share heirs (Quranic heirs) include: husband, wife, daughter, son's daughter (how low soever), father, mother, grandfather (how high soever), grandmother (how high soever), full sister, consanguine sister, uterine brother, and uterine sister.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Residuary heirs — After Quranic shares are allocated, residue passes to residuary heirs: son, son's son (how low soever), father (as residuary), grandfather, full brother, consanguine brother, full nephew, consanguine nephew, full first cousin, etc.
chunks.text: Residuary heirs — After Quranic shares are allocated, residue passes to residuary heirs: son, son's son (how low soever), father (as residuary), grandfather, full brother, consanguine brother, full nephew, consanguine nephew, full first cousin, etc.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Husband's share — If wife has no child: husband gets 1/4. If wife has child: husband gets 1/8.
chunks.text: Husband's share — If wife has no child: husband gets 1/4. If wife has child: husband gets 1/8.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Wife's share — If husband has no child: wife (or wives collectively) gets 1/4. If husband has child: wife (or wives collectively) gets 1/8. If multiple wives, they share equally in the share.
chunks.text: Wife's share — If husband has no child: wife (or wives collectively) gets 1/4. If husband has child: wife (or wives collectively) gets 1/8. If multiple wives, they share equally in the share.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Daughter's share — One daughter: gets 1/2. Multiple daughters (2+): get 2/3 collectively. Daughter with son: daughter takes half of son's share (son:daughter = 2:1).
chunks.text: Daughter's share — One daughter: gets 1/2. Multiple daughters (2+): get 2/3 collectively. Daughter with son: daughter takes half of son's share (son:daughter = 2:1).

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Mother's share — If no child: mother gets 1/3. If child exists: mother gets 1/6. If spouse and both parents survive: mother gets 1/3 of the remainder after spouse's share.
chunks.text: Mother's share — If no child: mother gets 1/3. If child exists: mother gets 1/6. If spouse and both parents survive: mother gets 1/3 of the remainder after spouse's share.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Father's share — If no child: father gets 1/6 (as Quranic heir) plus residue (as residuary). If child exists: father gets 1/6.
chunks.text: Father's share — If no child: father gets 1/6 (as Quranic heir) plus residue (as residuary). If child exists: father gets 1/6.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Full sister — If no child, no father, no brother: full sister gets 1/2. Multiple full sisters (2+): 2/3. Full sister with full brother: 2:1 ratio.
chunks.text: Full sister — If no child, no father, no brother: full sister gets 1/2. Multiple full sisters (2+): 2/3. Full sister with full brother: 2:1 ratio.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Grandfather — When no father exists, grandfather takes father's place in inheritance.
chunks.text: Grandfather — When no father exists, grandfather takes father's place in inheritance.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Exclusion from inheritance — Grounds of exclusion: (a) homicide (killing the testator/intestate); (b) difference of religion (Muslim/non-Muslim); (c) slavery. A valid will (wasiyat) can distribute up to 1/3 of the estate to non-Quranic heirs.
chunks.text: Exclusion from inheritance — Grounds of exclusion: (a) homicide (killing the testator/intestate); (b) difference of religion (Muslim/non-Muslim); (c) slavery. A valid will (wasiyat) can distribute up to 1/3 of the estate to non-Quranic heirs.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Wasiyat (Will) — A Muslim may bequeath up to 1/3 of his estate to any person not already an heir. Bequest to an heir requires consent of all other heirs after death. Will must be in writing, signed by testator and two witnesses.
chunks.text: Wasiyat (Will) — A Muslim may bequeath up to 1/3 of his estate to any person not already an heir. Bequest to an heir requires consent of all other heirs after death. Will must be in writing, signed by testator and two witnesses.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Gift (Hiba) — A gift inter vivos (hiba) must be made with: (a) declaration by donor; (b) acceptance by donee; (c) delivery of possession. Gift to a minor may be accepted by guardian. Gift of property requires registration.
chunks.text: Gift (Hiba) — A gift inter vivos (hiba) must be made with: (a) declaration by donor; (b) acceptance by donee; (c) delivery of possession. Gift to a minor may be accepted by guardian. Gift of property requires registration.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Succession Certificate — The Family Court grants succession certificates entitling the holder to collect debts, securities and other assets of the deceased. Application includes: names of all legal heirs, their shares, and details of the deceased's assets.
chunks.text: Succession Certificate — The Family Court grants succession certificates entitling the holder to collect debts, securities and other assets of the deceased. Application includes: names of all legal heirs, their shares, and details of the deceased's assets.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Letters of Administration — Where the deceased dies intestate (without will), letters of administration are granted by the court to the person entitled to administer the estate (usually the nearest heir willing to administer).
chunks.text: Letters of Administration — Where the deceased dies intestate (without will), letters of administration are granted by the court to the person entitled to administer the estate (usually the nearest heir willing to administer).

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Probate — Where the deceased left a will, probate is granted by the court confirming the will's validity and the executor's authority. Probate is mandatory in the four major cities (Karachi, Lahore, Rawalpindi, Islamabad) for immovable property.

chunks.title: Muslim Personal Law of Succession, Inheritance and Wills
chunks.chunkTitle: Non-Muslim succession — Non-Muslims (Christians, Hindus, Parsis) are governed by their respective personal laws for succession. The Succession Act 1925 applies to certain non-Muslim communities.
chunks.text: Non-Muslim succession — Non-Muslims (Christians, Hindus, Parsis) are governed by their respective personal laws for succession. The Succession Act 1925 applies to certain non-Muslim communities.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930) — Defines the law relating to the sale of goods in Pakistan. Source: Pakistan Code (pakistancode.gov.pk). Status: CURRENT.
chunks.text: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930) — Defines the law relating to the sale of goods in Pakistan. Source: Pakistan Code (pakistancode.gov.pk). Status: CURRENT.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Definitions — 'Buyer' means a person who buys or agrees to buy goods. 'Seller' means a person who sells or agrees to sell goods. 'Goods' means every kind of movable property other than actionable claims and money. 'Price' means the money consideration for a sale.
chunks.text: Definitions — 'Buyer' means a person who buys or agrees to buy goods. 'Seller' means a person who sells or agrees to sell goods. 'Goods' means every kind of movable property other than actionable claims and money. 'Price' means the money consideration for a sale.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Sale and agreement to sell — A contract of sale may be absolute or conditional. If transfer of property in goods is immediate, it is a sale. If transfer is to occur at a future time or subject to a condition, it is an agreement to sell. An agreement to sell becomes a sale when time elapses or condition is fulfilled.
chunks.text: Sale and agreement to sell — A contract of sale may be absolute or conditional. If transfer of property in goods is immediate, it is a sale. If transfer is to occur at a future time or subject to a condition, it is an agreement to sell. An agreement to sell becomes a sale when time elapses or condition is fulfilled.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Essential elements — A valid contract of sale requires: (a) two parties (buyer and seller); (b) goods (existing or future); (c) transfer of property; (d) price (money consideration); (e) consent; (f) lawful object.
chunks.text: Essential elements — A valid contract of sale requires: (a) two parties (buyer and seller); (b) goods (existing or future); (c) transfer of property; (d) price (money consideration); (e) consent; (f) lawful object.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Existing and future goods — Goods may be existing (owned and possessed by seller), future (to be manufactured or acquired), or contingent (dependent on specified event). Sale of future goods operates as an agreement to sell.
chunks.text: Existing and future goods — Goods may be existing (owned and possessed by seller), future (to be manufactured or acquired), or contingent (dependent on specified event). Sale of future goods operates as an agreement to sell.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Perished goods — Where goods have perished without seller's knowledge at the time of the contract, the contract is void.
chunks.text: Perished goods — Where goods have perished without seller's knowledge at the time of the contract, the contract is void.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Condition and warranty — A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract. A warranty is a stipulation collateral to the main purpose. Breach of condition may be treated as breach of warranty.
chunks.text: Condition and warranty — A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract. A warranty is a stipulation collateral to the main purpose. Breach of condition may be treated as breach of warranty.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Implied conditions — Implied conditions include: (a) condition as to title (seller has right to sell); (b) condition as to description (goods correspond with description); (c) condition as to fitness for purpose; (d) condition as to merchantable quality.
chunks.text: Implied conditions — Implied conditions include: (a) condition as to title (seller has right to sell); (b) condition as to description (goods correspond with description); (c) condition as to fitness for purpose; (d) condition as to merchantable quality.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Caveat emptor — There is no implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for any particular purpose (buyer beware). Exceptions: (a) buyer makes known the purpose; (b) goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in such goods.
chunks.text: Caveat emptor — There is no implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for any particular purpose (buyer beware). Exceptions: (a) buyer makes known the purpose; (b) goods are bought by description from a seller who deals in such goods.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Transfer of property — Property in goods passes when the parties intend it to pass. For specific goods in deliverable state: property passes when contract is made (regardless of payment or delivery).
chunks.text: Transfer of property — Property in goods passes when the parties intend it to pass. For specific goods in deliverable state: property passes when contract is made (regardless of payment or delivery).

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Delivery — Delivery may be actual, constructive or symbolic. Unless otherwise agreed, delivery and payment are concurrent conditions.
chunks.text: Delivery — Delivery may be actual, constructive or symbolic. Unless otherwise agreed, delivery and payment are concurrent conditions.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Acceptance — Buyer is deemed to have accepted goods when: (a) buyer intimates acceptance; (b) goods are delivered and buyer does any act inconsistent with seller's ownership; (c) buyer retains goods beyond a reasonable time without rejection.
chunks.text: Acceptance — Buyer is deemed to have accepted goods when: (a) buyer intimates acceptance; (b) goods are delivered and buyer does any act inconsistent with seller's ownership; (c) buyer retains goods beyond a reasonable time without rejection.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Rejection of goods — Buyer has the right to reject goods that do not conform to the contract. Buyer may accept part and reject part.
chunks.text: Rejection of goods — Buyer has the right to reject goods that do not conform to the contract. Buyer may accept part and reject part.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Remedies of seller — Seller may sue for: (a) the price if property has passed; (b) damages for non-acceptance; (c) interest on the price when due.
chunks.text: Remedies of seller — Seller may sue for: (a) the price if property has passed; (b) damages for non-acceptance; (c) interest on the price when due.

chunks.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930 (Act III of 1930)
chunks.chunkTitle: Remedies of buyer — Buyer may sue for: (a) damages for non-delivery; (b) specific performance; (c) damages for breach of warranty; (d) interest.
chunks.text: Remedies of buyer — Buyer may sue for: (a) damages for non-delivery; (b) specific performance; (c) damages for breach of warranty; (d) interest.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877) — Relates to specific relief available in civil courts in Pakistan. Source: Pakistan Code (pakistancode.gov.pk). Status: CURRENT.
chunks.text: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877) — Relates to specific relief available in civil courts in Pakistan. Source: Pakistan Code (pakistancode.gov.pk). Status: CURRENT.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Specific relief defined — Specific relief is relief in the form of a decree for specific performance of a contract, or for an injunction, or for a declaratory decree.
chunks.text: Specific relief defined — Specific relief is relief in the form of a decree for specific performance of a contract, or for an injunction, or for a declaratory decree.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Specific performance of contract — The court may decree specific performance of a contract when: (a) damages are not an adequate remedy; (b) the contract is for the transfer of identified immovable property; (c) the contract is for the transfer of unique movable property; (d) damages cannot be ascertained.
chunks.text: Specific performance of contract — The court may decree specific performance of a contract when: (a) damages are not an adequate remedy; (b) the contract is for the transfer of identified immovable property; (c) the contract is for the transfer of unique movable property; (d) damages cannot be ascertained.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Contracts which cannot be specifically enforced — Contracts for personal service or dependent on personal qualifications; contracts requiring continuous supervision; contracts where consent was not free; contracts where defendant could not be compensated by damages.
chunks.text: Contracts which cannot be specifically enforced — Contracts for personal service or dependent on personal qualifications; contracts requiring continuous supervision; contracts where consent was not free; contracts where defendant could not be compensated by damages.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Discretion of court — Specific performance is a discretionary remedy. The court may refuse if: (a) claimant's conduct has been unfair; (b) contract is unfair or oppressive; (c) enforcement would cause undue hardship; (d) claimant has failed to perform his part.
chunks.text: Discretion of court — Specific performance is a discretionary remedy. The court may refuse if: (a) claimant's conduct has been unfair; (b) contract is unfair or oppressive; (c) enforcement would cause undue hardship; (d) claimant has failed to perform his part.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Declaratory decrees — Any person entitled to any legal character or right to any property may institute a suit for a declaration of his right, against any person denying or interested in denying that right.
chunks.text: Declaratory decrees — Any person entitled to any legal character or right to any property may institute a suit for a declaration of his right, against any person denying or interested in denying that right.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Effect of declaratory decree — A declaratory decree binds only the parties and those claiming through them. The court may not make a declaration which is useless or which relates to a matter which has already been decided.
chunks.text: Effect of declaratory decree — A declaratory decree binds only the parties and those claiming through them. The court may not make a declaration which is useless or which relates to a matter which has already been decided.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Injunctions — An injunction is a judicial order requiring a person to do or refrain from doing a particular act. Injunctions may be: (a) temporary (pending disposal of suit); (b) perpetual (final decree); (c) mandatory (requiring positive act); (d) prohibitory (restraining from act).
chunks.text: Injunctions — An injunction is a judicial order requiring a person to do or refrain from doing a particular act. Injunctions may be: (a) temporary (pending disposal of suit); (b) perpetual (final decree); (c) mandatory (requiring positive act); (d) prohibitory (restraining from act).

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Temporary injunctions — Governed by CPC Order 39. The court may grant temporary injunction where: (a) property is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated; (b) defendant threatens to dispossess plaintiff; (c) defendant threatens to remove/dispose of property.
chunks.text: Temporary injunctions — Governed by CPC Order 39. The court may grant temporary injunction where: (a) property is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated; (b) defendant threatens to dispossess plaintiff; (c) defendant threatens to remove/dispose of property.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Perpetual injunctions — Granted by final decree to permanently restrain the defendant from doing a particular act. The existence of a legal right and its actual or threatened infringement must be established.
chunks.text: Perpetual injunctions — Granted by final decree to permanently restrain the defendant from doing a particular act. The existence of a legal right and its actual or threatened infringement must be established.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Mandatory injunctions — Compel the defendant to perform a positive act to remedy a wrong. Granted where the plaintiff has a strong case and damages are inadequate.
chunks.text: Mandatory injunctions — Compel the defendant to perform a positive act to remedy a wrong. Granted where the plaintiff has a strong case and damages are inadequate.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Quia timet injunctions — Preventive injunctions granted where an injury is imminent or threatened, before actual harm occurs. The plaintiff must show a strong probability of injury.
chunks.text: Quia timet injunctions — Preventive injunctions granted where an injury is imminent or threatened, before actual harm occurs. The plaintiff must show a strong probability of injury.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Recovery of specific immovable property — A person entitled to possession of specific immovable property may recover it by a suit for possession. Title must be proved.
chunks.text: Recovery of specific immovable property — A person entitled to possession of specific immovable property may recover it by a suit for possession. Title must be proved.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Recovery of specific movable property — A person entitled to possession of specific movable property may recover it. If the property has been wrongfully taken, the suit must be within 3 years.
chunks.text: Recovery of specific movable property — A person entitled to possession of specific movable property may recover it. If the property has been wrongfully taken, the suit must be within 3 years.

chunks.title: Specific Relief Act, 1877 (Act I of 1877)
chunks.chunkTitle: Pre-emption — A right to pre-emption allows a co-sharer or neighbor to purchase property sold to a third party, subject to fulfilling conditions and making payment. Governed by provincial pre-emption laws (Punjab Pre-emption Act 1991).
chunks.text: Pre-emption — A right to pre-emption allows a co-sharer or neighbor to purchase property sold to a third party, subject to fulfilling conditions and making payment. Governed by provincial pre-emption laws (Punjab Pre-emption Act 1991).

chunks.title: Elections Act, 2017 (Act XXXIII of 2017)
chunks.chunkTitle: Elections Act, 2017 (Act No. XXXIII of 2017) — Regulates conduct of elections in Pakistan. Source: Election Commission of Pakistan (ecp.gov.pk). Status: CURRENT.
chunks.text: Elections Act, 2017 (Act No. XXXIII of 2017) — Regulates conduct of elections in Pakistan. Source: Election Commission of Pakistan (ecp.gov.pk). Status: CURRENT.

chunks.title: Elections Act, 2017 (Act XXXIII of 2017)
chunks.chunkTitle: Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) — The ECP is a constitutional body under Article 218 of the Constitution. It consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and four Members (one from each province). ECP conducts elections for: National Assembly, Provincial Assemblies, Senate, and Local Government.
chunks.text: Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) — The ECP is a constitutional body under Article 218 of the Constitution. It consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and four Members (one from each province). ECP conducts elections for: National Assembly, Provincial Assemblies, Senate, and Local Government.

chunks.title: Elections Act, 2017 (Act XXXIII of 2017)
chunks.chunkTitle: Delimitation of constituencies — ECP delimits constituencies after each census. Constituencies must be contiguous and have approximate equality of population. Reserved seats for women and minorities are allocated proportionally.
chunks.text: Delimitation of constituencies — ECP delimits constituencies after each census. Constituencies must be contiguous and have approximate equality of population. Reserved seats for women and minorities are allocated proportionally.

chunks.title: Elections Act, 2017 (Act XXXIII of 2017)
chunks.chunkTitle: Voter registration — Every citizen of Pakistan aged 18+ is entitled to be registered as a voter. Voter lists are updated annually. NADRA provides computerized national identity cards (CNIC) required for voting.
chunks.text: Voter registration — Every citizen of Pakistan aged 18+ is entitled to be registered as a voter. Voter lists are updated annually. NADRA provides computerized national identity cards (CNIC) required for voting.

chunks.title: Elections Act, 2017 (Act XXXIII of 2017)
chunks.chunkTitle: Candidates — Qualifications: citizen of Pakistan, 25+ for National Assembly, 30+ for Senate, sound mind, not convicted of moral turpitude. Disqualifications: convicted of corruption, default on loans/bills, dual nationality (for certain positions), and Section 62/63 of Constitution.
chunks.text: Candidates — Qualifications: citizen of Pakistan, 25+ for National Assembly, 30+ for Senate, sound mind, not convicted of moral turpitude. Disqualifications: convicted of corruption, default on loans/bills, dual nationality (for certain positions), and Section 62/63 of Constitution.

chunks.title: Elections Act, 2017 (Act XXXIII of 2017)
chunks.chunkTitle: Election schedule — Elections must be held within 60 days after the expiry of the assembly term (if dissolved after full term) or within 90 days (if dissolved prematurely). Polling is held on a non-working day.
chunks.text: Election schedule — Elections must be held within 60 days after the expiry of the assembly term (if dissolved after full term) or within 90 days (if dissolved prematurely). Polling is held on a non-working day.

chunks.title: Elections Act, 2017 (Act XXXIII of 2017)
chunks.chunkTitle: Campaign finance — Candidates have spending limits prescribed by ECP. Political parties must submit annual statements of accounts. Foreign funding is prohibited for political parties.
chunks.text: Campaign finance — Candidates have spending limits prescribed by ECP. Political parties must submit annual statements of accounts. Foreign funding is prohibited for political parties.

chunks.title: Elections Act, 2017 (Act XXXIII of 2017)
chunks.chunkTitle: Election offences — Offences include: (a) personation (voting in another's name); (b) bribery; (c) undue influence; (d) false statements; (e) illegal voting. Punishment: imprisonment up to 2 years or fine.
chunks.text: Election offences — Offences include: (a) personation (voting in another's name); (b) bribery; (c) undue influence; (d) false statements; (e) illegal voting. Punishment: imprisonment up to 2 years or fine.

chunks.title: Elections Act, 2017 (Act XXXIII of 2017)
chunks.chunkTitle: Election petitions — Disputes regarding election results may be filed in the High Court within 45 days of the Gazette notification. Grounds: corrupt practice, illegal practice, improper rejection of nomination, or improper counting.

chunks.chunkTitle: Citizenship — Citizenship is governed by the Pakistan Citizenship Act 1951. Modes of acquisition: (a) by birth (born in Pakistan); (b) by descent (born abroad to Pakistani parent); (c) by naturalization (residence, marriage); (d) by incorporation of territory. Dual citizenship is permitted with 19+ countries but not all.

Modes of acquisition: (a) by birth (born in Pakistan); (b) by descent (born abroad to Pakistani parent); (c) by naturalization (residence, marriage); (d) by incorporation of territory. Dual citizenship is permitted with 19+ countries but not all.

chunks.title: Immigration, Passport and Citizenship Laws of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Foreigners Act, 1946 — Regulates entry, presence and exit of foreigners. All foreigners must have valid visa/passport. Overstay is penalized. Registration with police required for stays exceeding 30 days in certain categories.
chunks.text: Foreigners Act, 1946 — Regulates entry, presence and exit of foreigners. All foreigners must have valid visa/passport. Overstay is penalized. Registration with police required for stays exceeding 30 days in certain categories.

chunks.title: Immigration, Passport and Citizenship Laws of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Visa categories — (a) Diplomat visa; (b) Business visa; (c) Tourist visa; (d) Student visa; (e) Work visa; (f) Religious visa; (g) Transit visa. Online visa system available for eligible countries.

chunks.title: Immigration, Passport and Citizenship Laws of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: NADRA records — National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) maintains: CNIC (Computerized National Identity Card), CRIC (Children), NICOP (overseas Pakistanis), POC (Pakistan Origin Card). CNIC mandatory for voting, property, banking, passports.

chunks.title: Immigration, Passport and Citizenship Laws of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Refugee law — Pakistan hosts Afghan refugees under UNHCR arrangements. Proof of Registration (PoR) cards issued. Pakistan is not a signatory to the UN Refugee Convention 1951 but cooperates with UNHCR.

chunks.title: Immigration, Passport and Citizenship Laws of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Immigration offences — (a) Illegal entry into Pakistan; (b) overstaying visa; (c) using forged documents; (d) human trafficking; (e) employing illegal foreigners. Penalties: fine, imprisonment, deportation.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Court Hierarchy and Structure in Pakistan — The judicial system of Pakistan established under the Constitution of Pakistan 1973, Article 175: Courts are independent and separate from the executive. Source: Constitution, Law and Justice Commission.
chunks.text: Court Hierarchy and Structure in Pakistan — The judicial system of Pakistan established under the Constitution of Pakistan 1973, Article 175: Courts are independent and separate from the executive. Source: Constitution, Law and Justice Commission.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Supreme Court of Pakistan — The apex court under Article 175. Composition: Chief Justice of Pakistan and other judges. Jurisdiction: (a) Original (Article 184): fundamental rights of public importance (suo motu); (b) Appellate (Article 185): appeals from High Courts; (c) Advisory (Article 186): Presidential reference; (d) Review (Article 188): review of its own judgments.
chunks.text: Supreme Court of Pakistan — The apex court under Article 175. Composition: Chief Justice of Pakistan and other judges. Jurisdiction: (a) Original (Article 184): fundamental rights of public importance (suo motu); (b) Appellate (Article 185): appeals from High Courts; (c) Advisory (Article 186): Presidential reference; (d) Review (Article 188): review of its own judgments.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: High Courts — Each province has a High Court under Article 175 read with Article 192-203: (1) Lahore High Court (Punjab); (2) Sindh High Court (Karachi); (3) Peshawar High Court (KPK); (4) Balochistan High Court (Quetta); (5) Islamabad High Court (ICT). High Courts have: (a) Original constitutional jurisdiction under Article 199; (b) Appellate jurisdiction over civil/criminal decisions of subordinate courts; (c) Revisional jurisdiction; (d) Writ jurisdiction (habeas corpus, certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, quo warranto).
chunks.text: High Courts — Each province has a High Court under Article 175 read with Article 192-203: (1) Lahore High Court (Punjab); (2) Sindh High Court (Karachi); (3) Peshawar High Court (KPK); (4) Balochistan High Court (Quetta); (5) Islamabad High Court (ICT). High Courts have: (a) Original constitutional jurisdiction under Article 199; (b) Appellate jurisdiction over civil/criminal decisions of subordinate courts; (c) Revisional jurisdiction; (d) Writ jurisdiction (habeas corpus, certiorari, prohibition, mandamus, quo warranto).

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Federal Shariat Court — Established under Article 203-C. Examines laws for conformity with Islam (Injunctions of Islam). Appeals from FSC lie to the Supreme Court's Shariat Appellate Bench. FSC also exercises appellate jurisdiction in Hudood cases.
chunks.text: Federal Shariat Court — Established under Article 203-C. Examines laws for conformity with Islam (Injunctions of Islam). Appeals from FSC lie to the Supreme Court's Shariat Appellate Bench. FSC also exercises appellate jurisdiction in Hudood cases.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: District and Sessions Court — At district level. The District and Sessions Judge is the highest judicial authority in the district. Jurisdiction: (a) Criminal: Sessions cases (murder, rape, dacoity, etc.); (b) Civil: original suits above the pecuniary limits of civil judges; (c) Appellate: appeals from civil judges and magistrates; (d) Administrative: controls subordinate judiciary in the district.

Jurisdiction: (a) Criminal: Sessions cases (murder, rape, dacoity, etc.); (b) Civil: original suits above the pecuniary limits of civil judges; (c) Appellate: appeals from civil judges and magistrates; (d) Administrative: controls subordinate judiciary in the district.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Civil Judge / First Class Magistrate — Lowest tier of regular judiciary. Civil Judges hear civil suits up to prescribed pecuniary limits. Judicial Magistrates (1st Class) try criminal cases punishable with up to 3 years imprisonment (varies by province).
chunks.text: Civil Judge / First Class Magistrate — Lowest tier of regular judiciary. Civil Judges hear civil suits up to prescribed pecuniary limits. Judicial Magistrates (1st Class) try criminal cases punishable with up to 3 years imprisonment (varies by province).

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Family Courts — Established under the Family Courts Act 1964. Exclusive jurisdiction over: marriage, divorce (talaq/khula), maintenance, custody, dower, dowry, guardianship. Summary procedure with mandatory conciliation. Appeals to the High Court.
chunks.text: Family Courts — Established under the Family Courts Act 1964. Exclusive jurisdiction over: marriage, divorce (talaq/khula), maintenance, custody, dower, dowry, guardianship. Summary procedure with mandatory conciliation. Appeals to the High Court.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Anti-Terrorism Courts (ATC) — Established under Anti-Terrorism Act 1997. Try terrorism-related offences. Summary procedure. Judge holds office for 3 years. Appeals to High Court within 30 days.
chunks.text: Anti-Terrorism Courts (ATC) — Established under Anti-Terrorism Act 1997. Try terrorism-related offences. Summary procedure. Judge holds office for 3 years. Appeals to High Court within 30 days.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Banking Courts — Under Banking Companies Ordinance. Exclusive jurisdiction over banking disputes above PKR 500,000. Appeals to High Court within 30 days.
chunks.text: Banking Courts — Under Banking Companies Ordinance. Exclusive jurisdiction over banking disputes above PKR 500,000. Appeals to High Court within 30 days.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Accountability Courts — Under NAB Ordinance. Try corruption cases referred by NAB. Exclusive jurisdiction. Trial must conclude in 30 days (max 90 days). Appeals to High Court.
chunks.text: Accountability Courts — Under NAB Ordinance. Try corruption cases referred by NAB. Exclusive jurisdiction. Trial must conclude in 30 days (max 90 days). Appeals to High Court.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Consumer Courts — Under provincial Consumer Protection Acts. Try consumer complaints. Summary procedure. No court fee (or nominal fee). Appeals to High Court.
chunks.text: Consumer Courts — Under provincial Consumer Protection Acts. Try consumer complaints. Summary procedure. No court fee (or nominal fee). Appeals to High Court.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Labour Courts — Under Industrial Relations Act 2012. Jurisdiction: individual and collective disputes, unfair labour practices, wrongful termination. Appeals to the Labour Appellate Tribunal.
chunks.text: Labour Courts — Under Industrial Relations Act 2012. Jurisdiction: individual and collective disputes, unfair labour practices, wrongful termination. Appeals to the Labour Appellate Tribunal.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Rent Tribunals — Under provincial Rent Acts. Exclusive jurisdiction over landlord-tenant disputes (eviction, rent, repair). Summary procedure. Appeals to District Judge/high court.
chunks.text: Rent Tribunals — Under provincial Rent Acts. Exclusive jurisdiction over landlord-tenant disputes (eviction, rent, repair). Summary procedure. Appeals to District Judge/high court.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Tax Tribunals — (a) Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue: income tax and sales tax appeals; (b) Customs Appellate Tribunal: customs appeals. Appeals to High Court on substantial questions of law.
chunks.text: Tax Tribunals — (a) Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue: income tax and sales tax appeals; (b) Customs Appellate Tribunal: customs appeals. Appeals to High Court on substantial questions of law.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Environmental Tribunals — Under Pakistan Environmental Protection Act 1997. Adjudicate environmental offences. Judicial and technical members. Appeals to High Court.
chunks.text: Environmental Tribunals — Under Pakistan Environmental Protection Act 1997. Adjudicate environmental offences. Judicial and technical members. Appeals to High Court.

chunks.title: Court Hierarchy and Structure of Pakistan
chunks.issuingAuthority: Law and Justice Commission of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Special Courts — (a) Special Judge (Central): drug offences; (b) Special Court (Offences in Banks): bank robbery, fraud; (c) Special Judge (Child Protection): child abuse cases (some provinces); (d) Provincial Motor Vehicle Special Judges: traffic offences.

chunks.chunkTitle: Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) — CPC Section 89: Courts may refer disputes to mediation/conciliation. DNA testing, medical reports and other scientific evidence increasingly used.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Fundamental Rights — Constitution of Pakistan 1973, Part II (Articles 7-28). Source: Constitution of Pakistan. Status: CURRENT.
chunks.text: Fundamental Rights — Constitution of Pakistan 1973, Part II (Articles 7-28). Source: Constitution of Pakistan. Status: CURRENT.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 9: Right to Life and Liberty — No person shall be deprived of life or liberty save in accordance with law. Courts have interpreted 'life' broadly to include: right to livelihood, clean environment, health, shelter, and dignity.
chunks.text: Article 9: Right to Life and Liberty — No person shall be deprived of life or liberty save in accordance with law. Courts have interpreted 'life' broadly to include: right to livelihood, clean environment, health, shelter, and dignity.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 10: Safeguards as to Arrest — (1) Arrested person must be informed of grounds of arrest within 24 hours. (2) Right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner. (3) Produced before magistrate within 24 hours. (4) Not detained beyond 24 hours without magistrate's authority. (5) No special preventive detention beyond 1 month without review board approval.
chunks.text: Article 10: Safeguards as to Arrest — (1) Arrested person must be informed of grounds of arrest within 24 hours. (2) Right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner. (3) Produced before magistrate within 24 hours. (4) Not detained beyond 24 hours without magistrate's authority. (5) No special preventive detention beyond 1 month without review board approval.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 10A: Right to Fair Trial — Every citizen is entitled to a fair trial and due process for determination of civil rights and obligations or criminal charges. Includes: right to present evidence, cross-examine witnesses, impartial tribunal, and reasoned judgment.
chunks.text: Article 10A: Right to Fair Trial — Every citizen is entitled to a fair trial and due process for determination of civil rights and obligations or criminal charges. Includes: right to present evidence, cross-examine witnesses, impartial tribunal, and reasoned judgment.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 11: Slavery, Forced Labour Abolished — Slavery and forced labour are prohibited. No child below 14 may be employed in hazardous employment. Bonded labour is a criminal offence.
chunks.text: Article 11: Slavery, Forced Labour Abolished — Slavery and forced labour are prohibited. No child below 14 may be employed in hazardous employment. Bonded labour is a criminal offence.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 12: Protection against Retrospective Punishment — No law shall authorize punishment for an act that was not an offence at the time of commission. No penalty greater than that applicable at the time of the offence.
chunks.text: Article 12: Protection against Retrospective Punishment — No law shall authorize punishment for an act that was not an offence at the time of commission. No penalty greater than that applicable at the time of the offence.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 13: Double Jeopardy — No person shall be prosecuted or punished for the same offence more than once.
chunks.text: Article 13: Double Jeopardy — No person shall be prosecuted or punished for the same offence more than once.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 14: Dignity and Privacy — The dignity of man is inviolable. No person shall be subjected to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. Right to privacy of home and correspondence.
chunks.text: Article 14: Dignity and Privacy — The dignity of man is inviolable. No person shall be subjected to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. Right to privacy of home and correspondence.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 16: Freedom of Assembly — Citizens have the right to assemble peacefully and without arms, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interest of public order.
chunks.text: Article 16: Freedom of Assembly — Citizens have the right to assemble peacefully and without arms, subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the interest of public order.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 17: Freedom of Association — Citizens have the right to form associations or unions, subject to law. Political parties must not be formed on sectarian/religious hate basis. Internal party democracy required.
chunks.text: Article 17: Freedom of Association — Citizens have the right to form associations or unions, subject to law. Political parties must not be formed on sectarian/religious hate basis. Internal party democracy required.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 18: Freedom of Trade and Profession — Every citizen has the right to enter any lawful profession or occupation, and to conduct any lawful trade or business, subject to qualifications prescribed by law.
chunks.text: Article 18: Freedom of Trade and Profession — Every citizen has the right to enter any lawful profession or occupation, and to conduct any lawful trade or business, subject to qualifications prescribed by law.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 19: Freedom of Speech — Freedom of speech and expression is guaranteed, subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of: (a) glory of Islam; (b) security of Pakistan; (c) public order; (d) decency; (e) morality; (f) contempt of court; (g) defamation; (h) incitement to offence.
chunks.text: Article 19: Freedom of Speech — Freedom of speech and expression is guaranteed, subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of: (a) glory of Islam; (b) security of Pakistan; (c) public order; (d) decency; (e) morality; (f) contempt of court; (g) defamation; (h) incitement to offence.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 19A: Right to Information — Every citizen has the right to access information held by public bodies. Exercise of this right must not impinge on national security, personal privacy, or commercial confidentiality.
chunks.text: Article 19A: Right to Information — Every citizen has the right to access information held by public bodies. Exercise of this right must not impinge on national security, personal privacy, or commercial confidentiality.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 20: Freedom to Profess Religion — Subject to law, public order and morality: (a) every citizen has the right to profess, practice and propagate his religion; (b) every religious denomination has the right to establish and maintain religious institutions.
chunks.text: Article 20: Freedom to Profess Religion — Subject to law, public order and morality: (a) every citizen has the right to profess, practice and propagate his religion; (b) every religious denomination has the right to establish and maintain religious institutions.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 21: Protection against Taxation for Religious Purposes — No person shall be compelled to pay taxes for the propagation or maintenance of any religion other than his own.
chunks.text: Article 21: Protection against Taxation for Religious Purposes — No person shall be compelled to pay taxes for the propagation or maintenance of any religion other than his own.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 22: Safeguards as to Educational Institutions — No person shall be required to receive religious instruction other than his own. Educational institutions maintained by religious communities may require religious instruction of their own faith.
chunks.text: Article 22: Safeguards as to Educational Institutions — No person shall be required to receive religious instruction other than his own. Educational institutions maintained by religious communities may require religious instruction of their own faith.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 23: Right to Hold Property — Every citizen has the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property subject to law. Property may be compulsorily acquired only for public purpose and with compensation.
chunks.text: Article 23: Right to Hold Property — Every citizen has the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property subject to law. Property may be compulsorily acquired only for public purpose and with compensation.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 24: Protection against Deprivation of Property — No person shall be compulsorily deprived of property save by law for a public purpose. Adequate compensation must be provided. Parliament may define 'public purpose' and 'compensation'.
chunks.text: Article 24: Protection against Deprivation of Property — No person shall be compulsorily deprived of property save by law for a public purpose. Adequate compensation must be provided. Parliament may define 'public purpose' and 'compensation'.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 25: Equality — All citizens are equal before law and entitled to equal protection of law. The State may make special provisions for the protection of women and children. Non-discrimination on grounds of sex alone.
chunks.text: Article 25: Equality — All citizens are equal before law and entitled to equal protection of law. The State may make special provisions for the protection of women and children. Non-discrimination on grounds of sex alone.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 25A: Right to Education — The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 5 to 16 years in such manner as determined by law.
chunks.text: Article 25A: Right to Education — The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 5 to 16 years in such manner as determined by law.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 26: Access to Public Places — No citizen shall be denied access to public places (hotels, restaurants, parks, entertainment venues) on grounds of race, religion, caste, sex, residence or place of birth.
chunks.text: Article 26: Access to Public Places — No citizen shall be denied access to public places (hotels, restaurants, parks, entertainment venues) on grounds of race, religion, caste, sex, residence or place of birth.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 27: Safeguard against Discrimination in Service — No citizen shall be discriminated against for public employment on grounds of race, religion, caste, sex, residence or place of birth.
chunks.text: Article 27: Safeguard against Discrimination in Service — No citizen shall be discriminated against for public employment on grounds of race, religion, caste, sex, residence or place of birth.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Article 28: Maintenance of Culture — Any section of citizens with distinct language, script or culture has the right to preserve and promote it. Admission to public educational institutions cannot be denied on linguistic grounds.
chunks.text: Article 28: Maintenance of Culture — Any section of citizens with distinct language, script or culture has the right to preserve and promote it. Admission to public educational institutions cannot be denied on linguistic grounds.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Right to Remedy — The right to invoke writ jurisdiction under Article 199 (High Court) and Article 184 (Supreme Court) for enforcement of fundamental rights. This is the primary remedy for any violation of fundamental rights.
chunks.text: Right to Remedy — The right to invoke writ jurisdiction under Article 199 (High Court) and Article 184 (Supreme Court) for enforcement of fundamental rights. This is the primary remedy for any violation of fundamental rights.

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Limitation on Fundamental Rights — Fundamental rights are not absolute. They are subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law for the purposes specified. Rights may be suspended during a Proclamation of Emergency (Article 233).
chunks.text: Limitation on Fundamental Rights — Fundamental rights are not absolute. They are subject to reasonable restrictions imposed by law for the purposes specified. Rights may be suspended during a Proclamation of Emergency (Article 233).

chunks.title: Fundamental Rights under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1973
chunks.chunkTitle: Non-discrimination and Minority Rights — Article 36: Protection of minorities. The State shall protect the legitimate rights and interests of minorities, including their due representation in Federal and Provincial services.
chunks.text: Non-discrimination and Minority Rights — Article 36: Protection of minorities. The State shall protect the legitimate rights and interests of minorities, including their due representation in Federal and Provincial services.

chunks.title: Expanded Situation-to-Action Legal Remedies Guide
chunks.chunkTitle: FIR refused by police — Remedy: (a) Written complaint to Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) or District Police Officer (DPO); (b) Application under Section 22-A/22-B CrPC to Sessions Judge/Justice of Peace; (c) Complaint to the Judicial Magistrate under Section 190 CrPC; (d) Constitutional writ under Article 199 to High Court.

chunks.chunkTitle: Unlawful arrest — Remedy: (a) Produce before magistrate within 24 hours; (b) Bail application under CrPC Section 496/497; (c) Habeas corpus petition under Article 199; (d) Suit for damages for wrongful arrest (tort of false imprisonment).

chunks.title: Expanded Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Pre-arrest bail procedure — (1) File application before Sessions Court (or High Court) under CrPC Section 498-A. (2) Notice to prosecutor. (3) Court may grant bail with or without surety. (4) For anticipatory bail: show that arrest is apprehended and not on reasonable grounds. (5) If granted: complies with bail bond, surrenders passport, regular appearance.

(3) Court may grant bail with or without surety. (4) For anticipatory bail: show that arrest is apprehended and not on reasonable grounds. (5) If granted: complies with bail bond, surrenders passport, regular appearance.

chunks.title: Expanded Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Post-arrest bail procedure — (1) File bail application in trial court (Magistrate/Sessions). (2) If refused: file in Sessions Court (if from Magistrate) or High Court. (3) Prosecutor may oppose on grounds of gravity, evidence, flight risk. (4) Court considers: nature of offence, evidence, criminal record, community ties. (5) Bail granted with/without surety and conditions.

chunks.title: Expanded Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Constitutional writ petition procedure (Article 199) — (1) File petition in High Court with supporting affidavit. (2) Relief sought: certiorari (quash orders), mandamus (compel performance), prohibition (restrain proceedings), habeas corpus (produce detainee), quo warranto (challenge appointment). (3) Court issues notice to respondents. (4) Hearing: interim relief may be granted. (5) Final order: petition allowed or dismissed.

(3) Court issues notice to respondents. (4) Hearing: interim relief may be granted. (5) Final order: petition allowed or dismissed.

chunks.title: Expanded Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Civil suit procedure — (1) Filing of plaint in Civil Court (within limitation period). (2) Court issues summons to defendant (Order 5 CPC). (3) Defendant files written statement (Order 8 CPC) within 30 days. (4) Issues framed by court (Order 14). (5) Plaintiff's evidence (examination-in-chief, cross-examination). (6) Defendant's evidence. (7) Arguments. (8) Judgment and decree. (9) Execution of decree (Order 21).

chunks.title: Expanded Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Criminal trial procedure — (1) FIR registration. (2) Investigation (Section 156-173 CrPC). (3) Challan (police report) filed in court. (4) Framing of charge (Section 221-240). (5) Prosecution evidence. (6) Statement of accused (Section 342). (7) Defense evidence. (8) Arguments. (9) Judgment: conviction or acquittal. (10) Sentence hearing if convicted.

chunks.title: Expanded Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Appeal procedure — Criminal appeal: (a) Sessions Court to High Court: 30 days; (b) High Court to Supreme Court: 30 days (leave to appeal). Civil appeal: (a) Civil Judge to District Judge: 30 days; (b) District Judge to High Court: 90 days; (c) High Court to Supreme Court: 90 days (subject to substantial question of law).

chunks.title: Expanded Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Execution petition procedure — (1) File execution application under Order 21 CPC in the court that passed the decree. (2) Court issues notice to judgment debtor. (3) Modes of execution: (a) delivery of property; (b) attachment and sale of property; (c) arrest and detention of judgment debtor; (d) appointment of receiver. (4) Garnishee orders against third parties.

chunks.title: Expanded Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Legal notice procedure — (1) Draft notice: state facts, legal basis, demand/relief sought. (2) Send via registered post (AD) and courier with acknowledgment. (3) Mandatory for: consumer complaints (15 days), cheque cases (30 days), breach of contract, property disputes. (4) Recipient must respond within specified time. (5) Failure to comply: file suit/complaint.

(4) SECP issues Certificate of Incorporation within 24 hours (e-services). (5) Obtain NTN, register for Sales Tax (if required).

chunks.chunkTitle: Inheritance procedure — (1) Death certificate. (2) Collect Fard (land record), bank details, property documents. (3) File application for succession certificate in Family Court. (4) Notice to all heirs (public notice if some unknown). (5) Court determines legal heirs and shares. (6) Grant of succession certificate. (7) Mutation (Inteqal) at Board of Revenue for land. (8) Transfer of bank accounts, shares.

chunks.chunkTitle: Family Court procedure — (1) File petition (khula, maintenance, custody, etc.) in Family Court. (2) Court attempts conciliation (Section 12 Family Courts Act). (3) If conciliation fails: recording of evidence. (4) DNA test may be ordered for parentage disputes. (5) Judgment: Family Court must decide within 6 months. (6) Appeals to High Court.

chunks.title: Expanded Legal Workflows & Procedures
chunks.chunkTitle: Consumer court procedure — (1) File complaint in writing to District Consumer Court (no court fee or nominal). (2) Complaint must state: facts, deficiency of goods/services, relief sought. (3) Pre-notice to opposite party (15 days). (4) Court issues notice to respondent. (5) Summary trial. (6) Decision within 90 days. (7) Appeal to Provincial Consumer Commission within 30 days.

chunks.chunkTitle: Asma Jilani v. Government of Punjab (PLD 1972 SC 139) — Supreme Court rejected the doctrine of revolutionary legality. Held: the recognition of a revolutionary government by the courts applies only to the law of the previous regime and does not validate extra-constitutional acts. Significance: foundational case on constitutional continuity. Source: PLD 1972 SC 139 (verified via nasirlawsite.com, recordoflaw.in, multiple academic papers).

chunks.title: Overseas Pakistanis: Consular Services & Pakistani Missions Abroad
chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Consular services for overseas Pakistanis are provided by Pakistan's diplomatic missions abroad — Embassies, High Commissions and Consulates General — under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) of Pakistan. MOFA official portal: https://www.mofa.gov.pk. A Pakistani national living or travelling abroad should first identify the Pakistani mission with consular jurisdiction over the region/city where they are located, because services are delivered by the mission responsible for that area. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04. Note: The exact list of services, fees and processing times at each mission can change; always confirm current requirements on the relevant mission's official website before acting.

chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Terminology: an EMBASSY is the diplomatic mission headed by an Ambassador, usually located in a country's capital. A HIGH COMMISSION is the equivalent mission exchanged between Commonwealth countries (e.g., Pakistan High Commission in London, Ottawa, Canberra). A CONSULATE GENERAL is a mission located outside the capital that serves a specific region and handles consular work such as passports, attestation and visas. This app does not claim to know every mission; it directs users to the official MOFA directory of missions for verified, current contact details. Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, https://www.mofa.gov.pk. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

MOFA maintains the authoritative and current list of Pakistan's missions, their addresses and consular jurisdictions. Do not rely on unverified phone numbers or addresses from blogs or social media. This knowledge base deliberately does not hardcode individual mission addresses or phone numbers because they change; the official MOFA directory is the authoritative source. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: Overseas Pakistanis: Consular Services & Pakistani Missions Abroad
chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Pakistani passports issued or renewed abroad are processed through Pakistan missions using the Directorate General of Immigration & Passports (DGIP) online systems. The DGIP official portal is https://www.dgip.gov.pk and its online Machine Readable Passport (MRP) facility is accessed through the DGIP e-services used by missions. Typical services include: new passport, renewal/replacement, and emergency certificates. Applicants generally need their existing CNIC/SNIC or NICOP and biometric verification. Fees, validity and processing times are set by DGIP and can change — confirm current figures on https://www.dgip.gov.pk and on the relevant mission's website. Jurisdiction note: passport issuance is a PAKISTAN (federal) matter executed abroad by the mission, not a foreign-law matter. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: Overseas Pakistanis: Consular Services & Pakistani Missions Abroad
chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: If a Pakistani passport is lost or stolen abroad, the usual first steps are: (1) file a police report / loss report with the local police of the country where it happened and keep the report; (2) contact the nearest Pakistani embassy/high commission/consulate (find it via https://www.mofa.gov.pk); (3) apply for an Emergency Certificate (EC) or replacement passport as directed by the mission. An Emergency Certificate is commonly used for a single return journey to Pakistan when a full passport cannot be issued immediately. Required documents, fees and timelines vary by mission and change over time — the mission is the authoritative source. Do not assume a foreign authority will replace a Pakistani passport; only Pakistan's own missions issue Pakistani travel documents. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.chunkTitle: An Emergency Certificate (EC) / emergency travel document is issued by Pakistani missions to citizens who need to travel but do not hold a usable passport (for example after a loss abroad). It is normally valid for a limited purpose such as return to Pakistan and is not the same as a passport. Eligibility, validity and whether onward travel is permitted depend on the issuing mission and the destination country's rules. Confirm the specific conditions with the relevant Pakistani mission and the immigration authority of the country you intend to enter. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Pakistani documents (educational certificates, marriage certificates, experience certificates, etc.) used abroad usually require attestation. The typical Pakistan-side chain is: relevant issuing authority / department, then the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) Pakistan attestation, then attestation by the embassy/consulate of the country where the document will be used (where that country requires it). MOFA attestation information is published at https://www.mofa.gov.pk. Whether a document additionally needs legalization or an apostille depends on the destination country's rules. This app does not fabricate country-specific attestation requirements — users must verify the destination country's official requirements. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: Overseas Pakistanis: Consular Services & Pakistani Missions Abroad
chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Two common ways a public document is recognised across borders: LEGALIZATION (a multi-step authentication ending with the destination country's mission) and APOSTILLE (a single certificate under the Hague Apostille Convention for countries that are parties to it). Whether Pakistan's documents and a given destination country use the apostille route or the legalization route is jurisdiction-specific and subject to change. The correct route must be confirmed with (a) MOFA Pakistan for the outbound side and (b) the official authority of the destination country for the inbound side. This knowledge base does not claim a specific country's current apostille/legalization status; it directs users to the authoritative source. Jurisdiction: cross-border (both a Pakistan side and a foreign side exist). Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: Overseas Pakistanis: Consular Services & Pakistani Missions Abroad
chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: A Power of Attorney (POA / Mukhtar Nama) executed by an overseas Pakistani for use in Pakistan generally must be attested so that Pakistani authorities will accept it. Commonly the POA is signed before, and attested by, the Pakistani embassy/high commission/consulate with jurisdiction over the area where the person resides, then forwarded to Pakistan for use (for example in property, banking or court matters). The specific format, attestation process and any registration requirement depend on the purpose and on Pakistani law (including the relevant registration and evidence rules). Because a POA can have serious legal effect, obtaining proper attestation and, where needed, legal advice is important. Jurisdiction: PAKISTAN law governs a POA to be used in Pakistan, even when it is signed abroad. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Overseas Pakistanis can register certain civil events with Pakistan's authorities even while abroad. Birth and death of Pakistani citizens occurring abroad can be registered through the relevant Pakistani mission under the applicable registration rules, and the National Database & Registration Authority (NADRA, https://nadra.gov.pk) maintains Pakistani civil registration records including for overseas Pakistanis (e.g., NICOP/POC and related records). Marriage registration recognition can be more complex across borders (see foreign marriage recognition). Exact procedures, accepted documents and channels change; confirm with the mission and NADRA's official channels. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.chunkTitle: NADRA issues identity documents for Pakistanis connected to Pakistan but living abroad, including the NICOP (National Identity Card for Overseas Pakistanis) and the POC (Pakistan Origin Card). These documents are used to access services in Pakistan such as banking, property transactions, and certain benefits. Applications and renewals are handled through NADRA and, abroad, sometimes through missions/NADRA overseas centres. NADRA official portal: https://nadra.gov.pk. Eligibility categories, fees and processing times change — verify current details on NADRA's official site. Jurisdiction: PAKISTAN (federal) matter. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: Overseas Pakistanis: Consular Services & Pakistani Missions Abroad
chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: If a Pakistani national is arrested or detained in a foreign country, the applicable criminal law and procedure are those of that FOREIGN country, not Pakistani law. A Pakistani mission can typically provide CONSULAR ASSISTANCE — such as seeking access to the detained citizen, helping communicate with family, providing a list of local lawyers, and ensuring the citizen is treated humanely and with due process under the local law and applicable international consular norms — but the mission CANNOT act as a lawyer, interfere in the foreign country's judicial process, secure release, or pay legal/bail costs. Immediate practical steps usually include contacting the nearest Pakistani mission (via https://www.mofa.gov.pk) and engaging a qualified LOCAL lawyer in that country. The right to consular notification/access is widely recognised under the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations; specific entitlements depend on the country. Safety-first guidance, not legal advice on the foreign case. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: Overseas Pakistanis: Consular Services & Pakistani Missions Abroad
chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Consular assistance by Pakistani missions is bounded: missions help with lost/emergency travel documents, attestation, welfare checks, referrals to local lawyers, and communication with family, and can raise a citizen's case with local authorities on humanitarian/due-process grounds. Missions do NOT provide legal representation, do NOT override local law, and do NOT guarantee outcomes of foreign legal or immigration processes. When a matter turns on foreign law, the correct authority is the foreign country's own system plus a qualified local lawyer; the Pakistani side (mission/consular) handles the Pakistan-facing aspects. This distinction (which law applies) is central to cross-border guidance. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: For problems specifically involving recruitment/employment abroad (fraudulent agents, unpaid wages, passport withholding) Pakistani workers can use Pakistan-side channels under the Ministry of Overseas Pakistanis and Human Resource Development and the Bureau of Emigration & Overseas Employment: official portals https://ophrd.gov.pk and https://beoe.gov.pk, and the mission in the country of work for local enforcement. For general consular help, contact the relevant Pakistani mission via https://www.mofa.gov.pk. Where a complaint requires enforcement in the foreign country, the foreign country's labour/immigration authorities are the primary route, with consular support. Do not treat an overseas workplace dispute as governed by Pakistani labour law alone — jurisdiction matters. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.issuingAuthority: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Government of Pakistan
chunks.chunkTitle: Pakistanis returning to Pakistan should travel on a valid Pakistani passport (or Emergency Certificate accepted for the journey) and, where relevant, ensure their visa/status in the host country allows lawful departure. On re-entry, customs rules on bringing goods, currency and restricted items apply and are set by Pakistani authorities (e.g., FBR customs rules) — these change, so verify current allowances before travelling. If a person holds foreign nationality as well, entry/exit and visa rules for Pakistan depend on which passport is used and Pakistan's nationality/dual-nationality rules (see dual nationality). Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: International Travel, Visa & Immigration Basics for Pakistani Citizens
chunks.chunkTitle: For a Pakistani citizen travelling abroad, two separate legal layers always apply and must not be mixed: (A) the PAKISTAN side — holding a valid Pakistani passport and complying with any Pakistani exit/entry requirements; and (B) the DESTINATION-COUNTRY side — that country's visa, immigration and entry rules, set by that country's own government. This knowledge base provides Pakistan-facing cross-border guidance and points to the official foreign authority; it does not claim to reproduce every country's current rules. Any country-specific requirement must be confirmed on the destination country's official government/immigration website. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: International Travel, Visa & Immigration Basics for Pakistani Citizens
chunks.chunkTitle: Before any international travel, a Pakistani traveller needs a valid passport issued by the Directorate General of Immigration & Passports (DGIP, https://www.dgip.gov.pk). Many countries require that a passport remain valid for a period (commonly around six months) beyond the intended date of entry or departure — this is a destination-country rule that varies and changes. Travellers should check the destination country's official entry requirements for the required passport validity rather than assuming a single rule. Renew a Pakistani passport well before travel, especially because renewals abroad go through missions and can take time. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.chunkTitle: A visa is permission granted by a FOREIGN country to enter/stay for a purpose (tourism, study, work, transit, family, business). The application must be made to that country's official immigration/visa authority or its designated mission/visa-processing partner. General, jurisdiction-neutral preparation steps for a Pakistani applicant: (1) identify the correct visa category on the destination's official site; (2) assemble required documents (usually valid passport, application form, photographs, proof of funds, itinerary/invitation, accommodation, and category-specific items); (3) use only the official application channel and pay fees to the official authority; (4) allow realistic processing time. This app does NOT guarantee visa approval and does NOT invent per-country document lists — the destination country's official source is authoritative. Jurisdiction: the visa decision is FOREIGN law, made by the foreign state. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: International Travel, Visa & Immigration Basics for Pakistani Citizens
chunks.chunkTitle: No agent, service or app can guarantee that a visa will be approved; the decision rests solely with the destination country's immigration authorities applying their own law and discretion. Beware of anyone promising a "sure" visa or asking for payment for a guaranteed outcome — that is a common fraud pattern. Legitimate help (form review, document preparation) is fine, but the approval decision and the criteria belong to the foreign state. Always apply through, and verify requirements with, the destination country's official immigration/embassy channel. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: International Travel, Visa & Immigration Basics for Pakistani Citizens
chunks.chunkTitle: Common immigration terms relevant to Pakistanis abroad: VISA (permission to seek entry for a purpose/duration); RESIDENCE PERMIT / VISA (permission to live in a country for a longer period, often tied to work or study); WORK PERMIT / LABOUR AUTHORISATION (permission to work, separate from a visit visa in many countries); OVERSTAY (remaining beyond the permitted period — usually a violation with penalties); DEPORTATION / REMOVAL (formal expulsion by the state); ASYLUM / REFUGEE STATUS (protection claimed under the host country's law and international instruments). Each is governed by the specific country's law; details vary widely and change. Verify against the official authority of the country concerned. Jurisdiction: FOREIGN (host country). Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.

chunks.title: International Travel, Visa & Immigration Basics for Pakistani Citizens
chunks.chunkTitle: Overstaying a visa or working without the required work authorisation is typically a violation of the DESTINATION country's immigration law and can lead to fines, detention, removal/deportation, and bans on future entry. Consequences are determined by foreign law and vary by country and circumstances. A deported or removed Pakistani may still need Pakistan-side help (travel document to return — see consular services). This app gives general risk awareness and directs to the foreign authority and the Pakistani mission; it does not state specific penalties as if universal. If facing overstay/deportation issues, obtain advice from a qualified lawyer in that country and notify the nearest Pakistani mission via https://www.mofa.gov.pk. Status: CURRENT. Verified: 2026-09-04.
