chunks.chunkTitle: Workflow: What to do when police refuse to register an FIR (escalation ladder)
chunks.text:
Workflow: What to do when police refuse to register an FIR (escalation ladder)
Authority: CrPC Sections 154, 22-A/22-B, 200; Constitution Article 199 (as recorded in the court procedures digest).
Ladder: (1) written application to the SHO requesting FIR registration — keep a copy; (2) if refused, written complaint to the Superintendent of Police (SP) or Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) of the area (DSP Complaint Cell); (3) application to the Sessions Judge sitting as ex-officio Justice of Peace under Sections 22-A/22-B CrPC — the Sessions Judge can direct the SHO to register the FIR; (4) private complaint directly before the Magistrate under Section 200 CrPC; (5) in extreme cases, a writ petition before the High Court under Article 199; (6) complaint through the Pakistan Citizen Portal (Helpline 8171); (7) contact the IGP Complaint Cell.
Note: an FIR must be registered for cognizable offences; refusal is a dereliction of duty (Police Order 2002 / CrPC as recorded in the police digest). The FIR itself is free of charge and the complainant is entitled to a free copy.
Source: Indexed corpus procedures digest (rag/documents/procedure/procedures.txt) and police digest (rag/documents/police/police.txt)
Source URL: https://pakistancode.gov.pk/ (as recorded in the digest)
Status: Corpus-derived workflow (statutory anchors as recorded)

chunks.chunkTitle: Workflow: Registration of foreigners present in Pakistan
chunks.text:
Workflow: Registration of foreigners present in Pakistan
Authority: Foreigner registration office (FRO) framework of the Pakistan Online Visa System (Government of Pakistan/NADRA).
Situation: Who must register — all foreigners are exempted from police registration EXCEPT nationals of Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Israel, Nigeria, Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) and Somalia, and any other foreign national directed by the immigration authorities to report to the FRO for registration (a stamp to this effect is affixed on the passport).
Exemption nuance: nationals in the managerial category who are issued a Work Permit/Visa from the listed countries are exempted from police registration, except Indians and foreigners of Indian origin.
Effect: on registration, the FRO issues the residential permit that governs the period of stay — the period of stay is counted from the date of arrival, and is governed by the residential permit, not by the date of issue of the visa.
Steps: (1) enter Pakistan within the visa validity (six months from date of issue; unused visas become invalid); (2) report to the FRO if the passport is stamped for registration or if the holder is a national of a listed country; (3) obtain the residential permit at registration; (4) to stay beyond the permit, apply for an extension of the relevant visa category.
Source: Pakistan Online Visa System — Important Terms (official)
Source URL: https://visa.nadra.gov.pk/important-terms/
Status: Active (verified 2026-09-06; FRO locations and forms per the visa portal)

chunks.chunkTitle: Case: Service 17945/25 (Baber Maseeh Vs Cantonment Executive Officer Sargodha etc).
chunks.text:
Case: Service 17945/25 (Baber Maseeh Vs Cantonment Executive Officer Sargodha etc).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Service 17945/25. Title: Service 17945/25 (Baber Maseeh Vs Cantonment Executive Officer Sargodha etc). Official Ref: 2026LHC5569. Author Judge: Justice Ms. Shireen Imran. Judgment Date (as displayed): 04-09-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5569.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 10 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Stereo . H C J D A 38
JUDGMENT SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT , LAHORE
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Writ Petition No. 17945 of 20 2 5 .
Baber Masih V ersus Cantonment Executive Officer, Sargodha & another
JUDGMENT
Date of hearing: 0 3 . 09 .2026 .
Petitioner by: Syed Hamid Raza Bukhari, Advocate.
Respondent s by: M ian Asghar Ali, Advocate .
SHIREEN IMRAN, J : Through this petition, petitioner has called in question order dated 13.12.2024 passed by respondent No.2, whereby the departmental appeal filed by him was partly accepted and consequently vide order dated 10.01.2025 , he was reinstate d in service w.e.f. 26.11.2012 , the date when he was dismissed from service , however, his claim qua back benefits was declined while treating his period of absence from duty as Extra Ordinary Leave (EOL) .
2. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that the petitioner
was appointed as a Sanitary Worker on 06.10.2011 and his services were regularized on 30.12.2011 ; that , being implicated in a baseless criminal case bearing FIR No.655/2012 , he remained in judicial W.P. No. 17 945 of 202 5 . 2 custody , due to which he remained absen t from duty and consequently , the department stuck off him from service vide order dated 12.02.2014 and that after his acquittal from the aforesaid criminal case by this Court vide judgment dated 11.11.2021 passed in Criminal Appeal No.166 - J/2017 th ough the departmental appeal filed by the petitioner for his reinstatement in to service was accepted and he was reinstated in service w.e.f. 26.11.2012 but his claim q ua back benefits w as declined without considering the fact that all acquittals are h onourable . Reliance has been placed upon the judgments reported as Dr. Muhammad Islam v. Government of N. - W.F.P. through Secretary, Food, Agriculture, Livestock and Cooperative Department, Peshawar and 2 others ( 1998 SCMR 1993 ) , Attaullah Sheikh v.
WAPDA and others [ 2001 PLC (C.S .) 316 ] , Tahir Kazmi and another v. Inspector General of P o lice, Punjab , Lahore and others [ 2026 PLC (C.S.) 5 10 ] , The Province of Sindh through Chief S e cretary Government of Sindh and others v. Raj Kumar Lohana and others [ 2026 PLC (C.S.) 40 4 ] and Ghulam Murtaza v. District Police Officer, Gujrat & others ( 2026 SCMR 843 ) .
3. Conversely, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the
respondents submits that the instant petition is misconceived and has been filed to secure an undue benefit. It is contended that no fundamental right of the petitioner has been infringed and as the petitioner remained absent from duty and did not perform any work, no mala fide or ill - will can be attributed to the departmental authorities while declining his request for grant of back benefits.
W.P. No. 17 945 of 202 5 . 3 Reliance has been placed upon the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Civil Petition Nos.1935 to 1938 of 2018 and connected matters, titled Shafique Ahmed & three others v. Provincial Police Officer, KP & others , dated 03.12.2025.
4. Arguments heard. Record perused.
5 . Firstly, taking up the objection raised by the learned counsel for the respondents against maintainability of this petition in absence of infringement of any fundamental right , this Court is of the view that t he petitioner seeks enforcement of his fundamental rights guaranteed under Article s 10 - A of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan (the Cons titution) and service rights , arising from orders of the competent authorities, and the impugned orders are amenable to judicial review where they are alleged to be without lawful justification. Likewise, absence of any specific finding against an authority does not preclude this Court from examining whether the impugned action is lawful, particularly where the challenge concerns the denial of consequential service benefits following reinstatement .
T hus , instant petition cannot be dismissed on the point of maintainability , resultantly the objection under discussion is hereby spurned .
6 . Now reverting to merits of the case, it is observed that the controversy essentially relates to the petitioner’s entitlement to back benefits for the period intervening his removal and reinstatement. The petitioner was appointed as Sanitary Worker on 06.10.2011 and his services were regularized on 30.12.2011. During service, he was W.P. No. 17 945 of 202 5 . 4 implicated in a criminal case and remained in judicial custody, owing to which he could not attend his duties . He was ultimately acquitted by this Court vide judgment dated 11.11.2021. Though the petitioner has been reinstated in service by treating the period of his absence as EOL but his request for grant of back benefits has been declined despite the fact that the authority, while reinstating him in service, itself admitted that his absence was due to the circumstances beyond his control. Once the authority itself admitted that the absence of the petitioner was not intentional rather it was due to circumstances beyond his control, his request for grant of back benefits was to be considered leniently. It is trite law that discretion vested in an authority should be exercised justly and fairly . Dealing with somewhat similar situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pak istan in the case of Shafique Ahmed & three others (supra) has, inter alia, concluded as under: - “ 5. ***** The core requirement for any legitimate and legal administration of power now hinges on its justification. Sound justification for government actions involves establishing the cogency and persuasiveness of the rationale behind government actions and requires such actions to be scrutinised for their rationality and reasonableness. Thus, if Article 10 - A of the Constitution serves as a decisive departure from the restrictive culture of authority, it becomes evident what it aims to transition towards:
a culture of justification. In this new model, every exertion of power must stand on its own merits, compelling authorities to substantiate their decisions through sound reasoning rather than relying on the fear associated with the force they command … … …
7. It is crucial to emphasise that similar
provisions are prevalent across nearly all Civil Servants Acts applicable at both the Federal and W.P. No. 17 945 of 202 5 . 5 provincial levels. The pivotal focus of our discussion lies in the second proviso to Section 17. The straightforward language of the second proviso clearly indicates that discretion to determine back pay is conferred upon the authority responsible for reinstating a civil servant into service. Notably, the command of the law is unequivocal; the granting of such arrears is not an automatic consequence but rather a decision for which the authority possesses discretion, emphasising the equitable nature of such power. However, it must be recognised that this legislation that bestows these discretionary powers lacks a clearly defined set of conditions, circumstances, and standards to guide the authority in exercising its powers. This absence of specificity is deliberate and serv es a distinct purpose as the discretion is inherently tied to the latitude granted by the legislative enactment and allows the designated official or authority to make determinations within a defined spectrum. The decisionmaker is not confined to the belief that there exists only one correct resolution. Instead, while the authority’s choices should align with established legal principles of reason and justice, its judgment must be rooted in careful consideration and not arbitrary preferences.
Exercising dis cretion is a grave responsibility, a sacred trust that demands utmost diligence, vigilance, and fairness. This power should be wielded with precision, rationality, and an unwavering commitment to the principles underpinning natural justice. Any deviation from this meticulous duty threatens to compromise the integrity of the decision - making process and jeopardises the foundational elements of governance. The authority, serving as the custodian of this discretion, is mandated by both the Constitution and serv ice laws to act with impartiality, fairness, and transparency. It must consciously avoid actions that appear arbitrary or whimsical and instead embrace a thoughtful approach that acknowledges and balances the diverse interests and rights of all parties involved.
The decision - making process must be guided by relevant factors, with precise articulation and disclosure of the reasons for decisions. At its core, the principle of fairness — central to administrative law - compels the authority to act without bias, prejudice, or ulterior motives, to guarantee that all civil servants receive equitable treatment. Any failure to adhere to this principle constitutes a breach of the duty of fairness and invites judicial scrutiny.
…… W.P. No. 17 945 of 202 5 . 6
12. After it is determined whether the civil servant
was employed anywhere during the intervening period or not, the next stage is to determine how back pay should be granted. The question of awarding back pay in cases where a civil servant has been unfairly dismissed is guided by a general principle: such pay should ordinarily be granted to those civil servants who have been unlawfully deprived of their positions. However, this principle is not absolute and is subject to various conditions.
The decision could grant back pay in full or in part, or it could deny back pay altogether. There is no rigid formula that dictates under what specific circumstances back pay should be authorised. The determination depends heavily on the unique facts and circumstances of each case. It would be erroneous to assume that entitlement to back pay is warranted solely based on technical legalities that invalidate a dismissal order. Instead, the awarding of back pay — whether in whole or in part, or none at all — requires a nuanced evaluation of several factors.
These factors may include the nature of the civil servant’s appointment, the length and quality of his service, any proven misconduct, his financial situation, and other relevant considerations. This careful analysis seeks to balance the competing interests at play. Due to the diverse nature of such cases, there is no one - size - fits - all approach for providing relief in the form of back pay. Each situation must be assessed on its own merits, and this evaluation is often entrusted to the discretion of the relevant authority. However, it needs to be emphasised that while granting full back pay is generally the standard, it falls upon the authority to demonstrate compelling reasons that would justify a deviation from this norm. At this stage, the authority is tasked with exercising its discretion judiciously and consistently with established legal standards.
This discretion must be exercised thoughtfully , based on a clear and convincing rationale that is evident from the official record. The exercise of discretion should adhere to the principles of reason and justice — based on law rather than whim — and must avoid arbitrary or capricious decisions . ”
14.***** This deprivation connects directly to
Article 9 of the Constitution, which guarantees the right to life. The term ‘life’ encompasses a broader interpretation, encapsulating not only mere existence but also the means to sustain it. ” … … (emphasis provided) W.P. No. 17 945 of 202 5 . 7 7 . The question of reinstatement of an employee came under consideration before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of The Province of Sindh through Chief Secretary, Government of Sindh and others (supra) . The Hon’ble Supreme Court, while considering the said question, settled the matter by, inter alia, observing as follows: - “ 10. In unison, a quick look to the glossary of the expression Reinstatement communicates the meaning of restoring something to a former, original, normal, or unimpaired condition. If we gaze it into the framework of employment, it characteristically ensues when a terminated, dismissed or laid off employee is sent back to his former occupation status which includes the reestablishing and protection of his seniority rights, privileges or other benefits that were previously lost. The doctrine of reinstatement also affirms a legal precept that allows a party to bring back a contract or agreement to its original terms after it has been terminated or breached. For all intent and purposes, this doctrine applies with diversity and miscellany that includes different situations including the reinstatement of an employee in the labour and/or civil service laws to his job after an unjust/wrongful termination or dismissal from service and also the renaissance or reactivation of a contract/agreement etc. Furthermore, this also facilitates to rectify errors, settle disputes, and make sure that person concerned is not unjustifiably penalized which is in fact a fundamental perception of guaranteeing justice and upholding unprejudiced relationship in the legal and contractual agreements or terms and conditions of employment/service . ” 8 . Moreover, the question of grant of back benefits upon reinstatement of an employee has been elaborately considered and settled by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Tahir Kazmi and another (supra), wherein the Hon’ble Court, inter alia, observed as follows: - W.P. No. 17 945 of 202 5 . 8 “ 4. The core issue is the entitlement to back benefits. Grant of back benefits while not expressly defined in the service laws of Pakistan is a well established remedy in Pakistan as well as other jurisdictions. As defined in Black's Law Dictionary, "back pay" refers to the salary an employee should have received but was denied due to unlawful employer action. A "back pay award" restores the economic status quo ante, compensating for the loss incurred. In our jurisdiction, the term "back benefits" typically includes arrears of salary and related service entitlements. Although broader meanings may exist, this discussion confines "back benefits" to arrears of pay and other emoluments denied due to wrongful dismissal or removal.
… …
11. This constitutional foundation finds
affirmation in judicial precedent, most notably in Tariq Mahmood and Muhammad Sharif where this Court reaffirmed that the grant of back benefits is the norm and denial of service benefits to such reinstated employee is an exception. Any deviation from this must be justified by clear evidence that the employee was gainfully employed elsewhere during the intervening period . The logic is straightforward when a court declares an official action unlawful, it must undo not only the decision but the resulting harm. Restitution is therefore integral to corrective justice, not an exercise of discretion. ” 9 . In the present case, petitioner’s absence was occasioned by his incarceration in a criminal case in which he was ultimately acquitted. More importantly, the departmental appellate authority expressly found his absence to be beyond his control and did not find any misconduct surviving against him. The respondents have also not produced any material showing that the petitioner was gainfully employed elsewhere or earned any income during the intervening period. In t hese peculiar circumstances, mere fact that the petitioner did not physically perform his duties cannot constitute sufficient justification for denying him the back benefits upon reinstatement .
W.P. No. 17 945 of 202 5 . 9 1 0 . That regardless of the extent of financial benefits granted, the intervening period between a civil servant's removal and subsequent reinstatement must be regularized to maintain the continuity of service. This is, however, a separate theme from back benefits. The reason for grant of extraordinary leave without pay or "leave of the kind due" is to ensure that the service record of the civil servant remains unbroken , thereby safeguarding eligibility for pension, promotion, seniority, and other ancillary service benefits. As held by the Hon ’ble Supreme Court, any failure to recognize such intervening periods , results in an unlawful forfeiture of rights .
1 1 . The direction to treat the intervening period as EOL does not answer the question of back benefits. EOL may regulate the manner in which an absence is accounted for in the service record but it cannot, without lawful basis, be used to defeat the consequences of reinstatement where the competent authority has it self recognized that the absence was beyond the employee’s control and that no misconduct remained against him .
1 2 . The judgment relied upon by the respondents in Shafique Ahmed & three others (supra), instead of lending support to the respondents, goes otherwise, as in the said judgment it has been held that grant of back benefits be determined justly and fairly in light of the circumstances attending the employee’s a bsence, nature and basis of reinstatement, findings recorded by the competent authority and the guidelines provided by the superior courts on the subject .
W.P. No. 17 945 of 202 5 . 10 1 3 . For the foregoing reasons, it is held that the question regarding grant of back benefits has not been dealt with in accordance with the guidelines provided by the superior courts and law on the subject. Consequently, I deem it appropriate to remit the matter back for decision afresh on the point of back benefit s.
1 4 . Accordingly, this petition is allowed . The impugned order s dated 13.12.2024 and 10.01.2025 , to the extent of denial of back benefits , are set aside and the matter is remitted to respondent No.2 for decision afresh , in view of the observations made hereinabove, especially the observations of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, contained in paragraphs No. 5, 7, 8, 11, 12 and 14 of Shafique Ahmed & three others (supra) , The Province of Sindh through Chief Secretary, Government of Sindh and others (supra) and Tahir Kazmi and another (supra) . This shall be done within a peri od of two (02) months , from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this judgment .
(SHIREEN IMRAN)
JUDGE
Approved for reporting.
JUDGE
U mar

Form No: HCJD/C-121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Crl. Misc. No. 43416-B of 2026 Ali Shahzad alias Shan Ali Versus The State etc.
Sr. No. of order/ Proceeding Date of order/ Proceeding Order with signature of Judge, and that of parties or counsel, where necessary.
31.08.2026 Malik Ali Ahmad Noul, Advocate for the petitioner.
Hafiz Asghar Ali, DPG with Afzal, SI for the State.
Syed Qalb Abbas, Advocate for the complainant.
Through the instant petition under section 497, Cr.P.C., the petitioner, Ali Shahzad alias Shan Ali, seeks postarrest bail in case FIR No.135 of 2025, dated 25.02.2025, registered under Sections 324, 148 and 149, PPC, at Police Station Syed Wala, District Nankana Sahib.
2. The Complainant has alleged that the Petitioner, while
armed with a pistol, fired at Farooq Ahmad, son of the complainant, which allegedly struck the latter on the left side of his chest.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the
petitioner has been arrested since 03.03.2025. The challan was submitted before the learned Trial Court after significant delay, whereas the charge was framed only on 02.03.2026. The petitioner contends that the prosecution has failed to conclude the trial within the statutory period despite the petitioner’s continuous imprisonment and that the delay is not attributable to any act or omission on his part. Learned counsel, therefore, prays that the petitioner be released on bail on the statutory ground of delay in conclusion of the trial.
4. Conversely, learned Deputy Prosecutor General
assisted by the learned counsel for the complainant, while disputing the petition, submits that the petitioner is specifically nominated in the FIR with a direct role of causing a firearm injury to the injured witness. He further submits that the Crl. Misc. No.43416-B of 2026 2 prosecution witnesses were produced before the learned Trial Court but could not be examined or cross-examined due to the conduct of the defence. It is, therefore, maintained that the petitioner is unable to claim the benefit of a delay which he himself contributed to.
5. Arguments heard. Available record, including the
report furnished by the learned Trial Court, has been examined with the able assistance of learned counsel for the parties.
6. The petitioner seeks post-arrest bail on the ground of
statutory delay under the third proviso to Section 497(1), Cr.P.C. The history of the earlier bail proceedings has also been taken into account. The first post-arrest bail petition, bearing Crl. Misc.
No.47874-B of 2025, was dismissed for non-prosecution on
08.09.2025. The second petition, bearing Crl. Misc. No.52358-B
of 2025, was dismissed on merits on 29.09.2025. Another petition for the same relief, bearing Crl. Misc. No.42342-B of 2026, was not pressed and was disposed of accordingly on
10.07.2026. The applications moved before the courts below on
the statutory ground were also dismissed.
7. It is a settled principle that a successive bail petition is
maintainable only upon the availability of a fresh ground. This principle is elaborately enunciated in “ Muhammad Usman v. The State and another ” ( 2024 SCMR 28 ), relevant extract of which is reproduced as under:- "It is settled law that a second bail petition repeating the same grounds that were earlier taken is not competent. Moreover, the grounds raised by an accused in a subsequent bail application which were available at the time of filing of the earlier petition could also not be treated as fresh grounds nor urged for the purposes of seeking the same relief. This Court has already highlighted the principles regarding maintainability of a subsequent bail petition. If the ground on which bail has been sought subsists when a bail petition is withdrawn then such a ground can also not be taken again.
However, the exception to this rule is in the case of entitlement of bail on statutory grounds as has been held by this Court. If any act or omission of the accused has hindered the conclusion of trial within the period specified in the third proviso of section 497(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Cr.P.C.) then a right, as contemplated thereunder, will not accrue in the latter's favour and, therefore, he or she, as the case may be, would not become entitled to be released on bail on the statutory ground of delay in conclusion of the trial.
Nonetheless, if after the rejection of the plea of bail on Crl. Misc. No.43416-B of 2026 3 statutory grounds, the accused has subsequently corrected himself/herself and has abstained from doing any act or omission in the following period specified under the third proviso, then a fresh ground would accrue to the accused to invoke the jurisdiction of the court for grant of bail. The third proviso to section 497(1) of Cr.P.C. would thus become operative as and when the period specified therein has expired but the trial has not concluded without any fault on part of the accused".
In the present case, the petition is competent because a fresh ground of delay in conclusion of trial had become available to the petitioner.
8. The third proviso to Section 497(1), Cr.P.C. reads as
under:
"497(1). When bail may be taken in cases of non-bailable offence. — 3rd Proviso:- Provided further that the Court shall, except where it is of the opinion that the delay in the trial of the accused has been occasioned by an act or omission of the accused or any other person acting on his behalf, direct that any person shall be released on bail
(a) who, being accused of any offence not punishable with
death, has been detained for such offence for a continuous period exceeding one year, or in case of a woman exceeding six months, and whose trial for such offence has not concluded; or
(b) who, being accused of an offence punishable with death,
has been detained for such offence for a continuous period exceeding two years, and in case of a woman exceeding one year, and whose trial for such offence has not concluded:
Provided further that the provisions of the foregoing proviso shall not apply to a previously convicted offender for an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life or to a person who, in the opinion of the Court, is a hardened, desperate or dangerous criminal or is accused of an act of terrorism punishable with death or imprisonment for life." Under the third proviso to section 497(1), Cr.P.C., an accused facing an offence not punishable with death becomes entitled to the concession of bail where he has remained in continuous detention for a period exceeding one year and the trial has not concluded, unless the delay has been occasioned by an act or omission attributable to the accused or his counsel. The benefit may also be withheld where the accused falls within any of the statutory exceptions prescribed therein. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in Muhammad Usman case ( supra ), has Crl. Misc. No.43416-B of 2026 4 authoritatively held that the right recognized under the third proviso to Section 497(1), Cr.P.C. cannot be denied merely on the basis of discretionary powers of the Court.
"It has been held by this Court that the right recognized under the third proviso of section 497(1) Cr.P.C. cannot be denied to an accused on the basis of discretionary powers of the court to grant bail. The right has not been left to the discretion of the court, rather, its accrual is subject to the fulfillment of the conditions mentioned under the third proviso of section 497(1) Cr.P.C."
9. The statutory scheme has to be read alongside Section
173, Cr.P.C., which casts an obligation upon the investigating agency to complete the investigation without unnecessary delay and to submit the police report/challan in accordance with law.
The prosecution cannot first allow the investigation to remain incomplete beyond the prescribed period and thereafter seek to rely upon the resulting delay against the accused. In “ Hakim Mumtaz Ahmad and another v. The State ” ( PLD 2002 SC 590 ), the Hon'ble Supreme Court took serious notice of delay in submission of challan and emphasized the duty of the Investigating Officer to complete the investigation within the prescribed period and furnish justification where the challan has not been submitted.
"It is not only this case in which it has been noticed that the Investigating Agency as well as District Attorneys have failed to submit challan of the case registered against accused within the stipulated period but in majority of the case the police report/challan under section 173, Cr.P.C. is not filed despite expiry of stipulated period due to which accused persons involved in criminal case remain languishing in custody without trial "
10. In the present case, the record shows that the challan
was not submitted within the period as provided by Section 173, Cr.P.C. The FIR was lodged on 25.02.2025, the accused was arrested on 03.03.2025, whereas the report under Section 173, Cr.P.C. was submitted on 13.11.2025, resulting in a delay of approximately eight months and ten days from the date of arrest.
Nothing has been brought on record to establish that the petitioner either caused or contributed to such delay. The lapse, Crl. Misc. No.43416-B of 2026 5 therefore, was on the part of the investigating/prosecuting machinery and cannot be converted into a ground for depriving the petitioner of the statutory protection available under Section 497(1), Cr.P.C.
11. The matter, however, does not end with submission of
the challan. The subsequent period during which the trial remained inconclusive must also be examined to determine whether any part thereof is legally attributable to the petitioner.
In Muhammad Usman (supra), the Hon'ble Supreme Court further held that, "While ascertaining the delay, the cumulative effect in disposal of the case has to be considered and its assessment cannot be determined on the basis of mathematical calculations by excluding those dates for which adjournments had been sought by the accused or the latter's counsel. The main factor for consideration is the attendance of the witnesses and whether, despite the matter having become ripe for the recording of evidence, whether the delay was caused by the defence. The recording of the statement of a last witness would also not defeat the right recognized under the third proviso and it would be unreasonable to conclude that the trial has been completed." The principal consideration is whether the matter had become ripe for recording of evidence and whether the delay was actually caused by the defence. The same principle is equally reflected in “ Haq Nawaz v. The State and another ” ( 2025 YLR 673 ), wherein, while relying upon Muhammad Usman (supra), “ Shakeel Shah v. The State and others ” ( 2022 SCMR 1 ), “ Nadeem Samson v. The State and others ” ( PLD 2022 SC 112 ) and “ Rohan Ahmad v. The State and others ” ( PLD 2024 SC 492 ), the Court reiterated that the prosecution must establish that the accused intentionally prolonged the trial through unjustified adjournments or other conduct having the effect of delaying the proceedings.
12. A bare perusal of the report furnished by the learned
Trial Court reveals that, after framing of the charge, prosecution witnesses were present on certain dates, yet their evidence could not be recorded or completed on account of the absence or nonavailability of defence counsel. However, such circumstance, Crl. Misc. No.43416-B of 2026 6 without a corresponding finding as to the actual effect of those adjournments on the progress of the trial, cannot ipso facto render the entire period attributable to the petitioner. The relevant consideration is whether, on the dates sought to be counted against him, the prosecution witnesses were available and ready to depose, the prosecution was prepared to examine them, and the recording of their evidence was nevertheless frustrated by a specific and unjustifiable act or omission of the petitioner or a person acting on his behalf. In the present case, admittedly, no evidence of any prosecution witness was actually recorded during the period in question. The order sheets do not disclose any specific instance where a prosecution witness, being present and ready, could not be examined solely because of a deliberate or unjustified act of the petitioner. The prosecution was required not merely to produce its witnesses before the Court but to demonstrate that their evidence was ripe for recording and that the petitioner was responsible for its nonrecording. The mandate of Muhammad Usman case ( supra ) equally requires the Court to assess the cumulative effect of the proceedings and the actual impact of the alleged adjournments, rather than mechanically treating every date on which the defence sought an adjournment as delay attributable to the accused.
13. The impact of returning unrecorded prosecution
witnesses on a bail application based on statutory delay (Section 497, Cr.P.C.) is significant, particularly when the Trial Court fails to record a speaking order. Under Pakistani jurisprudence, the right to an expeditious trial is fundamental, and any delay not directly attributable to the accused such as the court's failure to record present witnesses operates in favor of the accused for the purposes of statutory bail. Section 344 Cr.P.C relates to the adjournment of proceedings in criminal cases, which is reproduced herein for ready reference:
"344. Power to postpone or adjourn proceedings. (1) If, from the absence of a witness, or any other reasonable cause, it becomes necessary or advisable to postpone the commencement of, or Crl. Misc. No.43416-B of 2026 7 adjourn any inquiry or trial, the Court may, if it thinks fit, by order in writing, stating the reasons therefor, from time to time, postpone or adjourn the same on such terms as it thinks fit, for such time as it considers reasonable, and may by a warrant remand the accused if in custody..." Under Section 344, Cr.P.C., a Trial Court is mandated to record reasons in writing for any adjournment. If prosecution witnesses (PWs) are present but returned without being examined, and the Trial Court fails to provide a "speaking order" justifying this delay, such periods are generally not excluded from the calculation of the statutory period for bail. Such omissions by the court or the prosecution are not considered "acts or omissions of the accused" under the third proviso to Section 497(1), Cr.P.C. Similarly, the Rules & Orders of Lahore High Court (Vol. III, Chapter I, Part-A) Rule 4 :
"4. Speedy disposal of cases.- Magistrates shall give priority to criminal cases when an accused person is in custody. A criminal case shall be proceeded with from day to day as far as practicable and disposed of quickly. Witnesses, who are present, should be examined promptly and shall not be detained longer than may be absolutely necessary. Adjournments, when necessary, shall be as short as the circumstances permit." Part-E, Rule-14 of the Chapter 1 speaks in following words:- “ 14. Record to contain a brief note of all material orders passed.-Each record or memorandum of evidence should be dated and the record of a case made by a Magistrate or Sessions Judge should not only contain depositions or memoranda of evidence, according as the evidence is or is not recorded by him in full, but also, in its proper place, a short note of every material order made during the inquiry or trial, with the date on which such order was made. Every order of adjournment must be entered, and the date on which the inquiry was resumed should be apparent.
Notes- Orders to be written by the Magistrate in his own hand.- All notes and orders recorded by Presiding Officer (e.g., orders of adjournment, notes regarding the presence of witnesses) other than depositions, orders deciding any matter in dispute and the final judgment, should be written by the Presiding Officer in his own handwriting or dictated by him and be dated and appended to the record. Each "order" or "note" should be clearly marked as such." Crl. Misc. No.43416-B of 2026 8 Chapter-11, Part-B, Rule 10 makes a distinction between police remand and judicial remand and that too requires recording of reasons for adjournment to judicial remand:- "10. Procedure when a remand for more than 15 days is required for completion of the case.- If the limit of 15 days has elapsed, and there is still need for further investigation by the Police, the procedure to be adopted is that laid down in section 344, Criminal Procedure Code. The case is brought on to the Magistrate's file and the accused, if detention is necessary, will remain in magisterial custody. The case may be postponed or adjourned from time to time for periods of not more than 15 days each, and as each adjournment expires the accused must be produced before the Magistrate, and the order of adjournment must show good reasons for making the order ." Chapter 24, Part-B, Rule-2 also requires the recording of reasons for adjournment in Sessions trial other than day to day.
"2. Reservation of several days for possible Sessions cases.- The trial of a Sessions case shall, as a rule, be held from day to day and unless there be compelling reasons for adjournment, there should be no adjournment."
14. The Hon'ble Superior courts have clarified the
consequences of unreasoned adjournments and the return of present witnesses in following ways:- The august Supreme Court of Pakistan in “ ABDUR RASHID V. THE STATE ” ( 1998 SCMR 897 ) held for the right of accused to bail in case of any slackness or incapacity of prosecution to conclude trial within the time frame mentioned in clauses (a) & (b) of section 497 CrPC .
However, if the delay occasioned is due to any act or omission on the part of the accused, it may cause exception to the said general rule. The apex court ruled as:
"Any slackness or incapacity of prosecution to conclude the prosecution side within the time frame mentioned in clauses (a) and (b), supra, will provide all advantage to the accused for being released on bail. However, exception contained in third proviso unambiguously imposes a responsibility upon the accused for ensuring that delay in disposal is not occasioned or caused on account of him or any person acting on his behalf.
Therefore, it is crystal clear that if for any reason accused or his authorized agent which necessarily includes the advocate engaged for defence causes delay, then in such eventuality protection contained in the third proviso cannot be invoked. It may further be noticed that while ascertaining cumulative effect of ultimate delay in disposal of the case, it would not be merely Crl. Misc. No.43416-B of 2026 9 mathematical calculation of excluding such days for which adjournment was obtained by the accused or his counsel."
15. The circumstances of the present case become even
more significant when it is noticed that the charge was framed almost one year after the petitioner's arrest, whereas the substantial period preceding the framing of charge has neither been explained by the prosecution nor attributed, through any specific act or omission, to the petitioner. A careful examination of the order sheets, particularly the proceedings after framing of charge, further belies the assertion that the delay in conclusion of the trial was attributable to the petitioner. On several dates, the complete prosecution evidence was not available and adjournments were sought from the complainant/prosecution side for producing the complete evidence. On one occasion, even the learned Presiding Officer was not available.
Conversely, the record reflects that adjournment was sought on behalf of the accused only on two occasions. Thus, the order sheets, when examined cumulatively and in their true perspective, do not demonstrate that the petitioner or anyone acting on his behalf repeatedly or deliberately obstructed the recording of prosecution evidence. Rather, the record indicates that on several dates the prosecution itself was not in a position to proceed with its complete evidence. The subsequent report of the learned Magistrate merely records, in general terms, that the delay in conclusion of the trial was attributable to the accused, but identifies neither the particular dates nor the proceedings nor any specific conduct of the petitioner which occasioned such delay. Such conclusion is not borne out by the contemporaneous order sheets. The statutory exception contemplated by the third proviso to Section 497(1), Cr.P.C. cannot be invoked on the basis of a generalized assertion of attribution; the alleged delay must be demonstrably traceable to an act or omission of the accused or a person acting on his behalf. Had the record shown that, despite the presence and readiness of a prosecution witness and the prosecution's preparedness to examine him, the Crl. Misc. No.43416-B of 2026 10 petitioner had deliberately and without justification prevented the recording of his evidence, or had failed to cross-examine after his examination-in-chief was recorded despite adequate opportunity, the period so occasioned could legitimately have been taken into account. That is not the case here. In the absence of any such specific finding or supporting material in the order sheets, the petitioner cannot be saddled with responsibility for a period during which the prosecution evidence was, in fact, not recorded. The statutory right available under the third proviso to Section 497(1), Cr.P.C. thus cannot be defeated merely on the strength of an unsupported conclusion that the delay was attributable to the petitioner.
16. It is equally substantial that the prosecution has not
asserted that the petitioner is a previous convict, a hardened or desperate criminal, or that he poses a serious threat and danger to the community if released on bail. Nothing has been placed on record to bring his case within any of the exceptions contemplated by the third proviso to Section 497(1), Cr.P.C. The principles laid down in “ Noor Agha v. The State and another ” ( 2025 SCMR 1679 ) and “ Adnan Shafai v. The State and another ” ( 2024 SCMR 1543 ) may also be relied upon in this context.
17. The right to a fair and expeditious trial is an essential
component of due process. Pre-trial detention cannot be permitted to assume the character of punishment, particularly where the accused has remained incarcerated beyond the statutory period and the trial is not likely to conclude in the immediate future. The prosecution's allegations may be grave, but the gravity of an accusation, by itself, is unable to defeat a statutory entitlement where the prescribed conditions stand satisfied.
18. In the present case, the delay in submission of the
challan is attributable to the prosecution. No material has been brought on record showing that the petitioner caused or contributed to that delay. As regards the subsequent period, the Crl. Misc. No.43416-B of 2026 11 report of the learned Magistrate does not identify any particular act or omission of the petitioner which materially obstructed the progress of the trial. The order sheets likewise do not disclose that, on the dates relied upon, the prosecution was ready to record its evidence and the petitioner deliberately prevented such recording. The mere presence of prosecution witnesses in Court, without recording of their evidence and without a specific order-sheet explanation as to why such evidence could not be recorded, is insufficient to deprive the petitioner of his statutory right.
19. Consequently, without commenting upon the merits of
the case, lest it prejudice either party during the trial, the instant petition is allowed . The petitioner, Ali Shahzad alias Shan Ali, is admitted to post-arrest bail, subject to furnishing bail bonds in the sum of Rs. 1,00,000/- (one lac) with one surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the learned Trial Court.
20. The observations recorded herein are tentative in
nature and shall not influence the learned Trial Court, which shall decide the case strictly on the basis of the evidence produced before it.
(GHULAM SARWAR NIHUNG)
JUDGE
Announced, dictated, prepared and signed on 31.08.2026.
Approved for reporting .
JUDGE
Iftikhar

Stereo HCJDA 38
JUDGMENT SHEET
LAHORE HIGH COURT LAHORE
( JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT)
Writ Petition No.17594 of 2020 All Pakistan Markazi Union Pan, Beri, Cigarette, Mashroob Retailers through its President V ersus Federation of Pakistan through Secretary National Health Services Regulation & Coordination and others Petitioners by:- Khawaja Haris Ahmad, Sr. ASC.
M/s Syed Tassadaq Mustafa Naqvi, Syed Tassadaq Murtaza Naqvi, Barrister Naqsh Fatima Naqvi and Muhammad Usman, Advocates (W.P. No17595 of 2020) Respondents by : Mr. Nauman Khalid, Assistant Attorney General for the Federation of Pakistan.
Mr. Salman Asif Warraich and Umar Farooq Khan, Assistant Advocates General, Punjab with Dr. Hafiz Asim Hussain, Addl. Director office of D.G. Health & Population Department, Punjab.
Dates of hearing: - 04.06.2026, 08.06.2026, 15.06.2026,
19.06.2026, 23.06.2026, 29.06.2026
JUDGMENT
RAHEEL KAMRAN, J.: Through the titled writ petition under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 ( “ the Constitution ” ) , the petitioner has called in question the vires of S.R.O.72(I)/2020 dated 30.01.2020 ( “ the impugned Notification ” ) , issued by the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination, whereby the advertisement, promotion and sponsorship of tobacco and tobacco products has been comprehensively prohibited through the various media and other modes specified therein. As id entical
-2-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 challenge arises in Writ Petition No.17595 of 2020, both petitions were heard together and are disposed of through this common judgment.
2 . Learned counsel for the petitioners, adopting substantially common grounds of challenge, contended that the impugned Notification dated 30.01.2020 is ultra vires the Prohibition of Smoking and Protection of Non - Smokers Health Ordinance, 2002 (“the Ordinance of 2002”) .
According to them , Section 7 contemplates only the regulation of tobacco adv ertisements through guidelines prescribed by the Committee constituted thereunder and does not authorize a complete prohibition. It was argued that the expression “ if such advertisement is not in accordance with guidelines ” necessarily presupposes that som e form of advertisement must remain permissible , therefore, the Committee lacked authority to recommend a blanket prohibition. It was further contended that no guidelines, as contemplated by Section 7, were ever framed by the Committee itself and that the impugned Notification merely gives effect to recommendations of a sub - committee, thereby lacking statutory foundation. Learned counsel also submitted that Section 7 is confined to “ advertisement ” and does not extend to promotion, sponsorship or restriction s relating to the display and visibility of tobacco products at points of sale, with the result that the impugned Notification travels beyond the parent statute. Learned counsel further relied upon the expression “except as provided by the Federal Excise R ules, 2005” occurring in clause (a) of the Guidelines 2013 as well as the impugned Notification , contending that the said exception itself demonstrated that the competent authority understood the statutory scheme as permitting at least some form of tobacc o advertisement. According to learned counsel, the existence of such an exception was inconsistent with the respondents’ assertion that Section 7 authorized a complete prohibition.
Much emphasis has been laid by the learned counsel for the petitioners that the impugned Notification violates Articles 4 and 18 of the Constitution by imposing what is, in substance, a complete prohibition upon a lawful commercial activity under the guise of
-3-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 regulation. According to them, although a lawful trade may be subjected to reasonable restrictions, regulation cannot be stretched to the point of extinction. It was also contended that the Notification is based upon an excessive delegation of legislative power and is arbitrary, disproportionate and violative of Articles 9, 10-A, 14, 18, 25, 37 and 38 of the Constitution. Learned counsel further submitted that the exclusion of any representative of the tobacco industry from the Committee offended the principles of natural justice as well as Section 24-A of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
Developing the challenge further, learned counsel contended that the Committee travelled beyond its statutory mandate by seeking to implement Article 13 of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control ( “ WHO FCTC ” ) , although the Convention has never been incorporated into municipal law. According to learned counsel, Pakistan follows the dualist theory of international law and treaty obligations cannot be enforced domestically without legislative incorporation. It was also argued that after the Eighteenth Constitutional Amendment, the subject of health stands devolved to the Provinces and the Federation consequently lacked constitutional competence to issue the impugned Notification. In this context, considerable emphasis was laid upon the historical merger of the Tobacco Control Cell with the Health Services Academy under the Inter-Provincial Coordination Division, from which it was argued that implementation of tobacco-control measures fell within the domain of the Council of Common Interests rather than the Federal Government.
3 . Notice under Order XXVIIA of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, was issued to the Attorney General for Pakistan, in response to which parawise comments were submitted on behalf of the Federation in Writ Petition No.17594 of 2020 .
4 . L earned Assistant Attorney General for Pakistan opposed the petitions principally on the basis of the parawise comments. He also raised a preliminary objection to t he maintainability of the petitions on
-4-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 the grounds stated therein. On merits, he maintained that the impugned Notification neither prohibits nor regulates the manufacture, import, distribution or sale of tobacco products but merely restricts their advertisement, promotion and sponsorship in furtherance of the legislative policy embodied in the Ordinance of 2002 for the protection of public health. According to him, Article 18 does not confer an independent constitutional right to advertise tobacco products; Section 7 authorizes the Committee to prescribe appropriate guidelines in furtherance of the statutory object; the Committee acted strictly within the authority conferred by the Ordinance; and the WHO FCTC was relied upon only as a legitimate guide in exercising powers independently conferred by domestic law. He further submitted that the continuing operation of the Ordinance after the Eighteenth Amendment is protected by Article 270AA(6) of the Constitution and that the Federation remained constitutionally competent to administer the statutory framework established thereunder.
5 . The learned Assistant Advocate General, Punjab remained present during the hearing but did not advance any independent submissions either supporting or opposing the challenge.
6 . In support of their respective submissions, the learned counsel for the petitioners as well as the learned Assistant Attorney General placed reliance upon numerous statutory provisions, constitutional provisions and judicial precedents, which shall be referred to, to the extent necessary, while examining the respective questions arising for determination.
7 . Having heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record with theirable assistance, it is appropriate first to dispose of the preliminary objection to maintainability raised by the learned Assistant Attorney General. The objection is two-fold: first, that the petitioners, being retailers rather than manufacturers of tobacco products, are not persons aggrieved; and secondly, that the petitions are misconceived because neither the Ordinance of 2002 nor the notifications dated
-5-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020
26.09.2018 and 31.05.2019 have been challenged. Neither objection
merits acceptance. The petitioners are associations representing retailers dealing in tobacco products. The impugned Notification expressly regulates various aspects of retail sale, including the display and visibility of tobacco products at points of sale and certain dealings between suppliers and retailers. Its provisions are thus directly applicable to the members of the petitioner associations, whose conduct is governed by the impugned instrument and who may be affected by its enforcement. They, therefore, possess a sufficient and direct interest to question its legality under Article 199 of the Constitution. Reliance in this regard is placed on the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of “Mian Fazal Din v.
Lahore Improvement Trust, Lahore and another” (PLD 1969 SC 223) , wherein it has been held:
“The right considered sufficient for maintaining a proceeding in writ jurisdiction is not necessarily a right in the strict juristic sense but it is enough if the applicant discloses that he had a personal interest in the performance of the legal duty which if not performed or performed in a manner not permitted by law would result in the loss of some personal benefit or advantage or the curtailment of a privilege or liberty or franchise.” The preliminary objection is, therefore, overruled and the petitions are held to be maintainable.
8 . Turning now to the merits of the case, it is convenient to address first the petitioners’ principal constitutional challenge, as the determination of the remaining questions substantially depends upon its resolution. The foundation of the petitioners’ case is that the impugned Notification, by comprehensively prohibiting the advertisement, promotion and sponsorship of tobacco products, impermissibly abridges their fundamental right to carry on a lawful trade and business guaranteed by Article 18 of the Constitution. The said Article undoubtedly accords constitutional protection to the freedom of every citizen to enter upon a lawful profession, occupation, trade or business. Economic liberty is an
-6-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 important facet of individual autonomy and a recognized constitutional value. The guarantee, however, is not absolute, unqualified or unfettered but subject to regulation and reasonable restrictions which may be imposed by law in the larger interest of the society or for public welfare .
The opening words of the Article 18 expressly make its operation “subject to such qualifications, if any, as may be prescribed by law” . The word “qualification” has been used to confer a right upon a citizen to enter upon any lawful profession or occupation and not to conduct and unlawful trade or business. The word “lawful” qualifies the right of the citizens in the relevant field and envisages that the State can by law ban a profession, occupation, trade or business by declaring it to be unlawful which in common parlance means anything forbidden by law .
It is not the petitioners’ case that the impugned Notification prohibits the manufacture, import, distribution or sale of tobacco products. The tobacco trade in this country is lawful and as such, continues to remain independently regulated . The petitioners’ grievance is confined to the prohibition of the advertisement, promotion and sponsorship of tobacco products. It is well settled that reasonable restriction s which bear true relation to business or trade can be validly imposed for the purp ose of promoting general welfare . By qualifying the right to business and trade, the Constitution makers wanted to create a balance between the societal needs and the right of an individual .

Tobacco products are inherently addictive and scientifically established to cause serious disease, affecting not only users but also those involuntarily exposed to second-hand smoke .
