It was argued that, since the notification constituting the Committee required it to frame guidelines compliant with Article 13 of the WHO FCTC, the Committee effectively exercised a power derived from an unincorporated treaty rather than from the Legislature , thereby rendering the impugned Notification legally unsustainable. The submission raises an important question concerning the relationship between international obligations and municipal law. It, however, proceeds u pon a misconception as to the true source of the Committee ’ s authority. The issue is not whether the WHO FCTC forms part of the law of Pakistan , rather, it is whether, while exercising a statutory discretion already conferred by domestic legislation, the C ommittee could legitimately draw guidance from an international convention to which Pakistan is a party. That distinction is fundamental and lies at the heart of the present controversy.
29 . The distinction as noted above, becomes apparent upon a brief notice of the two principal theories governing the relationship between international law and municipal law. Under the monist theory, international and domestic law are regarded as forming a single legal order, with the consequence that a treaty, once validly ratified, ordinarily becomes capable of direct application within the municipal legal system, subject always to the constitutional framework of the State concerned.
The dualist theory, on the other hand, proceeds upon the premise that
-25-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 international law and municipal law constitute two distinct legal systems.
Under that approach, a treaty binds the State upon the international plane by virtue of ratification, but does not, merely for that reason, become enforceable within domestic courts. For a treaty to create rights or obligations enforceable under municipal law, its provisions must ordinarily be incorporated through legislation enacted by the competent law-making authority. The controversy in the present case falls to be examined against the backdrop of the latter principle, which has consistently informed the jurisprudence of the superior Courts of Pakistan.
30 . Pakistan has consistently followed the dualist approach .
The superior Courts have repeatedly held that, unless incorporated into municipal law through legislation or otherwise reflected in an existing statutory framework, the provisions of an international convention do not, merely by virtue of ratification, become independently enforceable in domestic courts. At the same time, the jurisprudence has drawn a clear distinction between enforcing a treaty as an autonomous source of municipal rights and obligations, on the one hand, and referring to it as an interpretative aid while construing domestic legislation, on the other.
Where a municipal statute is reasonably capable of more than one interpretation, or confers a statutory discretion to be exercised consistently with its legislative object, courts and public authorities may legitimately have regard to an international convention to which Pakistan is a party, provided such reliance neither conflicts with municipal law nor treats the treaty itself as the source of the legal power being exercised. In that limited but important sense, international conventions perform a persuasive and interpretative function without acquiring the force of municipal law. The above view finds support in the jurisprudence of the superior Courts. In the case of “ Mst. Shehla Zia and others v. WAPDA ” (PLD 1994 SC 693) , while considering the relevance of international “Societe Generale De Surveillance S.A. v. Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of Finance Revenue Div ision, Islamabad” ( 2002 SCMR 1694) .
-26-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 environmental instruments, the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that an international agreement, though binding upon the State at the international plane, does not become enforceable as municipal law unless incorporated through legislation. At the same time, the Court recognised that such instruments possess persuasive value. Relevant extract from the said judgment is as under:- “ An international agreement between the nations if signed by any country is always subject to ratification, but it can be enforced as a law only when legislation is made by the country through its legislature. Without framing a law in terms of the international agreement the covenants of such agreement cannot be implemented as a law nor do they bind down any party. This is the legal position of such documents, but the fact remains that they have a persuasive value and command respect. ” (Emphasis supplied by this Court).
The same principle was reiterated by the Peshawar High Court in the case of “ Haji Lal Muhammad v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of Interior, Islamabad ” (PLD 2014 Peshawar 199) , wherein it was held that international law unless in direct conflict with municipal law ought to be applied and respected by municipal courts in deciding matters arising therefrom . More recently, the Islamabad High Court, in the case of “ Yassa Khan v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary, Minis try of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination ” (2023 CLC 744) , while dealing with issues relating to tobacco control under the Ordinance of 2002, likewise referred to the WHO FCTC and its guiding principles in issuing directions for the eff ective enforcement of domestic law. These authorities thus illustrate a consistent judicial approach that international conventions do not operate as an independent source of enforceable municipal law, yet they may legitimately be consulted as persuasive i nterpretative aids where such use advances, rather than contradicts, the purpose of the governing domestic legislation.
31 . Applying the above principles, the petitioners ’ objection cannot be sustained. The impugned Notification does not owe its legal
-27-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 existence to the WHO FCTC, nor does it purport to enforce Article 13 thereof as an independent source of municipal law. The authority to constitute the Committee, to prescribe tobacco-advertisement guidelines and to issue the impugned Notification flows exclusively from Section 7 of the Ordinance of 2002. The notification dated 26.09.2018, whereby the Committee was reconstituted, merely required the Committee, while discharging the statutory function entrusted to it by the Legislature, to take appropriate steps to make the guidelines compliant with Pakistan ’ s obligations under Article 13 of the WHO FCTC and to review them periodically in the light of national and international commitments. In doing so, the Federal Government neither purported to incorporate the Convention into municipal law nor delegated legislative authority to an international instrument. It simply identified the normative considerations which the Committee was expected to bear in mind while exercising a statutory discretion already conferred by domestic legislation. Such recourse to an international convention as an interpretative and policy guide is entirely consistent with the dualist doctrine recognised in Pakistan and does not transform the Convention into the source of the Committee ’ s legal authority. The impugned Notification, therefore, derives its validity from Section 7 of the Ordinance, whereas the WHO FCTC merely informed the manner in which that statutory power was exercised.
32 . The petitioners nevertheless sought to derive suppor t from the language of Article 13 of the WHO FCTC itself by contending that the Convention contemplates a comprehensive prohibition of tobacco advertising only “ in accordance with a Party ’ s constitution or constitutional principles ” and, therefore, does not invariably mandate a complete ban. The submission proceeds on a mistaken premise. The qualification contained in Article 13 defines the extent of a Contracting State ’ s obligation under international law; it neither confers legislative authority upon d omestic institutions nor circumscribes the powers already conferred by municipal law. The present controversy is not
-28-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 concerned with the minimum obligations imposed by the Convention upon Pakistan, but with the extent of the authority delegated by the Legislature through Section 7 of the Ordinance. As already held, that provision authorizes the Committee to prescribe guidelines consistent with the legislative policy of protecting public health and contains no statutory limitation requiring that some category of tobacco advertisement must invariably remain permissible. Whether Article 13 obliged Pakistan to adopt a comprehensive prohibition, or merely permitted such a course consistently with its constitutional framework, is therefore of no legal consequence to the validity of the impugned Notification. Once the measure is found to be independently authorized by Section 7 of the Ordinance of 2002, its validity cannot be made to depend upon the precise content of Pakistan ’ s treaty obligations under the WHO FCTC. Indeed, the flexibility recognized by Article 13 itself — that implementation is to be undertaken in accordance with each State ’ s constitutional order — reinforces the conclusion that the Convention leaves the choice of domestic regulatory measures to municipal law rather than itself prescribing their legal source.
33 . The view expressed in the preceding paragraphs that the Committee merely employed the WHO FCTC as an interpretative guide, while exercising powers independently conferred by Section 7 of the Or dinance of 2002 , is further borne out by the notification dated
26.09.2018 whereby the Federal Government reconstituted the
Committee contemplated by that provision. Significantly, the notification expressly records that it was issued “ in exercise of power s conferred by section 7 of the Prohibition of Smoking and Protection of Non - Smokers Health Ordinance, 2002 ” , thereby identifying the Ordinance — not the Convention — as the sole legal source of the Committee ’ s authority. The functions assigned to the Committe e likewise demonstrate that compliance with Article 13 of the WHO FCTC was intended to guide the exercise of the statutory discretion conferred by the Legislature , rather than to substitute or enlarge it. The reference to Article 13 in the
-29-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 impugned Notification appears only while describing the considerations to be borne in mind in framing and periodically reviewing the guidelines.
The Convention thus informed the content of the guidelines, whereas the authority to formulate and enforce them continued to flow exclusively from the Ordinance.
34 . The petitioners next assailed the impugned Notification on the ground that, even if Section 7 of the Ordinance of 2002 authorized the measures embodied therein, the Federal Government ceased to possess constitutional competence to exercise that authority after the Constitution (Eighteenth Amendment) Act, 2010. It was contended that, upon the abolition of the Concurrent Legislative List and the devolution of the subject of health to the Provinces, the regulatory power under Section 7 could no longer be exercised by the Federation. Learned counsel further referred to the Rules of Business framed by the Government of the Punjab, whereby the administration of the Ordinance of 2002 was assigned to the Provincial Health Department, and argued that the continued constitution of the Committee by the Federal Government and the issuance of the impugned Notification in exercise of Section 7 were constitutionally incompetent. The plea is misconceived. International treaties, conventions, etc and their implementations are federal legislative subjects in terms of entries 3 and 32 of the Fourth Schedule read with Article 70(6) of the Constitution. In terms of Article 97 of the Constitution, executive authority of the Federation extends to the matters with respect to which the Parliament has power to make laws. Once the Federal Government signed WHO FCTC prior to the Constitution (Eighteenth Amendment) Act, 2010, it remained a Federal subject.
Whether the provisions of existing law i.e., the Ordinance of 2002 were sufficient to give effect to obligation under WHO FCTC or otherwise, was exclusively for the Federal Government to consider. At the time of passing of the Constitution (Eighteenth Amendment) Act, 2010, the subject matter in question was never a concurrent subject to be devolved upon the Provinces as canvassed by the learned counsel for the
-30-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 petitioners covered by Article 270AA(6) of the Constitution.
Furthermore, the constitutional validity of the Ordinance of 2002 has not been questioned before this Court. Consequently, the statutory framework established thereunder — including the authority conferred by Section 7 to constitute a Committee and prescribe guidelines regulating tobacco advertisements — likewise continued to remain operative after the Eighteenth Amendment.
35 . It may also be noted that following the Eighteenth Amendment, the Federal Government continued to administer the Ordinance of 2002 as a subsisting federal enactment and, in exercise of the same power under Section 7, notified the Tobacco Advertisement Guidelines through S.R.O.1086(I)/2013 dated 31.12.2013. Those Guidelines, as already noticed, imposed restrictions substantially similar to those embodied in the impugned Notification. Significantly, neither the Provincial Governments nor any person affected thereby questioned the constitutional competence of the Federation to constitute the Committee or to issue the Guidelines under Section 7. Likewise, when the Committee was reconstituted through the notification dated
26.09.2018, it included nominated representatives of the Governments of
Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, thereby ensuring provincial participation in the formulation of the recommendations ultimately culminating in the impugned Notification. There is nothing on the record to suggest that any Province objected either to the constitution of the Committee or to the exercise of powers under Section 7 on the ground that such authority had ceased to vest in the Federation after the Eighteenth Amendment. Although the absence of a constitutional challenge cannot, by itself, determine the existence of legislative competence, it is nevertheless a relevant circumstance demonstrating the contemporaneous constitutional understanding of the Federation and the Provinces alike that the Ordinance of 2002 continued to operate as a subsisting federal law until altered by the competent legislature. That understanding is entirely consistent with the constitutional scheme.
-31-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 36 . An allied consti tutional objection advanced by the learned counsel for the petitioners was founded upon the role of the Council of Common Interests (CCI). It was contended that the Tobacco Control Cell, originally established in 2007 as an attached department of the then Ministry of Health for implementation of Pakistan ’ s obligations under the WHO FCTC , ceased to remain under the Federal Ministry of Health after the Eighteenth Amendment. Learned counsel pointed out that, by notification dated 20.06.2011 issued by the Cabin et Division, the Tobacco Control Cell was merged with the Health Services Academy, which was thereafter placed under the Inter - Provincial Coordination Division. Since inter - provincial coordination is a matter falling within Part II of the Federal Legislati ve List, it was argued that the formulation and implementation of tobacco - control measures thereafter became a matter requiring consideration by, or falling within the constitutional domain of, the Council of Common Interests. According to the learned coun sel, the Committee constituted under Section 7 and the impugned Notification, having been issued without recourse to the Council of Common Interests, were therefore constitutionally incompetent. In this regard, it is pointed out that t he Tobacco Control Ce ll owes its existence to an executive decision of the Federal Government and not to the Ordinance of 2002. Neither Section 7 nor any other provision of the Ordinance assigns to that Cell any statutory function in relation to the constitution of the Committ ee or the prescription of tobacco advertisement guidelines. The impugned Notification was issued by the Federal Government in exercise of the delegated authority expressly conferred by Section 7 through the Committee constituted thereunder, and not by the Tobacco Control Cell in exercise of any independent statutory power. Consequently, the administrative placement of the Tobacco Control Cell under one Division or another, or its merger with any other institution, cannot determine the constitutional validit y of the exercise of powers under Section 7 of the Ordinance of 2002 . It may also be noted that the Council of Common interests is concerned with
-32-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 formulation and regulation of policies in relation to the matters enumerated in Part II of the Federal Legislative List , whereas t he source of the impugned Notification remains under entries in Part I of the Federal Legislative List, the Federal statute and the authority delegated thereunder, not the executive location of an administrative unit established to fac ilitate tobacco - control policy.
37 . Adverting now to the remaining constitutional objections, learned counsel for the petitioners contended that the impugned Notification offends Article 4 of the Constitution on the premise that Section 7 of the Ordinance of 2002 contemplates regulation of tobacco advertisements rather than their complete prohibition and that, where a statutory provision admits of two possible constructions, the interpretation advancing a fundamental right ought to be preferred. In this regard, it may be pointed out that as held in the preceding paragraphs, neither Article 18 nor Article 19 confers an independent constitutional right to advertise tobacco products, and Section 7 of the Ordinance of 2002, when construed in the light of the legislative policy embodied in the Ordinance as a whole, authorizes the prescription of such guidelines as are reasonably necessary to advance its object of protecting public health. As such no competing interpretation favourable to the petitioners survives so as to attract the principle of adopting a rights-consistent construction. On the contrary, where welfare legislation enacted for the protection of public health and preservation of healthy environment as guaranteed under Article 9A of the Constitution is reasonably capable of a construction that furthers its legislative purpose, the Court must prefer an interpretation that gives full effect to that purpose rather than one which defeats or substantially impairs it . The challenge founded upon Article 4 is, therefore, without substance.
“Privatization Commission through Secretary and others v. Aftab Hussain and others” (PLD 2022 SC 267) .
“Director General, FIA and others v. Kamran Iqbal and others” (2016 SCMR 447) , “ Saif - Ur - Rehman vs. Additional District Judge, Toba Tek Singh and 2 others” (2018 SCMR 1885) .
-33-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 38 . Coming now to the petitioners’ contention that no representative of the tobacco industry was included in the Committee constituted under Section 7 of the Ordinance of 2002 , thereby offending the rule of audi alteram p artem as well as Section 24 - A of the General Clauses Act, 1897 , it may be noted that the Committee contemplated by Section 7 is an expert statutory body constituted to assist the Federal Government in furthering the public - health objectives embodied in the Ordinance. The Legislature neither prescribed any representative composition for the Committee nor required the inclusion of every commercial or other interest likely to be affected by the guidelines framed thereunder. In these circumstances, no legal rig ht accrued to the petitioners to claim representation in the Committee. Likewise, Section 24 - A of the General Clauses Act does not engraft an inflexible requirement of prior hearing before every exercise of delegated legislative or policy - making authority. It requires statutory discretion to be exercised fairly, justly, reasonably and in furtherance of the purpose for which it has been conferred. There is nothing on the record to suggest that the Committee acted arbitrarily, in bad faith or for any purpose alien to the Ordinance of 2002 . On the contrary, it is manifest that the committee acted within the limits of the authority conferred by Section 7 and in furtherance of the legislative objective of protecting public health.
The challenge founded upon the p rinciples of natural justice and Section 24 - A of the General Clauses Act is, therefore, without merit.
39 . The petitioners also invoked Articles 9, 10 - A, 14, 25, 37 and 38 of the Constitution and contended that the impugned Notification would encourage illicit trade in tobacco products. These submissions were, however, advanced only in general terms and were not supported by any independent or particulari z ed argument demonstrating how the impugned Notification infringes any of the aforesaid constitutiona l provisions. Article 10 - A, which guarantees the right to a fair trial and due process, has no application to the framing of subordinate legislation of general application. Likewise, no material has been placed before the
-34-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 Court to establish any infringement of Articles 9, 14 or 25 beyond the contentions already examined and rejected while dealing with the principal constitutional challenge. As regards Articles 37 and 38, they embody the Principles of Policy which, by virtue of Article 30 of the Constitution, are not enforceable by any court, though they undoubtedly reinforce the constitutional commitment to measures advancing public welfare and the protection of public health. The apprehension that comprehensive restrictions on tobacco advertising may stimulate illicit trade is equally speculative. Such a consequence, even if assumed, concerns the efficacy or enforcement of the regulatory regime rather than the constitutional or statutory validity of the impugned Notification. The possibility of regulatory evasion cannot furnish a ground for invalidating an otherwise lawful exercise of delegated legislative power. These residual objections are, therefore, repelled.
40 . At this stage, it is appropriate to notice the citations relied upon by the learned counsel for the petitioners. The propositions laid down therein, such as delegated legislation must remain within the limits of the parent statute and that restrictions upon a lawful trade must satisfy constitutional scrutiny, ar e well settled and admit of no controversy.
Those principles have been kept in view throughout the judgment in hand . The relied upon precedents, however, arose in materially different statutory and factual contexts. They were concerned either with restrict ions directly imposed upon the carrying on of a lawful trade or with subordinate legislation found to have transgressed the limits of the enabling statute. The case in hand stands on a fundamentally different footing. As already held, the impugned Notification neither prohibits nor regulates the petitioners ’ underlying trade in tobacco products; it regulates only the advertisement, promotion and sponsorship of such products in furtherance of the legislative policy expressly embodied in the Ordinance of 2002 . Equally, for the reasons already recorded, the Committee acted within the authority conferred upon it by Section 7 and the impugned Notification does not travel beyond the scope of the parent
-35-
W.P. No.17594 of 2020 statute. The authorities relied upon by the petitioners are, therefore, distinguishable and do not advance their case.
41 . For the foregoing reasons, both petitions are found to be devoid of merit and are dismissed . There shall be no order as to costs .
Before parting with the judgment, this Court places on record its appreciation for the valuable assistance rendered by the learned counsel for the parties as well as learned Law Officer, whoseable submissions and assistance have greatly facilitated the Court in arriving at the conclusions recorded herein.
(RAHEEL KAMRAN)
JUDGE
Announced in the Open Court on 02.09.2026.
JUDGE
Approved for reporting.
JUDGE
Azhar*

Case: Service 45728/24 (Azim Uddin Zahid Vs Government of Punjab etc.).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Service 45728/24. Title: Service 45728/24 (Azim Uddin Zahid Vs Government of Punjab etc.). Official Ref: 2026LHC5482. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Raheel Kamran. Judgment Date (as displayed): 02-09-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5482.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 26 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Stereo HCJDA 38
JUDGMENT SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT LAHORE
( JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT)
Writ Petition No.45728 of 2024 Azim uddin Zahid V s .
Government of the Punjab through Secretary Law and Parliamentary Affairs, etc.
Petitioner by:- Barrister Muhammad Umer Riaz and Rana Rehan, Advocates.
Respondents by : Mr. Imran Khan, Assistant Advocate General, Punjab.
Dates of hearing: - 09.06.2026 , 30.06.2026
JUDGMENT
RAHEEL KAMRAN, J:- Through the instant petition filed under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (“the Constitution”) , the petitioner has called in question the vires of the Punjab Healthcare Commission (Amendment) Act, 2024 (VI of
2024) dated 14.06.2024 (“the impugned a mendment ”) , whereby
sub - section (1a) was inserted in Section 6 of the Punjab Healthcare Commission Act, 2010 (“the Act of 2010”) providing that a Comm issioner of the Punjab Healthcare Commission (“the Commission”) shall serve during the pleasure of the Government. The petitioner has also assailed the notification dated 18.07.2024 (“the impugned notification”) , whereby he, along with the other Commission ers, was removed from the Commission pursuant to the impugned a mendment. The principal challenge is founded upon the contention that vesting the Government with an unfettered power to remove Commissioners at its pleasure undermines the statutory W.P.No.45728 of 2024 independence of the Commission and is contrary to the Constitution and the scheme and object of the Act of 2010.
2 . As per the contents of the petition, the Commission was established under section 3 of the Act of 2010 as an autonomous regulatory body for regulating healthcare services in the Province. Its functions include, inter alia , registration and licensing of hea lthcare providers, regulation of quality and standards, accreditation, inspection and investigation, issuance of regulatory directions and imposition of penalties and sanctions. Under the unamended section 6, a Commissioner was to hold office for a term of three years, subject to resignation, death or disqualification in terms of section 7. In October 2023, an amendment was introduced through an Ordinance empowering the Government to remove a Commissioner before expiry of his term without assigning any reas on. The said amendment was challenged before this Court and interim protection was granted. A similar provision was subsequently introduced through another Ordinance in February 2024, which was also challenged and interim relief was granted. After the seco nd Ordinance lapsed, the Provincial Assembly enacted the impugned amendment on
14.06.2024, whereby sub - section (1a) was inserted in section 6,
providing that a Commissioner shall serve during the pleasure of the Government. Pursuant thereto, the petitioner and the other Commissioners were removed vide notification dated 18.07.2024.
3 . Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the Commission is an autonomous regulatory body established to regulate healthcare services in both the public and private sectors and that its extensive regulatory, investigative and enforcement powers require institutional independence from governmental control. According to him, making the tenure of Commissioners subject to the pleasure of the Government enables the executive to exercise control over the very regulator which may be required to regulate governmental healthcare institutions, thereby defeating the object and scheme of the Act of 2010.
He submitted that the impugned provision confers an unguided and W.P.No.45728 of 2024 unfettered discretion to terminate a fixed statutory tenure without assigning reasons or following any prescribed procedure and is consequently inconsistent with the constitutional requirements of fairness, non-arbitrariness and lawful exercise of public power. Reliance was placed, inter alia , upon “Muhammad Yasin v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary, Establishment Division, Islamabad and others” ( PLD 2012 SC 132), “ Aman Ullah Khan and others v. The Federal Government of Pakistan through Secretary, Ministry of F inance, Islamabad and others” (PLD 1990 SC 1092), “ Baz Muhammad Kakar v. Federation of Pakistan through Ministry of Law and Justice, Islamabad” (PLD 2012 SC 870) , “Ms.
Imrana Tiwana and others v. Province of Punjab and others” (PLD 2015 Lahore 522), “Barrister Sardar Muhammad v. Federation of Pakistan and others” (PLD 2013 Lahore 343), and “Babar Sattar v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Ministry of Water and Power and 4 others” (2016
CLD 134) .
Learned counsel further contended that the impugned amendment amounted to regulatory capture and was person-specific, having been preceded by two unsuccessful attempts through Ordinances to secure the removal of the existing Commissioners. He also referred to the statutory regimes governing other regulatory bodies, including OGRA, NEPRA and PEMRA, to submit that autonomous regulators are ordinarily protected against arbitrary removal through defined grounds and procedural safeguards. He maintained that the impugned notification was independently liable to be set aside for having removed the Commissioners collectively without assigning reasons. He additionally invoked Articles 4, 9, 10-A, 14 and 25 of the Constitution, submitting that the independence of the Commission was necessary for effective protection of the public ‟ s right to healthcare. In the alternative, he prayed that the impugned provision be read down so as to preserve the independence of the Commission.
4 . Learned Assistant Advocate General, Punjab, controverted the submissions and contended that the impugned W.P.No.45728 of 2024 amendment neither compromised the autonomy of the Commission nor amounted to regulatory capture. He emphasized that section 5 provides a broad-based mechanism for constitution of the Board, under which seven Commissioners are nominated on the recommendation of a committee comprising representatives of various stakeholders, while two Commissioners are nominated by the Government. Relying upon the case of “ LDA v. Imrana Tiwana ” (2015 SCMR 1739) , he submitted that governmental participation in appointments to a regulatory body does not, by itself, establish regulatory capture, particularly where the Government itself falls within the regulatory sphere. He further argued that the concept of regulatory capture could not furnish a ground for striking down legislation in the absence of conflict with a constitutional provision.
Learned Law Officer further submitted that the allegation of person-specific legislation was misconceived and amounted to attributing mala fide to the legislature. Relying upon “Baz Muhammad Kakar v.
Federation of Pakistan through Ministry of Law and Justice, Islamabad” (PLD 2012 SC 870) he contended that the validity of legislation is to be tested with reference to legislative competence and conformity with the Constitution, rather than the alleged motive behind its enactment. He maintained that the Provincial Assembly was competent to amend the Act and that the petitioner had failed to identify any constitutional provision expressly prohibiting the impugned arrangement. According to him, the doctrine of pleasure could not be rendered inapplicable merely because the office was previously subject to a fixed tenure, nor could the possibility of its arbitrary exercise render the legislation itself unconstitutional.
Learned Assistant Advocate General also distinguished the case of “M uhammad Yasin v. Federation of Pakistan ” (PLD 2012 SC 132) on the ground that it concerned the legality of appointment to the office of Chairman, OGRA, for non-compliance with statutory qualifications and did not directly involve removal under a statutory pleasure clause.
W.P.No.45728 of 2024 Finally, he submitted that none of the petitioner ‟ s fundamental rights had been infringed and that the asserted effect upon the right to healthcare was speculative. He also contended that the petitioner ‟ s tenure had, in any event, expired and, therefore, no effective relief survived, relying upon the case of “ Munawar Iqbal Gondal v. Mrs. Nasira Iqbal and others ”
(2014 SCMR 860) .
5 . In rebuttal, learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that the challenge to the vires of the impugned amendment was maintainable under Article 199 and could not be defeated by any alternate statutory mechanism. He reiterated that the Commission regulates both public and private healthcare establishments and that its licensing, inspection, investigation and enforcement powers require Commissioners to act independently, including when dealing with governmental institutions. He contended that a tenure terminable at the unfettered pleasure of the Government would inevitably impair such independence and that the non-obstante clause contained in the impugned provision could not override the Constitution or the fundamental scheme of the Act of 2010. He further maintained that collective removal of the Commissioners without reasons or hearing was independently unlawful for being violative of Article 10A of the Constitution and that premature removal from a fixed tenure could also attract constitutional protection where it carries stigma. He distinguished the judgment relied upon by the respondents concerning the effect of an overriding statutory provision and reiterated that, in the alternative, the impugned provision could be read down to preserve the independence and effectiveness of the Commission.
6 . Since vires of Section 6(1a) of the Act of 2010 was assailed in this petition for alleged violation of fundamental rights and constitutional guarantees, therefore, notice under Order XXVIIA of the CPC was issued and reply thereto was also filed by the office of the Advocate General, Punjab in this and the connected Writ Petition No.50857 of 2024. The said writ petition filed by the Pakistan Medical W.P.No.45728 of 2024 Association, was fixed and heard along with the petition in hand till
09.06.2026 when that was consigned to record room for want of
instructions to the counsel.
7 . L earned counsel for the parties have been heard and record examined . Before adverting to the constitutional challenge, it would be appropriate to notice an objection raised by the learned Assist ant Advocate General that the petitioner‟s tenure has, in any event, expired and, therefore, no live controversy survives for adjudication.
Reliance in this regard has been placed upon the case of “M unawar Iqbal Gondal v. Mrs. Nasira Iqbal and others ” (2014 SCMR 860) , wherein the Supreme Court declined to examine an issue which had become academic after expiry of the relevant term, while leaving it open to the parties to agitate the substantive question in a future live controversy.
The objection, thoug h attractive at first sight, does not warrant disposal of the instant petition in its entirety. The petition in hand assails two distinct acts: first, the constitutional validity of sub - section (1a) inserted in Section 6 of the Act of 2010 through the impu gned amendment ; and secondly, the notification dated 18.07.2024 whereby the petitioner was removed from office pursuant thereto. It is correct that with expiry of the petitioner‟s original tenure, relief qua restoration of the petitioner to the office of t he Commissioner for the unexpired portion of that tenure has lost its practical significance . However, t he challenge to the vires of the impugned amendment, however, stands on a different footing. The impugned provision continues to remain on the statute b ook and constitutes a threat of removal of every Commissioner of the Commission before expiry of his/her tenure . Its constitutional validity is, therefore, not a question confined to the petitioner ‟ s individual grievance.
The Supreme Court has observed tha t a constitutional question cannot be regarded as a mere academic exercise where its determination is necessary for clarification of the relevant constitutional provisions. In the case titled “ Sh. Riaz - ul - Haq and another v. Federation of Pakistan ” (PLD 2013 SC 501) , while considering questions relating to the constitutional scheme concerning the judiciary, the Supreme Court declined to treat the W.P.No.45728 of 2024 interpretation of the relevant constitutional provisions as academic and observed that such exercise was „very essential and necessary‟ for making the constitutional position clear. The same principle is attracted here because the question concerns a continuing statutory provision governing the tenure and removal of Commissioners of an important institution of the healthcare regulatory body.
8 . The next question is whether a statutory provision enacted by the Provincial Assembly conferring upon the Government the power to remove a Commissioner “during the pleasure of the Government” is immune from judicial revie w merely because the legislature was competent to enact the amendment. The answer, in the considered view of this Court , is in the negative. The legislative competence of the Provincial Assembly and the constitutional validity of the legislation are two se parate inquiries. The fact that the Assembly possesses legislative competence over the subject does not mean that every legislative choice made in exercise of that competence is beyond constitutional scrutiny.
Legislation, like every other exercise of Stat e power, remains subject to the Constitution and to the fundamental principles of law which inform the exercise of public power under our constitutional order. The question is whether, in its legal operation and effect, the impugned provision is consistent with the constitutional guarantees and limitations applicable to the exercise of legislative and public power. In the present case, as shall presently be examined, the impugned provision falls to be tested, inter alia , against the guarantees contained in Article 10A of the Constitution.
9 . The Commission is not an ordinary departmental office nor is a Commissioner merely an incumbent of an executive post terminable at the will of the appointing authority. The statutory scheme of the Act of 2010 reveals that the Commission was conceived as a distinct institutional and regulatory body, entrusted with functions of regulating and improving the quality and standards of healthcare services in the Province. Section 3(2) gives the Commission a separate corporate personality by declaring it to be a bo dy corporate having perpetual W.P.No.45728 of 2024 succession and a common seal, with powers to enter into contract, sue and be sued by its name . The regulatory character of the institution is further evident from section 4, which is reproduced below for reference:
“4. Functio ns and powers of the Commission . – (1) The Commission shall perform such functions and exercise such powers as may be required to improve the quality of healthcare services and clinical governance and to ban quackery.
(2) Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions of subsection (1), the Commission shall –
(a) maintain register of all healthcare service providers;
(b) grant, revoke and renew licenses to persons involved
in the provision of the healthcare services and to vary terms and conditions and purposes of the licenses;
(c) monitor and regulate the quality and standards;
(d) operate accreditation programmers in respect of the
healthcare services and to grant accreditation to such healthcare service providers who meet the standards;
(e) enquire and investigate into maladministration,
malpractice and failures in the provision of healthcare services and issue consequential advice and orders;
(f) impose and collect fees and charges on registration,
licensing and accreditation under this Act;
(g) impose and collect penalties on violation, breach or
non-compliance of the provisions of the rules, regulations, standing orders and instructions issued under this Act;
(h) advocate rights and responsibilities of recipients and
providers of the healthcare services;
(i) hold seminars, conferences and meetings on developing
awareness about provision of high quality healthcare services;
(j) enter into agreement or arrangement with the Federal
Government or a Provincial Government, any authority, board, council or entity, nongovernmental organization, domestic or international institution or agency for the purposes of this Act;
(k) coordinate, liaise and network with any person, agency
or institution;
(l) take on lease land, buildings for the purpose of offices
or premises of the Commission at such price and on such term as may be necessary; W.P.No.45728 of 2024
(m) appoint, engage, authorize and terminate employees,
consultants, advisors, attorneys, inspection teams, contractors, agents and experts on such terms and conditions as deemed fit and assign, delegate or entrust them with such functions and powers as are expedient for the performance of functions of the Commission;
(n) take measures for the welfare of the present and past
employees of the Commission as well as its all registered members;
(o) issue regulations, guidelines, instructions and
directives to persons involved in the provision of Healthcare services;
(p) grading of the healthcare establishments; and
(q) take necessary steps to ban quackery.
(3) The Commission may assign any of its functions to a person on such terms and conditions as may be agreed between the Commission and the person.
(4) In the performance of its functions, the Commission shall –
(a) take into consideration the policy advice of the
Technical Advisory Committee; and (b) co-ordinate with the Government.
(5) Subject to sub-section (6), the Commission shall conduct third party evaluation through independent performance audit of healthcare establishments in a phased manner.
(6) The Commission shall not conduct third party evaluation through independent performance audit of healthcare establishments in the private sector other than tertiary care hospitals.
(7) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, the Commission may –
(a) on a complaint by any aggrieved person; or
(b) on a complaint by any aggrieved healthcare service
provider; and shall –
(c) on a reference by the Government or the Provincial
Assembly of the Punjab; or
(d) on a motion of the Supreme Court of Pakistan or the
Lahore High Court made during the course of any proceedings before it, undertake investigation into allegations of maladministration, malpractice or failures on the part of a healthcare service provider, or any employee of the healthcare service provider.
W.P.No.45728 of 2024 (8) The Commission shall take cognizance of any case of harassment of a healthcare service provider or damage to a healthcare establishment and may refer such a case to the competent forum.
(9) The Commission shall take measures and devise a strategy to counter sale of drugs without prescription.
(10) The Commission may exercise the same powers as are vested in a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (V of
1908), in respect of the following matters: –
(a) summoning and enforcing the attendance of any person
and examining him on oath;
(b) compelling the production of documents;
(c) receiving evidence on affidavits; and
(d) issuing commission for the examination of witnesses.
(11) The Commission shall not investigate or inquire into any matter subjudice before a Court of competent jurisdiction on the date of the receipt of a complaint, reference or motion.
(12) The Commission may authorize members of the staff to administer oaths and to attest various affidavits, affirmations or declarations which shall be admitted in evidence in all proceedings under this Act without proof of the signature or seal or official character of such person. ” The perusal of above section 4 shows that the statutory functions assigned to the Commission are regulatory in nature and extend well beyond the performance of ordinary administrative or departmental functions. Section 4 ibid empowers and requires the Commission to maintain a register of healthcare service providers; grant, revoke and renew licences and regulate their terms and conditions; monitor and regulate the quality and standards of healthcare services; operate accreditation programmes; enquire and investigate into maladministration, malpractice and failures in the provision of healthcare services and issue consequential advice and orders; impose and collect penalties for violations and non-compliance; issue regulations, guidelines, instructions and directives to persons involved in the provision of healthcare services; grade healthcare establishments; and take necessary measures to ban quackery.
W.P.No.45728 of 2024 10 . The regulatory character of the Commission is further reinforced by the institutional structure prescribed for its governance under section 5 of the Act, which vests the general superintendence, direction and management of its affairs, as well as overall policy - making in respect of its operations, in the Board of Commissioners. For reference, section 5 is reproduced hereunder: - “ 5. Constitution of the Board . – (1) The general superintendence, direction and management of the affairs of the Commission and overall policy making in respect of its operations shall vest in the Board which may exercise all such powers and do all such acts, deeds and things that may be exercised or done by the Commission under this Act.
(2) The Government shall notify the Board which shall consist of nine Commissioners, seven of whom shall be nominated on the recommendation of the committee.
(3) A person shall not be eligible to be nominated as Commissioner unless he possesses a minimum of fifteen years experience in public or private sector.
(4) The committee shall recommend to the Government a panel of two persons for each vacant post of the seven Commissioners to be nominated on the recommendation of the committee.
(5) The Government shall nominate a former Judge of the Lahore High Court and a financial expert as Commissioners.
(6) The Board shall regulate the conduct of its meetings, quorum and minutes of the meetings.
(7) The Government shall prescribe the remuneration payable to a Commissioner for attending a meeting of the Board.
(8) A decision of the Board shall not be valid if decided in a meeting without quorum.
(9) The committee, for the purpose of recommendation for nomination of Commissioners under this section, shall consist of the following:
(a) Secretary to the Government, Health Department; Chairman
(b) Vice Chancellor of a health sector University
nominated by the Government; Member
(c) a representative of the Pakistan Medical Association; Member
(d) a representative of the private healthcare
establishments nominated by the Government; Member
(e) a representative of the general practitioners
W.P.No.45728 of 2024 nominated by the Government; Member
(f) a representative of the Council for Tibb; Member
(g) a representative of the Council for Homeopathy. Member ”
From perusal of the section 5 it is vivid that the Board is constituted as the principal governing organ of the Commission and is empowered to exercise all such powers and perform all such acts, deeds and things as may be exercised or done by the Commission under the Act. The composition of the Board is also significant. It consists of nine Commissioners, seven of whom are nominated on the recommendation of a committee comprising representatives of the Government, the health sector, the Pakistan Medical Association, private healthcare establishments, general practitioners, the Council for Tibb and the Council for Homeopathy. A person is not eligible to be nominated as a Commissioner unless he possesses a minimum of fifteen years ‟ experience in the public or private sector. In addition, the Government is required to nominate a former Judge of the Lahore High Court and a financial expert as Commissioners. The statutory scheme, therefore, contemplates a multi-member governing body comprising persons possessing professional, institutional and specialized experience, rather than a conventional departmental hierarchy in which the relevant officeholder functions as a subordinate of the executive Government. The legislature has deliberately placed the general superintendence, direction, management and overall policy-making of the Commission in the Board and has prescribed a structured mechanism for the nomination of its members. This structural arrangement assumes that the Commissioners are to discharge their statutory responsibilities as members of an institutional regulatory body, rather than merely execute the policy or directions of the Government. This aspect becomes particularly relevant when the tenure of a Commissioner is examined. The original scheme of section 6(1) provided that a Commissioner “shall hold office for a term of three years” and was eligible for re-nomination in accordance with section 5. The statutory conferral of a defined term of office, read W.P.No.45728 of 2024 together with the nature of the functions vested in the Commission and the governing authority assigned to its Board, indicates that the office of Commissioner was conceived as a tenure-based statutory office rather than an ordinary executive appointment. The distinction is material. A regulator is required to apply the law even when the result may be inconvenient to the Government, a governmental institution, a politically influential person or any other entity falling within its regulatory jurisdiction. The effectiveness of such regulation necessarily depends upon the ability of the regulator to act without apprehension that an adverse regulatory decision may result in the loss of office of the person who made it.
11 . It is in this context that the institutional independence of the Commission assumes substantive significance. Such autonomy cannot be treated as a mere matter of nomenclature, but must be gathered from the statutory scheme, the nature of the functions entrusted to the Commission and the field over which those fun ctions are to be exercised.
Significantly, subsection (4) of section 1 provides that the Act of 2010 shall apply to all healthcare establishments, public or private hospitals, non - profit organizations, charitable hospitals, trust hospitals, semi government and autonomous healthcare organizations. Thus, the regulatory jurisdiction of the Commission extends not only to privately operated healthcare establishments but also to public and semi government healthcare institutions. The Commission may, therefore, be required in the discharge of its statutory functions to exercise regulatory, investigative and enforcement powers even in respect of healthcare institutions falling within or associated with the governmental sphere.
An institution entrusted with regulating entities falling within the sphere of the executive Government cannot meaningfully discharge that function if the same executive authority retains an unrestricted power to remove, at any time and for no ascertainable reason, the persons constituting the regulatory body. Security of tenure is thus not an incidental privilege of a Commissioner. In the context of an autonomous W.P.No.45728 of 2024 regulator, it constitutes an important structural safeguard designed to enable the office-holder to perform the statutory mandate with the requisite independence. The significance of the independence of a regulatory body finds support in the observations of the Supreme Court in the case of “ Muhammad Yasin v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary, Establishment Division, Islamabad and others ” (PLD 2012 SC
132) . In that case, while examining the doctrine of pleasure in its
historical and constitutional context, the Supreme Court traced the doctrine to the British constitutional scheme, under which important State functionaries held office during the pleasure of the Crown in its absolute and unfettered discretion. The Court observed that Pakistan, having adopted a democratic Constitution founded upon the rule of law, had retained the doctrine in its broad form only in respect of a few constitutionally identified offices, and significantly held that such discretionary powers do not exist in statutes relating to autonomous regulatory bodies such as OGRA.
12 . Of particular significance are the observations of the Supreme Court in Muhammad Yasin case regarding the importance of institutional autonomy in the functioning of regulatory bodies. While examining the regulatory framework governing OGRA, the Supreme Court observed:
“Vital autonomous institutions such as OGRA can function „effectively and efficiently‟ only if their autonomy is respected.
This is the letter as well as the spirit of the law. Such autonomy is only possible when appointments to key positions in these regulators are made in a demonstrably transparent manner; that is, by ensuring the implementation of the checks which the Ordinance lays down for such appointments.” The Court further explained the rationale underlying such institutional autonomy in the following terms:
“These bodies have explicitly been made autonom ous to ensure that they remain free from political or other interference and thus remain focused on the objectives of their parent statutes.” W.P.No.45728 of 2024 The principle emerging from these observations is of wider application.
Independence of a regulatory institution is not merely a formal attribute; it has to be understood in the context of the statutory safeguards intended to preserve the institution ‟ s capacity to discharge its mandate without improper interference. While the case of Muhammad Yasin was concerned, in particular, with the statutory safeguards governing appointment to key positions in OGRA, the underlying rationale is equally relevant when examining the effect of a statutory power of removal upon the independence of a regulatory body. A transparent or participatory process of appointment may protect the initial constitution of a regulator; it does not, by itself, ensure the subsequent independence of its office-holders if their tenure remains liable to be terminated at the unfettered pleasure of the executive. The manner of appointment and security of tenure, though distinct safeguards, may operate together to secure the institutional independence necessary for the discharge of regulatory functions. In the case in hand, this distinction assumes particular importance because the Commission regulates provision of healthcare services which constitute an essential and integral facet of the right to light and human dignity as guaranteed under Articles 9 and 14 of the Constitution. The legislature prescribed a structured mechanism for the constitution of the Board and, in the original enactment, conferred upon a Commissioner a defined term of three years. The subsequent insertion of subsection (1a) in section 6, providing that a Commissioner shall serve during the pleasure of the Government, therefore cannot be examined in isolation from the nature of the institution, the functions entrusted to it and the statutory scheme governing its constitution and tenure. The doctrine of pleasure cannot be treated as a talisman which, merely by its use in statutory language, places the resulting power beyond judicial scrutiny. Indeed, the Supreme Court in Muhammad Yasin case itself observed that, even where appointments are to be made in the exercise of discretionary powers, such powers are required to be employed reasonably and their exercise is amenable to judicial review.
Whether a statutory power of removal is legally sustainable must, W.P.No.45728 of 2024 therefore, depend upon the nature of the office, the statutory scheme, the purpose for which the institution was created and the effect which the power of removal is capable of producing upon the discharge of its statutory functions.
13 . The precise difficulty lies not in the existence of a power of removal as such, but in the nature and extent of the power conferred by subsection (1a) of section 6. The impugned provision does not make premature termination of a Commissioner‟s tenure dependent upon misconduct, incapacity, conflict of interest, failure to discharge statutory functions, or any other ascertainable circumstance mentioned in section 7 of the Act of 2010. Nor does it prescribe any procedure for exercise of the power or require the Government to disclose the basis upon which the tenure is brought to an end. The power is thus vested without any discernible statutory standard governing its exercise. This is materially different from a scheme under which a Commissioner may be removed for specified causes and in accordance with a defined procedure. In the latter case, the tenure remains subject to accountability within a legal framework; in the former, its continuation is made dependent solely upon the continuing satisfaction of the executive authority. The constitutional question must, therefore, be examined not in the abstract, but in the context of the nature of the office, the regulatory functions entrusted to the Commission and the constitutional guarantees governing the exercise of a power having such consequences for the holder of the office. The fact that an actual instance of governmental interference may not have been demonstrated does not conclude the matter. The validity of an institutional arrangement is capable of being examined by reference to the legal power which the arrangement itself creates and the manner in which that power is capable of affecting the discharge of statutory functions.
14 . The foregoing statutory position must, however, be examined in the light of the constitutional guarantees governing the exercise of public power. Article 10A guarantees to every person the W.P.No.45728 of 2024 right to a fair trial and due process for the determination of his civil rights and obligations. The constitutional guarantee of due process is not confined to proceedings before ordinary courts or tribunals. In the case of “Naveed Asghar and 2 others v. The State” (PLD 2021 SC 600) it has been held that principles of fair trial guaranteed by Article 10A are to be read as an integral part of every sub-constitutional legislative instrument that dealt with determination of civil rights and obligations of any person.
15 . The expression “civil rights and obligations” employed in Article 10A is of particular significance in the present context. The impugned amendment concerns a statutory office carrying a defined tenure, while the power conferred thereby, when exercised, results in premature termination of that tenure and thereby produces direct and adverse civil consequences for the incumbent. The mere fact that the power is conferred by legislation does not, by itself, place its exercise beyond the discipline of due process. As noticed above, the constitutional guarantee of fair trial and due process under Article 10A extends not only to judicial proceedings but also to administrative proceedings involving the determination of civil rights and obligations. Likewise, in the case of “Justice Qazi Faez Isa and others v. President of Pakistan and others” (PLD 2022 SC 119) , the Supreme Court explained the wide amplitude of the expression “civil rights and obligations” and recognized the right of hearing as an essential component of fair trial and due process. The Supreme Court in the case of “ Commissioner Inland Revenue v. Messrs RYK Mills ” ( 2023 SCMR 1856 ), while considering the constitutional guarantees contained in Articles 4 and 10A in the context of administrative adjudication, emphasized that the principles of natural justice require a fair and meaningful opportunity to respond before an adverse order affecting rights or interests is passed. The Court specifically recognized the importance of notice, opportunity to present one ‟ s case, impartiality and reasons in securing a fair and transparent decision-making process.
W.P.No.45728 of 2024 16 . Tested against these constitutional standards, subsection (1a) of section 6 presents a difficulty of a fundamental nature. It authorizes the premature termination of a Commissioner‟s defined tenure at the pleasure of the Government, yet prescribes neither any substantive ground or ascertainable standard for such termination nor any procedure regulating the exercise of the power. The provision does not require the Government to disclose the basis upon which the tenure is proposed to be brought to an end, afford the Commissioner an opportunity to respond, or record reasons for the adverse decision. The vice, therefore, is not merely that a power of removal has been conferred upon the executive; rather, it is that a power carrying serious civil consequences has been conferred without any discernible legal standard or procedural safeguard. The exercise of such an unstructured power, which permits adverse action against the statutorily secured tenure of a healthcare regulator without affording the safeguard of due process, cannot be reconciled with the guarantee enshrined in Article 10A of the Constitution.
17 . It is necessary to emphasize that the constitutional objection is not directed against the existence of a power of removal as such. A legislature may, consistently with the constitutional scheme, provide for premature termination of a statutory tenure upon specified grounds and through an appropriate procedure. The constitutional difficulty arises where a defined tenure, conferred as part of the statutory architecture of an autonomous regulatory institution, is made terminable at the unstructured pleasure of the executive, without any ascertainable standard or process by which the exercise of that power can be tested.
The expression “during the pleasure of the Government” may identify the source of the power, but it cannot, merely by its use, immunize the exercise of that power from the constitutional requirements of lawful and fair process. The statutory discretion of the executive remains subject to the Constitution and to judicial review.
18 . The foregoing constitutional considerations acquire particular significance when examined in the context of the pleasure W.P.No.45728 of 2024 doctrine itself. The Supreme Court has recognized that, under the present constitutional order, the doctrine is not a general reservoir of executive power but an exceptional constitutional arrangement confined to specified offices. In Muhammad Yasin case (supra) the Supreme Court, while considering the independence of an autonomous regulatory body, explained the constitutional position in the following terms:
“ 29. Much has changed since then. Pakistan now has a democratic Constitution which provides for the government of laws and not of men. It is for this reason that in our Constitution there remain few positions where the incumbents "hold office during the pleasure" of someone else based on broad discretion.
In its undiluted form this convention exists only in Article 100(2), Article 101(3) and Article 140(3) which relate to the appointments of a Governor, the Attorney General and the Advocates General respectively. Similarly, such discretionary powers do not exist in those statutes which relate to autonomous regulatory bodies like
OGRA. ”
(Emphasis supplied by this Court).
The above pronouncement is of particular relevance to the controversy before this Court. The Supreme Court drew a clear distinction between the limited constitutional offices in respect of which the Constitution itself employs the language of pleasure and statutory offices forming part of autonomous regulatory bodies. The observation that such discretionary powers do not exist in statutes establishing autonomous regulatory bodies is directly germane to the present case, where the impugned provision has introduced an unrestricted pleasure-based removal power in relation to a Commissioner of an autonomous healthcare regulator. The mere use of the expression “during the pleasure of the Government” in a statute, therefore, cannot by itself be treated as sufficient to confer upon the executive the same broad discretionary authority which the Constitution has expressly recognized in respect of the specified offices.
19 . Comparative legislative practice within Pakistan also does not support the proposition that an executive pleasure power is an inherent or necessary incident of the regulation of healthcare establishments. The Sindh Healthcare Commission W.P.No.45728 of 2024 Act, 2013 provides that a Commissioner shall hold office for a term of three years and specifies statutory disqualifications, while reserving the pleasure provision in section 8(2) to the office of Chairperson, whose continuation in that capacity depends upon the pleasure of the majority of Commissioners.
Likewise, the Islamabad Healthcare Regulation Act, 2018 establishes the Islamabad Healthcare Regulatory Authority as a body corporate and provides that a member of its Board shall hold office for three years, eligible for one further term, while prescribing specific disqualifications; it contains no corresponding provision authorizing the Federal Government to terminate a Board member merely at its pleasure. These legislative models are significant because they demonstrate that healthcare regulation can be entrusted to statutory bodies whose governing members enjoy a defined tenure, while accountability is secured through specified statutory qualifications and disqualifications rather than through an unrestricted executive power of removal. Furthermore, neither the impugned amendment shows nor the learned Law Officer has beenable to point out any legislative necessity for an autonomous healthcare regulator to be subjected to an unrestricted executive pleasure power.
20 . Furthermore, the significance of due process and procedural fairness in the exercise of executive removal powers, as well as the relationship between security of tenure and institutional independence, is also illustrated by comparative jurisprudence. Although the constitutional framework of the United States is materially different from our own, the decision of the Supreme Court of the United States in Trump v. Cook, 609 U.S. ___ (2026), is instructive in both respects.
The case concerned the attempted removal of a Governor of the Federal W.P.No.45728 of 2024 Reserve Board, whose office was held for a defined term and from which she could be removed only for cause. The Court emphasized that the Federal Reserve operates at a deliberate remove from the ordinary political process and that not only the fact of its independence but also the appearance of independence is integral to its design. In that context, the Court held that the statutory expression “cause” could not be construed as conferring an unrestricted power of removal and that the cause relied upon must genuinely relate to unfitness for office rather than serve as a pretext for securing a more congenial replacement. The Court further held that the fixed statutory tenure and for-cause protection carried with them a right to notice and an opportunity to respond before removal; as the requisite procedural safeguards had not been afforded to the office-holder, the attempted removal could not, at that stage, be sustained.
21 . The relevance of Trump v. Cook (supra) to the present controversy lies not in importing the constitutional law of the United States into our constitutional framework, but in the manner in which the Court approached the relationship between defined tenure, grounds of removal, procedural fairness and institutional independence. The decision demonstrates that these considerations are not necessarily separate or competing concerns. Where an office is entrusted with functions requiring independence from ordinary political influence, security of tenure serves not merely to protect the individual office-holder but also to preserve the institutional character of the body. At the same time, where premature removal is sought on the basis of adverse allegations or considerations, procedural fairness requires that the affected office-holder be informed of the basis of the proposed action and afforded an opportunity to respond before the decision is finalized.
22 . This conclusion finds support in the reasoning adopted by this Court in the case titled “Nabila Hakim Ali Khan v. Government of the Punjab, etc.” , (PLD 2025 Lahore 759) , wherein, while examining a statutory office carrying a defined tenure, the importance of security of W.P.No.45728 of 2024 tenure to the independent and fearless discharge of statutory functions was recognized, particularly where the office-holder was required to deal with the Government or persons wielding influence. It was further noticed that permitting termination without a defined legal process could impair the independence and impartiality expected of the office.
Although the statutory office considered therein was different, the principle concerning the relationship between defined tenure, institutional independence and accountability through law is directly apposite to the controversy in the case in hand.
23 . The contention that the impugned provision cannot be subjected to constitutional scrutiny merely because no provision of the Constitution expressly declares that a Commissioner of a provincial healthcare regulator shall not hold office during the pleasure of the Government also cannot be accepted. The constitutional challenge in the present case does not rest upon the existence of an express constitutional provision prescribing a particular tenure for Commissioners. Rather, the impugned provision is challenged on the ground that the power which it confers, in its legal operation and effect, is inconsistent with the constitutional guarantees of lawful treatment and due process embodied in Articles 4 and 10A of the Constitution, read with the constitutional consequence prescribed by Article 8. Constitutional adjudication is not confined to identifying a textual provision which reproduces, in identical terms, the precise prohibition sought to be enforced. The exercise of legislative power remains subject to the Constitution, while the exercise of public power created by legislation remains subject to the requirement that such power be exercised within the limits and for the purposes for which it has been conferred. The Supreme Court‟s decision in Muhammad Yasin case (supra) is instructive in this regard. The relevance of Muhammad Yasin (supra) to the present controversy, therefore, lies in the constitutional principle that the independence and autonomy of a statutory regulator cannot be divorced from the legal framework governing the exercise of public power in relation to its office-holders.
W.P.No.45728 of 2024 24 . The same conclusion follows from the settled principle that statutory discretion is not synonymous with arbitrary power. Even where legislation confers a broad discretion upon a public authority, the power must remain connected with the object of the enactment and must be exercised within the legal and constitutional framework applicable to that authority. Article 4 of the Constitution, in particular, requires that every action detrimental to a person be taken in accordance with law; statutory conferment of a power cannot, therefore, be construed as an authorization to exercise it arbitrarily or without regard to the constitutional requirements governing its exercise. The expression “during the pleasure of the Government” may identify the source and character of the power conferred, but it does not, by itself, answer the question whether the power is subject to constitutional limitations. The Court is consequently required to examine the legal effect of the provision within the statutory scheme as a whole. Here, the legislature established a specialized regulatory institution, vested its Board with extensive regulatory and coercive functions, prescribed qualifications and a structured mechanism for constitution of the Board, and originally secured the office of Commissioner through a defined term of three years. The question is whether that statutory design is compatible with a subsequent provision which makes the continuation of that tenure dependent upon the unstructured pleasure of the executive. In the considered view of this Court, the two features cannot be reconciled without substantially diminishing the institutional protection which the original scheme was designed to provide.
25 . The nature of the field regulated by the Commission further reinforces this conclusion. As discussed in the preceding paragraphs, the Commission regulates provision of healthcare services which constitute an essential and integral facet of the right to light and human dignity as guaranteed under Articles 9 and 14 of the Constitution.
Jurisdiction of the Commission extends to public as well as private healthcare establishments and its statutory powers include licensing, monitoring, investigation, inspection, issuance of regulatory directions W.P.No.45728 of 2024 and imposition of penalties. Its decisions may, therefore, affect governmental institutions as well as private healthcare providers and other entities operating within the healthcare sector. The statutory mandate is consequently not one of ordinary departmental administration but one requiring the application of regulatory standards across institutional interests that may, at times, include those of the Government itself. In such a setting, the ability of the regulator to take decisions according to the statute, rather than according to the perceived wishes of the executive, assumes particular importance. The constitutional values embodied in Articles 9 and 14, insofar as those protect life and dignity of the citizens, provide an additional contextual reason for insisting upon an effective regulatory mechanism. The conclusion reached herein rests upon the statutory character of the Commission, the functions entrusted to it and the constitutional requirements governing the exercise of public power.
26 . The contention raised by the learned counsel for the petitioner that the impugned amendment constitutes persons-specific legislation also requires consideration. This Court does not consider it necessary to determine the subjective motive of the legislature as an independent ground for invalidating the enactment.
27 . The argument concerning stigma does not require separate determination as a basis for the present decision. Learned Assistant Advocate General has correctly distinguished between removal at pleasure, which does not necessarily carry any stigma, expiry of tenure, which likewise carries none, and removal founded upon an allegation of misconduct, which may have stigmatic consequences. The Court accepts that distinction for the purposes of the submission. The conclusion reached herein does not depend upon the proposition that the petitioner‟s removal was stigmatic or that Article 14 is attracted on that account.
28 . At the same time, it is necessary to make clear what this judgment does not hold. An autonomous regulatory body does not require that its Commissioners be placed beyond accountability, nor does a defined tenure render an office-holder immune from removal in every W.P.No.45728 of 2024 circumstance. Misconduct, incapacity, conflict of interest or other legally recognized grounds may furnish a legitimate basis for premature removal where the legislature so provides and the competent authority acts in accordance with law. Independence and accountability are complementary, rather than competing, requirements of a sound regulatory framework . The constitutional difficulty arises where the law dispenses altogether with the standard by reference to which premature termination may be justified and leaves the continuation of office solely to the unfettered will of the executive. Such an arrangement does not merely provide a mechanism for accountability; it alters the character of a defined statutory tenure by making it inherently precarious. The distinction is therefore between lawful accountability and executive control at will. The former is compatible with institutional independence; the latter may substantially impair it.
29 . For the foregoing reasons, subsection (1a) inserted in section 6 of the Punjab Healthcare Commission Act, 2010, insofar as it provides that a Commissioner shall serve during the pleasure of the Government without prescribing any substantive ground or procedural safeguard for premature termination of the defined statutory tenure, cannot be sustained. In the context of the statutory scheme, the provision places the continuation of the office- holder‟s tenure entirely at the discretion of the executive, notwithstanding the autonomous and regulatory character of the institution and the nature of the functions vested in it. It thereby creates a legal regime in which the independence of the healthcare regulator is capable of being compromised through the exercise of an unstructured removal power. More importantly, insofar as the provision permits adverse action carrying serious civil consequences without any ascertainable standard or procedural safeguard for fair and lawful decision-making, it is inconsistent with the guarantees embodied in Article 4 and 10A of the Constitution. Being inconsistent with a fundamental right, the provision cannot be sustained in view of Article 8 of the Constitution. Therefore, the petition in hand is allowed and consequently, the impugned subsection (1a) of the Punjab Healthcare W.P.No.45728 of 2024 Commission Act, 2010 is declared void to the extent of such inconsistency and of no legal effect.
30 . In consequence of the declaration made above, the impugned notification dated 18.07.2024, insofar as it purported to remove the petitioner in exercise of the power conferred by subsection (1a) of section 6, cannot be sustained. The petitioner‟s original three-year tenure has, however, expired during the pendency of these proceedings.
No effective order for his restoration to an office the term of which has already elapsed can, therefore, presently be made. The declaration made herein concerning the invalidity of subsection (1a), being directed against the statutory provision itself and not merely against the individual notification of removal, shall nevertheless operate according to law.
(RAHEEL KAMRAN)
