VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 11 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Stereo. HCJDA 38
JUDGMENT SHEET
LAHORE HIGH COURT
BAHAWALPUR BENCH, BAHAWALPUR
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025 Muhammad Arsalan Vs. The State and another
JUDGMENT
Date of hearing : 30 . 0 6 .202 5 For the Appellant : Malik Saeed Ejaz, Advocate.
For the Respondent s :
Rao Riaz A hmad Khan , Deputy Prosecutor General , with Muhammad Tayyab Ameer / T - SI .
Tariq Saleem Sheikh, J. – The Appellant is facing trial in connection with FIR No. 147/2022 dated 12.03.2022, registered under section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997 ( “ CNSA ” ) at Police Station Samma Satta, Bahawalpur. During the trial, the prosecution produced six witnesses whose evidence was recorded.
Thereafter, the case was fixed for recording the Appellant ’ s statement under section 342 Cr.P.C. On 26.08.2024, he filed an application under Article 59 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat, 1984 (the “ QSO ” ), read with Article 10-A of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (the “ Constitution ” ), praying that the Recovery Memo (Exh. PA), complaint (Exh. PB) and the rough site plan (Exh. PC) be sent to a handwriting expert for comparison with the handwriting of the Complainant/Respondent No.2, Muhammad Tayyab Ameer/T-SI (PW-3) who claimed that all those documents were in his handwriting.
The Additional Sessions Judge, Bahawalpur, dismissed the application vide order dated 22.04.2025 (the “ Impugned Order ” ). The Appellant has challenged that order through this appeal filed under section 48 of the CNSA.
The Impugned Order
2. The trial court observed that the evidence of all the
prosecution witnesses, including the Complainant/Investigating Officer Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025
- 2 -
Tayyab/T-SI (PW-3), had been recorded and that the defence had already conducted detailed cross-examinations. The case was fixed for the statement of the accused (Appellant) under section 342 Cr.P.C. If there were any contradictions in the prosecution ’ s case, their effect would be considered at the time of final arguments. The court added that under section 29 of the CNSA, a presumption arises against the accused unless proven otherwise. It further remarked that, according to settled case law, expert opinions on handwriting are generally weak and not conclusive, particularly when other direct evidence is available.
Referring to Syed Shabbir Hussain v. The State (1968 SCMR 1126), the court concluded that seeking expert opinion at this stage would serve no useful purpose and only prolong the proceedings. It therefore dismissed the Appellant ’ s application.
The submissions
3. The Appellant ’ s counsel contends that the Impugned
Order is perverse and not sustainable. He argues that the Appellant has been denied the right to a fair trial guaranteed under Article 10A of the Constitution. As such, it is liable to be set aside.
4. The Deputy Prosecutor General has controverted this
appeal and supported the Impugned Order.
Opinion
5. Muhammad Tayyab Ameer/T-SI (PW-3) is the
Complainant as well as the Investigating Officer of this case. He testified that on 12.03.2022, on a spy information, he along with other police officials apprehended the Appellant from Mouza Rama and recovered 1080 grams of crystal ICE from a polythene bag he was carrying. PW Tayyab/T-SI further stated that he separated 54 grams from the contraband and prepared a sealed sample parcel for chemical analysis. Then, he sealed the remaining ICE in another sealed parcel (P-1), affixed his stamp bearing the acronym “ TA ” on both the parcels in the presence of Sajid Nazir 462/HC (PW-2) and Riaz Hussain 1833/C (PW-5) and secured them vide Recovery Memo Exh. PA. After that, he drafted the complaint Exh. PB and sent it to the police station through Riaz Hussain 1833/C (PW-5) for the registration of FIR Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025
- 3 -
No.147/2022 (Exh. PD). He further stated that subsequently the investigation of the case was also entrusted to him, which he conducted. He prepared a rough site plan (Exh. PC) and recorded the statements of the witnesses (Exh. DA, Exh. DB, Exh. DC, and Exh. DD).
6. During cross-examination, the Appellant asked Tayyab/
T-SI (PW-3) various questions to establish that the documents mentioned in paragraph 1 were not in his handwriting and that the recovery proceedings were fabricated. PW Tayyab initially stated that he could not replicate the handwriting on Exh. DA, Exh. DB, Exh. DC, and Exh. DD because his index finger was swollen. Then, responding to another question, he stated that the finger injury had occurred a year earlier and that he had not been declared disabled or unfit. The relevant portion of the cross-examination reads:
“ I completed the investigation, I consumed 30 minutes in preparation of site plan. I reached the police station at 3:55 p.m.
Exh. DA, E xh. DB and Exh. DC are written by me … I cannot write down the same writing of Exh. DA, Exh. DB and Exh. DC due to the reason that my index finger is swelling condition … I cannot write down the same writing [like in] Exh. DD (statement of Sajjad Nazir under section 161 Cr.P.C.) as well as the hand writing on Exh.
PA, Exh. PB and Exh. PC due to the said reason. It is also incorrect to suggest that the reason given is absolutely wrong and that no index finger is swell (sic). At this stage, the witness again said that my finger is not swell, however, it was injured about one year back.
I am not declared disable neither by any doctor nor anyone from my police department. I was not declared unfit by my hand over other organ/fingers. I can write down through this finger. ” (sic) (emphasis added)
7. Given the above, the question arises as to whether the
Additional Sessions Judge rightly declined the Appellant ’ s request to refer the aforementioned documents to the handwriting expert.
Applicable l aw
8. Articles 59, 61, 78, 78-A, 79, and 84 of the QSO set out
the legal framework for proving a document and/or its handwriting or any signature thereon. In Mobarik Ali Ahmed v. State of Bombay (AIR 1957 SC 857), the Supreme Court of India (SCI) explained that the authorship of a document may be proved through various means, including direct testimony, handwriting comparison, internal consistency with related documents, or expert opinion. It emphasized Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025
- 4 -
that proof of authorship is simply proof of fact and may rest on direct or circumstantial evidence. Building on Mobarik Ali , the SCI in Gulzar Alishri Raj Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh (1998) 2 SCC 192, the SCI held that the evidentiary modes provided in sections 45 and 47 of the Indian Evidence Act 1872 – corresponding to Articles 59 and 60 of the QSO – are not exhaustive for proving the genuineness or authorship of a document.
9. Article 59 of the QSO provides that when the court has to
form an opinion upon a point of foreign law, or of science or art, or as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions or any other expert matter, the opinions upon that point of persons specially skilled in such foreign law, science or art, or in questions as to identity of handwriting or finger impressions, are relevant facts. This provision acknowledges that certain matters lie beyond judges’ knowledge or experience.
Therefore, in such cases, expert input becomes necessary. The term “ relevant fact ” signifies that expert opinion is not merely ancillary commentary but is admissible evidence that may assist the court in resolving technically complex or disputed issues, such as handwriting authenticity. However, such an opinion is not binding. Its evidentiary weight depends on the expert ’ s qualifications, the methodology, and reasoning. An unsupported or speculative opinion carries little value, and where conflicting expert opinions are presented, the court must determine which is more persuasive in light of the entire record.
10. Article 84(1) of the QSO stipulates that, in order to
ascertain whether a signature, writing, or seal is that of the person by whom it purports to have been written or made, any signature, writing, or seal admitted or proved to the satisfaction of the court to have been written or made by that person may be compared with the one in question, even if that signature, writing, or seal has not been produced or proved for any other purpose. Article 84(2) provides that the court may direct any person present in court to write any words or figures to enable it to compare those words or figures with any alleged to have been written by such person. Article 84(3) states that these provisions also apply to finger impressions with any necessary modifications.
Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025
- 5 -
11. In Brindra Kumar Ghose and others v. Emperor
(37 C 467 : 7 IC 359 : 11 Cr LJ 453), Jenkins, C.J. stated that section 73 of the Indian Evidence Act, which corresponds to Article 84 of the QSO, requires that the disputed writing must “ purport ” to have been written by the person to whom it is attributed, that is to say, the writing itself must state or indicate that it was written by that person.
According to this interpretation of the section, it is not competent to a court under the first paragraph of the section, to compare with an admitted or proved writing another writing which does not “ purport ” to have been written by a particular person, but is alleged to have been written by that person. A disputed writing which does not “ purport ” , but is alleged to be in a person ’ s handwriting, cannot be compared with an admitted or proved writing, but only with the words or figures which, under the second paragraph of the section, the alleged writer is made to write in court. According to Monir, this narrow interpretation of the section though followed in subsequent Calcutta cases and by the Oudh Court in another case, has not found favour with the Bombay and the Madras High Courts where it has, in substance, been held that the word “ purports ” , in the first paragraph of the section is equivalent to “ is alleged ” and that a court is competent to compare with an admitted or proved writing not only a writing which “ purports ” to be in the alleged writer ’ s handwriting but also a writing which is alleged to be in his handwriting without expressly purporting to be so.
12. Article 84 of the QSO is an enabling provision which is
indicated by the use of the word “ may ” . It confers discretion on the court. However, while this power exists, it should be exercised with caution, particularly in cases involving technical complexity or genuine dispute. Judges are not handwriting experts; relying solely on visual comparison may lead to error. In Kessarbai v. Jethabhai Jivan (AIR 1928 PC 277), the Privy Council observed that it is not always safe to stake a decision on the correct determination of the genuineness of a signature by mere comparison with admitted signatures, especially without the aid of microscopic enlargements or any expert evidence. In Brindra Kumar Ghose, the Court stated that comparison of M. Monir, Law of Evidence, Fourteenth Ed., Vol.2, p. 1316 Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025
- 6 -
handwriting is always a hazardous and inconclusive mode of proof, particularly when undertaken by someone not conversant with the subject and without the benefit of guidance from counsel ’ s arguments or expert evidence. In Galstaun v. Sanatan Pal (AIR 1925 Cal. 485, 78 IC 668), it was held that it is undesirable for a judge to undertake the task of comparing signatures to determine whether forgery has been committed in a case. Courts in Pakistan have also held the same view.
13. While Articles 59 and 84 of the QSO prescribe different
methods of proof, one involving expert assistance and the other judicial scrutiny, they are not alternatives in the sense of being mutually exclusive. They are rather complementary. Courts may resort to Article 84 in clear-cut or straightforward cases where the similarity or dissimilarity is obvious. In more complex situations, where the writing is distorted, disguised, or forged with sophistication, they may prefer or permit recourse to expert opinion under Article 59.
14. In addition to the provisions of the QSO, sections 510 and
540 Cr.P.C. are relevant in the present context. Section 510 governs the admissibility of reports by certain government experts, such as chemical examiners, serologists, and fingerprint analysts, and allows the court to summon them if their oral examination is necessary.
Handwriting experts are not among the categories expressly covered by this provision. Accordingly, their written reports are not per se admissible under section 510. The expert who authored the report must ordinarily be summoned for examination unless both parties consent to its admission without formal proof.
15. Section 540 Cr.P.C. empowers the court at any stage of the
inquiry, trial, or other proceeding to summon any person as a witness, or examine any person in attendance, if it considers his evidence essential to the just decision of the case. This provision is couched in the widest possible terms and is designed to enable the court to obtain all necessary evidence for reaching a just conclusion, even if such evidence is sought after the closure of the prosecution case. The See: Messrs Waqas Enterprises and others v. Allied Bank of Pakistan and others (1999 SCMR 85), Mst. Umatul Waheed and others v. Mst. Nasira Kausar and others (1985 SCMR 214), Ghulam Rasool and others v. Sardarul Hassan and another (1997 SCMR 976), and Rehmat Ali Ismailia v. Khalid Mehmood (2004 SCMR 361).
Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025
- 7 -
discretionary power under section 540 may be exercised to summon or refer matters to a handwriting expert when a material dispute arises and the court finds that such evidence is necessary for resolving it. The guiding principle is that the interest of justice must prevail over procedural formality.
16. Courts in Pakistan have consistently held that the opinion
of a handwriting expert is a weak type of evidence. In Syed Shabbir Hussain v. The State (1968 SCMR 1126), the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that “ the evidence of the handwriting expert is neither the only nor the best method of proving the handwriting or signature of a person. It is at best only opinion evidence. ” In Ch. Abdul Hamid v.
Deputy Commissioner and others (1985 SCMR 359), the Supreme Court cited the following excerpt from M. Monir Law of Evidence (Vol. l, page 621): “… of all kinds of evidence admitted in a Court, this is the most unsatisfactory. It is so weak and decrepit as scarcely to deserve a place in our system of jurisprudence. In view of this infirmity of expert testimony, it is the settled practice of courts not to base a finding merely on expert opinion. Conclusion based on mere comparison of handwriting must at best be indecisive, and yield to the positive evidence in the case. ” In Mst. Saadat Sultan and others v.
Muhammad Zahur Khan and others (2006 SCMR 193 : PLJ 2006 SC
1478), the Supreme Court reaffirmed that the opinion of a handwriting
expert, while relevant under the law, is a weak type of evidence and not conclusive. It is merely confirmatory or explanatory of direct or circumstantial evidence and cannot prevail over testimony that is confidence-inspiring and worthy of credence. Such opinion may be rebutted by independent and overwhelming evidence to the contrary.
The Court observed that it is always risky to base findings regarding the genuineness of handwriting solely on expert opinion. This form of evidence must be received with great caution, particularly because an expert, however impartial he may appear, may unconsciously develop a bias in favour of the party who has called him. The Court further stated that while such evidence must be critically examined, its rejection does not imply that the expert has acted dishonestly. Although corroboration is not a legal requirement, the degree of reliance that a court may place Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025
- 8 -
on expert opinion in any case depends on the facts and circumstances of that particular case.
17. Indian jurisprudence adopts a more nuanced view.
In Murari Lal v. State of Madhya Pradesh, AIR 1980 SC 531 :
(1980) 1 SCC 704, the SCI observed that there is no justification for equating the evidence of an expert with that of an accomplice or requiring corroboration as a rule. While it may be hazardous to base a conviction solely on the opinion of a handwriting expert, the risk arises not because experts are inherently unreliable but because all human judgment is fallible. An expert may err due to faulty observation, mistaken premises, or incorrect reasoning. The more developed and precise a scientific field is, the lower the risk of error. Fingerprint identification is highly reliable, whereas handwriting analysis is less exact and thus carries a greater margin of error. However, this does not justify a blanket requirement of corroboration in every case. The SCI emphasized that an expert deposes, not decides. His duty is to provide the judge with the necessary scientific criteria to assess the issue, enabling the judge to form an independent conclusion based on the facts and the expert ’ s reasoning. The Court further clarified that a judge is not precluded from comparing disputed and admitted writings under section 73 of the Indian Evidence Act (which corresponds to Article 84 of the QSO), even in the absence of expert evidence. It held that where expert testimony is available, it may assist the court, but where it is not, the court must perform the task itself. The duty to compare cannot be avoided on the ground that the court lacks expertise. Judges must discharge this function with or without expert guidance, using such aids as authoritative texts or personal experience where appropriate.
18. However, in Magan Bihari Lal vs State of Punjab
(AIR 1977 SC 1091), the SCI held that expert opinion must always be received with great caution, particularly the opinion of a handwriting expert. It is considered unsafe to base a conviction solely on such evidence without substantial corroboration. In that case, the Court found it especially hazardous to convict the accused solely on the strength of the expert ’ s opinion.
Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025
- 9 -
19. In Lalit Popli v. Canara Bank and others
(AIR 2003 SC 1796), the Supreme Court explained that handwriting identification is governed by sections 45, 47, and 73 of the Indian Evidence Act (which correspond to Articles 59, 61, and 84 of the QSO, respectively). Sections 45 and 47 deal with opinion evidence – either scientific or based on familiarity – while section 73 empowers the court to make a direct comparison. The Court clarified that these provisions are complementary. Although expert evidence need not be corroborated in every case, its weight depends on the surrounding circumstances.
Even in the absence of expert assistance, the court may compare the writings and reach its own conclusion.
20. To conclude, Articles 59 and 84 of the QSO are not
mutually exclusive. Where the writing is complex, disguised, or technically disputed, recourse to expert opinion under Article 59 is generally more appropriate. Nevertheless, if a party requests that a document be referred to a handwriting expert, such a request must be duly considered. If it is declined, reasons must be recorded, particularly where the authenticity of the document is material to the outcome of the case. This obligation flows from section 24A of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and the constitutional guarantee of a fair trial under Article 10A of the Constitution.
Application of l aw to the p resent c ase
21. The Appellant alleges that the recovery proceedings were
fabricated and that key documents – Recovery Memo (Exh. PA), complaint (Exh. PB), and site plan (Exh. PC) – were not written by Tayyab/T-SI (PW-3). During cross-examination, PW Tayyab gave contradictory statements regarding his ability to write. He initially claimed that he could not reproduce the handwriting on the documents due to a swollen index finger. However, he subsequently stated that the injury had occurred about a year earlier and that he had never been declared unfit or disabled. These contradictions cast doubt on his credibility and give rise to a serious factual dispute regarding the authorship of the documents. In these circumstances, referring them to a handwriting expert under Article 59 of the QSO is necessary. The court cannot undertake a comparison under Article 84 because no Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025
- 10 -
admitted or proved writing of PW Tayyab/T-SI is available on the record for that purpose. Expert opinion would provide relevant assistance in determining whether PW Tayyab was the author of the documents, which is central to the defence case.
22. The trial court declined the request partly on the ground
that handwriting expert opinions are generally weak and not conclusive. While this observation reflects settled jurisprudence, it does not justify the rejection of such evidence altogether. Article 59 of the QSO expressly recognises expert opinion as a relevant fact. Its admissibility is not precluded merely because it is rebuttable. The evidentiary weight to be attached to the expert ’ s findings is a matter to be assessed at trial. Where authorship of the documents is in dispute and direct evidence is contested, the expert ’ s opinion may still offer meaningful assistance to the court in arriving at a just conclusion.
23. The trial court also relied on section 29 of the CNSA,
which stipulates that in trials under the Act, it may be presumed that the accused has committed an offence unless the contrary is proved.
However, this reverse burden does not absolve the prosecution of its initial duty. The Supreme Court has consistently held that such presumptions are not automatic but are triggered only after the prosecution establishes a prima facie case through credible evidence.
Where the defence contests the recovery process and disputes the authorship of key documents, the presumption cannot be invoked to circumvent that burden. The accused must be afforded a reasonable opportunity to rebut the prosecution ’ s case through relevant evidence, including expert opinion.
24. The trial court’s reasoning that obtaining expert opinion
would delay the trial is also not tenable. Procedural convenience cannot override the need for fairness. The defence has specifically challenged the authenticity of critical prosecution documents. That challenge would remain untested without expert analysis, and resultantly, the adjudication would be incomplete. Procedural convenience cannot See paragraph 16, above.
Pir Mazharul Haq and others v. The State through Chief Ehtesab Commissioner
(PLD 2005 SC 63).
Criminal Appeal No. 221/2025
- 11 -
justify curtailing the accused ’ s right to lead evidence central to their defence. In Mrs. Kalyani Baskar vs Mrs. M. S. Sampoornam, (2007) 2 SCC 258, the SCI held that where the accused seeks to rebut the prosecution ’ s case using a document relied upon by the complainant (such as a cheque in a criminal proceeding), the court must not deny the opportunity to have that document examined by a handwriting expert. Refusing such a request deprives the accused of a meaningful chance to contest the prosecution ’ s case. A conviction rendered without affording the accused an opportunity to present material evidence amounts to a denial of a fair trial. A “ fair trial ” includes a fair and reasonable opportunity, guaranteed by law, to establish one ’ s innocence. The right to adduce evidence in support of the defence is fundamental, and its denial tantamounts to the denial of a fair trial.
Similarly, in Muhammad Tariq and others v. Asif Javed and another (2009 SCMR 264), the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that a party is entitled to every possible assistance from the court to prove its case.
Conclusion
25. The authenticity of the disputed documents is a material
issue in this case, and the defence is entitled to properly contest it. The trial court ’ s refusal to refer the documents for expert opinion, despite a genuine factual dispute, curtailed the Appellant ’ s right to a fair trial under Article 10A of the Constitution. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed and the Impugned Order dated 22.04.2025 is set aside. The Appellant’s application under Article 59 of the QSO is accepted.
( Raja Ghazanfar Ali Khan) Judge (Tariq Saleem Sheikh) Judge Naeem Announced in open court on ________________ Approved for reporting ( Raja Ghazanfar Ali Khan) Judge (Tariq Saleem Sheikh) Judge This principle was reaffirmed in T. Nagappa vs Y.R. Muralidhar (2008) 5 SCC 633.

Case: Crl. Appeal-Against Conviction-Anti-Rape Act 572-24 (MUHAMMAD AZHAR VS THE STATE ETC).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Crl. Appeal-Against Conviction-Anti-Rape Act 572-24. Title: Crl. Appeal-Against Conviction-Anti-Rape Act 572-24 (MUHAMMAD AZHAR VS THE STATE ETC). Official Ref: 2025LHC8707. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Tariq Saleem Sheikh. Judgment Date (as displayed): 02-09-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2025LHC8707.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 8 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Stereo. HCJDA 38
JUDGMENT SHEET
LAHORE HIGH COURT
BAHAWALPUR BENCH, BAHAWALPUR
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Criminal Appeal No. 572 / 20 2 4 Muhammad Azhar Vs. The State etc.
JUDGMENT
Date of hearing : 0 3 . 1 2 .202 5 For the Appellant : Syed Asim Ali Bukhari, Advocate.
For the State : Ch. Asghar Ali Gill , Deputy Prosecutor General.
For the Complainant:
Mr. Muhammad Rizwan Nadeem, Advocate, assisted by Rao Nasir Mehmood Khan, Advocate.
Tariq Saleem Sheikh, J. – This appeal is directed against the judgment dated 27 . 11 .202 4 delivered by the Additional Sessions Judge, Minchinabad , in a private complaint under section 376 PPC.
2. On 08 .1 0 .20 23 , K.B. ( PW ‑ 1 ), aged about 18 or 19 years
(the “ Complainant ” ), submitted a written application (Exh. PA) to Muhammad Manzoor/ASI (CW ‑ 4) at Police Station Minchinabad, District Bahawalnagar, for registration of an FIR. She stated that she was unmarried and lived with her parents. According to her, Muhammad Azhar had an evil eye on her, and when she complained to her father, Azhar became angry and harboured a grudge. On 29.09.2023, her father went to attend a gathering of Saeed Ahmad Shah at Double Phatak, Minchinabad, around 9:00 p.m., while her mother had gone to visit her sister. Her brother was also not at home as he worked in Lahore. She was alone that night when Azhar and Shahzad entered the house armed with weapons and , a t gunpoint, threatened to kill her. Azhar grabbed her by the arm and forcibly took her into a r oom, where he removed her trouser and committed rape. During this time, Shahzad stood guard. The Complainant ’ s cries for help attracted Ghulam Ali and Muhammad Taj (PW - 2) to the scene. Upon seeing them, the accused fled, leaving the Complainant in a naked state. Azhar even left behind his slippers .
Based on this application, FIR No. 741/2023 (Exh. CW - 4/A ) was registered.
Crl. Appeal No. 572 / 20 2 4
- 2 -
3. The case was initially investigated by Shehnaz Akhtar/ASI
(CW ‑ 7), who opined that the Appellant was involved in the alleged offence.
S he endorsed the Complainant ’ s allegations without conducting any meaningful scrutiny . N otably , she failed to collect physical evidence from the scene. Although the Complainant and Muhammad Taj (PW - 2) claimed that the Appellant left behind his slipper, it w as not taken into possession.
The investigation was then entrusted to Faraz Ahmad/SI (CW - 8), who undertook a more thorough probe. He visited the place of occurrence, recorded statements of both parties, and examined the documentary record.
He identified ma terial inconsistencies in the Complainant ’ s version and expressed reservations about the reliability of the initial findings. Based on his analysis, he concluded that the case appeared to be false. During the reinvestigation, DSP Gul Hassan (CW ‑ 9) also int errogated both parties. He found that a dispute existed between them regarding property and drainage , and that the Appellant had submitted an application to the police on
03.10.2023 regarding obstruction of passage. He further found that the
Appellant was present at the house of a relative at the relevant time and concluded that the FIR had been lodged as a counterblast. It is relevant that the Complainant did not challenge this reinvestigation during trial, and no material was brought on record to impeach the DSP ’ s findings. Dissatisfied with the recommendation for cancellation, the Complainant instituted a private complaint (Exh. PA /CS ) titled “ Kousar Bibi v. Muhammad Azhar etc. ”
4. The Additional Sessions Judge recorded cursory evidence
adduced by the Complainant and summoned Azhar and Shahzad for trial. On
10.07.2024, the Additional Sessions Judge indicted them. They pleaded not
guilty and claimed a trial.
5. To prove the charge, the prosecution produced two witnesses.
Complainant K.B. (PW - 1 ) and Muha mmad Taj (PW - 2) furnished the ocular account. The Complainant gave up PW Ghulam Ali being unnecessary.
Besides, the Additional Sessions Judge examined nine persons as Court Witnesses. Ayesha Bibi/ASI (CW - 1) testified about the transmission of sealed parcel s of swabs to the office of the Punjab Forensic Science Agency (PFSA). Muzammil Bibi 1255/LC (CW - 2) got the Complainant ’ s medical examination conducted at the THQ Hospital, Minchinabad. She was also a Crl. Appeal No. 572 / 20 2 4
- 3 -
marginal witness of Recovery Memo Exh. CW - 2/A. Muhammad Imran 465/HC (CW - 3) was the Moharrar of the police station and testified about handing over two sealed parcels of swabs to Ayesha Bibi/ASI (CW - 1) for onward transmission to the office of PFSA. He was a marginal witness of Recovery Memo Exh. CW - 4/A. Dr. Muhammad Usama Nadeem (CW - 5) and Dr. Hadia Sarfraz (CW - 6) provided the medical evidence. Shehnaz Akhtar/ASI (CW - 7), Faraz Ahmad/SI (CW - 8), and Gul Hassan/DSP (CW - 9) deposed regarding the different stage s of investigation. PWs Ghulam Ali and Muhammad Kashif 1326/C were given up being unnecessary. The public prosecutor closed the evidence after tendering the report of the PFSA Exh. PB.
6 . After the prosecution was through with its evidence, the trial cour t recorded the statement s of Azhar and Shahzad under section 342 Cr.P.C. and confronted them with the incriminating material that was brought against them during the trial. They refuted the same and professed innocence. Neither did they opt to make a statement on oath under Section 340(2) Cr.P.C. nor examine any witness in their evidence. However, Azhar tendered certified copies of the application moved to the SHO and the cancellation report as Exh. DB and Exh. DC. In reply to the question as to why this ca se has been registered against him and why the witnesses had deposed against him, Azhar stated:
“ PWs are closely inter se related and highly inimical toward me and my co - accused. Actually, the Complainant lodged this false and fabricated case against me on the grudge of purchasing property by me from the Complainant ’ s relative/Baradri. Moreover, drainage water from house of the complainant party comes in my land, due to this reason, verbal quarrel took place between us, after that the complainant party blocked our way.
In this regard, I moved an application to SHO police station. Due to this grudge, the complainant party conc octed a false story and get register this false case against me and my co - accused in connivance with each other.
In fact, false story of prosecution also proved be second Investigating Officer, Gul Hassan/DSP and my version approved right. During the cours e of investigation, DSP/second I.O rightly cancelled the Complainant ’ s case. Moreover, medical officer also negates the prosecution ’ s story. ” 7 . On the conclusion of the trial, vide judgment dated 27 . 11 .202 4 , the Additional Sessions Judge acquitted Shah zad , but convicted Azhar under section 37 6 PPC and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for ten years with a fine of Rs.200,000/ - and , in default thereof, to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months. He was also directed to pay Crl. Appeal No. 572 / 20 2 4
- 4 -
Rs. 3 00,000/ - as compensation under section 544 - A Cr.P.C. to the Complainant and , in default thereof, to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months. The benefit of section 382 - B Cr.P.C. was extended to him. Aggrieved, Muhammad Azhar (hereinafter referred to as the “ Appellant ” ) has filed Crl. Appeal No.572/2024.
8 . In support of this appeal, Syed Asim Ali Bukhari, Advocate, contended that the prosecution failed to prove the charge against the Appellant beyond a reasonable doubt . The Additional Sessions Judge failed to properly appraise the evidence, which had caused a grave miscarriage of justice. He argued that there was an unexplained delay of nine d ays in lodging the FIR, which cast serious doubt on the veracity of the prosecution ’ s version. According to the counsel, the case was false and motivated, having arisen out of pr evious enmity between the parties relating to a property transaction, a disput e over drainage water, and obstruction of the right of passage. It was submitted that the Appellant had m ade an application to the SHO regarding this dispute before the registration of the FIR, and that FIR No. 741/2023 (Exh. CW - 4/A ) and the subsequent pri vate complaint (Exh. PA /CS ) w ere counterblast. Mr. Bokhari further contended that the Complainant materially improved her version while filing the private complaint as compared to the FIR, and that both the Complainant (PW ‑ 1) and Muhammad Taj (PW ‑ 2) intro duced further improvements during trial, which were duly confronted and undermined their credibility. He further argued that the prosecution evidence was riddled with material contradictions and lacked independent corroboration. Moreover, the medical and f orensic evidence did not support the allegation of rape. C ounsel prayed for acceptance of the appeal and acquittal of the Appellant.
9 . The Deputy Prosecutor General , assisted by the Complainant ’ s counsel, controverted the above contentions. He contended that the prosecution had proved the charge against the Appellant through credible evidence. There was no discrepancy or contradiction from which he could derive any benefit. He prayed for the dismissal of t he Appellant ’ s appeal.
1 0 . Arguments heard. Record perused.
1 1 . According to the prosecution, on 29.09.2023 at 9:00 p.m., the Appellant ravished the Complainant in her house . The prosecution examined Crl. Appeal No. 572 / 20 2 4
- 5 -
Complainant K.B. (PW - 1) and Muhammad Taj (PW - 2 ) to pro ve the charge against the Appellant. At the very outset, we have noted that the Complainant reported the incident to the police through an application Exh. P A on 08 . 10 .20 23 , i.e. , nine days later , whereupon FIR No. 741 /20 23 (Ex h . CW - 4/A ) was registered. However, it is settled law that a delay in reporting cases of sexual violence does not automatically vitiate the prosecution ’ s case. Reference in this regard may be made to Mehboob Ahmed v. The State (1999 SCMR 1102), Irfan Ali Sher v. The State (PLD 2020 SC 295), Zahid and another v. The State (2020 SCMR 590), Mubeen Ahmed v. The State and another (PLD 2021 Islamabad 431), Zahid v. The State (2022 SCMR 50) and Imdad Ullah v. The State and another (PLD 2025 Lahore 512) . In the present case, t he Complainant (PW ‑ 1), in her cross ‑ examination, stated that after the alleged occurrence , she and her family approached the police, but “ they did not turn an ear to our submission ” . However, she did not specify when this alleged approach wa s made, nor did she explain why she failed to submit an application to senior police officers or the Ex - Officio Justice of Peace, or why no medico - legal examination was sought during the intervening period. Therefore, in the circumstances of this case, the delay remains unexplained.
1 2 . The Complainant is the key witness for the prosecution. It is well established that in cases of sexual offen c es, the victim ’ s testimony is crucial, and unless there are compelling reasons to seek corroboration, the courts s hould have no difficulty in solely relying on the victim ’ s testimony to convict the accused. However, this is contingent on the testimony being independent, unbiased, and straightforward enough to substantiate the accusation. If the court finds it difficul t to accept the victim ’ s account, it may seek corroboration from other evidence that supports her version. Reliance is placed on Muhammad Aslam v. The State and others (2023 SCMR 397) and Atta - ul - Mustafa v. The State and another (2023 SCMR 1698). I t is in this legal context that the Complainant ’ s testimony must now be assessed.
1 3 . The Complainant ’ s testimony in court largely followed the one set out in the private complaint (Exh. PA /CS ), but she introduced significant embellishments and was at variance with her earlier version given to the police. During cross - examination, she admitted that she had not included key facts in the private complaint. She further stated that she had earlier warned Crl. Appeal No. 572 / 20 2 4
- 6 -
the Appellant to desist from harassing her and that he committed the offence in revenge. However, she acknowledged that this was not recorded in Exh. PA . Similarly, she stated in her examination - in - chief that the eyewitnesses attempted to apprehend the accused , but they fled , brandishing their weapons. This , too , was not mentioned in the private complaint. When confronted with these discrepancies, she was unable to offer any explanation and merely stated that she had narrated the full facts to her counsel whe n he drafted the private complaint .
1 4 . The Complainant also conceded that there was a pending dispute between her family and the Appellant regarding the drainage of water from her house into a watercourse adjoining the Appellant ’ s land. She denied that water flowed directly into his property but admitted that her family used to sprinkle the drainage water in the street. She further acknowledged that her family had forbidden the Appellant from using the street in front of their hou se after a quarrel. When asked about an application allegedly moved by the Appellant to the police on 03.10.2023, she admitted knowledge of it and confirmed that tensions had intensified after it . These facts are extremely relevant. Where animosity is admi tted, the possibility of false implication cannot be ruled out lightly, and the court must seek independent corroboration.
1 5 . Muhammad Taj (PW ‑ 2) claimed that on the night of
29.09.2023, he was irrigating his fields when he heard cries and rushed to
the house of the Complainant ’ s father. According to him, he saw the Appellant committing rape with the Complainant while co - accused Shahzad stood guard. He stated that he was accompanied by Ghulam Ali and that they both attempted to apprehend the accused. The Appellant allegedly raised a lalkara and asked his co - accused to fire at them, upon which they stepped back . He further asserted that the accused had fled, leaving behind a slipper, and that the slipper was subsequently secured by the police .
1 6 . Muhammad Taj (PW ‑ 2) was confronted with his statement under section 161 Cr.P.C. (Exh. DA) during cross - examination. He conceded that several core elements of his deposition were not recorded in it . These included the claim that he witnessed the rape, the Appellant ’ s alleged threat to shoot, the fact that the victim was left naked, and the recovery of the slipper. His only explanation was that the police did not Crl. Appeal No. 572 / 20 2 4
- 7 -
record his version accurately. While such a claim may occasionally be true, it cannot override the settle d evidentiary rule that a witness who materially improves upon his initial statement must be viewed with caution.
17. The Complainant herself admitted during her cross -
examination that “ prior to the arrival of Taj PW my uncle Ghulam Muhammad (read Ghulam Ali) had approached the place of occurrence. Taj reached the place of occurrence after about 15 minutes of arrival of Ghulam Muhammad (read Ghulam Ali). ” This admission clearly shows that PW Taj was not the eyewitness. The prosecution should have produced Ghulam Ali, but he was given up. Under Illustration (g) of Article 129 of the Qanun - e - Shahadat, 1984, the presumption would be that if he had been produced, he would not have supported the prosecution. Reliance is placed on Lal Khan v. The State (2006 SCMR 1846).
1 8 . There is another point: if PWs Muhammad Taj , Ghulam Ali and 15 to 20 people , as claimed, ha d gathered at the crime scene, why did they not make any attempt to apprehend the Appellant and his co - accused. In incidents of this nature, it is commonly observed that the victim ’ s relatives or bystanders, without regard for their own safety, typically try to capture the culprit to prevent their escape and to hold them accountable for their misconduct. The prosecution has not given any satisfactory explanation in this regard.
19. During cross - examination, Muhammad Taj (PW ‑ 2) conceded
that he was a close relative of the Complainant. He described her as his niece and confirmed that his own residence is approximately one acre away from the scene of the occurrence. He stated that his house is situated inside his agricultural land and that he reached the Complainant ’ s house only after hearing the cries. When asked about the timing of the incident and his movements, he could not recall the time. He also a cknowledged that the Complainant ’ s sister Nusrat resided in the same house, but was not cited as a witness.
2 0 . For the reasons discussed above, the testimony of Muhammad Taj (PW - 2) is unreliable and cannot be used to corroborate the Complainant.
2 1 . It is significant that both the Complainant and Muhammad Taj (PW ‑ 2) stated that the Appellant left behind his slippers while fleeing the Crl. Appeal No. 572 / 20 2 4
- 8 -
scene. However, those were neither secured during the investigation nor produced in evidence at trial. Furthermore, the w eapon allegedly used to threaten the Complainant was never recovered.
2 2 . The Complainant was medically examined on 05.10.2023 by Dr. Hadia Sarfraz (CW 6), who initially noted that the hymen was ruptured and mild hyperemia was present at the introitus. H owever, she found no signs of injury, resistance , or trauma on any part of the body. In her final opinion, given after receipt of the PFSA report, she concluded that “ nothing can approve the act of sexual offence. ” She confirmed that the absence of seminal material, coupled with the lack of clinical findings, did not support the allegation. In her cross - examination, she clarified that hyperemia is not necessarily a sign of rape and may result from infection. She also admitted that there were no injuries on the hips, thighs, knees, or genitals of the victim.
According to the PFSA report (Exh. PB) , no seminal material was detected on the vaginal swabs or clothing of the victim. The Agency did not conduct DNA profiling due to this absence. Taken together, the m edical and forensic material does not corroborate the allegation of rape.
2 3 . It is a cardinal principle of criminal jurisprudence that the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt arising from any deficiency in the prosecution case. In this instance, the evidence as a whole does not meet the standard required to sustain a conviction under s ection 376 PPC. The finding of guilt recorded by the Additional Sessions Judge appears to be based on an inadequate appraisal of the evidence and cannot be maintained. Accordingly, we accept Crl. Appeal No.572/2024 and set aside the Appellant ’ s conviction and sentence. He shall be released from jail if not required to be detained in another case.
( Muhammad Amjad Rafiq) (Tariq Saleem Sheikh) Judge Judge Naeem

Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Writ Petition-Service-Suspension 4833-26. Title: Writ Petition-Service-Suspension 4833-26 (SHAHBAZ ANWAR VS PROVINCE OF PUNJAB ETC.). Form No:HCJD/C - 121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT
BAHAWALPUR BENCH BAHAWALPUR
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
W.P. No.4833 of 2026 Shahbaz Anwar Vs The Province of Punjab etc.
S.No. of order/ proceeding Date of order/ proceeding Order with signature of Judge, and that of parties or counsel, where necessary
24.08.2026 Mr. Muhammad Yaseen Ataal, Advocate for the
petitioner.
The petitioner has filed the instant petition under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan , 1973 (‘ the Constitution ’) seeking grant of the following prayers :
i. T he impugned Office Order No.SO ( E - III)WL / 3 - 3/2026 dated 16.08.2026, may kindly be set aside as illegal, without lawful authority, coram non judice , mala fide, arbitrary and violative of the PEEDA Act, 2006 and the principl e s of natural justice.
ii. I t is also humbly prayed that the operation of the impugned Office Order No.SO (E - III)WL / 3 - 3/2026 dated 16.08.2026, may kindly be suspended and the respondent No.1 may kindly be restrained for tak ing any further coercive/adverse action against the petitioner on the basis of the impugned proceedings.
iii. A ny other relief deemed just and proper in the circumstances of the case may kindly be granted.
2. The necessary facts, as set out in the petition and
relevant for the adjudication of the present controversy, are that the petitioner is an employee of Pakistan Museum of Natural History, Pakistan Science Foundation, Ministry of Science & Technology, Islamabad . Since 10.04.2023, the W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 petitioner has been with the respondent department and presently he is posted as the Curator, Bahawalpur Zoo, Bahawalpur, vide office order dated 19.08.2025 .
Petitioner was issued a letter dated 15.08.2026 seeking his explanation as to why he failed to report the death of 330 chicks of different species to respondent No.4/Deputy Chief Wildlife Ranger , Bahawalpur Region, Bahawalpur , which he had already replied . Subsequently, through o rder dated
16.08.2026, respondent No.1 has placed the petitioner
under suspension for a period of 90 days with immediate effect (the ‘ Impugned Order ’) under Section 6 of the Punjab Employees Efficiency, Discipline and Accountability Act, 2006 ( ‘ PEEDA or the Act’ ) that has been challenged in this Writ Petition.
3. The sole argument advanced by the petitioner is
that the Impugned Order has been passed by the B orrowing Organization without taking ‘ prior approval ’ f rom the L ending O rganization , which i s mandatory requirement under Section 15(1)(a) & (b) of the Act before placing a deputationist, like Petitioner, under suspension .
Consequently , the I mpugned O rder placing him under suspension is illegal, unlawful, without jurisdiction and void ab initio , hence, liable to be set aside. While addressing the maintainability of this Writ Petition, learned counsel contends that he is on deputation with the respondent department , so the bar contained in Article 212(2) of the Constitution does not apply to the p etitioner in view of Section 2(1)(b)( i ) of the Punjab Civil Servant s Act, 1974 whereby a person on deputation to the Province from the Federation or any other Province or A uthority does not fall in the definition of civil servant . A ccording to him, this W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 Writ Petition is maintainable. In these facts and circumstances, the Petitioner prays for the acceptance of this Writ Petition by setting aside the Impugned Order of his suspension.
4. At the very outset, learned counsel was confronted
qua the maintainability of this Writ Petition. Besides , he was inquired if he ha d any precedent to substantiate his submissions made at the bar. Learned counsel sought time to furnish case law in support of his petition and to refute the propositions of law expounded by this Court , which have duly been formulated and reproduced herein below.
Subsequently , the case was taken up at the end of the cause list after conclusion of all court work, whe n the learned counsel for the petitioner frankly conceded that he could not find any precedent favouring his p etition. However, he quibbled that he could also not find anything supporting the propositio n s of law as canvassed by this Court. He, therefore, insisted that Writ Petition is maintainable and the Impugned Order be set aside being illegal and without jurisdiction.
5. Be that as it may. A rguments have been heard at
great length and the record of this case has been perused with the able assistance of learned counsel for the petitioner.
6. For complete determination of the controversy
agitated in this petition , it is imperative to reproduce the following relevant provisions of PEED A :
Section 5. Initiation of proceedings. — (1) If on the basis of its own knowledge or information placed before it, the c ompetent authority is of the opinion that there are sufficient grounds for initiating proceedings against an employee under this Act, it shall either —
(a) p roceed itself against the accused by issuing a
show cause notice under Section 7 and , for W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 reasons to be recorded in writing, dispense with the enquiry :
Provided that no opportunity of showing cause or personal hearing shall be given where —
(i) the competent authority is satisfied
that in the interest of security of Pakistan or any part thereof, it is not expedient to give such an opportunity; or
(ii) an employee has entered into plea
bargain under any law for the time being in force or has been convicted of the charges of corruption which have led to a sentence of fine or imprisonment; or
(iii) an employee is involved in
subversive activities; or
(iv) it is not reasonably practicable to give
such an opportunity to the accused; or
(b) get an enquiry conducted into the charge or
charges against the accused, by appointing an enquiry officer or an enquiry committee, as the case may be, under Section 10 :
Provided that the competent authority shall dispense with the enquiry where --
(i) an employee has been convicted of
any offence other than corruption by a court of law under any law for the time being in force; or
(ii) an employee is or has been absent
from duty without prior approval of leave:
(Emphasis Added) Section 6 . Suspension. --- An employee against whom action is proposed to be initiated under Section 5 may be placed under suspension for a period of ninety days, if in the opinion of the competent authority, suspension is necessary or expedient, and if the period of suspension is not extended for a further period of ninety days within thirty days of the expiry of W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 initial period of suspension, the employee shall be deemed to be reinstated:
Provided that the continuation of the period of suspension shall require the prior approval of the competent authority for each period of extension .
(Emphasis Added) Section 15. Procedure of i nquiry against officers lent to other government s , etc. — (1) Where the services of an employee are transferred or lent to any other government , department, corporation, corporate body , autonomous body, authority, statutory body or any other organization or institution, hereinafter referred to as the borrowing organization, the competent authority for the post against which such employee is posted in the borrowing organization may --
(a) suspend him under Section 6; and
(b) initiate proceedings against him under this Act :
Provided that the borrowing organization shall forthwith inform the lending organization of the circumstances leading to the order of his suspension and the commencement of the proceedings :
Provide d further that the borrowing organization shall obtain prior approval of the lending organization before taking any action under this Act, against an employee holding a post in Basic Pay Scale 17 or above.” (Emphasis Added)
7. Perusal of the above basic provisions of law
reveals the scheme of PEEDA, where under the Competent Authority has two options available to it , if and when it is of the opinion that there are sufficient grounds for initiating proceedings against an employee under PEEDA . First , the Competent Authority can proceed itself against the employee under Section 7 of the Act by dispensing with the regular enquiry OR Second the Competent Authority can get an enquiry conducted by appointing an W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 Enquiry Officer or Enquiry Committee (as the case may be) under Section 10 ibid . It would not be out of the place to briefly mention that there are procedural safeguards in built by the legislature and also those introduced by the Courts, from time to time, for structuring this discretionary power of the Competent Authority and guiding as to when a regular enquiry can be dispensed with or under what circumstances a regular enquiry is mandatory as well as for safeguarding and protecting the rights of the accused employee, but since they are not the subject matter of the instant writ petition, therefore, they are not being referred to herein below.
8. The first set of questions that need to be answered
are whether the Competent Authority under the Act has the power or authority to place an employee under suspension. At what point in time, this power can be exercised by the Competent Authority ? Are there any pre - requisites or condition precedent for exercise of power of suspension? Answers to all these questions are found in Section 6 of the Act. This power of the Competent Authority to issue a suspension order against an employee is derived fr om Section 6 ibid and is exercised if the suspension is necessary or expedient in the opinion of the Competent Authority a t the time when the Competent Authority is proposing or contemplating to initiate any action against an employee under PEED A . Except this rider , there is no other pre - requisite for exercise of such power by the Competent Authority f or issuance of a suspension order . It is c lear as day that t he act of placing an employee under suspension precedes the initiation of proceedings under Section 5 of the Act and the passing of any adverse order in consequence thereof. By the bare reading of this Section , one is W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 constrained to note that it is a stand - alone provision containing no reference, neither express nor implied, to any other s ection of the Act. In Section 6, there is no concept of seeking permission, prior or later, for placing the name of an employee under suspension for 90 days. Section 6, unlike Section 15, does not have any controlling proviso, which makes it obligatory upon the Competent A uthority to seek prior approval of the L ending O rganization. Section 6 i s self contained s ection of law without having any pre requisites for exercise of such power, except the opinion of the Competent Authority that suspension is necessary or expedient. This exercise of power under Section 6 has not been made subject to or subservient to Section 15 ibid .
9. When interpreting different , apparently
incongruent, provisions of a statu t e, the first and the foremost duty of the Court is to read , explain and apply th ose provisions harmoniously in such a manner that no part of law made by the legislature is made redundant , rendered surplus or made otiose .
By following this cardinal principle of law , when these two provisions of the Act , Section s 6 & 15 , are p ut in juxtaposition and read harmoniously , it cumulatively follows that under Section 6 the Competent Authority, before initiation of any action as stated in Section 5, can place an employee under suspension for 90 days , if in the opinion of Competent Authority suspension is necessary or expedient.
However, in case the employee in question has been lent, transferred or sent on deputation from one government to other government, department, corporation or authority etc., as explained in S ection Aftab Shahban Mirani and others vs. Muhammad Ibrahim and others ( PLD 2008 SC 779 ) Lucky Cement Ltd. vs. Commissioner Income Tax, Zone Companies, Circle - 5, Peshawar ( 2015 SCMR 1494 ) , Haji tooti and another vs. Federal Board of Revenue, Islamabad and others ( 2023 SCMR 1980 ) W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 15, then the Competent Authority in the Borrowing Organization can (i) suspend him under Section 6, meaning thereby that the procedure as set out in Section 6 ibid would apply i.e. if in opinion of the Competent Authority suspension is necessary or expedient ; and (ii) initiate proceedings against him under the Act i.e. either of the two actions stated in Section 5 ibid would take place . T he only extra step, added in the case of an employee on deputation, is that the Borrowing Organization shall forthwith inform the Lending Organization of the circumstances leading to the order of suspension and commencement of proceedings . To reach to this conclusion, t his Court has noted that the word s ‘prior approval ’ ha ve only been used in the 2 nd proviso to Section 15 stating to the effect that prior approval of the Lending Organization is required by the Borrowing Organization before taking any action under this Act. 2 nd proviso does not supersede, overrides or control the 1 st proviso. Rather these two provisos address two different subjects. 1 st proviso casts obligation on the Competent Authority about rel a ying the information to the Lending Organization qua the circumstances leading to the issuance or passing of the order of suspension and the fact the proceedings under PEEDA have been initiated or commenced or begun against a deputationist employee. It is a Post f acto obligation communicating of what has already transpired. On the other hand, 2 nd proviso imposes a duty on the Competent Authority to obtain prior approval of the Lending Organization before taking any action under this Act against an employee on deputation holding a post in BPS - 17 or above. This is an ex - ante or before the event obligation . Legislature’s conscious W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 omission of word s ‘prior consent ’ in the 1 st proviso to Section 15 ibid , is instructive of legislature’s true intent that no prior approval, advance permission or previous consent of the Lending Organization is needed for placing an employee under suspension and for initiation of enquiry against a deputation ist. Had the legislature wanted so, it would have said so in the st proviso.
10. Besides i t is also trite law that while
interpreting a statute, the heading or title of s ection or provision is also useful internal aid or tool for interpretation . The title / heading of Section 1 5 reads ‘ Procedure of enquiry against officers lent to other governments, etc. ’ , so prima facie Section 15 only relates to the procedure of e nquiry not the procedure of suspension. As opined earlier, the initiation of enquiry has a separate and distinct meaning in the Act whereas the passing of a suspension order is not an enquiry, it is just preface to an Enquiry . Nowhere in Section 15 , the passing of an order of suspension been clogged or initiation of enquiry has been blocked. 2 nd proviso to Section 15 relates to taking of action under this Act , which , prima facie , means order(s) that is to be passed by the Competent Authority on receipt of the report from the Enquiry Officer or Committee (as the case may be) under S ection 13 or where enquiry has been dispensed with, before passing an order under Section 7.
11. In view of the foregoing facts and the
applicable law, this Court is of the firm view that for the suspension order issued under Section 6, there is , as such , no requirement of seeking prior approval or consent of the Lending Organization by the Mst. Rehmat Begum vs. Mehfooz Ahmed and others ( PLD 2024 SC 1108 ) W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 Borrowing Organization. All that the Borrowing Organization is required to do is to forthwith inform the Lending Organization of the circumstances leading to the order of the suspension and the commencement of the proceedings. In other words, what has led to the suspension of the officer concerned and beginning of an enquiry that is to be conveyed to the Lending Organi z ation by the Borrowing Organi z ation.
12. At this juncture, it would not be out of the
place to refer to, although in passing, the meaning and purport of phrase ‘ forthwith ’ as used in 1 st proviso to the Section 15. According to Black’s Law Dictionary (12th Edition), edited by Bryan A. Garner on 05 th April, 2024 and published by Thomson Reuters, the term “forthwith” is defined as follows :
1. Without unnecessary delay. 2. Within a
reasonable time under the circumstances; with all convenient dispatch. The U.S. Supreme Court has stated that “(t)here are many cases which turn upon the question whether a person was not too late in complying wit h a requirement that a thing must be done forthwith.” Dickerman v. Northern Trust Co., 176 U.S 181, 193, 20 S. Ct. 311, 315 (1900).
That was an anomalous case in which it was argued that the person required to do something forthwith did it too quickly. The Court held there was no good argument that the actor had “acted with too great haste.” Id. The court cited with approval, however, a lexicographic authority stating that the word “has a relative meaning, and will imply a longer or shorter period, according to the nature of the thing to be done.” Id. Cf.
IMMEDIATELY; PROMPTLY.
( Emphasis Added ) On the other hand, t he word ‘ forthwith ’ in its ordinary parlance , as opposed to legal, means immediately, instantly, at once and promptly. Reference is made to Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary of Current English (10th Edition) by A.S. Hornby published by W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 Oxford University Press in the year 2020 , where term “forthwith” means immediately; at once . This term ‘forthwith’ has come under judicial scrutiny more than once, mostly, in the context of Order XVII Rule 3 CPC, where this term has been interpreted as ‘within reasonable time’ , without delay and was not equated with words ‘at once’ . So the judicial consensus is that the word ‘forthwith’ does not mean ‘immediately’ but ‘with all reasonable celerity’ . It has a relative meaning depending on the nature of the thing to be done. If the legislature wanted the C ompetent A uthority to straightaway communicate the circumstances leading to the order of suspension and commencement of proceedings from Borrowing Organization to the Lending Organization, it would have used the words like ‘ immediately ’ or ‘ promptly ’ that imply urgency . The use of word ‘ forthwith ’ leaves the Competent Authority with reasonable time to do the needful. What is reasonable time is a fact specific question that will invariably fluctuate on case to case basis as it has, rightly, been pointed out in the above quoted definition from the Black’s Law Dictionary.
13. At this juncture, after having addressed the
merits of arguments and submissions made by the learned counsel for the Petitioner, it would not be out of the place to recall that the Petitioner has only challenged the order whereby he has been suspended.
To comment upon with the nature and effect of an order of suspension, let us begin by remembering that an order of placing an employee under suspension has never been termed, treated and accepted as a penalty Maulvi Abdul Aziz Khan vs. Mst. Shah Jahan Begum and 2 others ( PLD 1971 SC 434 ) Lutfullah Virk vs. Muhammad Aslam Sheikh ( PLD 2024 SC 887 ) Muhammad Aslam vs. Nazir Ahmed ( 2008 SCMR 942 ) Inspector General, Frontier Corps, Baluchistan, Quetta vs. The Superintendent, Central Jail, Mach, & 3 others ( 1990 MLD 2258 ) W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 by the superior courts. Suspension is a temporary measure, effect whereof is to merely stop an official from performing his duties for the time being.
Suspended employee continues to hold his office, receive pay or subsistence allowance, as the case may be, but is restrained from performing the actual functions of his office during the period of his suspension. It is not permanent removal from service, which order may only be passed upon completion of the enquiry. Thus, an order of suspension pending a departmental enquiry is not a penalty as it does not violat e any legal right vesting in the suspended officer. Seminal judgment by a Full Bench of Hon’ble Supreme Court on this score is Mian Muhammad Hayat v. The Province of West Pakistan reported as ( PLD 1964 SC 321 ) that was later approvingly followed in the case of Abdul Khaliq Bangash v. The Secretary, Government of West Pakistan, Co - Operative Department, Lahore & 2 others ( 1970 SCMR 103 ), wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court, after referring to the above exposition of law, was pleased to make the following important observation :
“The petitioner continues to remain in service in spite of his suspension and if he is ultimately exonerated in the enquiry, he can be re - instated and paid all the arrears of his salary that may be found due to him”.
Subsequently, the above principle of law was followed in the case titled The Divisional Superintendent, Pakistan Railways, Lahore v.
Muhammad Halim through Legal Representatives and others ( PLD 2000 SC 55 ).
14. As a necessary corollary of the discussion in
the foregoing paragraph s , since this writ petition is aimed against an interim order of suspension that is W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 not a penalty under the service laws, so this writ petition against an order of interlocutory nature is premature, non - maintainable and liable to be dismissed on this score alone. In this respect, r eliance is placed on case s titled Muhammad Sadiq Khokhar v. Engineer - in - Chief, Pakistan Army, GHQ and another reported as ( 1981 PLC (C.S.) 123 ) , Professor Dr. Zafar Iqbal Chaudhry v. Province of Punjab and others reported as ( 2017 PLC (C.S.) 583 ) , Ahmed Raza Sultan etc. v. Senior Member Board of Revenue reported as ( PLJ 2014 Lahore 265 ) and Muhammad Amin Mughal v. Secretary Local Government and Rural Development Department/Chairman Punjab Local G overnment Board, Government of the Punjab, Civil Secretariat, Lahore and 4 others reported as ( 2002 PLC (C.S . ) 816 ) , where this Court was pleased to observe as follows :
“The suspension order or the holding of inquiry is step towards passing of the final order and no writ petition is maintainable against interim order. As if the inquiry the petitioner is found guilty of the charge and thereupon some action is taken against him, the petitioner has the remedy to file an appeal before the Service Tribunal. The High Court cannot interfere in such like interim orders in view of dictum laid down by the Karachi High Court in Abdul Bari's case (PLD 1981 Karachi 290, 303 and 309), M uhammad Mahmood Ali's case (1984 CLC 142 at page 145) and Nazir Ahmad Sheikh's case (1998 PLC (C.S.) page 607).
In the light of the above discussion the writ petition is not maintainable and the same is dismissed.
15. Since the petitioner has only challenged the
order of his suspension under Section 6 of the Act , whereas the Competent Authority is yet to initiate proceedings against him either through a regular W.P. No. 4833 - 2026 enquiry under Section 10 or by dispensing with it under Section 7 , let alone conclude the same , and the petitioner has other remed ies available to him under the hierarchy of the Act as and when the enquiry proceeds, therefore, i n the view of the aforementioned legal position , this petition is held to be premature, devoid of any merit and not deserving any interference by this Court at this stage. Hence , this Writ Petition is dismissed in limine .
(Muhammad Usman Ghani Rashid Cheema) Judge Approved for reporting Judge
*M.Rizwan*
