Stereo HCJDA 38
JUDGMENT SHEET
LAHORE HIGH COURT LAHORE
( JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT)
Writ Petition No.33829 of 2026 Lahore Electric Supply Company (LESCO) through its Company Secretary V ersus Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Ministry of Information and Broadcast, and others Petitioner by:- Barrister Muhammad Umer Riaz, Rana Rehan, Barrister Ch. Abubakar, Ch.
Haseeb Tariq and Dahhar Hussain, Advocates with Ch. Imtiaz Ilahi, C.O.
LESCO.
Respondents by : Mr. Nauman Khalid, Assistant Attorney General for the Federation of Pakistan with Laeeq Ahmad Bajwa, Deputy Director Ministry of Information & Broadcasting, Islamabad.
Barrister Mian Adnan Tariq and Muhammad Sheraz Sultan, Advocates for respondent No.3 (Ateeq Ahmad Khan) .
Date of hearing: - 24.06.2026
JUDGMENT
RAHEEL KAMRAN, J.: Th rough this petition filed under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 ( “the Constitution” ), the petitioner has called in question the order dated
04.05.2026 passed by the Chief Information Commissioner, Camp
Office, Lahore, whereby Appeal No.5240 - 12/25 filed by respondent No.3 Ateeq Ahmad Khan, was allowed and the petitioner - Lahor e Electric
-2-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 Supply Company ( “LESCO” ), was directed to furnish to the applicant as well as the Information Commission the information sought by him within ten days.
2 . The controversy emanates from an information request made by respondent No.3 Ateeq Ahmad Khan seeking certified copies of the minutes of the 144 th HR Meeting held on 27.02.2023 and the 261 st Board of Directors Meeting held on 04.05.2025 concerning the promotion of Muhammad Ramzan Butt, who, at the relevant time, was serving as an officer of LESCO. The requisite information was not furnished by LESCO, whereafter respondent No.3 preferred an appeal before the Pakistan Information Commission under section 17 of the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017 ( “the Act of 2017” ). The petitioner- LESCO contested the appeal by filing a written reply, principally maintaining that the requested record was excluded from public record under section 7(a), (b), (c) and (g) of the Act of 2017 and was otherwise exempt from disclosure under section 16 thereof. The Commission, however, allowed the appeal through the impugned order, holding that the final decision regarding the promotion had already been taken and, consequently, the minutes of the meetings no longer enjoyed the exclusion contemplated by section 7(b) of the Act of 2017. Hence, these petitions.
3 . Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the impugned order is contrary to the statutory scheme governing the right of access to information. It was submitted that the minutes sought by respondent No.3 relate to the promotion and service matters of identifiable employees and contain, inter alia , information from their service records, ACRs, remarks and observations, disclosure of which would invade their personal privacy and is therefore excluded under section 7(g) of the Act of 2017. Learned counsel further contended that the fact that a final decision had been taken by LESCO did not render the deliberations leading to such decision open to disclosure, as sections 7(a), (b) and (c) expressly protect noting on files, minutes of meetings and intermediary opinions or recommendations subject to a final decision by the public
-3-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 body. According to learned counsel, section 6(d) makes final orders and decisions public record, but does not convert the minutes or deliberations preceding such decision into public record. Reliance was also placed upon section 16(1)(c), relating to invasion of personal privacy, and section 16(1)(i)(iii), which exempts information the disclosure of which is likely to undermine the deliberative process in a public body by inhibiting the free and frank provision of advice or exchange of views.
Learned counsel also referred to the judgment of the Islamabad High Court reported as “ Pakistan Telecommunication Authority v. Pakistan Information Commission ” (2024 YLR 929 Islamabad) , contending that the protection available to deliberative material does not cease merely because a final decision has subsequently been made. It was further argued that the Information Commission had acted beyond its lawful mandate by keeping the matter for implementation after passing the impugned order and directing LESCO to furnish the information within a specified period. To substantiate his contentions, learned counsel has also placed reliance on cases reported as “Muhammad Nawaz v. Additional District and Sessions Judge and others” (PLD 2023 SC 461) , “Akhtar Ali v.
Muhammad Shoaib Ahmad” (2011 CLD 1 Lahore) and “Shahbaz Akmal Jandran v. Province of Punjab through Director General, Excise and Taxation, Lahore and another” (PLD 2025 Lahore 649) . Learned counsel also took the Court through case law from Indian jurisdiction such as “ Girish Ramchandra Deshpande v. Central Information Commissioner and others ” (2013) 1 Supreme Court Cases 212 and “ R.K. Jain v. Union of India and another ” (2013) 14 Supreme Court Cases 794 .
4 . Learned Assistant Attorney General for the Federation, as well as learned counsel appearing for respondents No.2 and 3, supported the impugned order. Learned counsel for respondent No.3 submitted that section 7(b) does not confer an absolute or perpetual exclusion upon minutes of meetings; rather, the exclusion is expressly made subject to a final decision by the public body. Since the decision concerning the promotion in question had already been finalized and acted upon, the statutory condition attached to the exclusion no longer remained
-4-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 operative. It was further contended that the information sought relates to the functioning and decision-making of a public body concerning an official matter and cannot be withheld merely by invoking personal privacy. Learned counsel maintained that the petitioner ’ s reliance upon the exemptions contained in section 16 of the Act of 2017 was equally misconceived and that the impugned order correctly applied the statutory scheme. The objection regarding the Commission ’ s direction for furnishing the information within a specified period was also controverted on the ground that the Commission is expressly empowered under the Act of 2017 to order disclosure and ensure implementation of its decisions.
5 . I have heard learned counsel for the parties and examined the record as well as the relevant provisions of the Right of Access to Information Act, 2017 (“the Act of 2017”).
6 . Before examining the specific objections raised by the petitioner, it would be appropriate to appreciate the constitutional and statutory scheme governing the right of access to information. Article 19A of the Constitution provides the foundational guarantee in the following terms: — “19A . Every citizen shall have the right to have access to information in all matters of public importance subject to regulation and reasonable restrictions imposed by law. ” The language of Article 19A makes access to information a constitutionally guaranteed right of every citizen, albeit subject to such regulation and reasonable restrictions as may be imposed by law. The constitutional guarantee, therefore, does not render every piece of information held by a public body unconditionally accessible; at the same time, any restriction upon the exercise of the right must have the sanction of law and remain within the parameters prescribed by the law. The right is intended to facilitate access to information concerning matters of public importance and thereby promote transparency and accountability in the functioning of public bodies.
-5-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 7 . The Right of Access to Information Act, 2017 was enacted to give effect to the aforesaid constitutional guarantee. The legislative purpose underlying the enactment is expressly set out in its Preamble, which, insofar as relevant, provides as follows: — “WHEREAS Government believes in transparency and the right to have access to information to ensure that the people of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan have improved access to records held by public authorities and promote the purposes of making the Government more accountable to its people, of improving participation by the people in public affairs, of reducing corruption and inefficiency in Government, of promoting sound economic growth, or promoting good governance and respect for human rights; AND WHEREAS it is expedient to provide for a law which gives effect to the fundamental right of access to information, as guaranteed under Article 19A of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan and international law, whereby everyone shall have the right to have access to all information held by public bodies subject only to reasonable restrictions imposed by law and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto;” The Preamble thus makes it vivid that the legislation is not merely procedural in character; rather, it constitutes the statutory mechanism for giving effect to a fundamental right and is designed to advance transparency, governmental accountability, public participation, good governance and respect for human rights. The expr ession “subject only to reasonable restrictions imposed by law” is also significant, as it reflects the constitutional balance between the citizen ’ s right of access and the legitimate restrictions which the Legislature may prescribe.
8 . The general rule governing access to information is then expressly enacted in section 3 of the Act of 2017, which provides: — “ 3. Right to have access to information not to be denied .---(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, no applicant shall be denied access to information or record held by a public body.
(2) This Act shall be interpreted so as to advance its purposes as set out in the preamble and to---
-6-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026
(a) promote the right of access to information; and
(b) facilitate and encourage promptly the
disclosure of the information at the lowest and reasonable cost.” Section 3 thus establishes the basic statutory rule that access to information or record held by a public body shall not be denied, while expressly making that right subject to the provisions of the Act itself.
More importantly, subsection (2) prescribes the interpretive approach to be adopted in applying the Act: its provisions are to be construed so as to advance the purposes stated in the Preamble, promote the right of access to information and facilitate its prompt disclosure. Consequently, the exclusions and exemptions contained elsewhere in the Act cannot be construed independently of this overarching legislative policy. They must be applied according to their language, purpose and statutory limits, without either defeating the right of access or enlarging an exception beyond the scope intended by the Legislature.
9 . Against the above constitutional and statutory framework, the controversy may now be examined with reference to the particular record sought by respondent No.3 and the exclusions and exemptions relied upon by the petitioner. The first question which arises is whether the minutes of the meetings in question continued to enjoy the exclusion contemplated by section 7(b) of the Act after the decision concerning the promotion had been finally taken by the public body.
10 . The petitioner does not dispute that the requested minutes are in possession of the LESCO, which being a body falling within the defi nition of “public body” contained in section 2(ix) of the Act of 2017, is consequently subject to the obligations imposed by the Act. The controversy, therefore, is not whether the petitioner-LESCO is amenable to the Act, but whether the particular record sought by respondent No.3 falls within any subsisting exclusion under section 7 or exemption under section 16 thereof.
11 . To determine whether the minutes sought by respondent No.3 are presently accessible under the Act, it is necessary to examine
-7-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 the statutory scheme governing what constitutes public record and in particular, the treatment accorded by the Legislature to minutes of meetings and other deliberative material. Section 6, subject to the exclusions contained in section 7, declares specified categories of record to be public record. The relevant provisions read as follows: — “ 6.Declaration of public record .---Subject to the provisions of section 7, the following record of all public bodies is hereby declared to be the public record, namely;---
(a) - - - - -
(b) - - - - -
(c) - - - - -
(d) Final orders and decisions, including decisions relating to
members of public- - - ” The Legislature has, however, expressly qualified the operation of section 6 by enacting section 7, which provides, insofar as relevant to the controversy before this Court: — “ 7. Exclusion of certain record .---Nothing contained in section 6 shall apply to the following record of all public bodies, namely:---
(a) Noting on the files, subject to a final decision by the
public body;
(b) Minutes of meetings, subject to a final decision by the
public body;
(c) Any intermediary opinion or recommendation, subject to a
final decision by the public body;
(d) - - - - -
(e) - - - - -
(f) - - - - -
(g) Record relating to the personal privacy of any individual-
- - - ”
12 . The statutory language reproduced above is significant.
Section 6 declares, inter alia , final orders and decisions to be public record, but does so expressly subject to section 7. Section 7, in turn, creates specific exclusions from the operation of section 6. Insofar as minutes of meetings are concerned, however, the Legislature has not created an absolute or perpetual exclusion; rather, it has expressly made the exclusion “subject to a final decision by the public body”. The same qualification has been employed in respect of noting on files under clause
(a) and intermediary opinion or recommendation under clause (c). The
-8-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 duration of the exclusion is, therefore, controlled by the statutory condition expressly attached to it.
13 . In the present case, the minutes sought by respondent No.3 concern the consideration and decision regarding promotion of Muhammad Ramzan Butt. The Information Commission examined the record and found that the decision concerning his promotion had already been finalized and acted upon through the office order referred to in the impugned order. Once the public body had taken its final decision on the matter which was the subject of the deliberations, the statutory condition upon which the exclusion under section 7(b) rests ceased to operate. The petitioner ’ s contention that the minutes continue to remain excluded merely because they contain deliberations which preceded the final decision would render the words “subject to a final decision by the public body” redundant, which cannot be attributed to the Legislature. Reliance in this regard may be made to the cases of “Messrs Pakistan Television Corporation Limited v. Commissioner Inland Revenue (Legal), LTU, Islamabad and others” (2017 SCMR 1136), “ Searle IV Solution (Pvt.) Ltd.
and others v. Federation of Pakistan and others” ( 2018 SCMR 1444) , “ Justice Shaukat Aziz Siddiqui and others v. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Law and Justice, Islamabad and others” (PLD 2018 SC 538) and “ Directorate of Intelligence and Investigation - FBR, through Director and others v. Taj International (Pvt.) Ltd. and others” (2025 PTD 1270 ) .
14 . The submission that section 6(d) makes only the final decision public and consequently preserves the confidentiality of the deliberations leading thereto even after the decision has been made, does not withstand the plain language of section 7(b). Sections 6 and 7 have to be read harmoniously. Section 6 identifies the record declared to be public record, whereas section 7 specifies the record which, notwithstanding section 6, remains excluded and, in the case of minutes of meetings, expressly makes such exclusion subject to a final decision by the public body. To accept the petitioner’ s interpretation would be to render the qualifying words “subject to a final decision by the public body” practically meaningless. Such an interpretation cannot be adop ted
-9-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 when the Legislature has consciously attached a condition to the exclusion.
15 . The petitioner, however, seeks to sustain withholding of the requested record independently of section 7 by invoking the exemptions contained in section 16 of the Act. It is, therefore, necessary to examine the relevant provisions thereof. Section 16, insofar as material to the controversy, provides: — “ 16. Information exempt from disclosure .---(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act,---
(a) A public body shall not be required to disclose exempt
information,---
(i) provided that where only part of a record or the
information falls within the scope of the exceptions provided for in this Act, that part shall be severed and the residual record or information shall be provided to the applicant; and
(ii) - - - - -
(b) - - - - -
(c) Information is exempt if its disclosure under this Act
would involve invasion of privacy of an indentifiable individual, including a deceased individual, other than the applicant. This exception shall not apply where----
(i) - - - - -
(ii) - - - - -
(iii) the third party is or was an official of a public body
and the information relates to his functions as a public official;
(d) - - - - -
(e) - - - - -
(f) - - - - -
(g) - - - - -
(h) - - - - -
(i) Information may be exempt if its disclosure is likely to---
(i) cause prejudice to the effective formulation or
development of government policy;
(ii) frustrate the success of a policy, by premature
disclosure of that policy;
(iii) undermine the deliberative process in a public body
or inhibiting the free and frank provision of advice or exchange of views------ ” The above provisions make it clear that the exemptions contemplated by section 16 operate on a basis distinct from the conditional exclusion
-10-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 contained in section 7(b). While the latter ceases to operate upon the occurrence of the statutory event specified therein, i.e., a final decision by the public body, a claim under section 16 must independently satisfy the particular statutory requirements of the exemption invoked. The petitioner’ s reliance upon the deliberative nature of the meetings may, therefore, be examined on that footing.
16 . Section 16(1)(h)(iii) permits exemption where disclosure is likely to undermine the deliberative process in a public body by inhibiting the free and frank provision of advice or exchange of views.
The exemption, therefore, is not attracted merely because a record contains deliberations; the statutory test as to the likelihood of the specified prejudice must also be satisfied. In the present case, the petitioner has not demonstrated how disclosure of the minutes, after the decision concerning the promotion had been finalized and acted upon, is likely to undermine any continuing deliberative process. A general apprehension that disclosure of deliberations may inhibit frankness in future decision-making, without demonstrating the statutory prejudice contemplated by section 16(1)(h)(iii), cannot by itself justify withholding the record.
17 . The plea founded upon personal privacy also does not justify withholding the entire record. The petitioner has principally relied upon section 7(g), which excludes from public record “record relating to the personal privacy of any individual”, as well as section 16(1)(c), which permits exemption in respect of information the disclosure of which would constitute an unwarranted invasion of the privacy of an identifiable individual. The mere fact that the minutes concern an identifiable officer and relate to his promotion does not, however, make the entire record a thing of his personal privacy. The information sought concerns the decision-making process of a public body in relation to promotion to a public office and, in that sense, bears upon an official matter. Moreover, section 16(1)(c) itself recognizes an exception where the third party is or was an official of a public body and the information relates to his functions as a public official. The petitioner has not
-11-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 established that disclosure of the requested minutes, as a whole, would constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy within the meaning of the Act.
18 . This Court is conscious that the minutes of a meeting may, depending upon their contents, contain information which is genuinely personal or otherwise falls within a statutory exemption. However, that possibility cannot justify withholding the entire record. The Legislature has expressly provided in section 16(1)(a)(i) that where only part of a record falls within the scope of an exception, that part shall be severed and the residual record or information shall be provided to the applicant.
Therefore, if any specific portion of the minutes is demonstrably protected by a valid statutory exemption, the same may be severed in accordance with law; such possibility, however, does not revive the otherwise expired exclusion under section 7(b) or entitle the petitioner- LESCO to withhold the minutes in their entirety.
19 . The argument that respondent No.3 failed to disclose any public interest or reasons for seeking the information is also without substance. Section 11(5) of the Act of 2017 expressly provides that in no case shall an applicant be required to provide reasons for his request. The petitioner, therefore, could not lawfully require respondent No.3 to disclose the purpose or justification for which he sought the requested record. The statutory right is thus not made contingent upon the applicant first establishing his personal interest or demonstrating a particular purpose for seeking information.
20 . The petitioner’ s further objection that the Information Commission lacked jurisdiction to keep the matter for implementation is also misconceived. The statutory scheme itself contemplates implementation of decisions of the Commission. Section 19(2)(e) assigns to the Commission the responsibility to ensure implementation of the Act and the record to be made public under it, while section 20(1)(e) empowers the Commission to order a public body to disclose information to an applicant or to take such other reasonable measures as it may deem necessary to remedy any failure to implement the Act. The direction
-12-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 requiring LESCO to furnish the information within a specified period was, therefore, consequential to the decision allowing the appeal and fell within the statutory framework governing enforcement of the Commission’s decision. The mere fact that the matter was fixed for implementation could not, by itself, render the impugned order without lawful authority.
21 . It is also pertinent that, in an appeal under section 17, the public body bears the burden of proof to establish that it acted in accordance with the Act. The petitioner, despite raising several objections, has not established that the requested minutes fall within any subsisting exclusion under section 7 or satisfy the requirements of any exemption under section 16 so as to justify their complete withholding.
The impugned order, therefore, cannot be characterized as having been passed in disregard of the statutory scheme. On the contrary, the Information Commission correctly appreciated that the final decision having already been taken, the conditional exclusion contained in section 7(b) was no longer available to the petitioner-LESCO.
22 . The authorities relied upon by learned counsel for the petitioner do not alter the above conclusion, as the questions considered therein are materially distinguishable from the precise controversy arising in the present case. In the case of Pakistan Telecommunication Authority , the Islamabad High Court was concerned with a request for t he minutes of a meeting relating to a licence and while noticing section 7 of the Act of 2017, observed that the protection afforded to minutes was subject to a final decision by the public body and directed that the final decision be furnished. The judgme nt, however, did not examine the precise question whether the statutory exclusion of minutes under section 7(b) continues after the public body has taken the final decision to which the statutory qualification expressly relates. The said judgment, therefor e, does not lay down a contrary principle so as to displace the interpretation which follows from the plain language of section 7(b). Likewise, the cases of Muhammad Nawaz , Girish Ramchandra Deshpande and R.K. Jain principally concern the protection of per sonal information, service
-13-
W.P. No.33829 of 2026 records, ACRs and the right to privacy, rather than the duration or operation of the conditional exclusion relating to minutes of meetings under section 7(b) of the Act of 2017. The judgment in the case of Shahbaz Akmal Jandran likewise dealt with the scope of the right to information vis-à-vis the privacy of individuals under the Punjab Transparency and Right to Information Act, 2013 and not with the statutory consequence of the words “subject to a final decision by the public bo dy” occurring in section 7(b) of the federal Act of 2017. The remaining authorities cited by learned counsel also do not address the specific statutory question presently before the Court and, therefore, cannot be regarded as controlling the interpretation of section 7(b) in the facts of the present case.
23 . For the foregoing reasons, this Court finds no illegality, jurisdictional defect or misreading of the provisions of the Act of 2017 in the impugned order dated 04.05.2026. The petitioner ’ s objections seek to sustain exclusions and exemptions beyond the scope prescribed by the Legislature and, therefore, do not warrant interference in constitutional jurisdiction. Consequently, the petition in hand is dismissed. There shall, however, be no order as to costs.
(RAHEEL KAMRAN)
JUDGE
Announced in the Open Court on 01.09.2026.
JUDGE
Approved for reporting.
JUDGE
Azhar*

Case: Service 44193/22 (Muhammad Akram Vs Province of Punjab etc).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Service 44193/22. Title: Service 44193/22 (Muhammad Akram Vs Province of Punjab etc). Official Ref: 2026LHC5401. Author Judge: Justice Ms. Shireen Imran. Judgment Date (as displayed): 01-09-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5401.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 8 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Stereo . H C J D A 38
JUDGMENT SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT , LAHORE
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Writ Petition No. 44193 of 20 2 2 .
Muhammad Akram Vs. Province of Punjab & others
JUDGMENT
Date of hearing: 31 .08.2026 .
Petitioner by: Mr. Kashif Ali Chaudhry , Advocate.
Respondents by: Mr. Qamar Zaman Qureshi, Additional Advocate General.
SHIREEN IMRAN, J : Through this petition, petitioner has challenged order dated 24.06.2022 (impugned order) passed by the Divisional Forest Officer, Faisalabad Forest Division, Faisalabad (respondent No.4) , whereby earlier order dated 30.06.2021, qua his retirement on medical grounds , with effect from 18.06.2021 , along with encashment of 365 days in lieu of Leave Preparatory to Retirement (LPR), was withdrawn.
2. W hile assailing impugned order , dated 24.06.2022 passed by
respondent No.4 , learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the petitioner was initially retired from service on medical grounds vide order dated 30.06.2021, with effect from 18.06.2021, after having been declared medically incapacitated in Category “B”. It is submitted that pursuant to the said order, a vested and legitimate right had accrued in favour of the petitioner with regard to his retirement W.P . No. 44193 of 202 2 . 2 benefits, including the benefit of LPR and encashment of 365 days’ leave in lieu thereof. Learned counsel further submits that order dated
30.06.2021 was valid and operative and had attained legal efficacy
much prior to the subsequent clarification issued by the Finance Department, Government of the P u njab , dated 24.08.2021 , after which department passed impugned order , dated 24.06.2022. According to learned counsel, once the petitioner had already been retired and the consequential benefits had accrued to him, same could not subsequently be withdrawn or nullified retrospectively , merely on the basis of a later clarification . It is further argued that the impugned order has been passed in clear violation of the principles of natural justice as before withdrawing the earlier retirement order, petitioner was neither issued any show cause notice nor afforded any opportunity of hearing. Learned counsel has also questioned the competence and authority of the department to pass the impugned order on the basis of recommendations allegedly made by the Finance Department. It is contended that the question relating to the mode and manner of petitioner’s retirement falls within the domain of the Services & General Administration Department ( S&GAD ) and that the Finance Department has no substantive role in determining whether the petitioner was liable to be retired on medical grounds or otherwise , which was duly proceeded . Learned counsel , thus submits that impugned order , dated 24.06.2022 is without lawful justification, contrary to the settled principles of natural justice and liable to be set aside, especially when no prior notice or opportunity of hearing was W.P . No. 44193 of 202 2 . 3 afforded to the petitioner before taking any adverse action against him.
3. Conversely, learned Law Officer, while supporting the
impugned order submits that the authority empowered to pass an order can also recall /withdraw the same , t hus no exception can be taken to the impugned order, which has been passed on the basis of clarification dated 24.08.2021 issued by the Finance Department .
Further submits that the impugned order has caused no prejudice to the petitioner as only the nature of his reti rement has been changed.
Adds that if the argument of learned counsel for the petitioner qua his retirement falls within the domain of S&GAD is accepted as correct , then S&GAD having not been impleaded as party, th is petition is liable to be dismissed for non - joinder of necessary party.
4. Arguments heard. Record perused.
5. Admittedly, petitioner stood retired from government service
w.e.f. 18.06.2021 vide order dated 30.06.2021 passed by respondent No.4 on medical grounds. Later on, the said order w as withdrawn vide order dated 24.06.2022 , about one year of passing of earlier order on the basis of clarification issued by the Finance Department dated
24.08.2021 , which reads as under: -
“ In order to discourage the tendency of getting declaration of incapacitated /invitation on the veige of retirement as a matter of routine the benefit in question may not be allowed beyond the date of when the LPR is rule. ” W.P . No. 44193 of 202 2 . 4 After passing of order dated 30.06.2021, reasonable rights accrued in favour of the petitioner , which cannot be withdrawn later on. There is no cavil with the fact that an authority having power to pass an order can also recall /withdraw the same but the same is subject to the condition that no decisive step has been taken. So far as the case in hand is concerned, after passing of order dated 30.06.2021, certain decisive steps , including appointment of son of the petitioner under Rule 17 - A of the Punjab Civil Servants (Appointment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 1974 were taken , consequently the rights accrued in favour of the petitioner cannot be withdrawn in view of the principle of locus poenitentiae . The basic judgment on the principle of locus poenitentiae has been rendered in the case of Pakistan, through the Secretary, Ministry of Finance v. Muhammad Himayatullah Farukhi ( PLD 1969 SC 407 ), wherein the H o n ’ ble Supreme Court of Pakistan elaborated the scope of said principle as under: - “ There can hardly be any dispute with the rule as laid down, in these cases that apart from the provisions of section 21 of the General Clauses Act, locus poenitentiae, i.e., the power of receding till a decisive step is taken, is available to the Government or the relevant authorities. In fact, the existence of such a power is necessary in the case of all authorities empowered to pass orders to retrace the wrong steps taken by them. The authority that has the power to make an order has also the power to undo it. But this is subject to the exception that where the order has taken legal effect, and in pursuance thereof certain rights have been created in favour of any individual, such an order cannot be withdrawn or rescinded to the detriment of those rights. ” W.P . No. 44193 of 202 2 . 5
6. Further, the aforesaid view was followed by the Hon’ble
Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case s of Pakistan Railways through Chief Executive Officer/ Senior General Manager, Lahore and another v. Muhammad Aslam ( 2024 SCMR 97 ) and Shams Ur Rehman v.
Military Accountant General, Rawalpindi and another ( 2020 SCMR 188 ) . In the latter case, the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan has inter alia observed as under: - “… The case would, thus, be governed by the principle of locus poenitentiae and, in our view, the Department cannot retrace the steps already taken and lawfully acted upon by the petitioner." Foregoing the above discussion, after passing of order da ted
30.06.2021, certain decisive steps were taken and valuable rights
accrued including appointment of son of the petitioner , which cannot be taken back in view of the principle of locus poenitentiae .
7. Another important aspect of the matter is that whether the
clarification of the Finance Department can operate retrospectively.
The impugned clarification does not mention its retrospective or prospective effect and it is trite law that any policy/rules does not operative retrospectively until and unless the same has been given retrospective effect by the Legislator. Reliance in this regard can be made to the case of Secretary to Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Communication and Works Department, Civil Secretariat, Peshawar and others v. Inayat Ullah and another ( 2026 SCMR 558 ) , in which it was held as under: - “The fundamental principle governing the application of amended rules is that such amendment W.P . No. 44193 of 202 2 . 6 operates prospectively unless a contrary intimation is manifestly evident from the statute.” Likewise, in the case o f Controller General of Accounts, Government of Pakistan, Islamabad and others v. Abdul Waheed and others ( 2023 SCMR 111 ) , it was held that : - “ 6.***** The insertion or deletion of any provision in the rules or the law, if merely procedural in nature would apply retrospectively but not if it affects substantial rights which already stood accrued at the time when the un - amended rule or provision was in vogue …. ” As there was no mention of retrospective application of the subject clarification, the same was to operate prospectively.
8. Interestingly, before withdrawal of order dated 30.06.2021,
neither an opportunity of hearing was granted to the petitioner nor any show cause notice whatsoever in that regard was ever issued , which approach being against the principle of audi alteram partem cannot be authenticated. No one should be condemned unheard would be enough to vitiate even the most solemn proceedings. This principle has originated from the Islamic principles of justice. Reliance in this regard is placed in the case of Hyderabad Chamber of Commerce and Industry v. M/o Commerce Govt. of Pakistan. ( PLD 2024 Islamabad 353 ). Likewise, in the case of Central Development Authority through Chairman, Islamabad and others v. Shabir Hussain and others ( 2022 SCMR 627 ), it was held that: - “7***** Another shortcoming and unlawfulness is that no prior notice or justification was even shown in the cancellation letter which is flagrant violation of well settled principle of natural justice which is W.P . No. 44193 of 202 2 . 7 firmly established and deep rooted in the judicial conscience to be entrenched and embedded in every decision making function either judicial, quasi judicial or administrative which is a fundamental rule of law that no decision must be taken affecting the right of any person without first being informed of the case and affording an ample opportunity of defence…”
9. The requirement of hearing the parties is not an empty
formality , rather it constitutes an essential component of the principles of natural justice, due process and fair trial. The authority proposing to take an adverse action , must before reaching any conclusion against the person concerned , disclose the substance of the allegations and provide an effective opportunity to submit a response or defence.
10. Where an adverse or punitive action is taken without
following the prescribed procedure of law or without affording the person concerned a n adequate opportunity of hearing, such action is rendered vulnerable to judicial scrutiny. The violation of the principles of natural justice strikes at the very root of the proceeding s and any consequential order founded upon such defective proceedings cannot ordinarily be sustained merely on the ground that the authority otherwise possessed jurisdiction to take action.
1 1 . The requirement of observance of due process assumes greater significance where the proposed action carries civil consequences, affects the rights, status, employment, benefits, reputation or other legitimate interests of a person. An authority cannot bypa ss the requirement of providing a reasonable opportunity of defence and thereafter seek to validate the action on the basis of W.P . No. 44193 of 202 2 . 8 subsequent explanations or proceedings. The safeguards of natural justice are intended to prevent arbitrary exercise of power and to ensure fairness, transparency and impartiality in administrative and disciplinary decision - making. Reliance in this regard is placed o n the case of The Province of Sindh through Chief Secretary Government of Sindh and others v. Raj Kumar Lohana and others ( 2026 SCMR 278 ).
1 2 . In view of the foregoing discussion and having examined the matter in the light of the applicable law and the principles of natural justice, this Court is of the considered opinion that impugned order dated 24.06.2022 cannot be sustained i n the eye of law , having been passed without due observance of requisite procedure . Consequently, this petition is allowed and impugned order dated 24.06.2022 is set aside . As a result, order dated 30.06.2021 shall hold the field.
(SHIREEN IMRAN)
JUDGE
Approved for reporting.
JUDGE
U mar

VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 11 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Stereo. H C J D A 38.
Judgment Sheet
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT AT LAHORE.
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
W.P. No. of 46868 of 2026 Muhammad Aslam
VERSUS
Addl. Sessions Judge/Ex-Officio Justice of Peace etc.
JUDGEMENT
Date of Hearing: 27.8.2026 Petitioner by: Muhammad Afzaal, Advocate along with petitioner Muhammad Aslam.
Respondent by: Mr. Anwaar Hussain, Assistant Advocate General for respondent Nos.2 to 4, 9 and 10 along with Waheed, Station House Officer.
Mian H. M. Asim Mehmood and Malik Muhammad Atif, Advocates along with respondent Nos.5 and 6 and Mst. Hina Aslam (daughter of the petitioner) under the escort of Sana Nawaz 32407/C. Ms. Samra Yar Muhammad, Law Officer Child Protection and Welfare Bureau, Lahore MUNAWAR IQBAL DUGGAL, J. Through the instant constitutional petition under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 ( hereinafter to be referred as “the Constitution” ), the petitioner has called in question the legality and propriety of the order dated 06.08.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge/Ex-Officio Justice of Peace, Kasur, whereby the application filed by the petitioner under Sections 22-A and 22-B of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 ( hereinafter to be called as “Cr.P.C.”) seeking registration of a criminal case against respondent No.5/Muhammad Luqman and others was dismissed.
W.P. No.46868 of 2026 -2-
2. The facts necessary for adjudication of the instant petition are that
the daughter of the petitioner, namely Mst. Hina Aslam, went missing, whereupon the petitioner got registered FIR No.1121/2026 dated
20.05.2026 under Section 365-B of Pakistan Penal Code (Act XLV of
1860), ( he reinafter to be referred as “PPC” ), at Police Station Sattokatla,
Lahore, alleging that his daughter had been abducted by unknown persons for the purpose of illicit intercourse. During the course of investigation, however, Mst. Hina Aslam appeared before the learned Area Magistrate and got her statement recorded under Section 164, Cr.P.C., on 29.05.2026, wherein she stated that she had neither been abducted nor subjected to zina by anyone and that she had contracted marriage with respondent No.5/Muhammad Luqman of her own free will and consent. She further stated that her father had lodged a false and frivolous FIR and expressed no objection to its cancellation. On the basis of the aforesaid statement, the said FIR is stated to be under the process of cancellation.
3. Subsequently, upon coming to know about the alleged Nikah of his
daughter, the petitioner approached the Municipal Committee, Kasur, for verification of the Nikahnama. The Municipal Committee, Kasur, vide letter dated 23.06.2026, informed the petitioner that no record of the alleged Nikah was available in its office. The petitioner thereafter approached the Station House Officer, Police Station B-Division, Kasur, seeking registration of an FIR against respondent Nos. 5 to 9, alleging, inter alia, that a marriage had been solemnized with a minor girl in violation of the Punjab Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2026 and that the purported Nikahnama was forged and fictitious. As no action was taken on the application, the petitioner invoked the jurisdiction of the learned Ex-Officio Justice of Peace under Sections 22-A and 22-B, Cr.P.C.
4. The learned Additional Sessions Judge/Ex-Officio Justice of Peace,
Kasur, after hearing the parties and perusing the police report, dismissed the application vide order dated 06.08.2026 and suggested the petitioner W.P. No.46868 of 2026 -3to approach the Investigating Officer for addition of the relevant offences in FIR No.1121/2026. Hence, the instant petition.
5. Upon preliminary examination of the material available on record,
this Court, vide order dated 17.08.2026, directed respondents Nos.3 and 4 to produce Mst. Hina Aslam before the Court. In compliance therewith, she was produced before the Court. Respondent No.5/Muhammad Luqman and his father, namely Muhammad Ilyas, also appeared along with their learned counsel.
6. Learned counsel for respondent Nos.5 and 6 was confronted with
the Child Registration Certificate (CRC No.10818545) available on the record, issued by NADRA on 09.03.2017, wherein the date of birth of Mst. Hina Aslam is recorded as 01.03.2011. Thus, according to the document available on record, she was approximately fifteen years and two months old on the date of the alleged Nikah, i.e. 18.05.2026. Learned counsel for the respondents could not produce any contemporaneous and reliable document establishing that Mst. Hina Aslam had attained the age of eighteen years on the date of the alleged marriage. The respondents, however, submitted that she had represented herself to be nineteen years of age and that, relying upon her representation, the marriage was solemnized. Reliance was also placed upon her statement recorded under Section 164, Cr.P.C., wherein she stated that she was above eighteen years of age and had contracted marriage with respondent No.5 of her own free will and consent.
7. Learned counsel for petitioner has reiterated his earlier contentions
recorded in the interim order dated 17.08.2026. For sake of completion and brevity, the same are reproduced for ease of reference as under:
“ Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the petitioner’s daughter, namely Hina Aslam, is about fifteen years of age and is W.P. No.46868 of 2026 -4stated to have contracted marriage with respondent No.5. In this regard, learned counsel refers to the Nikahnama, according to which the marriage was solemnized on 18.05.2026 by a Nikah Khawan within the territorial limits of District Kasur. Learned counsel further relies upon a birth certificate issued by NADRA, wherein Hina Aslam is mentioned at Serial No.7 and her date of birth is recorded as 01.03.2011.
Learned counsel further submits that the petitioner approached the Municipal Committee, Kasur, for verification of the aforesaid Nikahnama , whereupon the Chief Officer, Municipal Committee, Kasur, vide report dated 23.06.2026, reported that no record of the said Nikah was available in the office. He further contends that the alleged Nikah was solemnized and the purported Nikahnama was prepared in violation of the provisions of the Punjab Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2026. The petitioner thereafter approached the Station House Officer, Police Station B-Division, Kasur, seeking registration of an FIR, but to no avail, whereupon he was constrained to invoke the jurisdiction of the learned Ex-Officio Justice of Peace under Sections 22-A & 22-B, Cr.P.C ”
8. Heard, the record perused.
9. At the outset, it is necessary to appreciate the legal effect of the
Punjab Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2026 published in official gazette on 11 th of May, 2026 with its commencement at once ( hereinafter to be called as “the Act , 2026 ”) . The Act defines a “child” as a person, male or female, who is under eighteen years of age, and defines “child marriage” to include an act of Nikah or solemnization of marriage where either of the contracting parties is a child. The statute further prohibits registration of a child marriage and creates penal consequences for an adult who contracts marriage with a child. More significantly, Section 5 declares that any form of cohabitation, before attainment of eighteen years of age, with or without consent, resulting from a child marriage, constitutes “child abuse” under the Act , ibid. The statutory scheme thus represents a material departure from the earlier legislative framework.
W.P. No.46868 of 2026 -5-
10. It is worthy to note that quite recently the Federal Constitutional
Court, in “ Shahbaz Masih v. Additional Sessions Judge, Lahore & others ” , F.C.P.L.A. No.536 of 2025, decided on 03.02.2026, considered the earlier legal regime applicable in Punjab and, after examining the judgments in “ Mst. Bakhshi v. Bashir Ahmad ” (PLD 1970 SC 323) and “ Mauj Ali v. Syed Safdar Hussain Shah ” (1970 SCMR 437), observed that the Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929, as then applicable, criminalized the solemnization of child marriage but did not expressly declare such marriage void or voidable. The Federal Constitutional Court consequently held that, in the absence of an express statutory provision invalidating the marriage, its validity was not affected merely by reason of the contravention of the penal provisions.
11. The aforesaid principle, however, may not be applicable to the
controversy before this Court. The alleged Nikah in the instant case was solemnized on 18.05.2026, i.e. after the enactment and coming into force of the Act, 2026. The new enactment has materially altered the statutory landscape by prescribing eighteen years as the minimum age for both male and female persons, criminalizing an adult's marriage with a child, and, most importantly, expressly characterizing cohabitation with a child arising from such marriage as “child abuse”, irrespective of consent. The present case must, therefore, be examined in the light of the law actually in force on the date of the alleged occurrence.
12. The Court is conscious that the question of age may, in an
appropriate case, require determination upon evidence and that constitutional jurisdiction is ordinarily not the forum for conclusively adjudicating disputed questions of fact. Nevertheless, at the stage of considering an application under Sections 22-A and 22-B, Cr.P.C., the Court is not required to finally determine the guilt or innocence of the proposed accused. The limited question is whether the information furnished to the police discloses commission of a cognizable offence W.P. No.46868 of 2026 -6warranting registration and investigation. The evidentiary value of the documents and veracity of the defence version are matters to be examined during investigation and, where necessary, determined at trial.
13. In the present case, the CRC issued by NADRA in 2017 records the
date of birth of Mst. Hina Aslam as 01.03.2011. The alleged Nikah took place on 18.05.2026. Prima facie, therefore, she was below eighteen years of age on the date of the alleged marriage. The respondents have not produced, at this stage, any equally reliable contemporaneous documentary material rebutting the said entry. Consequently, the material placed before the Court gives rise to a reasonable basis for treating the alleged occurrence as falling within the statutory framework of the Punjab Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2026.
14. The statement of Mst. Hina Aslam recorded under Section 164,
Cr.P.C., undoubtedly constitutes relevant material and her views cannot be disregarded merely because she is a child. At the same time, under the express statutory scheme introduced by Section 13 of the Act, 2026, her purported consent cannot, by itself, be treated as determinative of her residence, custody or protection where the Court is confronted with a prima facie case of child marriage and the consequent risk of child abuse.
The statute requires the Court to make an independent assessment of her safety, welfare and best interests.
15. This approach is also consistent with the contemporary
jurisprudence concerning the welfare of child, according to which the wishes of a child capable of forming an intelligent preference are a relevant consideration, but the paramount consideration remains the welfare and best interests of the child. The Supreme Court has emphasized that custody proceedings require a holistic assessment of the child's circumstances and that the best interests of the child, rather than W.P. No.46868 of 2026 -7the competing interests of the parents or other adults, remain the controlling consideration.
16. It is, therefore, not necessary for this Court, at the present stage, to
pronounce conclusively upon the validity or otherwise of the alleged Nikah. Such a determination may involve questions of fact and law which are appropriately left to the competent forum. What is material for the present proceedings is that there exists prima facie material disclosing an occurrence which, if established, may attract penal consequences under the Act, 2026. The police cannot decline to set the criminal law into motion merely because the alleged child has expressed willingness to reside with the adult contracting party.
17. The next question is whether registration of a separate FIR is barred
by the legal principle laid down in “ Mst. Sughran Bibi v. The State ” (PLD 2018 SC 595). The answer depends upon the nature of the occurrence alleged in the proposed FIR. The law laid down in Sughran Bibi is that a second FIR is not permissible merely to place before the police another version of the same occurrence already reported. At the same time, the investigating agency remains under a duty to investigate all aspects of the occurrence and all versions brought before it.
18. The facts of the instant case, however, prima facie disclose a
distinction between the occurrence forming the subject matter of FIR No.1121/2026 and the subsequent allegations now made by the petitioner.
The earlier FIR concerned the alleged abduction of Mst. Hina Aslam by unknown persons. The present complaint concerns the subsequent discovery and alleged solemnization of a child marriage on 18.05.2026, the alleged preparation/use of a purported Nikahnama and the alleged involvement of persons in solemnizing or facilitating the marriage of a child. The latter allegations are not merely a counter-version of the W.P. No.46868 of 2026 -8alleged abduction; rather, they relate to an identifiable statutory offence arising from a distinct transaction.
19. The distinction is further reinforced by the fact that the alleged
Nikah came to light during the investigation of the earlier case and that the Municipal Committee, Kasur, has reportedly stated that no corresponding record of the alleged Nikah exists in its office. Whether the Nikahnama is forged, whether the marriage was in fact solemnized, who participated in or facilitated it, and what offences, if any, were committed are matters requiring investigation. They cannot appropriately be foreclosed at the threshold by treating the complaint as merely a second version of the earlier allegation of abduction.
20. The principle enunciated in Sughran Bibi , therefore, does not, in the
peculiar circumstances of the instant case, furnish a lawful basis for refusing to entertain the petitioner's complaint altogether. The police shall, however, ensure that the investigation of the earlier FIR and the newly reported occurrence is investigated objectively and strictly in accordance with law, without any no duplication of proceedings or prejudice to any person.
21. It follows that the learned Additional Sessions Judge/Ex-Officio
Justice of Peace fell in error in declining to exercise jurisdiction on the sole premise that the petitioner should seek addition of offences in the earlier FIR. The impugned order has failed to take into consideration the subsequent and distinct allegation of child marriage and the statutory consequences flowing from the Act, 2026.
22. For what has been discussed above, the instant petition is allowed .
The impugned order dated 06.08.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge/Ex-Officio Justice of Peace, Kasur, is set aside.
Respondent No.4/SHO, Police Station B-Division, Kasur, is directed to proceed in accordance with Section 154, Cr.P.C., on the basis of the W.P. No.46868 of 2026 -9petitioner's application and, if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence, record the same and proceed with investigation strictly in accordance with law. Needless to observe that the registration of the case shall not be construed as an expression of opinion regarding the guilt of any person.
23. As regards the custody and protection of Mst. Hina Aslam, the
Court cannot lose sight of the fact that, prima facie, she is below eighteen years of age and that the alleged marriage was solemnized after the coming into force of the Act, 2026. Therefore, despite her statement that she wishes to go with respondent No.5, Mst. Hina Aslam cannot be allowed to go with respondent No. 5/Muhammad Luqman as any form of cohabitation, before attaining the age of eighteen years, with or without consent has been treated as child abuse under Section 5 of the Act, 2026 and punishment of seven years has been prescribed for any person who induces, forces, persuades, entices or coerces, a child bride to engage in child abuse. For ease of ready reference, the section 5 the Act, ibid is reproduced as under:- “5. Child abuse and its punishment- (1) Any form of cohabitation, before attaining the age of eighteen years, with or without consent, resulting from a child marriage shall be the child abuse under the Act.
(2) Any person who induces, forces, persuades, entices or coerces any child bride or child groom to engage in child abuse or commits child abuse shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years but shall not be less than five years and with fine which shall not be less than one million rupees.”
24. Section 13 of the Act, 2026 expressly requires the best interests of
the child to remain a primary consideration and contemplates immediate protective measures, including safe shelter and supervised custody where required. The statutory scheme further provides that the child's purported W.P. No.46868 of 2026 -10consent, by itself, shall not determine questions of custody or residence in proceedings under the Act, ibid.
25. At the same time, the Court must not disregard the expressed
wishes and dignity of Mst. Hina Aslam. Her statement before this Court indicates that she does not wish to return to her parental home and apprehends ill-treatment at the hands of family members. In these circumstances, neither immediate restoration to the parental home nor handing over of her custody to respondent No.5 would adequately address the competing considerations of safety, welfare, protection and her expressed wishes.
26. Consequently, and purely as a protective measure, Mst. Hina Aslam
shall remain in the safe custody of the Child Protection & Welfare Bureau, Government of the Punjab, through its duly authorized officer, pending further orders of the competent forum. The Bureau shall ensure her safety, dignity, education, psychological well-being and access to appropriate counselling and shall not permit any person to exercise coercion or undue influence upon her.
27. The learned Guardian Judge, Lahore, shall have jurisdiction to
determine the question of custody in appropriate proceedings under the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, upon an independent assessment of the welfare and best interests of the minor. Nothing contained in this judgment shall prejudice the determination of the competent Court regarding permanent custody, guardianship or the legal status of the alleged Nikah.
28. In view of the apprehension expressed by Mst. Hina Aslam
regarding her safety at her parental home, her interaction with her parents shall, for the present, be arranged only in a supervised environment by an authorized officer of the Child Protection & Welfare Bureau. Likewise, if W.P. No.46868 of 2026 -11- Mst. Hina Aslam expresses a desire to meet respondent No.5 or his parents, such interaction may be arranged by the Bureau in a safe and supervised environment, subject to the assessment of the child's welfare and without permitting any private or unsupervised meeting.
29. The Child Protection & Welfare Bureau shall submit a brief report
before this Court regarding the safety and welfare of Mst. Hina Aslam after an interval of four weeks and thereafter as and when required by this Court.
30. Before parting with the judgment, it is clarified that the
observations made herein are confined to the prima facie assessment necessary for deciding the petition under Article 199 of the Constitution and Sections 22-A and 22-B, Cr.P.C. The Investigating Officer shall conduct an impartial investigation without being influenced by any observation contained herein, and the competent criminal Court shall decide the matter strictly in accordance with the evidence and law.
31. The instant Writ Petition is allowed in the above terms.
( MUNAWAR IQBAL DUGGAL)
JUDGE
ANNOUNCED IN OPEN COURT on 31.08.2026.
JUDGE.
APPROVED FOR REPORTNG.
JUDGE.
Nadeem *

Case: Crl. Misc.-Post-arrest Bail 1313-B-26 (MUHAMMAD FAZIL VS STATE ETC ).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Crl. Misc.-Post-arrest Bail 1313-B-26. Title: Crl. Misc.-Post-arrest Bail 1313-B-26 (MUHAMMAD FAZIL VS STATE ETC ). Official Ref: 2026LHC5385. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Syed Farhad Ali Shah. Judgment Date (as displayed): 31-08-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5385.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 5 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Form No. HCJD/C-121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT
MULTAN BENCH MULTAN
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Crl. Misc. No.1313-B of 2026 Muhammad Fazil. Vs. The State etc.
Sr. No. of order / proceeding s Date of order / proceeding s Order with signature s of Judge, and that of p arties o r counsel, where necessary
24.08.2026 Mr. Muhammad Usman Sharif Khosa, Advocate for
petitioner.
Mr. Muhammad Abdul Wadood, Additional Prosecutor General with Muhammad Younas SHO.
Mr. Khizar Ali Khan Wadani, Advocate for complainant.
Muhammad Fazil (petitioner) seeks post arrest bail in case FIR No.175 dated 17.04.2015, offences under sections 302, 324, 365-B, 496-A, 337-A(i), 337-F(i), 148, 149, 201 P.P.C. registered at Police Station Saddar, District, Dera Ghazi Khan.
2. Succinctly stated, the case of prosecution as unfolded
from the crime report is to the effect that on 17.04.2015 Muhammad Sajjad (complainant) along with his family members was present at his home; that in the meanwhile, at about 04:30 p.m., Muhammad Fazil (petitioner) along with 14 co-accused while riding 05 motorcycles and armed with their respective weapons reached there and started indiscriminate firing; that Muhammad Fazil (petitioner) exhorted to teach a lesson to complainant party and fired a shot from his pistol which hit Muhammad Riaz on his right shin; that thereafter Muhammad Ismail (co-accused) inflicted six successive hatchet blows on the head and face of Muhammad Riaz; that co-accused Hanif and Masso inflicted injuries to complainant with their respective weapons and while leaving the place of occurrence the accused forcibly abducted Mst. Zulaikha Bibi Crl. Misc. No.1313-B of 2026 wife of sabir Hussain and took her to some unknown place, hence, this case.
3. Arguments heard. Record perused.
4. It is discernible from the tentative review of record that
instant case is arising out of an incident having occurred on 17 . 04 .201 5 at about 04 :30 p .m. during which one Muhammad Riaz lost his life aft er the receipt of multiple injuries, besides that complainant also endured traumas inflicted by the assailants . The burden of committing this crime was pointed towards a bunch of perpetrators comprising upon 1 5 persons including Muhammad Fazil (petitioner).
5. It is informed by learned law officer that the petitioner
applied for his post arrest bail on merits before Honorable Supreme Court of Pakistan, which was dismissed as withdrawn vide order dated 29.04.2025 passed in Crl. P.L.A. No.259/2025. The grant of instant post arrest bail is solely urged on the ground of delay in the conclusion of trial in terms of third proviso of Section 497 Cr.P.C., thus I intend to restrict myself only to this aspect. It is observed from the record that admittedly the petitioner initially remained fugitive from the process of law and was apprehended after a long and noticeable abscondance on 02.01.2024, whereas, the report under section 173 Cr.P.C. to the extent of petitioner was submitted in the Court on 07.05.2024. In pursuance of aforementioned police report, the petitioner was indicted by the trial court on 24.06.2024 and subsequent thereto the case was fixed for the recording of prosecution evidence. It is noticed that though approximately a period of 02-years, 07months and 23-days has elapsed but till now not even the statement of a single prosecution witness is recorded. I have carefully scanned the report submitted by learned trial judge and record of the case, from which it evinces that the pending proceedings were delayed mainly due to the reasons attributed Crl. Misc. No.1313-B of 2026 to the prosecution and complainant. According to record, the file of the case was placed before the trial court for the recording of prosecution evidence on 04.07.2024, 15.07.2024,
15.08.2024, 29.08.2024, 11.09.2024, 26.09.2024, 10.10.2024,
22.10.2024, 05.11.2024, 19.11.2024, 03.12.2024, 16.12.2024,
04.01.2025, 14.01.2025, 27.01.2025, 10.02.2025, 24.02.2025,
11.03.2025, 24.03.2025, 12.04.2025, 26.04.2025, 19.05.2025,
14.06.2025, 03.07.2025, 16.07.2025, 04.08.2025, 09.09.2025,
24.09.2025, 11.10.2025, 11.11.2025, 12.12.2025, 08.01.2026
and 09.02.2026. Out of the aforementioned dates, on
15.07.2024, accused was not produced from jail, whereas, on
15.08.2024, 29.08.2024, 11.09.2024 and 26.09.2024 the
presiding officer was not available. On 10.02.2025, 24.02.2025 and 11.03.2025 the case was adjourned on the joint request of both the sides and except the aforesaid dates no adjournment was sought on behalf of accused/petitioner.
6. The 3
rd proviso of section 497 Cr.P.C. unfolds that if the trial of a person accused of having committed an offence punishable with death is not concluded within two years of his detention, he becomes entitled to the concession of post-arrest bail. He can be held disentitled from the relief of post arrest bail under 3 rd proviso of section 497 Cr.P.C. only if it is demonstrated that such delay has been caused or occasioned by an act or omission of the accused seeking bail or by any other person acting on his behalf. It manifests from the report of the learned trial court and record that the delay in the conclusion of trial can in no manner be attributed to the petitioner or any person acting on his behalf. This is envisaged in the 4 th proviso that the benefit of 3 rd proviso of section 497 Cr.P.C will not be extended to a person, who is convicted in an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life or is a hardened, desperate or dangerous criminal or a person, who is involved in an act of terrorism punishable with death or Crl. Misc. No.1313-B of 2026 imprisonment for life. Needless to mention here that in order to bring the case of an accused within the 4 th proviso of section 497 Cr.P.C., the prosecution has to display its cards in reference to some material. In the instant case, no such stance is found present on the record, which may bring the case of the petitioner within the 4 th proviso of section 497 Cr.P.C. Reliance in this regard is placed upon the case reported as Noor Agha v. The state and another (2025 SCMR 1679) , wherein the Honorable Supreme Court held as under:
“The 3rd proviso to subsection (1) of section 497 of the Cr.P.C. governs the statutory right to claim release on bail on the ground of delay in the conclusion of trial. The legislature has explicitly used expression 'shall' in the 3rd proviso and it creates a right in favour of an accused to be released on bail provided the conditions stipulated for claiming such a right have been fulfilled. The 3rd proviso sets out the conditions for being released on bail on the ground of statutory delay. While the 4th proviso has described three distinct exceptions. Even if the conditions specified in the 3rd proviso are met but the case falls in one of the exceptions set out in the 4th proviso, the accused would not be entitled to claim bail on statutory ground as of right. The right would come into existence if the conditions explicitly set out in the 3rd proviso have been met and the exceptions in the 4th proviso are not attracted.
Further reliance is placed upon the case reported as Fayaz Khan v. Mohsin Shah and another (2026 SCMR 1076) .
7. In the given circumstances, the provisions of 3
rd proviso of Section 497 Cr.P.C. are inflexibly applicable in the instant case and petitioner is entitled to the concession of post arrest bail. While holding so, this Court is enlightened from the cases reported as Zahid Hussain Shah v. The State (PLD 1995 SC
49) and Muhammad Iqbal v. The State (1999 PCr.LJ 948)
Further reliance is placed upon the case reported as Muhammad Usman v. The State and another, (2024 SCMR
28) , wherein the Honorable Supreme Court of Pakistan granted
bail to an accused on the ground of statutory delay in the conclusion of trial with following observations:
“ On the touchstone of the principles highlighted herein above, a right has accrued in favour of the petitioner Crl. Misc. No.1313-B of 2026 under the third proviso of section 4 97(1) of the Cr.P.C., to be released on bail because the conditions have been met and the prosecution was not able to persuade us that the delay in conclusion of trial can be attributed to the petitioner nor that the mischief contemplated under the fourth proviso is attracted.”
8. The dismissal of instant post arrest bail is vociferously
urged by the learned Additional Prosecutor General on the ground that noticeable abscondance is attributed to the petitioner. Suffice it to say in this regard that if the case of an accused comes within the ambit of further inquiry, his previous abscondance cannot be used as hurdle for the grant of post arrest bail. Reliance in this regard is placed upon the case reported as Muhammad Aslam v. The State and others (2016 SCMR 1520) , an extract of which is reproduced hereunder:
“ It may be true that a person absconding after an occurrence and declared as a Proclaimed Offender may lose his claim to exercise of discretion in his favour by a court of law on the basis of proprie ty but at the same time it is equally true that an accused person the case against whom calls for further inquiry is to be admitted to bail as a matter of right. It goes without saying that whenever a question of propriety is confronted with a question of right the latter must prevail.” Further reliance is place upon the case reported as Hidayat Khan v. The State and another (2023 SCMR 172) .
9. For what has been discussed above, instant petition is
allowed and petitioner who is found incarcerated since
02.01.2024 and that too without any material progress in trial
is ordered to be released on bail subject to his furnishing bail bonds in the sum of Rs.10,00,000/- with two sureties in the like amount to the satisfaction of the learned trial court.
(SYED FARHAD ALI SHAH)
JUDGE
Approved for reporting.
JUDGE
Umer

Case: Crl. Misc.-Pre-arrest Bail-Under Section 498 Cr.PC 2930-B-26 (SYED TARIQ HUSSAIN BUKHARI VS THE STATE ETC).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Crl. Misc.-Pre-arrest Bail-Under Section 498 Cr.PC 2930-B-26. Title: Crl. Misc.-Pre-arrest Bail-Under Section 498 Cr.PC 2930-B-26 (SYED TARIQ HUSSAIN BUKHARI VS THE STATE ETC). Official Ref: 2026LHC5381. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Muhammad Usman Ghani Rashid Cheema. Judgment Date (as displayed): 31-08-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5381.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 4 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Form No.HCJD/C - 121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT ,
BAHAWALPUR BENCH, BAHAWALPUR .
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Crl.Misc.No. 2930 - B of 2026 Syed Tariq Hussain Bukhari v ersus The State , etc.
S.No.of order / Proceeding Date of Order/ Proceeding Order with signature of Judge, and that of parties’ counsel, where necessary 20 . 08 . 2026 Mr. Muhammad Naeem Bhatti , Advocate with the petitioner .
Mr. Javed Iqbal Bhayya, Assistant District Public Prosecutor alongwith Amanullah , S . I .
Through this petition , under s ection 498 Cr.P.C. , the petitioner seeks pre - arrest bail in case FIR No. 503/2026 dated 26 . 06 . 2026 , under s ection s 341, 188 PPC and Section 16 of the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960 registered at Police Station Kotwali, District Bahawalpur .
2 . Succinctly , the facts of the case are that on
26.06.2026 at about 11:00 p.m., the petitioner/accused, in his
capacity as administrator, took out a procession of Noha Khawani and Matam Dari in violation of the approved route, thereby causing obstruction on the road a nd inconvenience to the general public, in contravention of the relevant notification and applicable law. Hence, the instant FIR on
26.06.2026 .
3 . Contentions of the learned counsel for the petitioner and learned Assistant District Public Prosecutor have been heard and record of the case has been perused with theirable assistance.
Crl.Misc.No. 2930 - B of 20 2 6 2 4 . Although, it is a pre - arrest bail application but the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan has held, a number of times, whi le granting pre - arrest bail even merits of the case can be touched upon , or looked at and discussed . Reference is made to “Sajid Husain alias Joji v. The State” ( PLD 2021 SC 898), “ Javed Iqbal v. The State through Prosecutor General Punjab and another” ( 20 22 SCMR 1424) and “Muhammad Imran Nasrullah v. The State and others”
( 2022 SCMR 1946) .
5 . FIR and the material collected by police and presented before this Court reveals that the petitioner is nominated in FIR with the allegation of violation of the approved route while conducting the procession of Noha Khawani and Matam Dari by compl ainant/Sajid Nazir, S.I., Police Station Samma Satta . However, a copy of Certificate of Appreciation dated 09.07.2026 issued by the District Police Officer, Bahawalpur, h a s been submitted by the petitioner , the petitioner ha s been appreciated for his cooperation with the police and especially his efforts towards maintaining peace and law & order during Muharram - ul - Haram, particularly in connection wit h the peaceful conduct of Majalis, Noha Khawani and Matam Dari , were lauded .
Significantly, the said certificate was issued after the alleged occurrence dated 26.06.2026. The subsequent appreciation of the petitioner by the District Police Officer for his role in maintaining peace during the religious proceedings does not , prima facie , reconcile with the prosecution allegation that the petitioner had acted in a manner causing obstruction and disturbance that resulted in public nuisance . This peculiar circumstance casts serious doubt upon the prosecution version and makes the culpability of the petitioner a matter requiring further probe, to be determined by the learned trial Court after recording and evaluating the evidence. Hence, i n Crl.Misc.No. 2930 - B of 20 2 6 3 the facts and circumstances of this case, the possibility of false implication of the petitioner cannot be ruled out.
Reliance is respectfully placed on the case of “ Shahid Abbas v. The State and others ” ( 2021 SCMR 2082 ) .
6 . Learned ADPP has argued with vehemence that the petitioner has failed to point out any mala fide or ulterior motive on the part of complainant or the police party , which is sine qua non for confirmation of pre - arrest bail. It is well settled by now that it is not possible in each and every case to prove the mala fide and the same can be gleaned from the facts and circumstances of the case. I am fortif ied by the dictum laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in case s titled as “ Khalil Ahmed Soomro v. The State” (PLD 2017 SC 730) and “ Shahzada Qaiser Arfat alias Qaiser v.
The State and another” (PLD 2021 SC 708).
7 . Another aspect worth noticing is that out of the offences mentioned in the FIR, Sections 341 and 188 of PPC are bailable in nature. Though the offence under Section 16 of the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960 is non - bailable by virtue of Section 22 ibid , but the maximum punishment provided for is upto three years’ imprisonment, or fine, or both. Thus, the said offence does not fall within the prohibitory clause of Section 497(1), Cr.P.C. This circumstance, when considered alongside the material discussed above, further weighs in favour of the petitioner for the purposes of bail.
8 . Yet another facet of the nature of the offences mentioned in the FIR , not immaterial for decision of this bail application , is that no recovery of any sort is to be effected from the petitioner . learned ADPP has also not beenable to substantiate as to what lawful purpose, the intended arrest of the present petitioner, would serve in furtherance of Crl.Misc.No. 2930 - B of 20 2 6 4 prosecution’s case. T herefore, no useful purpose shall be served by causing the petitioner’s arrest. It is trite law that denial of bail in such like cases will amount to pre - tri al punishment, which is not permissible. Reference is made to the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of “ Naeem Qadir Sheikh and another v. The State and others ” ( 2022 SCMR
2068 ) .
9 . The epitome of above discussion is that the petitioner has succeeded in making out a case for confirmation of pre - arrest bail, hence, this petition is allowed and ad - interim pre - arrest bail already granted to the petitioner vide order dated 17 . 07 . 2026 is confirmed , subject to his furnishing of fresh bail bonds in the sum of Rs. 1 00,000/ - (Rupees one hundred thousand only) with one surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the learned trial court.
10. Before parting, it is clarified that the observat ions
made hereinabove are tentative in nature and the Trial Court shall be free to decide the case, on merits, without being influenced in any manner from the same, strictly in accordance with law .
( Muhammad Usman Ghani Rashid Cheema ) Judge Waqas* Approved for reporting Judge

Case: First Appeal Against Order(F.A.O.) 244285/18 (Mr. Ghulam Ali Zahid Chaudhry etc. Vs. Damas Jewellary LLC).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: First Appeal Against Order. Title: First Appeal Against Order(F.A.O.) 244285/18 (Mr. Ghulam Ali Zahid Chaudhry etc. Vs. Damas Jewellary LLC). Official Ref: 2025LHC8701. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Raheel Kamran. Judgment Date (as displayed): 31-08-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2025LHC8701.pdf.
