VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 6 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Stereo. H C J D A 38.
Judgment Sheet
LAHORE HIGH COURT LAHORE
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
F.A.O. No.244285 of 2018 Ghulam Ali Zahid Ch. And another Versus Damas Jewellary LLC
J U D G M E N T
Date of Hearing 13 .10.2025 For the appellants M/s Saqib Asghar and Mudassar Hassan, Advocates.
For the respondent Mr. Haseeb Zafar, Advocate.
Raheel Kamran J : - The instant First Appeal from Order (FAO) has been filed under Order XLIII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC) read with section 19 of the Intellectual Property Organization of Pakistan Act, 2012 challenging the vires of the order dated
01.08.2018 passed by the Intellectual Property Tribunal, Lahore (hereinafter
„the Tribunal‟) .
2 . By the impugned order, the Tribunal dismissed the application filed by the present appellants (who were the defendants in the suit) under Order VII Rule 10 CPC, seeking the return of the plaint to the respondent-plaintiff on the premise that the Tribunal lacked jurisdiction to adjudicate the dispute, as the matter was governed by the exclusive jurisdiction clause (Clause 6) of a prior Settlement Agreement dated 28.09.2010 (hereinafter, „Settlement Agreement‟) .
3 . Factual matrix of the matter is that the respondent Damas Jewellary LLC, instituted a suit against the appellants seeking declaration, injunction and damages under section 117 of the Trademarks Ordinance, 2001 for the alleged infringement of their registered trademark “DAMAS.” I t was the case of the respondent (hereinafter, „plaintiff‟) that the parties had a prior F.A.O. No.244285 of 2018 2 commercial relationship which was amicably settled through a comprehensive Settlement Agreement dated 28.09.2010. The agreement covered the use of the mark, the winding up of a joint venture company (Damas Toomban (Pvt.) Limited) and financial considerations. It was the stance of the plaintiff that the clause 2 of the Settlement Agreement allowed the defendant No.1 (appellant No.1 herein) to use the “ DAMAS ” trademark only till the completion date, however, following the failure of defendant No.1 to meet the original terms, the plaintiff granted an extension to the defendant No.1 for payment and trademark use. It was claimed in the plaint that during the grace period, the defendant No.1 struck off Damas Toomban (Pvt.) Limited on 27.07.2011 and misused the permission and got the plaintiff‟s trademark registered in his name through concealment and misrepresentation. It was further stated by the plaintiff that all obligations under the Settlement Agreement including the final payment were fully and finally discharged on 26.01.2017, thereby bringing the contractual relationship to an end; consequently, the right to the exclusive use of the trademark “Damas” reverted to the plaintiff as its rightful owner. The subsequent use of the trademark in Lahore by defendant No.1 constitutes a fresh act of infringement of the plaintiff‟s statutory intellectual property rights, thus necessitating the institution of the suit before the Intellectual Property Tribunal, which is the court of exclusive jurisdiction under the relevant statute.
4 . The appellants-defendants, in their written statement and subsequent application under Order VII Rule 10 CPC, asserted that the dispute regarding the use of the trademark was one of the subjects covered by the Settlement Agreement. They contended that any controversy relating to the mark‟s use must be resolved under Clause 6 of the said agreement, arguing that the true lis is contractual, not statutory, thus demanding the return of the plaint.
The appellants further pleaded that they had registered the mark in their name and that the terms of the settlement were never acted upon, or that the plaintiff was estopped due to acquiescence.
5 . The Tribunal dismissed the application under Order VII Rule 10 CPC by way of order dated 01.08.2018 by concluding that the dispute qua alleged infringement under the Trademarks Ordinance, 2001 is within its F.A.O. No.244285 of 2018 3 purview as the Settlement Agreement had reached its logical conclusion and born fruit. The dismissal of their application has been assailed by the appellants in this appeal.
6 . Learned counsel for the appellants contended that the Tribunal erred in dismissing the application. It was argued that the very subject matter of the suit i.e. the right to use the trademark, is directly linked to and flows from the Settlement Agreement dated 28.09.2010. Therefore, any dispute concerning this subject matter is mandatorily covered by Clause 6 of the Settlement Agreement, which governs the venue and mechanism for resolving contractual disputes. Learned counsel emphasized that the appellants have specifically pleaded in paragraph 10 of their written statement that the Agreement was never acted upon and alternatively, that the respondent had acquiesced in the a ppellants‟ continued use, thus demonstrating that the controversy necessarily involves the interpretation and enforcement of the Settlement Agreement.
7 . Conversely, learned counsel for the respondent fully supported the reasoning adopted by the Tribunal, submitting that the Settlement Agreement was a time-bound, executory contract, which has been fully performed, with all obligations discharged, including the final payment made in January 2017.
Once an agreement is fully performed and the company formed under it is wound up, the jurisdiction clause relating to disputes arising from its performance or validity ceases to apply to fresh commercial torts. He added that the present suit is based on a distinct statutory cause of action i.e. trademark infringement. Learned counsel maintained that the Intellectual Property Tribunal, having been established under the law, is the court of exclusive and specialized jurisdiction to try suits for infringement under the Trademarks Ordinance, 2001.
8 . Having considered the submissions of the learned counsel for the parties and examined the record, the fundamental question requiring determination is whether the plaintiff‟s suit qua infringement of the trademark “Damas” is a contractual dispute arising from the Settlement Agreement falling within the jurisdiction of foreign courts, or a distinct cause of action under the F.A.O. No.244285 of 2018 4 Trademarks Ordinance, 2001 falling squarely within the jurisdiction of the Intellectual Property Tribunal.
9 . The narrow inquiry at the stage of Order VII Rule 10 CPC is jurisdiction, not the merits of the defence. For a plaint to be returned, the court must find that it lacks the competence to try the suit as framed by the Plaintiff.
The plaintiff specifically asserted in paragraph No.23 of the plaint that final payment in pursuance of Settlement Agreement had been made by the appellant No.1 on 26.01.2017, as such the Settlement Agreement has been fully performed. In their written statement, the appellants did not specifically deny the plaintiff‟s assertion qua final payment in pursuance of the Settlement Agreement on 26.01.2017, rather they claimed that the plaintiff being fully aware of the use of trademark by the appellants acquiesced by not taking any legal action against them from 2012 to 2017. This plea of acquiescence while not specifically controverting the pl aintiff‟s assertion qua full performance of the Settlement Agreement reacts against the appellants. The jurisdiction clause of a private contract is meant to govern disputes concerning the terms, implementation, interpretation or validity of that contract. Where a contract, by its own terms, has been fully performed, its life as an executory instrument terminates. The subsequent alleged unauthorized use of a trademark is not a dispute over the breach of the completed contract; rather, it constitutes a new, independent tort of infringement, which is governed by the Trademarks Ordinance, 2001. The Tribunal rightly observed that the dispute no longer relates to the existence, validity, or termination of the Settlement Agreement, but is a dispute simpliciter for the enforcement of statutory trademark rights. To hold otherwise would imply that a jurisdiction clause in a settled contract operates in perpetuity, governing every future commercial dispute between the parties, regardless of the cause of action, which is an absurd proposition.
10 . The Intellectual Property Tribunal is a court of specialized jurisdiction, explicitly empowered under the Trademarks Ordinance, 2001 to deal with infringement suits. The respondent ‟ s plaint, on its face, pleads a cause of action for trademark infringement based on the a ppellants‟ conduct after January 2017. This is a purely statutory claim. The a ppellants‟ attempt to use F.A.O. No.244285 of 2018 5 the Settlement Agreement to divest the Tribunal of jurisdiction is misplaced because the new commercial activity creates a separate, statutory cause of action. Furthermore, the Tribunal derives its jurisdiction from a special statute.
Where a statutory right is sought to be enforced, the special court constituted for that purpose maintains jurisdiction, notwithstanding prior contractual dealings between the parties, unless the contract explicitly and validly bars future statutory claims, which the Settlement Agreement does not appear to do.
11 . Even assuming, arguendo, the claims of the appellants to the effect that the agreement was never acted upon or that the respondent is estopped due to acquiescence, are matters of evidence and trial. These involve mixed questions of fact and law which require the Tribunal to record evidence and interpret the parties ‟ conduct vis-à-vis the Settlement Agreement. The Tribunal cannot, at the interlocutory stage while deciding application under Order VII Rule 10 CPC, return the plaint merely because the defendant has raised complex factual defences. The power to return a plaint is based only on the ground that the court is not competent to entertain the suit, which is not the case here.
12 . The appellants raised several points which, while critical to the ultimate outcome of the suit, are defences on the merits and cannot be considered at the stage of deciding application under Order VII Rule 10 CPC.
The a ppellants‟ assertion that they have registered the trademark , is a formidable defence against the infringement claim, as it raises a question of concurrent rights or the validity of the r espondent‟s registration. However, the Tribunal is perfectly competent to decide whether an infringement has occurred, taking into account the a ppellants‟ claimed registration. The existence of a strong defence does not automatically extinguish the Tribunal‟s jurisdiction to hear the suit.
13 . In view of the foregoing detailed discussion, this Court finds no infirmity, illegality or jurisdictional error in the impugned order dated
01.08.2018 passed by the Intellectual Property Tribunal, Lahore. Consequently,
the appeal stands dismissed. No order as to costs.
F.A.O. No.244285 of 2018 6 Before parting with this order, it has been noticed that the civil suit from which instant appeal has arisen out, was filed in the year 2017. To prevent further delay in decision of the matter, the Intellectual Property Tribunal is directed to conclude the trial of the suit expeditiously, preferably within a period of six months.
(RAHEEL KAMRAN)
JUDGE
Azhar*

Case: Family 21804/20 (Dr. Rukhsana Kausar etc Vs Shahid Nazeer etc).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Family 21804/20. Title: Family 21804/20 (Dr. Rukhsana Kausar etc Vs Shahid Nazeer etc). Official Ref: 2026LHC5363. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Raheel Kamran. Judgment Date (as displayed): 31-08-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5363.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 18 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Stereo H C J D A 38.
Judgment Sheet
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Writ Petition No.21804 of 2020 Dr. Rukhsana Kausar and another Versus Shahid Nazeer and others Date of hearing 15.06.2026 Petitioner by : M /s Shaukat Umar Pirzada and Shujaat Umer Pirzada , Advocate s .
Respondent No. 1 by : Mr. Ijaz Feroz Kashmiri, Advocate.
RAHEEL KAMRAN , J.: This single judgment shall govern the titled petition as well as Writ Petition No. 26320 of 2020 (Shahid Nazir versus Dr. Rukhsana Kausar, etc), Writ Petition No. 23651 of 2026 (Shahid Nazir versus Addl. District Judge, Muzaffargarh, etc.) and Civil Revision No.23652 of 2026 (Shahid Naz ee r versus Fazal Hussain) as all these matte r s arise out of the same dispute and between the same pa rties.
2 . Facts relevant for decision of the controversy, precisely are that on 23.12.2011 Dr. Rukhsana Kausar (hereinafter to be referred to as “the petitioner” ) instituted a suit against Shahid Nazeer (hereinafter to be referred to as “the respondent” ) for dissolution of marriage, recovery of maintenance allowance for herself as well as her minor son namely Rohan Shahid (hereinafter to be referred to as “the minor” ) , recovery of dowry articles and delivery expenses. The petitioner’s case was that, durin g the negotiations preceding the marriage, the respondent and his family represented that a residential house and gold ornaments weighing 11 tolas would be given to her as dower. According to the petitioner, the respondent and his family lacked the financi al means to fulfil l the said commitment, W.P . No.21804 of 2020 2 whereupon, at their request and on the assurance that the amount would be repaid, her parents financed the purchase of the residential house as well as the 11 tolas of gold, although both were entered in the Nikahna ma as dower.
She further asserted that her parents also gave her dowry articles, including gold ornaments weighing 22 tolas, and that, owing to the respondent ’ s persistent neglect, failure to maintain her, and cruel conduct, she was ultimately compelled to leave the matrimonial home along with the minor child and return to her parental house. Besides dissolution of marriage, she sought recovery of maintenance, dowry articles, delivery expenses and the gold ornaments, while also disputing the respondent ’ s en titlement to claim restoration of the 11 tolas of gold or the house as Badl - e - Khula .
The respondent contested the suit by denying the material allegations. He maintained that the marriage was arranged by the elders of the families and that the suit house had been purchased by him from funds arranged through his brother before the marriage and was thereafter transferred in the petitioner ’ s favour as dower. He denied having borrowed any amount from the petitioner ’ s parents for purchase of either the house o r the jewellery and asserted that the entries relating to maintenance in the Nikahnama had been made by the petitioner herself. According to the respondent, he regularly maintained the petitioner and bore the expenses relating to the birth of the minor. He further pleaded that the petitioner voluntarily left the matrimonial home after taking with her all the gold ornaments, including the 11 tolas entered in the Nikahnama as dower, whereas only ordinary dowry articles remained in the house. He also questione d the validity of the subsequent gift ( Tamleek ) executed by the petitioner in favour of her father in respect of the suit house. On these premises, he prayed for dismissal of the suit.
3 . During the pendency of the suit, the Judge Family Court, by order d ated 28.04.2012, dissolved the marriage between the parties by way of Khula and observed that the petitioner was obliged to return the dower W.P . No.21804 of 2020 3 received by her as Badl - e - Khula , while keeping the remaining controversies pending for adjudication. Consequently, following issues were framed :
ISSUES .
1. Whether the plaintiffs are entitled for recovery of maintenance
allowance, if so for which quantum and for which period? OPP
2. Whether the plaintiff No.1 is entitled for recovery of dowry articles
as per list annexed w ith the plaint? OPP
3. Whether the suit of the plaintiffs is liable to be dismissed? OPD
4. Whether the defendant has paid/given Haq Mehar as mentioned in
column No.14, 15 and 16 of Nikahnama? OPD
5. Whether the defendant is entitled for recovery of Haq Mehar as
Za r - e - Khula? OPD
6. Whether the plaintiff No.1 has not received dower as mentioned in
column No.14, 15 and 16 of Nikahnama? OPP
7. Whether the plaintiff have not come into the court with clean
hands? OPD
8. Whether the plaintiffs have no cause of action? OPD
9. Relief.
ADDITIONAL ISSUE NO.2A .
Whether the plaintiff No.1 is entitled for recovery of Rs.63,000/ - as delivery expenses from the defendant? OPP After recording the evidence of the parties, the Family Court, through judgment and decree dated 31.10.2018, partly decr eed the suit by awarding maintenance to the petitioner for the period of iddat and to the minor son, directing recovery of dowry articles (excluding the gold ornaments) and requiring the petitioner to return 11 tolas of gold or its value to the respondent as Badl - e - Khula . The Family Court, however, declined the respondent ’ s claim for restoration of the suit house, holding that the same had not been proved.
Feeling aggrieved, both parties preferred separate appeals before the Additional District Judge. By judgment and decree dated
20.02.2020, both appeals were substantially dismissed, except that the
annual enhancement in the maintenance allowance awarded to the minor was reduced from 15% to 10%. Still dissatisfied, the petitioner has instituted W.P . No.21804 of 2020 4 Writ Petition No.21804 of 2020 challenging the concurrent findings whereby her claims relating to the gold ornaments, delivery expenses and certain ancillary reliefs were declined and she was directed to return 11 tolas of gol d or its value as Badl - e - Khula . Conversely, the respondent has filed Writ Petition No.26320 of 2020 questioning, inter alia , the findings relating to the suit house, maintenance and dowry articles.
4 . The controversy relating to the suit house did not end with the family litigation. After executing the Tamleek deed in favour of her father Fazal Hussain Asim, the petitioner gave rise to two independent civil proceedings before the Civil Court at Muzaffar garh. The respondent instituted a suit seeking declaration and cancellation of the Tamleek deed on the ground that the transfer was void and ineffective in law, whereas Fazal Hussain Asim instituted a separate suit seeking possession of the suit house and mesne profits on the strength of the said Tamleek. Since both suits involved common questions relating to the title and possession of the suit house, they were consolidated for trial. However, in view of the pendency of the family litigation, both suits w ere adjourned sine die awaiting the final determination of the issues arising therein. After the Family Court finally decided the controversy, the civil proceedings were revived. Ultimately, the suit instituted by the respondent for cancellation of the Tam leek deed was dismissed , whereas the suit filed by Fazal Hussain Asim was decreed and the respondent was directed to deliver possession of the suit house. Appeals preferred against both decisions were dismissed by the Additional District Judge, Muzaffarga rh. The respondent has assailed those concurrent decisions through Writ Petition No.23651 of 2026 and Civil Revision No.23652 of 2026.
Although the aforesaid proceedings originated within the territorial jurisdiction of the Multan Bench of this Court, bo th matters were ordered to be heard at the Principal Seat as they arise directly out of the same matrimonial dispute, involve substantially overlapping questions concerning the ownership and legal character of the suit house, and their W.P . No.21804 of 2020 5 adjudication is depe ndent, to a considerable extent, upon the findings recorded in the family litigation. To avoid the possibility of conflicting judicial determinations and in the interest of consistency, all the above matters have, therefore, been heard together and are bei ng disposed of by this common judgment .
5 . Learned counsel for the petitioner assailed the impugned judgments and decrees on the ground that they suffer from misreading and non - reading of material evidence, resulting in a manifest miscarriage of justice. He submitted that the respondent had failed to discharge the burden of proving that the dower entered in the Nikahnama, particularly the suit house and the 11 tolas of gold ornaments, had been financed or paid by him from his own resources. According to the learned counsel, the evidence produced by the petitioner unequivocally established that both the suit house and the 11 tolas of gold had been purchased from funds provided by the petitioner ’ s father at the request of the respondent and his family, and once the Courts below accepted that position in relation to the suit house, they committed a patent inconsistency in declining to extend the same conclusion to the gold ornaments despite the absence of any evidence demonstrating the respondent ’ s financial capacity. Learned counsel further contended that the concurrent findings whereby the petitioner was denied recovery of the 22 tolas of gold ornaments given to her by her parents as dowry are likewise unsustainable, as the evidence on record sufficiently es tablished that the said ornaments remained in the respondent ’ s possession. It was argued that the Family Court and the Appellate Court adopted an erroneous approach in appreciating the evidence and ignored material circumstances favourable to the petitione r ’ s case. He also challenged the dismissal of the petitioner ’ s claim for delivery expenses and assailed the reduction made by the Appellate Court in the annual enhancement of maintenance awarded to the minor.
Insofar as the connected civil proceedings are concerned, learned counsel submitted that once the petitioner had validly transferred the suit W.P . No.21804 of 2020 6 house to her father by way of Tamleek , the respondent ceased to have any subsisting right, title or interest therein. Consequently, the suit instituted by the r espondent for cancellation of the Tamleek deed was rightly rejected, whereas the suit filed by the petitioner ’ s father for possession was rightly decreed. It was, therefore, argued that the impugned judgments passed in the connected civil proceedings call for no interference. On these premises, learned counsel prayed that Writ Petition No.21804 of 2020 be allowed, whereas Writ Petition No.26320 of 2020, Writ Petition No.23651 of 2026 and Civil Revision No.23652 of 2026 be dismissed.
6 . Conversely, learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the petitioner had failed to substantiate her plea that the suit house and the 11 tolas of gold entered in the Nikahnama had been financed by her father.
According to him, the evidence produced by the petitioner was insufficient to displace the presumption arising from the entries recorded in the Nikahnama, whereas the respondent had satisfactorily established that the suit house formed part of the dower and that the petitioner was consequently obliged to restore the dower received by her as Badl - e - Khula . He further submitted that the petitioner also failed to prove that the 22 tolas of gold ornaments allegedly gifted by her parents remained in the respondent ’ s possession and, therefore, the concurrent findings declining recovery thereof call for no interference. Learned counsel further submitted that the respondent ’ s own challenge to the impugned judgments, insofar as they r elate to the suit house, the award of maintenance in favour of the minor and other reliefs granted to the petitioner, is equally well - founded and deserves acceptance.
I n relation to the connected civil proceedings, learned counsel argued that the Tamleek deed executed by the petitioner in favour of her father did not confer any valid title, as she herself had acquired no lawful ownership in the suit house. He further contended that, in any event, the alleged gift was legally defective for want of delivery of possession, which, according to the learned counsel, constitutes an essential ingredient of a valid gift under the W.P . No.21804 of 2020 7 applicable principles of law. Consequently, it was submitted that the respondent ’ s suit seeking declaration and cancellation of the Tamlee k deed was maintainable, whereas the suit instituted by the petitioner ’ s father for possession was liable to dismissal. He, therefore, prayed that Writ Petition No.21804 of 2020 be dismissed, whereas Writ Petition No.26320 of 2020, Writ Petition No.23651 o f 2026 and Civil Revision No.23652 of 2026 be allowed.
7 . Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and gone through the record, it has been noticed that t he concurrent findings recorded by the Courts below regarding maintenance do not call for interference. The evidence on record unmistakably establishes that the respondent is a professionally qualified engineer who, after initially serving in the private sector, joined the Government Service and was drawing a substantial salary.
The Family Cour t rightly observed that despite being in possession of the best evidence, the respondent withheld his complete salary record and produced only a certificate reflecting his basic pay, thereby entitling the Court to draw an adverse inference while assessing his actual financial capacity. The maintenance awarded to petitioner No.1 was confined only to the period during which she remained legally entitled thereto, whereas maintenance of the minor was determined keeping in view his growing educational and other day - to - day needs. The Appellate Court further moderated the respondent’s financial burden by reducing the annual enhancement from 15% to 10%. This Court finds the quantum so determined to be fair, reasonable and commensurate with the circumstances brought on record.
8 . It has been noted that qua his financial capacity, the respondent took inconsistent stance. While asserting his claim over the suit house, he maintained that he had sufficient financial resources to purchase a house worth Rs.19,50,000/- in the year 2006, claiming that although part of the sale consideration had initially been arranged through financial assistance from his brother, the same was repaid by him within a period of two to three W.P . No.21804 of 2020 8 years. During his cross-examination, he also asserted that he himself possessed sufficient funds to purchase the said property. Likewise, he claimed to have purchased 11 tolas of gold for the petitioner at the time of marriage. During cross-examination, he also referred to sources of income apart from his salary, including investments in business. Yet, when called upon to discharge his legal obligation of maintaining his own child, he projected himself as a person of meagre means. The inconsistency becomes even more apparent from the testimony of DW-3, the respondent ’ s own brother, who stated during cross-examination that the respondent owned a Honda Civic car. These circumstances, when viewed cumulatively, lend support to the conclusion reached by the Courts below that the respondent ’ s plea regarding his limited financial capacity did not inspire confidence. It scarcely needs reiteration that maintenance of a minor child is not merely a statutory liability but also a legal, moral and social obligation of the father.
The law does not countenance an attempt by a financially capable parent to understate his means with a view to reducing or avoiding his obligation towards a child who, owing to the breakdown of the matrimonial relationship, is being brought up by the other parent. Such pleas, if accepted without careful scrutiny, would defeat the very object of the beneficial provisions governing maintenance and would expose minor children to financial hardship for no fault of their own. The Courts are, therefore, required to examine such assertions in the light of the entire evidence rather than the income figures selectively projected by the obligor. Learned counsel for the respondent failed to point out any legal infirmity, misreading or nonreading of evidence or jurisdictional defect in the concurrent findings whereby maintenance has been awarded in favour of the petitioners.
9 . Adverting now to the petitioner ’ s claim for recovery of maternity expenses amounting to Rs.63,000/-, which too has been concurrently declined by the Courts below. Having examined the findings recorded by the Courts below on the said issue, no valid reason is found for taking a different view. The petitioner ’ s case was that the delivery expenses W.P . No.21804 of 2020 9 were initially borne by her parents and that at the respondent ’ s request, the receipts were prepared in his name on the representation that he intended to seek reimbursement from his employer and thereafter repay the amount to them. The respondent, however, categorically denied the said assertion.
Admittedly, the receipts pertaining to the delivery expenses stood in the respondent ’ s name. In the absence of any documentary evidence showing payment by the petitioner ’ s parents or any independent evidence, such as the testimony of the concerned medical practitioner, hospital official or any other person associated with the medical facility to substantiate the explanation furnished by the petitioner regarding issuance of the receipts in the respondent ’ s name, the Family Court rightly concluded that the claim had remained unsubstantiated. The Appellate Court, upon reappraisal of the record, affirmed the said finding. The concurrent conclusion is based upon a proper appreciation of the evidence available on record and suffers from neither misreading nor non-reading of evidence so as to warrant interference by this Court.
10 . Turning now to the controversy relating to the suit house, no legal infirmity is found in the concurrent findings recorded by the Courts below. The principal question before the Family Court was whether the respondent had in fact paid the sale consideration of the house, which admittedly stood transferred in the name of petitioner No.1 prior to the solemnization of marriage, or whether the entire purchase price and the ancillary transfer expenses had been borne by the petitioner ’ s father, as asserted by the petitioners. Upon an exhaustive appraisal of the oral as well as documentary evidence, the Family Court returned a categorical finding that the respondent had failed to establish that the property had been acquired from his own resources, whereas the petitioner had successfully proved that the entire consideration for the purchase of the house, together with the transfer expenses, had been provided by the petitioner ’ s father. The Appellate Court independently reappraised the evidence and affirmed the said conclusion.
W.P . No.21804 of 2020 10 11 . The record reveals that this finding does not rest merely upon oral assertions. Rather, the petitioner succeeded in establishing a coherent and unbroken chain of evidence tracing the source and movement of the funds utilized for the purchase of the property. The evidence showed that the petitioner ’ s father, who was serving abroad at the relevant time, arranged the requisite funds through his foreign currency account. Those funds were converted into Pakistani currency, whereafter, through his authorised representative, a demand draft was obtained and deposited into the bank account of the respondent ’ s brother, from whose account the sale consideration was ultimately transmitted to the vendor. The said transactions were substantiated not only through the testimony of the person who had acted on behalf of the petitioner ’ s father in arranging the financial transaction, but also by the relevant banking officials (PW-4, PW-5 and PW-6), who produced and verified the corresponding banking record before the Family Court. Significantly, material aspects of this chain of evidence remained substantially unchallenged during cross-examination. The Family Court also noticed that the respondent could not furnish any satisfactory explanation as to why the petitioner ’ s representative had participated in the registration process and executed the necessary documents on behalf of petitioner No.1 if, in fact, the respondent himself had financed the entire transaction. Conversely, the respondent ’ s plea that the property had been purchased from his own resources, or through financial assistance obtained from his brother, did not withstand judicial scrutiny. The evidence produced in support of that plea was found to be internally inconsistent and deficient in material particulars, particularly regarding the alleged source of funds, the financial capacity of the respondent and his brother to make such payment, and the manner in which the alleged financial arrangement had been made.
No documentary evidence was produced to substantiate the respondent ’ s assertion that the purchase price had been arranged by him or on his behalf.
Both the Courts below have discussed these aspects of the evidence in considerable detail and assigned cogent reasons for preferring the W.P . No.21804 of 2020 11 petitioner ’s version over that of the respondent. Learned counsel for the respondent has been unable to point out any instance of misreading or nonreading of evidence, much less any perversity, which may justify interference with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the Courts below in exercise of constitutional jurisdiction. The conclusion that the house had not been provided by the respondent as paid dower, and that no occasion therefore arose to direct its restoration as Badl-e-Khula , is thus fully borne out by the record.
12 . As regards the objection raised by the respondent pertaining to the validity of the Tamleek executed by petitioner in favour of her father, it is an admitted position that at the time when the Tamleek was executed, the suit house stood validly transferred and registered in the name of petitioner, who was the registered and lawful owner thereof. There existed no statutory or legal impediment restraining her from transferring the property in favour of any person of her choice, including her father, through a legally recognized mode of transfer. The respondent has, however, argued that the Tamleek was ineffective for want of delivery of possession, contending that actual possession of the house had never been handed over to the petitioner’s father. The argument overlooks the peculiar factual matrix of the case. The petitioner was admittedly the owner of the property and, by virtue of the subsisting marital relationship, continued to reside in the suit house as the legally wedded wife of the respondent. Her possession, though shared with or enjoyed through the marital relationship, was nonetheless lawful and referable to her title. In such circumstances, the absence of a formal physical change of possession does not, by itself, invalidate the transfer. The petitioner’s possession was juridical and lawful, though referable to the marital relationship and in the circumstances amounted to sufficient dominion over the property for the purpose of the transfer, which continued till the matrimonial relationship deteriorated. Therefore, when the transaction is appreciated in the backdrop of the attending facts and circumstances, the respondent’s objection regarding want of actual delivery W.P . No.21804 of 2020 12 of possession does not advance his case. No illegality or jurisdictional defect is found in the concurrent findings whereby the Courts below upheld the petitioner ’ s title in the suit house and the subsequent transfer thereof in favour of her father.
13 . The findings recorded hereinabove conclusively determine the challenge laid to the decree passed by the Civil Court in favour of the petitioner ’ s father for poss ession of the suit property . Once it has been found that the petitioner was the lawful owner of the suit house and that the subsequent Tamleek in favour of her father was legally valid, the latter ’ s entitlement to seek possession from the respondent, who c eased to have any lawful claim over the property, necessarily follows. The decree for possession, being a natural consequence of the lawful transfer of title and the findings concurrently recorded by the Courts below, suffers from no legal infirmity warran ting interference.
14 . Coming now to the controversy relating to the gold ornaments, b efore adverting to the rival claims, it would be advantageous to notice that although, by order dated 28.04.2012, the Judge Family Court dissolved the marriage between the parties by way of khula and observed that “ Plaintiff No.1 has an obligation to retur n the dower, received at the eve of marriage as Badl - e - Khula ” , the remaining disputes between the parties were kept pending for adjudication. Consequently, while proceeding with the suit, the Family Court framed, inter alia , Issues No.4, 5 and 6 specifical ly relating to payment of dower, entitlement of the respondent to its restoration as Badl - e - Khula and the petitioner ’ s plea that the dower mentioned in the Nikahnama had, in fact, never been paid. The onus to prove payment of dower was placed upon the respondent, whereas the petitioner was required to establish her plea that she had not received the dower mentioned in columns No.14 to 16 of the Nikahnama . This course adopted by the Family Court was consistent with the law as it then stood, since subsections (5) and (6) were inserted in Section 10 of the Family Courts Act, 1964 only subsequently (through the Punjab Family Courts (Amendment) Act 2015) W.P . No.21804 of 2020 13 and were not retrospectively in operation. Therefore, the contention of the learned counsel for the respondent that after passing the decree for dissolution of marriage the Family Court had become functus officio and lacked jurisdiction to determine the controversy regarding dower, is without substance.
15 . There is no dispute between the parties that the petitioner received gold ornaments weighing approximately 22 tolas from her parents at the time of marriage. Likewise, it is an admitted position that 11 tolas of gold were entered in the Nikahnama as dower and that the said ornaments were delivered to the petitioner. The principal controversy relating to the 11 tolas of gold entered in the Nikahnama, therefore, is to the source from which it was purchased. From the very inception of the litigation, the petitioner ’ s consistent case has been that the respondent lacked the financial means to provide either the suit house or the gold mentioned as dower and that, at the request of the respondent and his family, the petitioner ’ s father arranged the necessary funds for both. According to the petitioner, the house and the 11 tolas of gold were entered in the Nikahnama as dower merely to preserve the honour and social standing of her father within the family and the brotherhood, although the respondent had himself contributed nothing towards their purchase. This plea was reiterated not only by the petitioner herself but also by PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3, whose evidence remained materially consistent throughout. It is true that, unlike the purchase of the suit house, no documentary evidence or banking record was produced regarding the payment made for the purchase of the 11 tolas of gold.
Nevertheless, absence of documentary evidence is not by itself conclusive in civil proceedings where the rights of the parties are to be determined on the touchstone of balance of probabilities. The Court is required to appreciate the entire evidence cumulatively rather than in isolation. In the case in hand, the respondent completely failed to establish through any documentary or reliable oral evidence that he possessed the financial capacity to purchase 11 tolas of gold at the relevant time. The evidence available on the record W.P . No.21804 of 2020 14 sufficiently demonstrates the meagre financial resources of the respondent and his family and the improbability of their having independently financed both the house and the jewellery. An aspect of considerable significance is the suggestion put by the respondent’s counsel itself during the crossexamination of PW-3, the petitioner ’ s father, that:
“ یہ درست ہے کہ میں نے مدعا علیہ کو جو رقم ادھار دی اس کا لین دار ہوں۔ ”
By putting such suggestion, the defence itself acknowledged the advancement of money by PW-3 to the respondent, the only endeavour being to treat the transaction as a loan. This circumstance materially corroborates the petitioner ’ s consistent plea that the funds utilized for purchase of the jewellery had in fact been provided by her father.
Significantly, apart from a bare denial, the respondent neither produced any evidence regarding availability of his own funds nor furnished any satisfactory explanation regarding the source from which the purchase price of the jewellery was arranged.
16 . When the entire evidence is appreciated cumulatively, the consistent testimony of the petitioner and her witnesses, the established financial incapacity of the respondent, the absence of any evidence demonstrating availability of funds with the respondent, and the above admission emerging from the cross-examination of PW-3 collectively render the petitioner ’ s version more probable. Therefore, like the suit house, the amount utilized for purchase of the 11 tolas of gold had also been provided by the petitioner ’ s father. Consequently, the respondent cannot claim return of the said ornaments as Badl-e-Khula , for the simple reason that they did not represent dower financed or paid by him from his own resources.
17 . It is well s ettled that this Court while exercising constitutional jurisdiction under Article 199 of the Constitution, does not ordinarily interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by the courts below merely because another view of the evidence is possible. Such restraint, however, is not an inflexible rule. Where the findings suffer from misreading W.P . No.21804 of 2020 15 or non-reading of material evidence, omission to consider circumstances having a decisive bearing upon the controversy, or are otherwise unsupported by the record, the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court may legitimately be invoked to prevent miscarriage of justice. In the case in hand, the error committed by the Courts below lies not in their appreciation of any individual piece of evidence but in their failure to evaluate the entire evidentiary material in its cumulative effect. By treating the absence of documentary proof regarding payment of Rs.150,000/- as determinative, while overlooking other material circumstances which substantially corroborated the petitioner ’ s case, the Courts below arrived at a conclusion which is not borne out by the record as a whole. The concurrent findings relating to the 11 tolas of gold, therefore, cannot sustain.
18 . T he above conclusion, however, determines only the controversy relating to the source of funds utili z ed for the purchase of the 11 tolas of gold and, consequently, the respondent ’ s entitlement to claim its restoration as Badl - e - Khula . A distinct question re mains regarding the possession of the gold ornaments, particularly the petitioner ’ s claim for recovery thereof from the respondent. On this aspect, this Court find s no sufficient ground to differ from the concurrent findings recorded by the Courts below. T he petitioner ’ s consistent case was that when she finally left the matrimonial home, she departed merely in her wearing apparel, leaving behind not only the 11 tolas of gold entered in the Nikahnama but also the remaining 22 tolas of gold claimed to have b een given to her by her parents at the time of marriage. It was, however, never her case that the respondent or any member of his family had forcibly removed the jewellery from her person. The record further reveals material discrepancies regarding the cir cumstances in which she finally left the matrimonial home. While the petitioner maintained that she left permanently in July 2011, some of her own witnesses stated during cross - examination that she continued residing with the respondent until September/Oct ober 2011. Although this discrepancy may not, by itself, be decisive, it does impair the reliability of W.P . No.21804 of 2020 16 her version regarding the circumstances in which she allegedly left without the jewellery. Equally significant is the fact that the petitioner never ple aded nor did the evidence disclose that her final departure from the matrimonial home took place amidst any sudden or extraordinary circumstances which could reasonably explain her leaving behind ornaments of such considerable value. It was not her case th at immediately before her departure any altercation or violent incident had occurred, that she had been physically assaulted or forcibly expelled from the house, or that the respondent or any member of his family had prevented her from taking her personal belongings or had snatched the jewellery from her possession. On the contrary, her own case merely was that she left the matrimonial home along with her minor son wearing the clothes she had on. In the ordinary course of human conduct, where no such compel ling or coercive circumstances are shown to exist, it becomes difficult to accept, on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities, that a person would voluntarily leave behind valuable gold ornaments constituting her personal property without making a ny contemporaneous attempt to retrieve them or without alleging any impediment which prevented her from doing so. The absence of any such surrounding circumstances, therefore, constitutes an important factor while assessing the probability of the petitione r ’ s version. Furthermore, greater significance attaches to the evidence relating to the marriage of the petitioner ’ s sister which was solemnized after the petitioner left the matrimonial home for the last time . The petitioner ’ s father (PW - 3) admitted during cross - examination that the petitioner attended the marriage wearing jewellery. Likewise, when the petitioner herself was specifically asked whether she wished to produce the video recording of the marriage ceremony, she declined to do so. A suggestion was then put to her that the reason for withholding the video was that it would depict her wearing the disputed jewellery. Had the petitioner not been wearing the ornaments claimed in the present proceedings, the production of the video would have furnished the best available evidence to dispel the controversy. Her refusal W.P . No.21804 of 2020 17 to produce such evidence entitled the Family Court to draw an adverse inference in accordance with the settled principles governing appreciation of evidence.
19 . When the evidence in the case in hand is examined on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities, the concurrent findings of the Courts below that the petitioner failed to establish that the disputed jewellery remained in the respondent ’ s possession do not suffer from any misreading or non-reading of evidence, nor has any jurisdictional infirmity been pointed out warranting interference in exercise of constitutional jurisdiction.
Accordingly, while the findings relating to the source of funds for purchase of the 11 tolas of gold are liable to be modified for the reasons already recorded, the concurrent findings relating to possession of the jewellery call for no interference.
20 . For the foregoing reasons, Writ Petition No.21804 of 2020 succeeds partly and is accordingly allowed to the extent that the findings recorded by the Family Court and affirmed by the Appellate Court directing the petitioner to return 11 tolas of gold/jewellery or its value to the res pondent as Badl - e - Khula are set aside and the respondent is held not entitled to claim restoration of the said 11 tolas of gold or its value as consideration of Khula. The remaining findings recorded in the impugned judgments and decrees are maintained. T h e judgments and decrees impugned in Writ Petition No.21804 of 2020 stand modified accordingly .
Decree sheet be drawn. Writ Petition No.26320 of 2020 filed by the respondent is dismissed.
21 . The controversy involved in Writ Petition No.23651 of 2026 and Civil Revision No.23652 of 2026 substantially emanates from the respondent ’ s challenge to the petitioner ’ s title in the suit house and the validity of the Tamleek executed in favour of her father. Those very questions have been examined hereinabove and answered against the respondent. Once it has been held that the petitioner validly acquired title in W.P . No.21804 of 2020 18 the suit house, that the property had not been provided by the respondent as paid dower, and that the subsequent transfer in favour of Fazal Hussain Asim was legally valid, the very foundation of the respondent ’ s challenge to the rejection of his suit as well as to the decree passed in favour of Fazal Hussain Asim for possession ceases to survive. The findings recorded by the Civil Court and affirmed by the Appellate Court are fully consistent with the conclusions reached herein and disclose no legal infirmity warranting interference. Consequently, Writ Petition No.23651 of 2026 and Civil Revision No.23652 of 2026 are also dismissed. The judgments, decrees and orders impugned therein are affirmed. There shall, however, be no order as to costs.
( RAHEEL KAMRAN )
JUDGE
Announced in the Open Court on 31.08.2026.
JUDGE
Approved for reporting.
JUDGE
Azhar*

chunks.text:
Case: Crl. Misc.-Post-arrest Bail 5377-B-26 (RIAZ HUSSAIN VS STATE & 1 OTHER ).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Crl. Misc.-Post-arrest Bail 5377-B-26. Title: Crl. Misc.-Post-arrest Bail 5377-B-26 (RIAZ HUSSAIN VS STATE & 1 OTHER ). Official Ref: 2026LHC5349. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Tanveer Ahmad Sheikh. Judgment Date (as displayed): 28-08-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5349.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 7 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Form No: HCJD/C - 121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT,
MULTAN BENCH, MULTAN
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Cr iminal Misc ellaneous No. 5377 - B of 202 6 Riaz Hussain . Versus The State and another .
S.No. of order/ proceeding.
Date of order/ proceeding.
Order with signatures of Judge, and that of parties or counsel, where necessary.
20 . 0 8 .202 6 . Sardar Muhammad Akhtar Khan Leghari , Advocate for the petitioner .
Mr. Jamshaid Safdar, Advocate for the complainant.
Malik Ashfaq Ahmad, Deputy Prosecutor General with Khalid , S.I. The petitioner ( Riaz Hussain ), being arrayed as an accused in case F.I.R. No. 1101 of 2025, dated 15.11.2025, registered with Police Station Saddar Shujaabad, District Multan, for offence under Section 322 of PPC, seeks his post arrest bail, after the same was refused to him by the court of learned Magistrate Section 30, Shujaabad and then by the court of learned Additional Sessions Judge, Shujaabad, vide order dated
24.06.2026.
2. According to prosecution case as set
forth in the F.I.R. sons of Muhammad Shareef (complainant) namely Muhammad Abu Bakar and Ali Hamza were proceeding on motorcycle bearing registration No.3937-MNX along with their cousin namely Yasir and a friend Muhammad Amjad. Marriage of said Yasir was scheduled for the very next day. They Crl. Misc. No. 5377-B of 2026 2 were going on their left at Adda Nasir Mor at about 07.00 p.m. that a bus bearing registration No.6478-DGI coming negligently and rashly on wrong side collided with the motorcycle. All the four persons succumbed to the injuries at the very spot.
3. Learned counsel for petitioner ‘ while
canvassing for the bail ’ mainly focused on the points that petitioner was not nominated in the F.I.R. registered on 15.11.2025; he was introduced through supplementary statement got recorded by complainant on 23.12.2025, as such said infirmity alone was sufficient to bring the case with the purview of ‘further inquiry’; offence under Section 322 of PPC was not attracted to the case; from the bear perusal of the contents of FIR, the offence under Section 320 of PPC was made out, which was bailable; even otherwise offence under Section 322 of PPC was inviting the punishment only of Diyat as such was not hit by embargo contained under Section 497 of Cr.P.C., therefore, petitioner claims his release on bail as of right.
4. Conversely, the learned Deputy
Prosecutor General assisted by the learned counsel for complainant opposed present petition vehemently and rigorously on multiple grounds. Further added that since petitioner was not holding public service vehicle license, as such he was not authorized to drive the Bus, hence his act of driving, Crl. Misc. No. 5377-B of 2026 3 being illegal and unlawful, was fully covered by the mischief of Section 322 of PPC.
5. I have adhered to the submissions
made by all the concerned with utmost care.
In order to determine as to which of the penal provision of Section 320 PPC or 322 PPC would be attracted to the case, the combined study and critical analysis of the provisions of Sections 318, 319, 320, 321 and 322 is required. All the above said provisions are being reproduced below for the facility of reference:- Section 318. Qatl-i-khata. Whoever, without any intention to cause death of, or cause harm to, a person, causes death of such person either by mistake of act or by mistake of fact, is said to commit qatl-i-khata.
Section 319. Punishment for qatl-i-Khata.
Whoever commits qatl-i-khata shall be liable to diyat:
Provided that, where qatl-i-khata is committed by any rash or negligent act, other than rash or negligent driving, the offender may, in addition to diyat , also be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years as ta’zir .
Section 320. Punishment for qatl-i-khata by rash or negligent driving. Whoever commits qatl-i-khata by rash or negligent driving shall, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case, in addition to diyat , be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years.
Section 321. Qatl-bis-sabab. Whoever, without any intention to cause death of, or cause harm to, any person, does any unlawful act which becomes a cause for the death of another person, is said to commit qatl-bis-sabab .
Section 322. Punishment for qatl-bissabab. Whoever commits qatl-bis-sabab shall be liable to diyat.
Crl. Misc. No. 5377-B of 2026 4
6. Offence of qatl-i-khata has been
defined in Section 318 of PPC, which applies to a person, who causes the death of a person without any intention to kill or cause harm either by mistake of the act or mistake of the fact. Meaning thereby that the offence is committed inadvertently, without any intention or malice, but out of khata .
Offence of qatl-bis-sabab has been elaborated in Section 321 of PPC. It applies to a person who causes the death of other without any intention to kill by doing an unlawful act.
Intention or knowledge is not a “sine qua non” for the applicability of both the said offences.
7. The word “ unlawful act ” is of much
significance, which draws a line of demarcation between above said two offences.
I am of the confirmed view that when a person carrying a valid and effective license drives a vehicle and causes the death of a person by rash and negligent driving, his act would be covered by the offence of qatl-i-khata . He has no intention to kill, but his act of driving is lawful.
On the other hand where a person, not holding a license, or a valid/effective driving license causes the death of somebody by his rash or negligent driving, although he has also no intention to kill, but his act of driving is illegal and unlawful, therefore, his act Crl. Misc. No. 5377-B of 2026 5 squarely falls within the mischief of offence of “ qatl-bis-sabab ” and penal provisions of Section 322 of PPC shall be applicable to him.
8. It was borne out of the record that
petitioner was not named in the FIR registered on 15.11.2025. Certain persons Shakeel and Liaqat, owners of the Bus were joined in the investigation on 20.11.2025. They revealed in their statement under Section 161 of Cr.P.C. that petitioner was their driver and bus was handed over to him for driving.
Supplementary statement of complainant was recorded accordingly on 23.12.2025, nominating the petitioner. Name of the petitioner floated on the surface in the natural course of investigational steps. Circumstances were pointing accusing finger towards the petitioner. He failed to assign any malice or grudge on the part of complainant or owners of the vehicle to falsely involve him. Above delay in recording the statement of said persons cannot be resolved in favour of petitioner in any manner whatsoever.
9. In the case in hand, although
petitioner was holding HTV license, but he was not issued public service vehicle (PSV) license, which is required for driving the Bus.
“ Public service vehicle license ” is a special driving endorsement required to drive commercial passenger transport like van, coaster and bus. It is issued at least one year after holding LTV or HTV license with the minimum requirement of the age of 22-years.
Crl. Misc. No. 5377-B of 2026 6
10. It is matter of the record that
petitioner was not a holder of PSV license, therefore, he was not authorized to drive any public transport vehicle. A person driving the vehicle illegally/unlawfully puts not only his own life, but also life of the persons travelling with him as well as life of the public at risk.
Act of petitioner of driving the Bus could only be regarded as illegal and unlawful. It was also in flagrant violation of the provisions of Punjab Motor Vehicle Ordinance, 1965. Act of the petitioner triggered a crash causing a fatality and resulted into the death of four young boys, out of which marriage of a boy was scheduled for following day. Every sane person is presumed to know the consequences of his illegal/unlawful act or omission.
11. Offence of “ qatl-bis-sabab ”
punishable under Section 322 of PPC was inviting the punishment only of Diyat, but as per second schedule appended with Code of Criminal Procedure it was shown to be cognizable and non-bailable. Said provision was introduced following the amendment of Chapter XVI of the Pakistan Penal Code (Of offences affecting the human body) in 1990, which is manifesting the intention of legislature. The fact that it is punishable only with Diyat is not sufficient by itself for the release of an accused on bail, because each and every case has to be scrutinized in the light of its own surrounding circumstances. I Crl. Misc. No. 5377-B of 2026 7 have sought guidance from a case reported as ‘ Majid Nadeem Vs. The State and another ’ ( 2011 SCMR 1227 ), wherein five persons were crushed and done away with by rash and negligent driving of a car and post arrest bail was refused by apex Court.
12. Prima facie involvement of the
petitioner in the crime could not be ruled out.
There was even not an iota of the material suggesting that the case against him was requiring “ further inquiry ”. Circumstances appearing on the surface are presenting a dreadful picture. Act of petitioner was that of “extreme rash and negligent driving”, which neither can be condoned, nor discretionary powers can be exercised in his favour. I do not think it appropriate to allow this petition.
13. For what has been discussed above,
present petition has no force, hence dismissed .
14. Needless to mention that any
observation made in this order is tentative in nature and shall not influence the learned trial court in any manner.
(TANVEER AHMAD SHEIKH)
JUDGE
APPROVED FOR REPORTING.
JUDGE
* Shahzad Ahmad Nasir *

Case: Crl. Misc. 35608/26 (Muhammad Sarwar Vs The State etc).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Crl. Misc. 35608/26. Title: Crl. Misc. 35608/26 (Muhammad Sarwar Vs The State etc). Official Ref: 2026LHC5345. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Muhammad Amjad Pervaiz. Judgment Date (as displayed): 27-08-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5345.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 4 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Form No. HCJD/C - 121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT LAHORE
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Crl.Misc.No.35608-B of 2026 Muhammad Sarwar vs. The State and another.
Sr. No. of order/ proceedings Date of order/ proceedings.
Order with signatures of Judge, and that of parties or counsel, where necessary.
19.08.2026 Mr.Muhammad Abbas Ali Ansari, Advocate for the
petitioner.
Ch.Usman Ghani, Assistant Attorney General with Irfan SHO/FIA.
Through the instant petition under section 497 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Cr.P.C), the petitioner seeks bail after arrest in case FIR No.CCC-LHR- 20/2026 dated 02.03.2026 for offences under sections 489- B, 489-C P.P.C. registered at Police Station Corporate Crime Circle, Lahore (CCC).
2. As per contents of the F.I.R., the prosecution story,
precisely, is that pursuant to secret information regarding the involvement of a gang in the illegal business, possession and transportation of counterfeit Pakistani currency notes, a raiding team comprising officials of the F.I.A. apprehended the petitioner. Upon his personal search, counterfeit Pakistani currency notes amounting to Rs.200,000/- (200 notes of Rs.1,000/- denomination each) were allegedly recovered from his possession. It is further alleged that, at the time of his arrest, the petitioner confessed to counterfeiting of currency notes and sale thereof since last one year.
3. Arguments heard. Record perused.
4. At this stage of tentative assessment, it has been
observed that the raid has been conducted in pursuance of secret information and the petitioner was arrested at a busy public place yet no independent witness was associated during the proceedings. No evidence against the petitioner Crl.Misc.No.35608-B of 2026 is available on the record to support the allegations of counterfeiting currency notes or sale thereof in the market, except the above so-called confession which is inadmissible. There is no evidence as to any past or prospective buyer/customer. As of now, material available on record is not sufficient to attract the mischief of section 489-B P.P.C and the available evidence, at the most, makes out a case in terms of section 489-C P.P.C. In the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, the question of guilt of the petitioner qua the offence calls for further inquiry within the ambit of section 497(2) Cr.P.C, as per principles enunciated in various cases which are reproduced below.
Possession simpliciter of a counterfeit currency note does not constitute ingredients of section 489-B, P.P.C.
5. It is settled legal position that at the bail stage
deeper appreciation of the record cannot be gone into, but only a tentative assessment is to be made just to find out as to whether present applicants/accused are connected with the commission of offence or not. Applying the above settled legal position to the case in hand, it will be seen that prima facie ingredients of section 489-B, P.P.C. are not met in the circumstances of the case, but at best it can be a case of section 489-C, P.P.C. for which maximum punishment is prescribed to the extent of seven years or with fine or with both, which does not fall within the prohibitory clause of section 497, Cr.P.C.
6. It is for the learned trial Court to determine finally
whether provisions of sections 489-B or 489-C, P.P.C. are attracted in this case, of course, after recording evidence.
As of now, case against the petitioner calls for further enquiry falling within the ambit of section 497(2), Code of Criminal Procedure.).
1995, SCMR, 48, 1996 P Cr.LJ 815.
2012 YLR 1228
2021 SCMR 729
Crl.Misc.No.35608-B of 2026
7. It is since settled law that the benefit of doubt goes
to the accused even at bail stage.
The petitioner is behind the bars since his arrest. Nothing is to be recovered from him. In this case, evidence is documentary in nature which is already in possession of the prosecution and the question of tampering may not arise.
8. It is important to remember that bail is not to be
withheld as a punishment. There is no legal or moral compulsion to keep people in jail merely on the allegation that they have committed offences punishable with death or transportation, unless reasonable grounds appear to exist to disclose their complicity. The ultimate conviction and incarceration of a guilty person can repair the wrong caused by a mistaken relief of interim bail granted to him, but no satisfactory reparation can be offered to an innocent man for his unjustified incarceration at any stage of the case albeit his acquittal in the long run.
9. While dealing with the question of whether or not
bail is to be granted to an accused, it has to be kept in mind that the object of bail is to secure the attendance of the accused at the trial. The object is neither punitive nor preventive. Imprisonment of a person and deprivation of his liberty, cannot be described other than, being a punishment, unless no less restrictive alternative is available to ensure that the accused will stand his trial when called upon to do so. All civilized societies recognize the principle that punishment comes only after conviction, and the presumption of innocence subsist with the accused, till he is handed down punishment after trial.
10. Learned Law Officer has urged for refusal of bail to
the petitioner on the ground that further evidence may surface in the case of arrest of co-accused Muhammad Asif
PLD 1995 SC 34
2026 SCP 116
PLD 1972 SC 81
PLD 2020 SC 456
Crl.Misc.No.35608-B of 2026 yet to be arrested. Suffice it to say that surfacing of new facts and material tending to establish guilt of an accused is a valid ground to seek cancellation of bail.
11. For what has been discussed above, the instant
petition is accepted and the petitioner is admitted to post arrest bail subject to his furnishing bail bonds in the sum of Rs.1,00,000/- with one surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the learned trial court.
12. Before parting with this order, it is clarified that if
the petitioner or anyone else acting on his behalf, in any way, delays the conclusion of the trial, the other side (State or the complainant) shall be at liberty to file a petition for cancellation of bail.
13. It is also elucidated that the above observations are
tentative in nature only for the purpose of decision of this bail application and the same shall not influence the fate of the trial.
( Muhammad Amjad Pervaiz ) Judge Approved for reporting.
Judge M.J.Mehmood.
2020 SCMR 1115
2017 SCMR 1936
