Case: Crl. Misc.-Pre-arrest Bail-Under Section 498 Cr.PC 3115-B-26 (MUHAMMAD ISHFAQ ALIAS ISHTIAQ VS THE STATE ETC.).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Crl. Misc.-Pre-arrest Bail-Under Section 498 Cr.PC 3115-B-26. Title: Crl. Misc.-Pre-arrest Bail-Under Section 498 Cr.PC 3115-B-26 (MUHAMMAD ISHFAQ ALIAS ISHTIAQ VS THE STATE ETC.). Official Ref: 2026LHC5308. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Muhammad Usman Ghani Rashid Cheema. Judgment Date (as displayed): 24-08-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5308.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 5 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Form No: HCJD/C - 121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH C OURT
BAHAWALPUR BENCH, BAHAWALPUR
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Case No: Crl. Misc. No. 3115 - B of 2026 Muhammad Ishfaq @ Ishtiaq V ersus The State and another S.No. of order/ Proceeding Date of order/ Proceeding Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or counsel, where necessary .
19 . 08 . 2026
Mr. Muhammad Tariq Mahmood , Advocate with petitioner .
Mr. Javed Iqbal Bhayya, Assistant District Public Prosecutor alongwith Muhammad Abbas, SI.
Mr. Sohail Akhtar Alkara, Advocate for the complainant alongwith complainant in person .
Through this petition , under s ection 498 Cr.P.C. , the petitioner seek s pre - arrest bail in case FIR No. 130 / 2026 , dated 02 . 03 .2 026 , in respect of an offence under s ection 406 PPC , registered at Police Station City Haroonabad, District Bahawalnagar .
2 . At the very outset, learned counsel for the complainant alongwith complainant/Muneeb Alam states that the matter between the parties has been sorted out of Court and the complainant has no objection if ad - interim pre - arrest bail of the petitioner is confirmed. However, the learned ADPP has vehemently opposed this settlement and grant of b ail on basis thereof stating that offence of 406 PPC is not compoundable in nature and such a statement by the complainant does not amount to compounding of offence u/s 345 Cr.P.C. Hence, he requested that this bail petition be decided on merits and dismis sed in view of the facts of the case.
3 . Arguments heard and record perused with the able assistance of the counsel for the parties.
Crl.Misc.No. 3115 - B of 202 6 4 . F acts of this case, summarily, are that petitioner along co - ac c used took complainant’s motor car for temporary use but did not return the same, rather sold it to same one else.
Hence, he committed willful breach of trust , thus , this FIR.
5 . The above stance of the complainant brings to the fore the significance of an amicable settlement in the matter of bail, notwithstanding the non - compoundable character of the offence. Although an offence under section 406, PPC is non compoundable in nature , yet the factum of an amicable out of - Court settlement between the parties has consistently been regarded as a relevant circumstance while considering the question of bail, as such settlement tends to restore harmony between the parties and put an end to their hostility.
6 . Judicial notice has always been taken by the Courts where compromise / out of Court settlement was reached in ceases that were otherwise not compoundable. Reliance in this regard is placed on the case titled as “ Mukhtar Ahmad and 3 others vs. The State ” ( 1999 P.Cr.L.J. 1107 ), wherein paragraph No.4 reads as under:
“4. Unnatural offences as mentioned in section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code do not find mention in the table given in section 345, subsection (1) of the Criminal Procedure Code and, therefore, are not compoundable. Similarly, section 12 of the Offence of Zina (Enforcement of Hudood) Ordinance of 1979, (Ordinance No.VII of 1979) does not figure in the table mentioned under section 345, Cr.P.C. and, therefore, is not compoundable. However, the fact that the parties have themselves voluntarily forgotten and forgiven a certain crime and have entered into an outside Court settlement, may be considered as a ground for the grant of bail in the interest of justice and equity. If the comp lainant party is no longer willing to prosecute a matter any further then it is not for this Court or the Courts subordinate to it to compel the parties to do so, as the saying goes, "you can take the horse till the wate r but you cannot make him drink .” Crl.Misc.No. 3115 - B of 202 6 R eliance is also placed on “ Sohail Aslam vs. The State and another ” ( 2017 MLD 4 ), wherein, despite the allegations attracting non - bailable and non - compoundable offences, the complainant and the alleged victim had voluntarily forgiven the accused and suppo rted his plea for pre - arrest bail after an amicable settlement. This Court took into consideration their unequivocal no - objection, the apology tendered by the accused and the restoration of peaceful relations between the parties, and held that a voluntary out - of - Court settlement, though incapable of converting a non - compoundable offence into a compoundable one, could nevertheless constitute a relevant circumstance for grant of bail in the interest of justice and equity. Consequently, the ad - interim pre - arre st bail granted to the accused was confirmed.
Similar view has been taken by this Court in the cases titled as “ Muhammad Akram vs. The State ” ( 1995 MLD 1826 ) and “ Mst. Mussarat Elahi alias Bibi vs. The State ” ( 1997 P.Cr.L.J. 1193 ).
Another case, where compromise was effected in non compoundable case was appreciated by this Court is “ Shahid vs. The State and another ” ( 2017 YLR Note 81 ), where this Court was pleased to note the following: - “ Needless to say, compromise even in non comp oundable offences makes a crucial circumstance and a redeeming feature which helps the warring - parties come close to each other and live peacefully onwards. Let non - compoundable nature of the offences under sections 452, 354, P.P.C. not frustrate their nob le intentions. ” Crl.Misc.No. 3115 - B of 202 6 Most importantly, t he Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of “ Ghulam Ali v. The State and another ” ( 1997 SCMR 1411 ) also considered the factum of compromise in a non - compoundable offence and accepted the appeal while reducing the sentence of the accused.
7 . The principle that can safely be deduced from the above judicial pronouncements is that, notwithstanding the non - compoundable nature of an offence, an amicable settlement between the parties does not become altogether inconsequential while considering the question of bail.
Though such settlement cannot amount to compounding of the offence with in the contemplation of section 345, Cr.P.C., it may nevertheless be taken into consideration as a relevant circumstance in the exercise of judicial discretion, particularly where the complainant has voluntarily forgiven the accused, does not wish to pursu e the matter and raises no objection to the grant or confirmation of bail.
8 . In the present case, the complainant has appeared before this Court in person and categorically stated that the dispute has been amicably resolved outside the Court and that he h as no objection to the confirmation of ad - interim pre - arrest bail already granted to the petitioner. Therefore, while keeping the non - compoundable character of the offence intact and without expressing any opinion on the merits of the case, this Court hold s that the subsequent settlement between the parties and the unequivocal no objection extended by the complainant constitute relevant circumstances which can legitimately be taken into account for confirmation of the petitioner's pre - arrest bail.
9 . In vie w of the above - mentioned circumstances and without touching the merits of the case, this petition is allowed and the ad - interim pre - arrest bail already granted to Crl.Misc.No. 3115 - B of 202 6 the petitioner is confirmed , subject to his furnishing fresh bail bonds in the sum of Rs.1,00 ,000/ - (Rupees one lac only) with one surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the trial Court.
( Muhammad Usman Ghani Rashid Cheema ) Judge Waqas* Approved for Reporting Judge

chunks.text:
Case: Crl. Misc. 33563/26 (Muhammad Abbas Vs The State etc).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Crl. Misc. 33563/26. Title: Crl. Misc. 33563/26 (Muhammad Abbas Vs The State etc). Official Ref: 2026LHC5300. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Muhammad Amjad Pervaiz. Judgment Date (as displayed): 24-08-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5300.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 8 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Form No. HCJD/C - 121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT LAHORE
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Crl.Misc.No.33563-B of 2026 Muhammad Abbas vs. The State and another.
Sr. No. of order/ proceedings Date of order/ proceedings.
Order with signatures of Judge, and that of parties or counsel, where necessary.
20.08.2026 M/s Ijaz Ahmad Janjua and Saleem Ahmad Khan
Advocates for the petitioner.
Ch.Usman Ghani, Assistant Attorney General with Ayesha Masood SI/FIA.
Complainant with Mr.Junaid Sarvar, Advocate Through the instant petition under section 497 Cr.P.C., the petitioner seeks bail after arrest in case FIR No.1047 dated 31.12.2025 for offences under sections 17, 22 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1979 (hereinafter Ordinance) registered at Police Station FIA/AHTC, Lahore.
2. As per the contents of the FIR, the prosecution story,
precisely, is that in the year 2024, the petitioner, along with his co-accused, allegedly fleeced an amount of Rs.9,00,000/- from the complainant, partly in cash and partly through bank transactions, on the pretext of sending her abroad, i.e. to Muscat, Oman, for employment. However, neither was she sent abroad nor was the amount so received returned to her.
3. Arguments heard. Record perused.
4. Before I proceed to examine the case on merits, I am
constrained to first advert to a legal proposition which has arisen in this case during the course of arguments.
5. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that the
alternative punishments have been prescribed for offences under sections 17 and 22 of the Ordinance, hence, at bail stage lesser sentence is to be considered. He has placed reliance on Crl.Misc.No.33563-B of 2026 “ Messrs Askari Leasing Limited through Branch Manager vs.
Rana Muhammad Asif and 2 others ” ( 2005 P.Cr.L.J 1265 ), “ Muhammad Mustaqeem vs. The State ” ( 2004 YLR 68 ) and “ Hafiz Ahmad Khan vs. The State ” ( 1988 P Cr.LJ 338 ), “ Sohail Younas vs. The State and others ” ( 2015 P. Crl.LJ563 ) and “ Sohaib Ali Hashmat vs. The State and another ” ( 2025
MLD 925 ).
While concluding his arguments, learned counsel submitted that in cases of alternative punishment i.e.
imprisonment “or with fine”, the offence charged does not attract the mischief of prohibitory clause in terms of section 497 Cr.P.C.
6. On the other hand, learned Law Officer submits that
the above arguments are untenable in view of the principle enunciated by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Jabran’s case ( 2025 SCMR 199 ). He further submits that in view of the amendments introduced into various provisions of the Ordinance, including sections 17 and 22, the principle of alternative punishment is no more available in this case.
7. At this stage it is appropriate to reproduce ACT
No.VIII of 2025 (hereinafter Amendment Act), through which amendments have been brought into the Ordinance:- “ Whereas it is expedient further to amend the Emigration Ordinance, 1979(XVIII of 1979) for the purposes and in the manner hereinafter appearing; It is hereby enacted as follows:-
1. Short titled and commencement. (1) This Act shall be
called the Emigration (Amendment)Act, 2025
2. It shall come into force at once . (emphasis provided)
2. Amendment of Section 17, Ordinance XVIII of 1979 .
In the Emigration Ordinance, 1979 (XVIII of 1979), hereinafter referred to as the said Ordinance, in section 17, in sub-section (1), for the expression “, or with fine, or with both.” The words “and with fine up to one million rupees” shall be substituted. (underlining has been provided for emphasis) Crl.Misc.No.33563-B of 2026
3. Amendment of section 18, Ordinance XVIII of 1979.
In the said Ordinance,, in section 18, for the expression “, or with fine, or with both”, the words “ and with fine up to two million rupees” shall be substituted.
4 . Amendment of section 22, Ordinance XVIII of 1979 .
In the said ordinance, in section 22, for the expression “, or with fine, or with both” , the words “ and with fine up to two million rupees” shall be substituted. (emphasis supplied) As per sub-section 2 of section 1, the Amendment Act has come into force at once and without retrospective effect.
8. The simple question involved herein is as to whether
or not the provisions of the Amendment Act are applicable in this case wherein the occurrence has taken place prior to its promulgation.
Bare perusal of sections 2, 3 and 4 of the Amendment Act makes it clear that the punishment now prescribed is not alternative one as the expression “ or with fine ” has been substituted with the word “ and ” so it is clear that the amended provisions have authorized punishment for an offence by a penalty greater than or of different kind from, the penalty prescribed by law earlier. In this view of the matter, the above substitution attracts the protection against retrospective punishment guaranteed as fundamental right vide Article 12 Chapter 1 Part II of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (the Constitution). For ready reference same is reproduced hereunder:- “ Protection against retrospective punishment.
(1) No law shall authorize the punishment of a person:__
(a) for an act or omission that was not punishable by law at the time
of the act or omission; or
(b) for an offence by a penalty greater than, or of a kind different
from, the penalty prescribed by law for that offence at the time the offence was committed .
The scope of Article 12 of our Constitution and its principle has been matter of discussion by courts and jurists across Crl.Misc.No.33563-B of 2026 jurisdictions since ages, however, for the sake of brevity, I would hasten to rely upon recent pronouncement by Supreme Court of Pakistan in “ Anwar Saif Ullah Khan’s case (2026 SCP 129) is being reproduced hereunder:-
7. Article 12 is not a rule of convenience; it is a substantive
fundamental right enshrined in Chapter I of Part II of the Constitution. It embodies the ancient maxim “ nullum crimen, nulla poena sine lege praevia ”, no crime and no punishment without prior law. It also applies in a situation where, though it was previously a crime, but the punishment under the newly notified enactment was greater than the one provided in the previous law. As a non-derogable guarantee, it prohibits retrospective criminality and operates as an absolute bar on both the legislature and the courts. This principle is also reflected in Islamic jurisprudence. Allah Almighty states in the Qur’an: “ And We would never punish a people until We have sent a messenger to warn them” (17:15, Surah Al -Isra) . This establishes a foundational rule of justice: punishment is contingent upon prior communication of the law. Accordingly, retrospective punishment is impermissible, as liability of a specific charge arises only after the law has been enacted and duly conveyed. In practical terms, this means that individuals cannot be held accountable for actions committed before a relevant prohibition or obligation was imposed and consequently made known to them. This aligns with the broader legal maxim that there is no culpability without prior notice, typically ensured through publication in the official gazette, thereby safeguarding fairness and preventing arbitrary punishment. Although Section 2 of the NAO, 1999 purports to operate retrospectively from 01.01.1985, the decision of this Court in Asfandyar Wali v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2001 SC 607) establishes that Article 12 does not curtail the competence of the Legislature to enact laws having retrospective effect for all purposes, but it does prohibit, in the clearest possible terms, the imposition of criminal liability where, at the time of the act or omission, no offence or penalty existed in law, or where the later law seeks to impose a punishment greater in degree or different in kind from that which was prescribed when the offence was allegedly committed. The distinction is constitutional, not merely technical. A legislature may declare the general applicability of a statute to earlier periods; it may not, however, do so where the effect would be to fasten criminal guilt retrospectively. The moment the retrospective clause of a penal statute encounters the Article 12 barrier, the clause must yield and the barrier must prevail.” The above interpretation has been made by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in a Criminal Review Petition. Now the question is as to whether or not, the above principle is applicable in bail matters, the same has been answered in “ Sajjad Ha ider’s case Crl.Misc.No.33563-B of 2026 (2026 SCP 54), relevant portion whereof is reproduced hereunder:- “W e have heard the learned counsels for the parties and gone through the record in depth. In order to avoid unnecessary repetition, we have incorporated and addressed the submissions and contentions raised during the course of arguments throughout the ensuing discussion and analysis within this judgment. At the very outset, we have noted that the main offence for which the petitioners have been nominated is section 23 of the Act of 1947 where the offence is currently punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years or with fine or with both. It is relevant to state here that previously the punishment for the said offence was simple imprisonment extendable up to two years or fine or both and the same was amended in the year 2020 through the Act No. X of 2020 w.e.f.
27.02.2020. The date of occurrence as per FIR is year
2007-2015 which is before the ibid amendment of 2020.
As per the protections guaranteed by the Article 12 of the Constitution of Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (“ The Constitution ”), no law shall authorize the punishment of a person for an offence by a penalty greater than, or of' a kind different from, the penalty prescribed by law for that offence at the time the offence was committed. At a glance, protection against retrospective punishment as provided in Article 12 of the Constitution might appear as a notion dealing with procedural requirement, however it not as such. Article 12 of the Constitution does not state any procedural requirement of ordinary course rather it is one of the fundamental rights and highly guarded substantive right which is not to be taken lightly. This doctrine concerning ex post facto laws is well recognized in almost all jurisdictions with respect to administration of criminal justice. As per well recognized legal encyclopedia of American law i.e. Corpus Juris Secundum!, an ex post facto law is one which makes criminal and punishes an act which was done before the passage of the law and which was innocent when done, aggravates a crime or makes it greater than it was when committed, changes the punishment and inflicts a greater punishment than was prescribed when the crime was committed, or alters the legal rules of evidence and receives less or different testimony than was required to convict at the time the offence was committed. Further, an ex post facto law may be one which, assuming to regulate civil rights and remedies only, in effect imposes a penalty or the deprivation of a right for something which, when done, was lawful, deprives persons accused of crime of some lawful protection or defence previously available to them, such as the protection of a former conviction or acquittal, or of a proclamation of amnesty, or, generally, in relation to the offence or its consequences, alters the situation of an accused to his material disadvantage. Protection against such penal legislation is also provided by the Convention for the Crl.Misc.No.33563-B of 2026 Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms which was signed by members of the Council of Europe in 1950, and later ratified by the United Kingdom. The convictions and sentences to be recorded in the criminal jurisdiction under ex post facto law are also prohibited under Article 12 of the Constitution and well recognized by this court in its various judgments.
The benefit of the said interpretation must also be extended to an accused not only at the stage of trial but also at the stage of bail . Clearly, in the instant case, the offence was allegedly committed at the time between years 2007 and 2015, therefore, the punishment for the offence under section 23 ibid would be considered as two years or fine or both”
9. In view of the above enunciation of principle of law,
there is no manner of doubt that the constitutional protection against retrospective punishment at the anvil of Article 12 of the Constitution is available to the petitioner. Hence, the provisions of Amendment Act are not applicable in this case as the occurrence took place in the year 2024.
10. Now I proceed to examine the facts and merits of the
case tentatively to find out as to whether any case of bail after arrest is made out or not. It evinces that the F.I.R. in this case has been lodged with a delay of about one year. No time, date and place of alleged payment is mentioned in the F.I.R. There is no documentary proof of any payment to the petitioner. As per affidavit of Nasir Iqbal who is a prosecution witness, the alleged amount was paid to co-accused Iftikhar (since P.O).
The petitioner was arrested on 03.03.2026. His physical custody was remanded to the investigating officer but no incriminating material has been recovered from him. There is no evidence that the petitioner is beneficiary, so the question of guilt of the petitioner qua the alleged occurrence, at this stage, calls for further probe within the ambit of sub-section 2 of section 497 Cr.P.C. The investigation to the extent of the petitioner is complete and he is no more required for further investigation. His further incarceration would not serve any useful purpose rather, the same would amount to punishment before trial. It is settled law that bail cannot be withheld as Crl.Misc.No.33563-B of 2026 punishment. Reliance in this regard is placed upon “ Manzoor and 4 other v. State ” ( PLD 1972 SC 81 ), relevant portion whereof is reproduced hereunder:- “ It is important to remember that bail is not to be withheld as a punishment. There is no legal or moral compulsion to keep people in jail merely on the allegation that they have committed offences punishable with death or transportation, unless reasonable grounds appear to exist to disclose their complicity. The ultimate conviction and incarceration of a guilty person can repair the wrong caused by a mistaken relief of interim bail granted to him, but no satisfactory reparation can be offered to an innocent man for his unjustified incarceration at any stage of the case albeit his acquittal in the long run.”
11. The object of bail has been elaborated by the
Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in Khawaja Salman ’s case ( PLD 2020 SC 456 ), relevant portion whereof is reproduced hereunder:- “ While dealing with the question of whether or not bail is to be granted to an accused, it has to be kept in mind that the object of bail is to secure the attendance of the accused at the trial.
The object is neither punitive nor preventive. Imprisonment of a person and deprivation of his liberty, cannot be described other than, being a punishment, unless no less restrictive alternative is available to ensure that the accused will stand his trial when called upon to do so. All civilized societies recognize the principle that punishment comes only after conviction, and the presumption of innocence subsist with the accused, till he is handed down punishment after trial. It hardly needs any reiteration that the detention either pre-trial or during trial causes great hardship.”
12. Since the bail in this case has been granted in terms of
sub-section 2 of Section 497 Cr.P.C. I beg to be pardoned for venturing the opinion as to whether or not a case of alternative punishments would attract the mischief of prohibitory clause.
13. For what has been discussed above, this petition is
allowed and the petitioner is admitted to post arrest bail subject to his furnishing bail bonds in the sum of Rs.2,00,000/with one surety in the like amount to the satisfaction of the learned trial court.
Crl.Misc.No.33563-B of 2026
14. Before parting with this order, it is clarified that if the
petitioner or anyone else acting on his behalf, in any way, delays the conclusion of the trial, the other side (State or the complainant) shall be at liberty to file a petition for cancellation of bail under Section 497(5) Cr.P.C. before the learned trial court.
(Muhammad Amjad Pervaiz) Judge Approved for reporting.
Judge M.J.Mehmood

chunks.chunkTitle: Case: Service 6323/26 (Shafique Khushnood Vs MS General Hospital etc.).

Case: Service 6323/26 (Shafique Khushnood Vs MS General Hospital etc.).
Court: Lahore High Court, Lahore. Case No: Service 6323/26. Title: Service 6323/26 (Shafique Khushnood Vs MS General Hospital etc.). Official Ref: 2026LHC5289. Author Judge: Mr. Justice Malik Muhammad Awais Khalid. Judgment Date (as displayed): 19-08-2026. Record Type: FULL_TEXT_VERBATIM (complete judgment text extracted from the official court PDF). Source URL: https://sys.lhc.gov.pk/appjudgments/2026LHC5289.pdf. Verified: 2026-09-06 against the official court repository.
VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 11 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Stereo. H C J D A 38 Judgment Sheet
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
W.P . No. 6323 of 20 2 6 Shafique Khushnood .
Vs.
Medical Superintendent , Lahore General Hospital Lahore and two others .
JUDGMENT
Date of Hearing 20 . 5 .2026 Petitioner by M/s Sardar Ali Kamboh and Rai Riaz Ahmad Kharal , Advocate s .
Respondent s by Ch. Awais Ahmad Qazi, Addl. Advocate General & Mr. Faisal Nawaz, Legal Advisor for respondents.
MALIK MUHAMMAD AWAIS KHALID , J . T he petitioner has filed instant constitutional petition with the following prayer: - “ It is, therefore, most respectfully prayed that this writ petition may kindly be accepted and the impugned office order No.PF/ 468586 4 /LGH dated 24.7.2024 issued by the respondent No.2/Addl: Medical Sup erintendent, Lahore General Hospital, Lahore and impugned order No.PF/63503 dated 19.9.2024 passed by respondent No.1/Medical Superintendent, Lahore General Hospital, Lahore may kindly be set aside and the petitioner may graciously be reinstated in the ser vice with all back benefits, in the interest of justice.
2. Succinctly, the facts of the case are that
petitioner was serving as Security Guard (BS - 01/Permanent Basis) BOM created post in Lahore General Hospital, Lahore and has been performing his duties honestly and diligently . Thereafter, show cause notice W.P . No. 6323 / 20 2 6 2 No.PF/45035/LGH dated 15.7.2024 was issued to the petitioner by respondent No.2 while the inquiry was dispensed with. The petitioner submitted reply wherein he denied the allegations leveled aga inst him but respondent No.2 without conducting regular inquiry and providing opportunity of hearing, terminated his service vide order dated 24.7.2024. Feeling aggrieved, petitioner preferred departmental appeal before respondent No.1 which was dismi ssed vide order dated 19.9.2024. The appeal filed by the petitioner before Punjab Service Tribunal, Lahor e, was dismissed being not appropriate forum vide order dated
13.1.2026. Hence, this writ petition.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that
im pugned orders have been passed unlawfully and without mentioning any reason therein by the respondents; the word termination is alien to law; conducting of regular inquiry was dispensed with by the responden t - department against Article 10A of the Constitution of the Is lamic Republic of Pakistan 1973 (The Constitution).
4. Learned Law Officer and learned Legal Advisor
for respondent - department have opposed the petition on the ground that impugned orders have been passed quite in accordance with law and justifiable reasons.
5 . Arguments heard. Record perused.
6 . The allegation leveled against the petitioner was that he was c aught red handed while stealing A.C. pipes in W.P . No. 6323 / 20 2 6 3 ortho ward of Lahore General Hospital, Lahore on 0 1.5.2024 at 4:30 A.M. and remaine d absent from duty w.e.f. 15.6.2024 to 22.7.2024. Show cause notice was issued to the petitioner under section 7(b) read with Sections 5(1)(a) of Punjab Employees Efficiency Discipline & Accountability Act, 2006 ( the Act) with the direction to submit reply. The petitioner submitted his reply to the show cause notice with the contention that at about 4:30 a.m. night security supervisor called him that towards ortho ward someone was cutting A.C. pipe, he visited the s pot but no body was found there ; he was not absent from duty. Learned counsel for the petitioner took the stance that inquiry against the petitioner was dispensed with without mentioning any reason. Perusal of show cause notice depicts that no cogent and justifia ble reason has been enunciated therein for dispensing with inquiry.
Relevant portion is reproduced as under: - “AND WHEREAS, the undersigned is of the opinion that it is not necessary to hold an inquiry into the matter in view of the provision contained in section 5(1) (a) of the PEEDA Act 2006, therefore, proposed to proceed against you under Section 7(b) read with section 5(1)(a) of P EEDA Act, 2006 may not be imposed upon you. ” On the face of it , no reason has been mentioned by the competent authority in the show cause notice to dispense with the inquiry but has proceeded against the petitioner only on the basis of opinion which is unwarranted under law. With regard to absence of the petitioner, l earned W.P . No. 6323 / 20 2 6 4 counsel for the petitioner has produced copy of attendance register for the months of June and July 2024 which is apparently showing attendance of the petitioner on most of the dates. Complaint was filed against the petitioner by night supervisor Ra na Zeeshan on the pretext that there was theft of A.C. pipe of ortho ward of the hospital on
1.5.2024. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that
incident took place on 1.5.2024 but show cause notice was issued against the petitioner on 15.7.2024 with the delay of more than two months. It is important to note w hen the petitioner has denied the allegations levelled against him, right of confrontation is provided under Articles 4 & 10A of the Constitution and further u/s 10 of the Act , right of cross - exa mination is available to the petitioner to prove his innocence but denied arbitrarily . Authenticity or otherwise of the disputed facts cannot be considered without conducting a fair regular inquiry. Hon’ble Supreme Court in case s of Arbab and others Vs. Province of Sindh through Secretary Health Department and others ( 2026 SCMR 300 ) and The Vice - President (Admin.), National Bank of Pakistan and others Vs. Basharat Ali and others ( 1996 SCMR 201) held that paramount object of framing of the rules and enactment to provide a fair and reasonable opportunity to an employee to defend himself against the charge brought against him by his employer in order to ensure adherence of the principles of natural justice. The W.P . No. 6323 / 20 2 6 5 Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakist an in the case of Saad Salam Ansari Vs. Chief Justice of Sindh High Court, Karachi through Registrar (2007 SCMR 1726) held as under: - “The appellant has been subjected to a major penalty terminating his service prematurely. The spirit of the law namely PEE DA Act, 2006 is that such terminal punitive action against a civil servant should be taken after an inquiry has been conducted. In the present case, whether the appellant had a satisfactory explanation for his absence for the period mentioned in the show - c ause - notice has not been attended by the respondents. It is a matter upon which an opportunity to record evidence ought to have been granted. Likewise, the availability of documentary evidence, if any, with the respondents that justified dispensation of an inquiry ought to have been disclosed/confronted to the appellant.
In the absence thereof, we find that the impugned punishment has been imposed upon the appellant without complying with the provisions of the law.” The allegation of mis - conduct levelled against the delinquent could not be proved without conducting regular inquiry especially when major penalty is going to be imposed. The purpose for initiation of disciplinary proceeding is to find out whether charges of misconduct are proved or not and in case his guilt is established, what action should be taken against him under the applicable rules which may include the imposition of penalties minor or major. Reliance is placed on the case of Chief Engineer, Gujranw ala Electric Power Company (GEPCO) Gujranwala Vs.
Khalid Mehmood and others (2023 SCMR 291) wherein it has been held as under: - W.P . No. 6323 / 20 2 6 6 “ The allegations of dishonesty, corruption and negligence levelled against the respondent No.1 could not be proved without regul ar inquiry. The astuteness of triggering of disciplinary proceedings by the employer is to find out whether the charges of misconduct levelled against the delinquent are proved or not and, in case his guilt is established, what action should be taken again st him under the applicable Service laws which may include the imposition of minor or major penalties. There is no rigid or definitive rule that in each and every case after issuing show cause notice a regular inquiry should be conducted, but if the department aspires to dispense with the regular inquiry due to some compelling circumstances or exigency, then justifiable reasons should be assigned in writing before dispensing with the regular inquiry. No doubt if a charge is set up or stems from admitted doc uments, no full - fledged regular inquiry is obligatory, but if the allegations are based on disputed questions of facts, then obviously the employee cannot be denied a right of regular inquiry, specifically where the allegations cannot be resolved without l eading evidence and providing a fair opportunity to the parties to cross examine the witnesses. ” Further reliance can safely be placed on the case of Naseeb Khan Vs. Divisional Superintendent, Pakistan Railways, Lahore and another (2008 SCMR 1369) where in it has been observed as follows: - “ In case of imposing a major penalty, the principle of natural justice requires that a regular enquiry is to be conducted in the matter and opportunity of defence and personal hearing is to be provided to the civil servan t proceeded against as held by this Court in the case of Pakistan International Airlines Corporation v. Ms.
Shaista Naheed 2004 SCMR 316 and Inspector - General of Police, Karachi and 2 others v. Shafqat Mehmood 2003 SCMR
2007.
6. Keeping in v iew the facts and
circumstances of the case, we find that petitioner has been condemned unheard and major penalty of dismissal from service has been imposed upon him W.P . No. 6323 / 20 2 6 7 without adopting the required and mandatory procedure, resulting in manifest injustice. ” T he allegation s levelled in the show cause notice issued against the petitioner on the face of it could not be proved against the petitioner without proper inquiry and without providing an opportunity to adduce evidence not only to the complainant but also to the delinquent employee enabling him to defend against the charges, produce witnes s in order to prove his innocence as well as to avail the right to cross - examine the witnesses produced against him.
7. It is also pertinent to mention that in this
matt er the competent authority imposed major penalty of termination from service upon the petitioner whereas disciplinary proceedings were initiated under the Act and show cause notice was also issued under the said Act. The impugned order of the termination of the petitioner from service is alien to the Act. The Section 4 of the Act de scribes the penalties which is reproduced as under: - “ 4. Penalties. - (1) The competent authority may, notwithstanding anything contained in any law or the terms and conditions of service of the accused, by an order in writing, impose one or more of the following penalties, namely: -
a) Minor penalties -
(i) censure;
(ii) withholding of increment or
increments, for a specific period, subject to a maximum of five years; W.P . No. 6323 / 20 2 6 8
(iii) (iii) fine not exceeding basic
pay of one month;
(iv) (iv) reduction to a lower stage
or stages in pay scale, subject to a maximum of five stages; and
(v) wit hholding of promotion for a
specific period, subject to a maximum of five years; provided that this period shall be counted from the date when a person junior to the accused is considered for promotion and is promoted on regular basis for the first time;
(b) Major penalties –
(i) recovery from pay, pension or
any other amount payable to the accused, the whole or a part of any pecuniary loss caused to the Government or the organization in which he was employed, and if the amount due from any such person c annot be wholly recovered from the pay, pension or any other amount payable to him, such amount shall be recovered under the law for the time being in force;
(ii) reduction to a lower post and
pay scale from the substantive or regular post for a specific period subject to a maximum of five years;
(iii) forfeiture of past service for a
specific period subject to a maximum of five years;
(iv) compulsory retirement;
(v) removal from service; and
(vi) dismissal from service; and
(c) Penalties after retirement -
(i) withholding of pension or any
part thereof; (ii) withdrawing of pension or any part thereof; and (iii) recovery from pension or any other amount payable to the accused, of pecuniary loss caused to Government or the organization in which he was employed, an d if the amount due from any such person cannot be wholly recovered from the pension or any other amount payable to him, such amount shall be recovered under the law for the time being in force.
(ii) Dismissal from service under
this Ac t shall disqualify the employee for future W.P . No. 6323 / 20 2 6 9 employment under the Government or under any organization to which the pr ovisions of this Act apply.
PEED A Act, 2006 (iii ) Any penalty under this Act shall not absolve an employee or accused from liability to any punishment to which he may be liable for an offence, under any law, committed by him while in service.
Perusal of section ibid reveals that word ‘ termination ’ is not included in the Act rather , word dismiss , remove or compulsory retirement has been provided . The imposition of major penalty of ‘ termination from service’ is void being absent in the list pro vided by the Act , as show cause notice was issued to the petitioner under section 7 of the Act .
8. The principles of natural justice require that
delinquent should be given fair opportunity to contest charges levelled against him before he is found guilty.
No person is unjustly penalized without being given opportunity to present his complete defence, t herefore, impugned orders are against the principle of due process and transparency. Reliance is placed on the case of The Government of Balochistan, through Secretary Energy Department, Quetta and another Vs.
Muhammad Yasir (2025 SCMR 367) wherein it has been observed as follows:
“This action was in sheer contravention of Article 10 - A of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 ("Constitution"), and lacked due process of law. To enjoy the protection of law and to be treated in accordance with the W.P . No. 6323 / 20 2 6 10 law is a basic fundamental right of every citizen within the precincts ad confines of Article 4 of the Constitution which, in fact, assimilates the doctrine of equal protection of law and accentuates that no action detrimental to life and liberty can be taken without due process.” Reliance is also placed on the case of Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa through Secretary Elementary and Secondary, Education Department Peshawar and others Vs. Aurangzeb (Ex - Pr imary School Head Teacher) GPS W anna Khel Tehsil Takhtbhai District Mardan (deceased through L.Rs. (2025 SCMR 40) wherein it has been held as under: - “In our considered view, the allegations jotted down in the show cause notice, on the face of it, could not be proved without proper inquiry a nd without providing an opportunity to adduce evidence not only to the complainants but also to the delinquent employee for him to be able to defend himself against the charges, produce witnesses, if any, to prove his innocence, as well as avail the right to cross - examine the witnesses adducing against him. On the contrary, the competent authority imposed the major penalty of compulsory retirement from service upon the delinquent employee on the basis of a show cause notice alone, without following the prin ciple of natural justice and due process enunciated under the law.” The appellate authority also passed the impugned order in mechanical manner hence arbitrary in nature .
Respondents in a stereotype and perfunctory manner proceeded against the petitioner and imposed him major penalty of termination from service which is not warranted under law . While dispensing with the regular W.P . No. 6323 / 20 2 6 11 inquiry, logical reasons must be mentioned by the competent authority but in this case inq uiry has been dispensed with in a whimsical manner . The punishment awarded to the petitioner is in violation of Article s 4 & 10 - A of the Constitution and Section 4 of the Act. The impugned order s suffer from illegality hence, calling for interference by th is Court.
9 . As a sequel of above discussion , impugned orders are set aside and the petitioner is reinstated into service. The competent authority may order to conduct a regular i nquiry on the allegations leveled against the petitioner , under law and is directed to decide the issue of back benefits of the petitioner.
10 . The upshot of above discussion, instant writ petition is partly allowed in above terms.
( Malik Muhammad Awais Khalid )
JUDGE
Approved for reporting.
Judge Naeem*

VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 4 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Form No. HCJD/C - 121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT
MULTAN BENCH MULTAN
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT
Crl.Misc. No.5827 - B of 2026 Muhammad Akhta r & another. Vs. The State & another.
Sr. No. of order/ proceedings.
Date of order/ proceedings.
Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or counsel, where necessary.
17 .08.2026 Mr. Majeed Akbar Lodhi, Advocate for t he petitioners.
Rana Ghulam Hussain, Assistant Attorney General for Pakistan with M. Zeeshan Riaz, S.H.O, F.I.A. Through instant petition , the petitioners, namely Muhammad Akhtar and Muhammad Ansar, seek post - arrest bail in FIR No. 12/26 dated 04.07. 2026, registered under Sections 409, 420, and 109 PPC at Police Station FIA, District D.G. Khan .
2 . The allegations against the petitioners, namely Muhammad Akhtar and Muhammad Ansar (petitioners ) , in the FIR and from the evidentiary material collected during the course of the investigation produced before the Court, are that they both were involved in receiving various amounts from the beneficiaries of the Ehsaas Kafalat Program (BISP Scheme) for the release of amounts in their name s , and were also involved with an HBL Konnect biometric device and an Infinix mobile phone, retaining the Computerized Nati onal Identity Cards (CNICs) of the beneficiaries.
3 . I have heard the arguments of the learned counsel for the petitioners, the learned Assistant Attorney General for Pakistan in the presence of the complainant/investigating officer, and perused the record with theirable assistance.
4 . The petition in ha nd is a post - arrest bail petition, and only a tentative assessment of the evidentiary material produced before the Court can be made at this stage. In the FIR itself, it is mentioned that Crl.Misc.No.5827 - B of 2026 2 “ at the time of raid, two agents standing inside Ansar Mobile who we re intercepted were taking CNICs of the beneficiaries and a commission amount of Rs. 1,000 from ladies who came there to receive their amount) from each of the beneficiaries of the Ehsaas Kafalat Program (BISP Scheme ” . No allegations have been made against the petitioners that they were entrusted with any amount by any of the beneficiaries and that they then dishonestly misappropriated the same. When there is no allegation that they were entrusted with any amount by the beneficiaries, and the allegations are merely that they retained Rs. 1,000 out of the total amount which they handed over to each beneficiary of the Ehsaas Kafalat Program (BISP Scheme), then the case of the petitioners becomes one of cheating and not crim inal breach of trust.
Obviously, the offense of cheating is bailable in nature as per Schedule II of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898.
Therefore, an outward effort has been made by the investigating officer of the case to convert the offense of cheating into criminal breac h of trust, disregarding the narrative of the FIR as well as the statements recorded of the witnesses. In this backdrop, the culpability of the petitioners as to whether they were privy to the crime would be determined by the learned trial court after the recording of evidence. The petitioners were arrested in the case on 04.07.2026 and have since been behind the bars. Based on the particular facts and circumstances of the case, where there are no allegations that the petitioners would abscond or interfere with the witnesses, ke eping the petitioners behind bars would serve no useful purpose. It is not the prosecution's case that the petitioners are withholding any official record , or that the agents of a bank in whose name any machine/biometric apparatus was issued are withholdin g it. The relevant record and the evidence collected during the investigation are with the prosecution, and therefore, there is no Crl.Misc.No.5827 - B of 2026 3 question of tampering with the evidence. For what has been discussed above, case of the petitioners becomes one of further in quiry under Section 497 (2) Cr.P.C. Liability of petitioners for the offences would be determined by the learned trial court after sifting the evidentiary worth of the material produced before the same. Reliance in this regard in place on “Saeed Ahmed vs. The State” (1996 SCMR 1132) wherein it has been held as under: - “The learned counsel for the petitioner contended that there is no prohibition for grant of bail in respect of offences mentioned above, but with malafide intention subsequently offence under se ction 409 PPC .
The case entirely depends upon documentary evidence which seems to be in possession of the prosecution and challan has already been submitted. The objection of the learned counsel regarding addition of section 409, PPC may carry some weight while considering the bail, application. As there is no possibility of tampering with the evidence, which is entirely documentary in nature and in possession of the prosecution, in the circumstances, we convert the petition into an appeal and allow it, and grant bail to the petitioner on furnishing one surety in the sum of Rs.50,000/ - to the satisfaction of the Deputy Registrar, Supreme Court, Lahore.” Reliance is also placed on the case of “Muhammad Nawaz vs. The State through Chairman, NAB, Islamabad and another” (PLD 2008 SC 438). It has been observed by the Honorable Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Manzoo r and 4 others versus The State (PLD 1972 SC 81) as under: - “ It is important to remember that bail is not to be withheld as a punishment there is no legal or moral compulsion to keep people in jail merely on the allegation that they have committed offences punishable with death or transportation, unless reasonable g rounds appear to exist to disclose their complicity. ” Crl.Misc.No.5827 - B of 2026 4 In the reported case “ Muhammad Saeed Mehdi vs. The State and 2 others ” (2002 SCMR 282), it was observed that bail cannot be withheld as punishment in cases of non - bailable offence against the accused a nd that the basic idea was to enable the accused to answer the criminal prosecution against him rather than to make him not behind bars. In the same case, the apex Court observed that truth or otherwise of the allegation could only be determined at the tri al after analysis of evidence that might be adduced by the parties. Further reliance is place upon the case reported as Muhammad Sarfraz Ansari v. The State and others ( PLD 2021 Supreme Court 738 ) , wherein Honorable Supreme Court held as under:
“ We are ful ly cognizant of the well - settled principle that at the bail stage the court is not to make deeper examination and appreciation of the evidence collected during investigation or to conduct anything in the nature of preliminary trial to determine the accused ’s guilt or innocence. ” 5 . For what has been discussed above, this petition is accepted and petitioners are admitted to post - arrest bail subject to their furnishing bail bonds in the sum of Rs.1,00,000/ - (one lac only) each with two sureties each in t he like amount to the satisfaction of the learned trial court.
6 . It is clarified that the observations enumerated are absolutely tentative in nature and restricted only to the extent of this particular petition, having no nexus and relevance with the tr ial, which shall be concluded quite independently and purely on merit.
(SYED FARHAD ALI SHAH)
JUDGE
Approved for reporting .
JUDGE
Subhani *

VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 4 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
Form No: HCJD/C - 121
ORDER SHEET
IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE
( JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT )
Case No. Crl. Misc. No. 46375 - CB /20 26 Masood Aslam Versus The State, etc.
S r . No. of order / Proceedings Date of order / Proceedings Order with signatures of Judge, and that of parties or counsel, where necessary.
12.08.202 6 Ch. Tariq Mehmood, Advocate for the petitioner.
=====
This criminal miscellaneous has been filed in terms of Section 497(5) Cr.P.C. by the petitioner/complainant Masood Aslam for seeking cancellation of pre-arrest bail granted to respondent No.2 vide order dated 30.06.2026 passed by learned Addl. Sessions Judge, Lahore in case FIR No.506/2026 dated 14.05.2026, for offence under Section 406 PPC, registered at Police Station, Mozang Lahore.
2. As per contents of the FIR, the prosecution
story precisely is that the respondent borrowed car bearing registration No.KY-4443 from the complainant on 28.11.2025 for ten days in order to attend a marriage ceremony and later on, he did not return the same. He initially lingered on the matter for one pretext or another and ultimately refused to return it.
3. Arguments heard. Record perused.
4. For ready reference, the operative paragraph
of the order impugned is reproduced as under:- ‘ a) Alongwith police record, as well as bail petition of the petitioner, attested copies of suit for declaration, specific performance with permanent injunction along with consequential relief, titled "Muhammad Akram Khokhar Vs. Masood Aslam & another", alongwith order sheet of the Learned Civil court, regarding subject vehicle is attached according Crl. Misc. No.46375-CB/2026 2 to which petitioner filed the said suit on 18.02.2026, with the assertions that he purchased the subject vehicle from the complainant against the price of Rs.75,00,000/- and possession was also delivered to him, in the said suit, complainant appeared before Learned Civil court on 05.03.2026 and requested adjournment for written statement and written reply, on 21.04.2026, ex-parte proceedings were initiated against the complainant, on 11.05.2026, complainant filed application for setting aside the ex-parte proceedings, which was accepted on the statement of learned counsel for the plaintiff of the said suit, complainant filed the written statement in the suit on
11.05.2026, while taking the stance that petitioner
borrowed the subject vehicle for ten days for attending family function at Sargodha, but fraudulently retained the vehicle.
(b) The above referred two different versions of the
parties, to be determined by the learned Trial Court, during the trial regarding the constitution of offence of criminal breach of trust U/s 406 PPC.
c) Complainant didn't get register the FIR of this
case, after ten days from 28.11.2025, rather he got registered the instant FIR on 15.05.2026, after delay of about more than six months, that too after the submission of written statement in the above referred civil suit, which was submitted on 11.05.2026. It means that the complainant had got registered the instant FIR after due deliberation, consultation and after getting legal advice. This fact is creating a doubt in the case of complainant, regarding which petitioner is entitled for benefit of doubt, at bail stage.
d) Malice and malafide of the complainant
could not rule out that he implicated the petitioner for some ulterior motive, as a counter blast of the above referred civil suit.
e) All the above referred facts are establishing
case of further inquiry, at pre-arrest bail stage, regarding the involvement of the petitioner in this case.’ Crl. Misc. No.46375-CB/2026 3
5. The considerations for the grant of bail and
for cancellation of the same are altogether different. Once the bail is granted by a Court of competent jurisdiction, then strong and exceptional grounds would be required for cancellation thereof.
Sami Ullah ’s case has articulated the grounds to invoke and exercise jurisdiction in terms of the Section 497(5) Cr. PC. as under; Para
5…..
i) If the bail granting order is patently illegal,
erroneous, factually incorrect and has resulted into miscarriage of justice.
ii) That the accused has misused the concession of bail in any manner.
iii) That accused has tried to hamper prosecution evidence by persuading/pressurizing prosecution witnesses.
iv) That there is likelihood of absconsion of the accused beyond the jurisdiction of court.
v) That the accused has attempted to interfere with the
smooth course of investigation.
vi) That accused misused his liberty while indulging into similar offence.
vii) That some fresh facts and material has been collected during the course of investigation with tends to establish guilt of the accused. ’
6. The above view is being consistently
followed, in addition thereof, it has also been enunciated in Rab Nawaz’s case that the principles evolved for examining the bail granting order for purposes of its cancellation are that the Court shall interfere on two grounds i) the impugned order is perverse on the face of it and
PLD 1995 SC 34
2020 SCMR 1115
2025 SCMR 1357
Crl. Misc. No.46375-CB/2026 4
(ii) the case has been decided in clear disregard of
the settled principles of law .
7. Learned counsel for the petitioner was heard
at great length, who argued his cause well but could not demonstrate that any of the grounds mentioned above are attracted in this case. The order impugned is neither perverse nor factually incorrect, nor is it in disregard of any settled principle of law.
8. In view of the foregoing reasons, this Court
is not inclined to interfere with the impugned order, and thus, the petition in hand, being bereft of merit, is hereby dismissed in limine .
( Muhammad Amjad Pervaiz ) Judge Approved for R eporting .
JUDGE
Asif *

Through this Constitutional Petition filed under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, the petitioner has called in question the legality and propriety of the order dated 02.10.2025 passed by the learned Special Judge Rent/learned Rent Controller, whereby an application filed by respondent No.3 under Section 12(2), C.P.C. was allowed, the ex - parte ejectment order along with memo of costs dated 31.01.2024 was set aside and the ejectment petition was restored to its original position with a direction to the applicants therein to file an amended ejectment petition by incorporating the name of respondent No.3 in the memo of parties. The petitioner has also assailed the judgment dated 18.05.2026 passed by the learned R evisional Court, whereby the revision petition filed by the petitioner and respondent No.4 was dismissed.
2. The impugned orders have been assailed, inter alia ,
on the grounds that the learned Courts below misread , non - read the record and failed to appreciate the material available on record, exercised jurisdiction not vested in them, and committed material irregularity in allowing an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C. in proceedings governed by the Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009. It has further been contended that the ejectment order dated
31.01.2024 h ad already attained finality and had
Writ Petition No.4596 of 2026 - 2 been executed through delivery of possession, and, therefore, the learned Rent Controller had no lawful authority to recall the same.
3 . I have heard the learned counsel for the petitioner at the preliminary stage and have carefully examined the available record with his able assistance.
4 . At the outset, it may be observed that the controversy is required to be examined in the backdrop of the limited scope of Constitutional jurisdiction as well as the nature and extent of the jurisdiction exercised by a Rent Controller while dealing with an allegation that an order of ejectment has been procured through fraud, misrepresentation and concealment of material facts.
5. The record shows that the petitioner along with respondents
No.4 and 5 instituted the ejectment petition against respondent No.6 and procured a final eviction order dated 31.01.2024. However, said order was assailed by respondent No.3 through moving an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C. , which was allowed on 02.10.2025 and resultantly order dated 31.01.2024 was set - aside. The order dated 02.10.2025 was challenged by the petitioner and respondent No.4 through a revision petition , dismissed on 18.05.2026 , whereas respondent No.5 did not challenge the same. Respondent No.4 has also not joined the present proceedings. Consequently, the impugned orders have attained finality to the extent of resp o ndents No.4 and 5 . The controversy before this Court, therefore, survives only at the instance of the petitioner.
6 . The facts, in brief, are that the petitioner along with respondents No.4 and 5 (hereinafter referred to as the applicants) filed an ejectment petition on 31.07.2023 against respondent No.6 in respect of a property situated at Mohallah Banigran, Mouza Bahawalpur, measuring 18 marlas. The case set - up in the ejectment petition was that respondent No.6 had obtained possession of the premises as a tenant pursuant to a tenancy/lease agreement dated 02.02.2022 at a monthly rent of Rs.5,000/ for a period of one year and had subsequently failed to pay rent and hand over possession despite demand and notice. The applicants claimed ownership over the property in different shares. According to them, the Writ Petition No.4596 of 2026 - 3 petitioner and respondent No.4 were owners of 5 marlas each, whereas the remaining portion was claimed by respondent No.5 and her husband.
Despite service, publication and opportunities, respondent No.6 did not appear before the learned Rent Controller was proceeded against ex - parte on 07.10.2023. The petitioner and the applicants produced their evidence, including respondent No.4 as AW - 1, his affidavit as Exh.A - 1, Ghulam Nabi and Muhammad Mushtaq as attesting witnesses of rent agreement as AW - 2 and AW - 3 along with their affidavits as Exh.A - 4 and Exh.A - 5, the tenancy agreement as Exh.A - 2 and copy of the record of rights for the year 2019 - 20 as Exh.A - 3. On the basis of the ex - parte evidence, the learned Rent Controller allowed the ejectment petition and passed the final eviction order along with memo of costs dated 31.01.2024. In execution of the said order, possession of the disputed premises was delivered to the applicants.
7. The controversy, however, did not end with the delivery of
possession. Respondent No.3 thereafter approached the learned Rent Controller through an application under Section 12(2), C.P.C., asserting that the ejectment order had been procured by misdescription and concealment of the identity and ownership of the property. He maintained that the premises from which possession had been obtained did not belong to the applicants but formed part of property owned by him and situated in Khata Nos.36/32 and 38/34. He relied upon registered sale deed No.780 dated 19.03.1986 and asserted that the question of his title had already been adjudicated in his favour up to the Supreme Court of Pakistan. The applicants contested the application and maintained that the disputed premises belonged to them and that possession had lawfully been delivered in execution of the ejectment order. Respondent No.6, who had remained absent throughout the original ejectment proceedings, also appeared at that stage and submitted a written reply supporting the applicants.
8. During the proceedings, it became apparent that the real
controversy between the parties was not merely one of tenancy but concerned the identity and demarcation of the property in respect Writ Petition No.4596 of 2026 - 4 whereof the ejectment order had been obtained and executed. The parties, therefore, expressed consensus that the question of demarcation be determined through a Local Commission. Consequently, vide order dated
02.10.2024, the learned Rent Controller appointed the Tehsildar, Saddar,
Bahawalpur, as Local Commission with directions to demarcate the disputed property and submit his report. The Local Commission conducted demarcation proceedings in the presence of the parties. The parties agreed to have the property identified through Global Positioning System (GPS).
