VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 11 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
JUDGMENT SHEET
PESHAWAR HIGH COURT, PESHAWAR
( Judicial Department) C.R No. 35-P of 2013 .
Present:
Mr. Abdul Samad Khan, Advocate, for petitioners.
M/s Arshad Jamal Qureshi & Salman Fayaz Mir, Advocates, for respondents.
Date of hearing : 10.08.2026 & 19.08.2026.
JUDGMENT
MUHAMMAD NAEEM ANWAR, J.- Impugned through the instant Civil Revision Petition, filed under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, is the judgment and decree dated 11.10.2012 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-VI, Peshawar, whereby the appeal preferred by the respondents/plaintiffs against the judgment and decree dated 22.05.2009 passed by the learned Civil Judge-X, Peshawar, dismissing their suit, was allowed to the limited extent of cancellation of the tatimma prepared in respect of the disputed property and the consequential allocation of a specific portion thereof, while the alienation made by defendant No.1 in favour of defendant No.5 was maintained. The petitioners, who are aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment to the extent of cancellation of the tatimma, have invoked the revisional jurisdiction of this Court.
2. The facts giving rise to the present petition, in brief,
are that the respondents/plaintiffs instituted a suit for declaration, asserting that defendants No.1 to 4, including the present petitioners, were owners in possession of property comprised in Khasra No. 489 measuring 12 kanals 8 marlas, Khasra No. 310 measuring 8 kanals 7 marlas and Khasra No. 525 measuring 48 kanals 6 marlas, along with other properties situated in Revenue Estate Chughulpura, Tehsil and District Peshawar. There had been previous litigation between the parties concerning inheritance flowing from Mst. Sahib Jan Sultan, which controversy was ultimately decided by the Hon’ble Supreme Court through judgment dated 30.05.1990 passed in Civil Appeal No. 35-P of 1988. The plaintiffs asserted that proceedings for Rizwanullah Khan and others Vs Muhammad Usman Khan and others partition of the joint property had been initiated by them in 1983 and that a mode of partition had already been prepared, with the proceedings having reached an advanced stage. During the pendency of those proceedings, they came to know that defendant No.1 had purportedly transferred an area measuring 16 kanals in favour of Mst. Fahmida Begum, his wife, towards dower. It was further alleged that, during the pendency of the partition proceedings, defendants No.5 and 6, in collusion with officials of the Revenue Department, commenced construction over the disputed property. An application was accordingly moved before the Revenue Officer for restraining such construction, and the construction raised thereon was subsequently demolished pursuant to an order passed by the competent authority.
The plaintiffs specifically challenged the legality of Mutation No. 857 dated 10.03.1979, contending that the same had been attested in violation of the applicable land laws. Their principal grievance was that, in the absence of a lawful partition, preparation and carving out of a tatimma in respect of a specific portion of a jointly owned survey number amounted, in substance, to an unauthorized separation of a defined parcel from joint property, thereby affecting the rights of the remaining co-sharers. It was further asserted that defendant No.1, being entitled only to his share in the joint estate, could not lawfully alienate 16 kanals as a specific and separately identified portion of the joint property in a manner prejudicial to the rights of the other co-owners. Having failed to secure correction of the revenue entries from defendants No.1 and 5, the plaintiffs were constrained to institute the suit.
3. The suit was contested by defendants No.1 and 5 on
various factual and legal grounds. Their case was that the property had already been privately partitioned amongst the co-owners and each of them was in possession of his respective share. It was, therefore, maintained that the alienation reflected through Mutation No. 857 was lawful and could not validly be questioned by the plaintiffs. Defendant No.6 also filed a written statement. The parties were thereafter directed to produce their evidence. Muhammad Jamil, Patwari Halqa of Revenue Estate Chughulpura, appeared as a witness and produced the relevant revenue record, including the goshwara-e-Milkiyat. Muhammad Usman Khan appeared as attorney for the plaintiffs, whereafter the plaintiffs closed their evidence. Dr.
Rizwanullah Khan appeared as attorney for defendants No.1 and 5, who also closed their evidence. Upon conclusion of the trial, the learned Trial Court, through judgment and decree dated 22.05.2009, dismissed the suit. The plaintiffs preferred an appeal, which was initially allowed through judgment dated 07.01.2010. The matter thereafter came before this Court in Civil Revision No. 742-P of
2010. The revision petition was allowed, the judgment and decree of
the learned Trial Court were set aside and the matter was remanded to the learned Additional District Judge-VI, Peshawar, for a fresh decision after hearing the parties. Upon remand, the learned appellate Court, through the impugned judgment dated 11.10.2012, allowed the plaintiffs’ appeal to the limited extent of cancellation of the tatimma, while maintaining the alienation made by defendant No.1 in favour of defendant No.5. Hence, the present Civil Revision Petition.
4. Learned counsel for the petitioners, Mr. Abdus Samad
Khan, Advocate, contended that the learned appellate Court failed to appreciate the distinction between the right of a co-sharer to alienate his undivided share and the subsequent adjustment of such alienation in partition proceedings. Placing reliance upon Muhammad Muzaffar Khan v. Muhammad Yusuf Khan (PLD 1959 SC (Pak.) 9), Shah Hussain v. Abdul Qayum and others (1984 SCMR 427), Mst. Saima v. Paramount Spinning Mills Ltd. and others (2011 SCMR 1039) and Town Committee, Jalalpur Pirwala through Chairman v. Malik Mehr Bakhsh and another (2007 YLR 82), learned counsel argued that the predecessor-in-interest of petitioners No.1 to 5 possessed substantial ownership in the revenue estate and, therefore, his right to alienate his share in favour of his wife could not be curtailed merely because the property was jointly owned. It was further contended that Mutation No. 879 had subsequently been corrected through Mutation No. 5675 dated 25.06.2010 and that the latter mutation was itself assailable. Learned counsel, while referring to the statement of PW-1 and Exhibit PW-1/X-1, argued that Habibullah Khan was recorded as owner of 172 kanals 2 marlas, out of which 79 kanals 5 marlas had been alienated, leaving 92 kanals 17 marlas still standing in his ownership. On this basis, it was argued that the alienation did not exceed the transferor’s total entitlement in the estate and, consequently, could not be declared unlawful. The learned counsel thus sought restoration of the judgment and decree of the learned Trial Court.
5. Learned counsel appearing for the respondents, Mr.
Arshad Jamal Qureshi and Mr. Salman Fayaz Mir, Advocates, whose arguments were heard on 10.08.2026, confined their submissions to the preparation and attestation of tatimma pursuant to Mutation No.
857 dated 10.03.1979. According to learned counsel, the learned appellate Court had correctly found that the tatimma could not lawfully have been carved out from the jointly owned property in the absence of the consent of all the recorded co-owners or a lawful partition through the competent Revenue authority.
6. Arguments have been heard and the record perused.
7. At the outset, the objection concerning Mutation No.
5675 dated 25.06.2010 may conveniently be dealt with. The said mutation was founded upon the judgment of the learned Additional District Judge, Peshawar, in Civil Appeal No. 10/13. That judgment, however, had already been set aside by this Court in Civil Revision No. 742-P of 2010 and the matter was remanded to the learned appellate Court for a fresh decision. It is also significant that, even when Civil Revision No. 742-P of 2010 was decided on 11.06.2012, a copy of Mutation No. 5675 had not been brought on the record. In any event, once the judgment which constituted the foundation of the said mutation stood set aside and the learned appellate Court was directed to reconsider the matter afresh, Mutation No. 5675 could not confer any independent or enduring legal consequence. The revenue record, therefore, necessarily has to conform to the final adjudication of the rights of the parties.
8. The controversy concerning the alienation made by
defendant No.1 in favour of defendant No.5 stands on a different footing from the question of preparation of the tatimma. The learned appellate Court consciously maintained the alienation, and that part of the judgment was never challenged by the plaintiffs/respondents.
To that extent, therefore, the finding has attained finality. Even otherwise, a co-owner cannot be deprived of his fundamental right to alienate his own undivided share in joint property merely because the property has not yet been partitioned. A co-sharer may transfer his interest in the joint estate, but he cannot transfer a better title, a larger proprietary interest, or a specific parcel in excess of his own lawful entitlement. The controlling principle is that a co-sharer can transfer no better title than he himself possesses. Consequently, the validity of an alienation by a co-owner is necessarily subject to the upper limit of the transferor’s total entitlement in the entire joint estate. If a cosharer is in possession of a particular khasra number or a defined portion thereof in the column of cultivation, such possession does not, by itself, transform his possessory arrangement into exclusive proprietary title. His alienation of a specific parcel may, therefore, operate between the transferor and transferee, but its ultimate efficacy remains subject to the transferor’s proprietary share and the result of lawful partition. This principle is well settled in Itebar Shah and others v. Ahmad Shah and others (2001 CLC 1021) and Abdul Hameed through legal heirs and others v. Shamssuddin and others (PLD 2008 SC 140). The vendee steps into the shoes of the vendor and acquires precisely the interest which the vendor could lawfully convey—no more and no less.
9. The same principle was lucidly enunciated
in Muhammad Zafar Khan, wherein it was held that the vendee of a co-sharer, who owns an undivided khata jointly with others, acquires the same rights as his vendor. Even where the vendor is in exclusive possession of a particular portion of the joint land and transfers possession thereof, the vendee remains a co-sharer in the joint property to the extent of the area purchased, provided that such area does not exceed the share of the vendor in the entire joint estate.
The vendee may retain possession of the specific portion until partition, but such possession remains subject to adjustment at the time of partition. Thus, alienation of a specific portion by a co-sharer is not, by itself, rendered void merely because the joint property has not been partitioned; rather, the alienation remains subject to the vendor’s total proprietary entitlement and to adjustment in the eventual partition. If the specific area transferred exceeds the vendor’s share, the excess cannot be enforced against the other cosharers and has to be adjusted from the vendor’s remaining share in the joint estate or otherwise dealt with in the partition proceedings.
This principle has also been recognized in Mst. Saima (supra) and Shah Hussain (supra).
10. The distinction between the validity of an
alienation and the validity of a tatimma is, however, decisive for the present controversy. The learned counsel for the petitioners has correctly relied upon the principle governing alienation by a cosharer, but that principle does not authorize a unilateral separation of a specific parcel from a jointly owned survey number. A tatimma is essentially a revenue device for identifying and preparing a subdivision of an existing survey/khasra number. It is not, in itself, a mode of partition whereby the proprietary rights of all co-sharers can be separated or a defined parcel can be taken out of the joint character of the property at the unilateral instance of one co-sharer.
The preparation of a tatimma, where it has the effect of severing a defined portion of a jointly owned survey number and giving that portion a separate identity in the revenue record, necessarily affects the proprietary and possessory rights of every recorded coowner. Consent of all the co-owners is, therefore, a sine qua non for such a consensual sub-division; in the absence of such consent, separation of the joint property can only be achieved through lawful partition proceedings before the competent authority. This distinction assumes particular significance where the alienation is of a specific portion of a joint survey number. A transferor may validly alienate his undivided proprietary interest, or even transfer possession of a specific portion subject to adjustment, but he cannot, by the mere act of alienation, unilaterally transform that portion into a separately identified proprietary parcel to the exclusion of the remaining co-sharers. Such transformation would, in substance and effect, amount to partition without notice to, and without the consent of, the other recorded owners. The principle was expressly considered by this Court in Syed Muqaddar Shah and another v.
Haji Abdul Ahad Khan and another (1990 CLC 1596), where it was observed that where the vendor was in hissadari possession of an entire khasra number, preparation of a tatimma allocating a particular portion thereof to the vendee would have the effect of partitioning the khasra number without notice to and consent of the other recorded co-owners. The Court further recognized that a sale reflected in the column of cultivation, or preparation of a tatimma in consequence of sale of a portion of hissadari possession, remains subject to partition and adjustment of the rights of the recorded cosharers. The principle is also consistent with the law declared in Kala Khan v. Shah Hussain and 9 others (1983 CLC 684), where this Court held that sale of specific field numbers by a co-sharer remains subject to adjustment in partition proceedings. The duty of the authority conducting partition is to accommodate the vendee and make good any deficiency, where possible, from the vendor’s other joint land in the same estate. The rationale is simple: the co-sharer cannot convey more than his proprietary entitlement, but neither can the vendee be deprived of the benefit of a lawful purchase merely because the vendor happened to be in possession of a particular parcel at the time of sale. The rights of all concerned are ultimately reconciled through lawful partition and adjustment. The principle emerging from the above authorities may, therefore, be stated with precision: a co-sharer is competent to alienate his proprietary interest in the joint estate, and such alienation is valid to the extent of his total entitlement therein; however, where a specific portion of a joint survey number is identified for transfer, the identification of that portion cannot, by preparation of a tatimma, be converted into a separate proprietary parcel without the consent of all co-owners or without a lawful partition. The transferee acquires no better title than that possessed by the transferor, and the transfer remains subject to the transferor’s total share in the estate and to adjustment at the time of partition.
11. Applying the above principles to the case in hand,
there is no dispute that other co-owners were recorded in the joint property. Equally, there is nothing on record demonstrating that those co-owners had consented to the preparation of the tatimma in question. The order of the Revenue Officer endorsed on the reverse of Mutation No. 857 dated 10.03.1979 does not disclose the consent of all the recorded co-owners. In such circumstances, the Revenue Officer could not, merely on the basis of the alienation made by defendant No.1, confer upon the vendee a separate and identifiable portion of the joint khasra by carving out a tatimma, because doing so would have the legal effect of severing that portion from the joint estate without completion of the process of partition. The learned appellate Court, therefore, committed no error in directing cancellation of the tatimma. The cancellation of the tatimma does not, in the circumstances of the case, amount to cancellation of the underlying alienation. The two matters are legally distinct. The alienation has been maintained, and rightly so, subject always to the settled limitation that defendant No.1 could not transfer an interest greater than his own proprietary entitlement in the entire estate. The vendee, consequently, stepped into the shoes of defendant No.1 and acquired the rights of the transferor only to the extent of his lawful share. The specific portion mentioned in the transaction could remain relevant for the purposes of possession and subsequent adjustment, but it could not be treated as having been lawfully severed from the joint property through an unauthorized tatimma.
12. The reliance placed by learned counsel for the
petitioners upon the proposition that a co-sharer is competent to alienate his property is, therefore, unexceptionable as a general proposition, but it does not advance the petitioners’ case on the specific question before this Court. The issue is not whether defendant No.1 could alienate his proprietary interest. That question has already been answered in favour of the petitioners, and the respondents have not challenged that finding. The real question is whether, as a consequence of that alienation, the Revenue Officer could lawfully carve out a tatimma from a jointly owned survey number without the consent of the other co-owners or a lawful partition. The answer, in view of the settled legal position, must necessarily be in the negative.
13. Learned counsel for the petitioners also contended
that the joint property had subsequently been partitioned. In this regard, the record produced through C.M. No. 1265 reflects the order dated 27.09.2019 passed by Member-II, Board of Revenue, whereby the appeal preferred by Ali Hassan Durrani against Mst.
Fahmida Begum and others was dismissed and the order of the Additional Commissioner, Peshawar, was maintained. The order of the Additional Commissioner, Peshawar, dated 10.12.2018 relates to completion of the partition proceedings. The record further indicates that Writ Petition No. 6546-P of 2019, whereby the order of the Board of Revenue was questioned, was dismissed on 08.12.2018, and the proceedings reflect completion of partition with effect from
10.08.2011. These subsequent developments, however, do not
retrospectively validate an otherwise unauthorized tatimma prepared in 1979. The validity of the impugned revenue act has to be examined in the light of the legal position and the rights of the parties existing when that act was undertaken. If the joint estate has subsequently been partitioned, the rights flowing from the present judgment shall necessarily be incorporated and adjusted in the revenue record in accordance with the final determination of the competent forum. The subsequent partition may regulate the ultimate rights and possession of the parties, but it cannot retrospectively convert an unauthorized unilateral sub-division into a valid consensual partition. It is, therefore, clarified that the cancellation of the tatimma does not preclude the vendee from asserting such proprietary or possessory rights as may lawfully accrue to her through the alienation made by defendant No.1. Those rights shall, however, remain confined to the transferor’s total entitlement in the joint estate and shall be worked out in accordance with the final partition and adjustment of shares.
14. There is another important aspect which cannot be
overlooked. The respondents instituted the suit in 1994, whereas the impugned judgment of the learned appellate Court was rendered in
2012. The controversy relating to the tatimma, therefore, remained
sub judice before the civil Court during the intervening period. To the extent the subsequent revenue proceedings purport to deal with the same subject matter, the revenue entries must necessarily remain subject to the adjudication of the competent civil Court. Once a civil Court has adjudicated upon the legality of the act affecting proprietary rights, the revenue record cannot be permitted to operate contrary to such adjudication.
15. The cumulative effect of the foregoing discussion is
that three propositions govern the controversy: First, a co-sharer is competent to alienate his undivided proprietary interest in the joint estate, but he cannot transfer a title greater than his own; the validity and extent of the transfer are necessarily subject to his total entitlement in the entire estate. Second, where the transfer relates to a specific portion of a jointly owned survey/khasra number, the identification of that portion does not, by itself, effect partition or sever the parcel from the joint estate. The transferee merely steps into the shoes of the transferor and remains subject to the rights of the other co-sharers and the eventual adjustment in partition.
Third, a tatimma, being a revenue mechanism for sub-dividing a survey number and giving a distinct identity to a specified portion, cannot lawfully be used as a substitute for partition. Where its preparation has the effect of separating a specific portion from jointly owned property, the consent of all co-owners is indispensable; failing such consent, separation can only be achieved through lawful partition proceedings conducted by the competent authority. The learned appellate Court, therefore, correctly distinguished between the underlying alienation and the consequential preparation of the tatimma. While it preserved the alienation in favour of defendant No.5, it rightly declined to recognize the unilateral severance of a specific portion of the joint property through Mutation No. 857 and the tatimma prepared pursuant thereto.
16. For what has been discussed above, I find no illegality,
material irregularity or jurisdictional defect in the impugned judgment dated 11.10.2012 warranting interference in exercise of revisional jurisdiction under Section 115, C.P.C. The learned appellate Court has correctly applied the law to the facts of the case and has drawn a legally sustainable distinction between the right of a co-sharer to alienate his interest and the impermissibility of unilaterally severing a specific portion of joint property through preparation of a tatimma. Consequently, the instant Civil Revision Petition, being devoid of merit, is dismissed. The impugned judgment & decree dated 11.10.2012 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-VI, Peshawar, is maintained. It is, however, clarified that cancellation of the tatimma shall not be construed as cancellation of the underlying alienation in favour of defendant No.5, which shall remain subject to the transferor’s total proprietary entitlement in the joint estate and to the lawful adjustment of the parties’ rights in partition proceedings. There shall be no order as to costs.
Announced. JUDGE
19.08.2026.
(SB) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Muhammad Naeem Anwar.
Asif Jan Sr.S.S .

VERBATIM JUDGMENT TEXT (extracted from the official PDF at the Source URL; 12 pages; spelling, punctuation and lineation as in the PDF):
JUDGMENT SHEET
PESHAWAR HIGH COURT, PESHAWAR
( Judicial Department) C.R No.283-P of 2015 with C.M No.1803-P of 2025.
Present :
Nemo for petitioners.
Mr. Zar Badshah, Advocate, for respondents No. 10 to 18.
Mr. Abdul Rashid Pirzada Advocate for respondents No.
1,6,8,11,13,18 to 20 and 25. (Absent despite service) M/s Muhammad Amir Rafiq, Shakeel Zada and Shahid Zaman, and Qazi Salim, Advocates for added respondents.
Mr. Ghulam Ali, Advocate, for respondent No. 55.
Date of hearing : 12.08.2026.
JUDGMENT
MUHAMMAD NAEEM ANWAR, J.- Through the instant Civil Revision Petition, the petitioners have called in question the judgment & decree dated 19.01.2015 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-IV, Mardan, whereby the appeal preferred against the judgment and decree dated 06.12.2012 passed by the learned Civil Judge-XII, Mardan, in consolidated Civil Suits No. 168/1 and 167/1, was dismissed.
2. Before adverting to the controversy involved, it would be
appropriate to recapitulate the relevant facts and the chequered history of the litigation in their chronological sequence, as the matter has passed through various stages of adjudication and, during the pendency of the present revision, certain persons were brought on record pursuant to applications filed under section 12(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (“CPC”).
Background of the litigation.
3. The dispute essentially relates to the ownership and
revenue record of property originally claimed to have belonged to Faiz Talab Khan, who had seven sons, namely, Bawar Khan, Abdul Qadar Khan, Sher Afzal Khan, Mir Afzal Khan, Saadat Khan, Mir Akbar Khan and Raidullah Khan. The plaintiffs of Civil Suit No. 168/1 instituted their suit on 02.06.2009, claiming Zulfiqar Ali & others Vs Muhammad Amin Jan and others.
declaration of their ownership and possession on the basis of registered deed No. 1828 dated 26.10.1946. Their case was that the property had been transferred in their favour through the said registered deed, but the corresponding entries in the revenue record had either not been correctly incorporated or had been recorded on the basis of registered deed No. 1829 instead of registered deed No. 1828. They, therefore, sought declaration, perpetual injunction against alienation of the property on the basis of the allegedly erroneous revenue entries and correction of the revenue record in accordance with their registered title. On the other hand, the plaintiffs of Civil Suit No. 167/1 instituted a suit for declaration and perpetual injunction, claiming themselves to be owners in possession of 3000 kanals out of 31,023 kanals and 11 marlas of the disputed property. Both suits were contested by the respective defendants, consolidated and tried together. After recording of evidence and hearing the parties, the learned trial Court, vide judgment and decree dated 06.12.2012, dismissed Civil Suit No. 167/1, whereas Civil Suit No. 168/1 was decreed. The judgment and decree of the learned trial Court were assailed before the learned Additional District Judge-IV, Mardan, who, vide judgment and decree dated 19.01.2015, dismissed the appeal and maintained the findings of the learned trial Court. The aggrieved parties consequently invoked the revisional jurisdiction of this Court through Civil Revision No. 283-P/2015.
Compromise before this Court and subsequent proceedings.
4. During pendency of the Civil Revision, on 11.04.2016,
learned counsel appearing for the respective parties, namely, Mr.
Maazullah Khan Barkandi, Advocate, for the petitioners; Mr.
Abdur Rashid Khan, Advocate, for respondents No.1, 2, 10, 11 and 12; and Mr. Noor Hakam, Advocate, for respondents No.3 to 9 and 33, made a joint statement before the Court in the presence of the parties. The statement reads:
“ We have agreed that the parties admit registered deeds No. 1828 and 1829 in favour of the parties, therefore, the decree in suit No. 168/1 may be maintained while suit No.
167/1 may be decreed, both the registered deeds should be incorporated in the revenue record to the extent of the land mentioned therein. Parties may be left to bear their own cost .” On the basis of the aforesaid statement, the judgments and decrees of the Courts below were set aside and Civil Suit No. 167/1 was decreed. Thus, the litigation was sought to be brought to an end on the basis of the compromise and the admitted existence of registered deeds No. 1828 and 1829.
5. Subsequently, however, added respondents, who were not
parties to the aforesaid compromise proceedings, approached this Court through applications under section 12(2) CPC, challenging the judgment and decree dated 11.04.2016 on the ground, inter alia, that their independent rights and interests in the disputed property had neither been represented nor adjudicated upon.
Applications bearing C.M. No. 24-P/2018 were filed by the legal heirs of Amir Nosh, including Mst. Mufeed Begum and others.
Likewise, Said Bakht, Mubarak Zeb, Shah Zeb and Bakhtiar, being the legal heirs of Bawar Khan, also questioned the judgment of this Court. C.M. No. 10-P/2018 was filed by the daughters of Amir Nosh, namely Mst. Mufeed Begum, Farida Begum and Sadarat Begum. C.M. No.15-P/2018 was filed by persons claiming to be purchasers from Saadat Khan and Sher Afzal Khan, who alleged that the parties to Civil Revision No. 283-P/2015 had compromised the matter to their prejudice and had thereby purported to defeat their independent rights arising from subsequent transactions. All the applications were allowed through common judgement by this court on 17.03.2025 and the applicants were brought on record as added respondents in the Civil Revision and instant Civil Revision was revived/ restored.
Service upon the original petitioners.
6. There were six original petitioners, namely Zulfiqar Ali,
Sardar Ali, Afsar Ali, Mst. Falak, Mst. Bushra and Mst. Majmara, who were directed to be served through all possible modes. The matter being considerably old, it was taken up in pursuance of the order dated 22.06.2026. Mr. Aimal Khan Barkandi, Advocate, informed the Court that although his late father, Mr. Maazullah Khan Barkandi, Advocate, had represented the petitioners, after his father's death he had no contact or instructions from the petitioners. Learned counsel appearing for added respondents, namely, M/S Muhammad Amir Rafiq, Shakeel Zada and Shahid Zaman, Advocates, informed the Court that, as a compromise had earlier been affected between the parties, respondents No. 23 and 30 were relevant to the controversy and were believed to be in contact with the petitioners. Their cell numbers were accordingly furnished to the Court, whereafter directions were issued for service upon all the petitioners through all possible means. The Moharrir Branch of the Civil Revision submitted a detailed report regarding the efforts made for service through respondents No. 23 and 30. Cell numbers of petitioners No.2 and 3 were obtained and were found switched on; however, when attempts were made to contact them, the calls were not answered and the numbers were subsequently switched off. Thereafter, the SHO, Police Station Chura, Mardan, was also directed to effect service. The report submitted by the police reflects service upon Afsar Ali s/o Quresh Khan, (petitioner) bearing CNIC No. 16101-1148739-9 and cell No. 03059693513. Despite such service, neither Afsar Ali nor his brothers, sisters or mother, who are the remaining petitioners, appeared before this Court. One Badal Khan, step-brother of petitioners No.1 to 5 and step-son of Mst. Majmara, is present before the Court. He is also the husband of respondent No. 33, Mst. Musarrat. In these circumstances, and after giving due consideration to the repeated efforts made to secure the presence of the original petitioners and to protect the rights of all persons who had subsequently come on record, the matter has been heard on merits with the assistance of learned counsel who are present before the Court.
Nature of the original transactions.
7. The controversy, when examined against its historical
background, revolves around two registered deeds, namely, registered deed No. 1828 dated 26.10.1946 and registered deed No. 1829 dated 26.10.1946, both stated to have emanated from Faiz Talab Khan. The beneficiaries of registered deed No.
1828 were Abdul Qadar Khan, Sher Afzal Khan, Saadat Khan, Mir Akbar Khan and Raidullah Khan, sons of Faiz Talab Khan, whereas the beneficiaries of registered deed No. 1829 were the grandsons of Faiz Talab Khan. Thus, both sets of claimants trace their respective titles to the same predecessor, namely, Faiz Talab Khan. It is significant that the plaintiffs of Civil Suit No. 167/1, whose suit was dismissed by both Courts below, had not pleaded in their plaint the material fact of acquisition of the property through registered deed No. 1829. This omission substantially contributed to the dismissal of their suit. Nevertheless, the relationship of the beneficiaries of registered deed No. 1829 with Faiz Talab Khan has not been disputed. Similarly, the status of the beneficiaries of registered deed No. 1828 as sons of Faiz Talab Khan has not been seriously controverted.
8. The plaintiffs of Civil Suit No. 168/1 principally
complained that although their registered deed had been incorporated in the revenue record, the shares and the source of title had not been correctly reflected. According to them, the revenue record erroneously reflected alienation in their favour on the basis of registered deed No. 1829 rather than registered deed No. 1828, necessitating judicial intervention for correction and proper incorporation of their title. It is also apparent from the record that the plaintiffs of Civil Suit No. 167/1 claimed rights to the extent of 1800 kanals, whereas the plaintiffs of Civil Suit No.
168/1 claimed approximately 8937 kanals from the disputed property. When the matter came before this Court in Civil Revision No. 283-P/2015, the aforesaid position culminated in the joint statement dated 11.04.2016, whereby the parties then before the Court agreed that both registered deeds No. 1828 and 1829 be given effect to in the revenue record to the extent of the land mentioned therein. The difficulty, however, is that the matter did not end there.
Emergence of the rights claimed by the added respondents.
9. After the applicants under section 12(2) CPC were brought
on record, a materially different aspect of the controversy emerged.
The added respondents have asserted rights founded upon mutation No. 1107, which, according to learned counsel representing them, was attested pursuant to a decision of the Deputy Commissioner in Suit No. 8/6 dated 01.06.1949 and was subsequently incorporated in the revenue record. This assertion is of considerable legal and factual significance. It is not merely a collateral objection to the compromise between the original parties.
Rather, it constitutes an independent claim concerning the source, extent and subsistence of title in the disputed property. Learned counsel representing the added respondents were specifically asked whether the alienation made by Faiz Talab Khan through registered deeds No. 1828 and 1829 could subsequently be questioned by the legal heirs of Faiz Talab Khan. In response, Mr.
Shakeel Zada, learned Advocate, produced a copy of mutation No.
1107. Conversely, learned counsel representing respondents No.
10 to 18 contended that Faiz Talab Khan had ceased to be the owner of the property before execution and registration of the deeds in 1946. The first aspect, namely, whether an owner could alienate his property in favour of one or more persons, including to the exclusion of his legal heirs, is no longer res integra. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ghulam Muhammad v. Mian Muhammad and another (2007 SCMR 231) has recognized the unfettered right of an owner to alienate his property in favour of any person, including by excluding one or more of his prospective legal heirs. That principle, however, does not conclude the controversy before us.
Why the matter requires remand.
10. The decisive question is not simply whether registered
deeds No. 1828 and 1829 were executed and registered in 1946.
Nor is the controversy confined to the abstract proposition whether Faiz Talab Khan could alienate his property in favour of some of his descendants. The real difficulty is that mutation No. 1107 and the rights claimed thereunder were neither part of the original pleadings nor the subject of adjudication before the Courts below.
The persons now asserting rights on the strength of that mutation were not parties to the original litigation in a manner enabling their independent claims to be properly pleaded, controverted and adjudicated upon. Their assertions, therefore, could not have been effectively examined either by the learned trial Court or by the learned appellate Court. Equally important is the fact that, while exercising revisional jurisdiction, this Court cannot satisfactorily determine disputed questions of title which require examination of the original revenue record, the basis and legality of mutation No.
1107, the nature and extent of the alleged alienation thereunder, the relationship between the parties, the effect of the registered deeds and the competing claims of the persons deriving title from the beneficiaries thereof, without affording all concerned parties a meaningful opportunity to plead their respective cases and lead evidence. The issue is particularly important because the added respondents do not merely seek to support or oppose the original judgments. They assert independent and substantive rights in the property. Those rights may have a direct bearing upon the validity, extent and legal effect of the title claimed by the plaintiffs of both suits. Therefore, any attempt by this Court to finally determine those questions on the basis of the material presently available would not only amount to adjudicating disputed questions of fact in revisional jurisdiction but would also deprive the concerned parties of the opportunity to establish their respective claims through pleadings, production of the original revenue record and evidence.
11. The Court is conscious that litigation must ordinarily attain
finality and that remand should not be ordered merely to provide a party with an opportunity to fill gaps in its case. A remand becomes necessary, however, where an issue essential to the determination of the real controversy has emerged at a subsequent stage, where persons asserting independent rights have been brought on record, and where such rights were neither pleaded nor adjudicated upon by the Courts below. The present case falls squarely within that category.
The stance of the added respondents, particularly those claiming through mutation No. 1107 and those claiming as vendees from Saadat Khan and Sher Afzal Khan, was not before the Courts below. Consequently, there was no occasion for those Courts to examine the validity and legal effect of mutation No. 1107; the source and extent of the title claimed thereunder; its relationship with registered deeds No. 1828 and 1829; the alleged prior alienation by Faiz Talab Khan; or the effect of subsequent alienations made by the beneficiaries of the registered deeds.
These are not matters which can appropriately be determined for the first time in revisional jurisdiction. They require a proper trial, based upon complete pleadings, production of the relevant original revenue record and registration record, and an opportunity to all concerned parties to lead evidence and rebut the case of their opponents.
Necessary amendment and impleadment.
12. In order to bring the controversy to its logical conclusion
and to avoid further rounds of litigation, it is necessary that the pleadings themselves reflect the complete dispute now emerging from the record. Accordingly, the plaintiffs of both Civil Suit No.
167/1 and Civil Suit No. 168/1 shall be permitted to amend their respective plaints, to the extent necessary for incorporating the subsequent developments and the claims of the persons now brought on record. In particular, the plaintiffs shall array all the added respondents/applicants who have been brought on record in consequence of the proceedings under section 12(2) CPC as defendants in their respective suits. The plaintiffs of Civil Suit No.
167/1 shall also be at liberty to appropriately amend their prayer so as to clearly and comprehensively seek the relief which they claim on the basis of registered deed No. 1829 and the subsequent proceedings, rather than leaving the real nature of their claim to be inferred from the material brought before this Court. Both sets of plaintiffs shall submit their amended plaints before the learned trial Court, whereafter all the defendants, including the added respondents, shall be afforded an opportunity to file their respective written statements and to raise all lawful pleas available to them.
Scope of adjudication on remand.
13. The learned trial Court shall thereafter adjudicate the
consolidated suits afresh, strictly in accordance with law and on the basis of the pleadings and evidence brought on record. Without limiting the jurisdiction of the learned trial Court, the following material questions shall receive specific consideration:
i. Whether registered deeds No. 1828 and 1829 dated
26.10.1946 were validly executed, registered and attested and what
property and shares were transferred thereunder; ii. Whether Faiz Talab Khan was the lawful owner of the property, or of the relevant shares therein, at the time of execution and registration of the aforesaid deeds; iii. The nature, origin, validity and legal effect of mutation No.
1107, including the decision of the Deputy Commissioner in Suit No.
8/6 dated 01.06.1949 on the basis of which the mutation is stated to have been attested; iv. Whether mutation No. 1107 confers, recognizes or records any right, title or interest in favour of the added respondents and, if so, the extent and legal character of such rights; v. Whether the rights claimed on the basis of mutation No. 1107 are inconsistent with, subsequent to, or otherwise affected by registered deeds No. 1828 and 1829; vi. Whether the beneficiaries of registered deeds No. 1828 and 1829 acquired valid title to the extent claimed by them and whether the subsequent alienations made by Saadat Khan and Sher Afzal Khan in favour of the persons now arrayed as defendants created any legally enforceable rights; vii. Whether the fact that neither Bawar Khan nor his legal heirs, during his lifetime or thereafter within the relevant period, challenged the registered deeds No. 1828 and 1829 has any legal consequence for the claims now advanced by his legal heirs, and if so, to what extent; viii. Whether the revenue entries correctly reflect the registered instruments and the actual title of the parties, and whether any correction, cancellation, incorporation or consequential relief is warranted; and ix. Ultimately, what relief, if any, each of the plaintiffs and defendants is entitled to in accordance with law.
The learned trial Court shall not treat any observation made herein as a final determination of the aforesaid factual controversies. All parties shall remain at liberty to establish their respective claims by producing admissible evidence, including the original registered deeds, the complete revenue record, mutation No. 1107, the proceedings and order on the basis of which the mutation was attested, and any other relevant documentary or oral evidence permissible in law.
Conclusion.
14. For the foregoing reasons, this Court is of the considered
view that the judgments and decrees of the learned Courts below cannot be allowed to stand in their present form. The principal reason for remand is not merely the existence of a disputed claim but the emergence, after the earlier adjudication, of independent claims of persons who were not afforded an opportunity before the Courts below to plead and establish their rights, particularly rights asserted on the strength of mutation No. 1107 and subsequent transactions. Those claims may materially affect the determination of title and the relief sought by the plaintiffs. Their adjudication without a proper trial would offend the fundamental requirement of fair opportunity and would also risk an incomplete or inconclusive determination of the real controversy. The purpose of remand, therefore, is to ensure that the entire dispute is decided once and for all, on the basis of complete pleadings and evidence and after hearing every person whose proprietary rights may be affected by the ultimate judgment, rather than permitting the litigation to generate another round of proceedings at a later stage.
15. Consequently, the instant Civil Revision Petition is allowed.
The judgment and decree dated 19.01.2015 passed by the learned Additional District Judge-IV, Mardan, and the judgment and decree dated 06.12.2012 passed by the learned Civil Judge-XII, Mardan, in Civil Suits No. 168/1 and 167/1, are set aside. Both suits are remanded to the learned trial Court for fresh adjudication in accordance with the observations and directions contained herein. The plaintiffs of Civil Suit No. 167/1 and Civil Suit No.
168/1 shall file their respective amended plaints before the learned trial Court, incorporating such amendments as are necessary to disclose their complete claims and, in particular, the plaintiffs of Civil Suit No. 167/1 shall be at liberty to amend their prayer appropriately. All added respondents/applicants who have been brought on record in the proceedings under section 12(2) CPC shall be arrayed as defendants in the respective suits. Thereafter, the defendants shall be granted reasonable opportunity to submit their written statements and the learned trial Court shall frame appropriate issues on the basis of the amended pleadings. The learned trial Court shall decide the consolidated suits afresh after affording all parties a full and effective opportunity to produce documentary and oral evidence and to rebut the case of the opposite side. The Court shall examine the competing claims arising from registered deeds No. 1828 and 1829, mutation No.
1107 and subsequent transactions independently and strictly in accordance with law. Nothing contained in this judgment shall be construed as an expression of opinion on the ultimate merits of any of those claims. The learned trial Court shall bear in mind that the litigation is considerably old. It shall, therefore, proceed with expedition and shall not grant unnecessary adjournments. Subject to the cooperation of the parties and ordinary exigencies of judicial proceedings, the learned trial Court shall endeavour to conclude the proceedings within five months from the date of submission of the amended plaints. The parties shall appear before the learned Civil Judge-XII, Mardan, on 12.09.2026. Parties are left to bear their own costs.
Announced.
12.08.2026.
J U D G E
(SB) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Muhammad Naeem Anwar.
Asif Jan Sr.S.S .
