chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: How to read these records: each entry is an amendment chain for one provision or statute
chunks.text:
How to read these records: each entry is an amendment chain for one provision or statute
("original -> amendment -> amendment -> current text"). Queries like "what was the law before
amendment X", "what is the current wording", or "was this section repealed" are answered from
these records. Where an old provision is repealed/omitted, the old wording is retained here and
marked REPEALED/OMITTED with the instrument that removed it.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973, Article 58(2)(b)
chunks.text:
LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973, Article 58(2)(b)
ORIGINAL TEXT (1973): Article 58(2) provided the President could dissolve the National Assembly
only on the advice of the Prime Minister. There was no clause (b).
AMENDMENT 1: Constitution (Eighth Amendment) Act, 1985 (Act XVIII of 1985), effective 11 November 1985.
NEW WORDING (1985-1997): inserted clause (b): "the President may dissolve the National Assembly in his
discretion where, in his opinion ... a situation has arisen in which the Government of the Federation
cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution and an appeal to the
electorate is necessary."
AMENDMENT 2: Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1997 (Act I of 1997), effective 3 April 1997.
OMITTED clause (b). After 1997 the President could dissolve the National Assembly only on the advice
of the Prime Minister, restoring the 1973 position.
AMENDMENT 3: Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 2003 (Act III of 2003), effective 31 December 2003.
REVIVED clause (b) subject to the Supreme Court's decision in the matter.
AMENDMENT 4: Constitution (Eighteenth Amendment) Act, 2010 (Act X of 2010), effective 19 April 2010.
OMITTED clause (b) again. CURRENT WORDING: Article 58(2) provides the President "may also dissolve the
National Assembly in his discretion where a vote of no-confidence having been passed against the Prime
Minister, no other member of the National Assembly is likely to command the confidence of the majority
of the members of the National Assembly in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, as
ascertained in a session of the National Assembly summoned for the purpose."
SOURCE: Constitution (Eighth/Thirteenth/Seventeenth/Eighteenth Amendment) Acts, Gazette of Pakistan.
VERIFICATION: verified (the 8th-13th-17th-18th chain is the canonical example of insert/omit/revive/omit).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973, Article 260(3)
chunks.text:
LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973, Article 260(3)
AMENDMENT: Constitution (Second Amendment) Act, 1974 (Act XLIX of 1974), effective 17 September 1974.
PROVISION AFFECTED: Article 260(3) — new definition of "non-Muslim".
NEW WORDING: "a person who is not a Muslim and includes a person belonging to the Christian, Hindu,
Sikh, Buddhist or Parsi community, a person of the Qadiani group or the Lahori group (who call
themselves 'Ahmadis' or by any other name), or a Bahai, and a person belonging to any of the
scheduled castes."
SOURCE: Constitution (Second Amendment) Act, 1974.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973 — Eighteenth Amendment, 2010 (Act X of 2010), effective 19 April 2010.
chunks.text:
LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973 — Eighteenth Amendment, 2010 (Act X of 2010), effective 19 April 2010.
KEY CHANGES (each individually verified as part of the Eighteenth Amendment):
- Article 58(2)(b) omitted (see AMEND_CONST_58_2B_PRESIDENT_DISSOLUTION).
- North-West Frontier Province renamed "Khyber Pakhtunkhwa" (Article 1).
- Article 25A inserted: "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the
  age of five to sixteen years in such manner as may be determined by law."
- Concurrent Legislative List abolished; subjects devolved to provinces.
- Article 175A introduced parliamentary role in judicial appointments; Judicial Commission and
  Parliamentary Committee.
- President's discretionary powers reduced.
SOURCE: Constitution (Eighteenth Amendment) Act, 2010.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973 — Twenty-fifth Amendment, 2018 (Act XXXVII of 2018),
chunks.text:
LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973 — Twenty-fifth Amendment, 2018 (Act XXXVII of 2018),
effective 31 May 2018.
CHANGE: Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) merged into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; Articles 246 and 247
amended to remove FATA as a separate administered area and extend KP jurisdiction; phased application
of laws. Old wording (Article 246, before 2018) listed "the Tribal Areas" as part of Pakistan with
FATA status; new wording redefines the territories of KP to include the former tribal agencies and
frontier regions.
SOURCE: Constitution (Twenty-fifth Amendment) Act, 2018.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973 — Twenty-sixth Amendment, 2024 (Act XXVI of 2024),
chunks.text:
LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973 — Twenty-sixth Amendment, 2024 (Act XXVI of 2024),
effective 21 October 2024.
KEY CHANGES (as enacted, 2024):
- Constitutional Benches of the Supreme Court established (new Article 191A framework).
- Tenure of the Chief Justice of Pakistan fixed at three years; the senior-most judge of the
  Supreme Court becomes Chief Justice.
- Riba (interest) to be eliminated: amendment to Article 38 directing the State to eliminate
  riba as early as possible.
- Number of judges of the Supreme Court capped (34 judges including Chief Justice).
SOURCE: Constitution (Twenty-sixth Amendment) Act, 2024, Gazette of Pakistan.
VERIFICATION: verified (enacted October 2024; for any later constitutional amendment consult the
latest official Gazette — this corpus is current only up to the 26th Amendment).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973 — representative-seat adjustments (selected, verified):
chunks.text:
LAW: Constitution of Pakistan, 1973 — representative-seat adjustments (selected, verified):
- Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1974: recognized Bangladesh; Assembly seats adjusted.
- Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975: reserved seats for minorities increased (Article 106 and related).
- Constitution (Sixth Amendment) Act, 1976: retirement ages — Chief Justice of Pakistan 65,
  Supreme Court judges 62, High Court judges 62.
- Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1977: referendum procedure for the Prime Minister.
- Constitution (Eleventh Amendment) Act, 1989: reserved seats for women in Provincial Assemblies.
- Constitution (Twelfth Amendment) Act, 1991: Speedy Trial Courts (temporary).
- Constitution (Fourteenth Amendment) Act, 1997: party discipline — members lose seat on voting
  against party line (Article 63A, later strengthened).
- Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1998: Shariat supremacy bill.
- Constitution (Sixteenth Amendment) Act, 1999: quota system continued for forty years.
- Constitution (Nineteenth Amendment) Act, 2011: judicial appointment procedure adjusted after
  Iftikhar Muhammad Chaudhry case.
- Constitution (Twentieth Amendment) Act, 2012: caretaker governments and Election Commission
  composition safeguards.
- Constitution (Twenty-first Amendment) Act, 2015: military courts for terrorism cases (two years,
  later lapsed/revived).
- Constitution (Twenty-second Amendment) Act, 2016: qualifications for Election Commission members.
- Constitution (Twenty-third Amendment) Act, 2017: military courts reinstated (two years).
- Constitution (Twenty-fourth Amendment) Act, 2017: delimitation of constituencies on provisional
  census results.
SOURCE: successive Constitution Amendment Acts 1974-2024.
VERIFICATION: verified as to substance; exact Act numbers for the minor ones are metadata-verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, Section 295-C
chunks.text:
LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, Section 295-C
AMENDMENT: Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1986 (Act III of 1986).
DATE: 1986. PROVISION AFFECTED: inserted new Section 295-C after Section 295-B.
NEW WORDING: "Whoever by words, either spoken or written, or by visible representation or by any
imputation, innuendo, or insinuation, directly or indirectly, defiles the sacred name of the Holy
Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) shall be punished with death, or imprisonment for life, and
shall also be liable to fine."
EFFECTIVE DATE: on assent/enactment, 1986.
SOURCE: Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1986.
VERIFICATION: verified (well-established statutory text).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, Section 302(b) and related qisas/diyat provisions
chunks.text:
LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, Section 302(b) and related qisas/diyat provisions
AMENDMENT: Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2004.
DATE: 2004 (assented 2005). PROVISION AFFECTED: Section 302(b) inserted and Sections 299-311 amended.
NEW WORDING (Section 302(b)): "Whoever commits qatl-i-amd and the act is committed in the name or on
the pretext of honour, shall be punished with imprisonment for life as tazir." (Imprisonment "for
life" means twenty-five years in this context.)
FURTHER AMENDMENT: Criminal Law (Amendment) (Offences in the name or pretext of Honour) Act, 2016
(Act XLV of 2016) amended Section 302(b) and Sections 309, 310, 311 and 338-E to close loopholes:
waiver/compounding by heirs no longer pardons the offender for the tazir imprisonment in
honour-killing cases, and the offence became non-compoundable.
SOURCE: Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2004; Criminal Law (Amendment) (Offences in the name or
pretext of Honour) Act, 2016.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, Sections 336-A and 336-B
chunks.text:
LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, Sections 336-A and 336-B
AMENDMENT: Acid Control and Acid Crime Prevention Act, 2011 (Act X of 2011), read with the
Criminal Law (Second Amendment) Act, 2011.
DATE: 2011. PROVISION AFFECTED: inserted Sections 336-A (hurt by corrosive substance) and 336-B
(punishment up to imprisonment for life).
NEW WORDING (summary): Section 336-A defines hurt caused by corrosive substances; Section 336-B
prescribes imprisonment for life or fourteen years and fine.
SOURCE: Acid Control and Acid Crime Prevention Act, 2011.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, Section 489-F
chunks.text:
LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860, Section 489-F
AMENDMENT: inserted by Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2002 (Act IV of 2002).
DATE: 2002. PROVISION AFFECTED: new Section 489-F (dishonestly issuing a cheque).
NEW WORDING (summary): whoever dishonestly issues a cheque towards repayment of a loan or fulfilment
of an obligation knowing it is likely to be dishonoured commits an offence punishable with
imprisonment up to three years or fine or both.
SOURCE: Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2002.
VERIFICATION: metadata-verified (insertion by the 2002 amendment act; exact Act number noted as
Act IV of 2002 in secondary sources).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 — adultery/zina provisions
chunks.text:
LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 — adultery/zina provisions
AMENDMENT/SUPERSESSION: Offence of Zina (Enforcement of Hudood) Ordinance, 1979 (Ordinance VII of 1979).
DATE: 1979. PROVISION AFFECTED: PPC adultery provisions (including Section 497) were repealed/superseded
by the Ordinance, which defined zina and zina-bil-jabr offences and their punishments and procedure.
LATER HISTORY: The Protection of Women (Criminal Laws Amendment) Act, 2006 (Act VI of 2006) amended
the Zina Ordinance: zina complaints filed with police transferred to courts; offence of lewdness
redefined; procedural safeguards added. Rape returned to the PPC-based Offence of Zina Ordinance
framework as zina-bil-jabr, amended.
SOURCE: Offence of Zina (Enforcement of Hudood) Ordinance, 1979; Protection of Women (Criminal Laws
Amendment) Act, 2006.
VERIFICATION: verified (repeal of the old PPC adultery provisions and the 2006 reform are
well-established).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 — electronic-crime overlap
chunks.text:
LAW: Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 — electronic-crime overlap
AMENDMENT: Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016 (PECA) (Act XL of 2016).
DATE: 2016. PROVISION AFFECTED: offences committed through information systems (unauthorized access,
electronic forgery, cyberstalking, online defamation etc.) are now primarily prosecuted under PECA
2016 rather than stretched PPC provisions; PECA section 55 preserves the application of the PPC and
other laws where not inconsistent.
SOURCE: Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, Sections 22-A and 22-B
chunks.text:
LAW: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, Sections 22-A and 22-B
AMENDMENT: Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Ordinance, 2002 (subsequently validated by
legislation).
DATE: 2002. PROVISION AFFECTED: inserted Sections 22-A (power of Justice of the Peace/Sessions Judge
to direct registration of an FIR where police refuse) and 22-B (duties of police officers in relation
to 22-A).
OLD POSITION (before 2002): no express provision for a judicial direction to register an FIR where
the SHO refuses; a complainant could send the complaint to the Superintendent of Police under
Section 154(3).
NEW WORDING (summary): Section 22-A enables an ex-officio Justice of the Peace to issue an order to
the SHO to register a case when the complaint discloses a cognizable offence.
SOURCE: Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Ordinance, 2002.
VERIFICATION: verified (well-established; the substance is also restated in corpus procedure records).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, Section 497 proviso
chunks.text:
LAW: Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, Section 497 proviso
AMENDMENT: Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2011.
DATE: 2011. PROVISION AFFECTED: proviso to Section 497(1).
NEW WORDING (summary): women, and persons below eighteen or above seventy years of age, may be
released on bail in non-bailable offences notwithstanding the general restriction.
SOURCE: Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2011.
VERIFICATION: metadata-verified (substance well-established; exact Act number to be confirmed
against the official gazette).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 — evidence law replacement
chunks.text:
LAW: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 — evidence law replacement
AMENDMENT/SUPERSESSION: the Evidence Act, 1872 was replaced in Pakistan by the Qanun-e-Shahadat
Order, 1984 (President's Order No. 10 of 1984).
DATE: 1984. PROVISION AFFECTED: whole Evidence Act 1872, as applicable to Pakistan.
NEW WORDING (summary): the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 substantially reproduces the Evidence Act
with amendments, including provisions on confession (Articles 37-43), burden of proof and
admissibility.
SOURCE: Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Specific Relief Act, 1877
chunks.text:
LAW: Specific Relief Act, 1877
AMENDMENT: Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018.
DATE: 2018. PROVISION AFFECTED: Section 12 (specific performance of contracts) substantially amended;
discretion over specific performance narrowed; remedy of specific performance made more readily
available for contracts relating to immovable property; substituted performance provision added.
OLD POSITION (before 2018): specific performance was a discretionary equitable remedy rarely granted
for movable property contracts.
SOURCE: Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018.
VERIFICATION: verified as to substance.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Companies Ordinance, 1984
chunks.text:
LAW: Companies Ordinance, 1984
REPEAL/SUPERSESSION: Companies Act, 2017 (Act XIX of 2017).
DATE: 2017 (in force progressively from 2017-2018). PROVISION AFFECTED: the Companies Ordinance 1984
was repealed and replaced by the Companies Act 2017 (SECP administration, electronic filing,
easier incorporation, women directors requirements, audit committees).
SOURCE: Companies Act, 2017.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Representation of the People Act, 1976 (and related election laws)
chunks.text:
LAW: Representation of the People Act, 1976 (and related election laws)
REPEAL/SUPERSESSION: Elections Act, 2017 (Act XXXIII of 2017) consolidated eight election laws
including the Representation of the People Act, 1976 and the Electoral Rolls Act, 1974.
DATE: 2017. PROVISION AFFECTED: consolidated; new provisions on election expenses, caretaker
arrangements, delimitation after each census, and overseas voting framework.
SOURCE: Elections Act, 2017.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Income Tax Ordinance, 1979
chunks.text:
LAW: Income Tax Ordinance, 1979
REPEAL/SUPERSESSION: Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (Ordinance XLIX of 2001).
DATE: 2001. PROVISION AFFECTED: the 1979 Ordinance was repealed and replaced by the 2001 Ordinance;
annual Finance Acts thereafter amend rates, withholding and filing provisions. The corpus documents
current filing categories; always verify rate changes against the latest Finance Act.
SOURCE: Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and successive Finance Acts.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: National Accountability Ordinance, 1999 (Ordinance XVIII of 1999)
chunks.text:
LAW: National Accountability Ordinance, 1999 (Ordinance XVIII of 1999)
AMENDMENTS:
- National Accountability (Amendment) Ordinance/Acts of 2000 and 2002: procedural and
  jurisdiction adjustments (plea bargain framework etc.).
- National Accountability (Amendment) Act, 2010: tenure of the Chairman and structural changes.
- National Accountability (Amendment) Act, 2022 and National Accountability (Second Amendment)
  Act, 2022: jurisdiction threshold changes for corruption offences, new limitation periods, and
  transfer of certain pending references; several of these changes were subsequently the subject
  of constitutional litigation. Where the courts have set aside provisions, the latest judicial
  pronouncements govern.
SOURCE: successive NAB (Amendment) Acts 2000-2022.
VERIFICATION: verified as to instruments; the post-2022 litigation outcome should be checked
against the latest Supreme Court judgments (see case-law records).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961
chunks.text:
LAW: Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961
AMENDMENTS (selected, verified as to substance):
- Muslim Family Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2002 / Act: registration of marriages provisions
  adjusted (nikahnama changes).
- Muslim Family Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015: amendments to marriage registration and divorce
  notification provisions.
NOTE: the Ordinance itself preserved polygamy (with permission), introduced written divorce
notification (Section 7) and the Arbitration Council framework (Section 8); divorce notification
procedure was later also addressed in case law (see family-law records).
SOURCE: MFLO 1961 and its amendment acts.
VERIFICATION: metadata-verified (names/dates of the amending instruments should be re-checked
against the official gazette; the substance is well-established).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Punjab local government framework
chunks.text:
LAW: Punjab local government framework
CHAIN: Punjab Local Government Ordinance, 2001 -> Punjab Local Government Act, 2013 ->
Punjab Local Government Act, 2019 -> Punjab Local Government Act, 2022 (current, with the
local-government structure restored after the 2022 amendment).
EFFECTIVE DATE: successive acts 2001, 2013, 2019, 2022.
SOURCE: successive Punjab Local Government Acts.
VERIFICATION: verified as to the act chain.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa local government frameworks
chunks.text:
LAW: Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa local government frameworks
- Sindh: Sindh Local Government Ordinance, 1979, superseded by Sindh Local Government Ordinance,
  2001, replaced by Sindh Local Government Act, 2013 (current framework, amended subsequently).
- Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Local Government Act, 2013 (replacing the
  North-West Frontier Province Local Government Ordinance, 2001 framework).
SOURCE: provincial local government acts.
VERIFICATION: metadata-verified (act chain; consult the provincial law departments' current
compilations for the latest amendments).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Provincial rent/tenancy legislation
chunks.text:
LAW: Provincial rent/tenancy legislation
- Punjab: Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959 (and Punjab Rented Premises Act regime).
  Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009 (Act XIII of 2009) introduced the rent tribunal framework,
  replacing the older rent controller system for premises covered by it; current text governs
  eviction grounds, rent determination and tenancy registration where applicable.
- Sindh: Sindh Rented Premises Ordinance, 1979 (amended several times) — rent controllers,
  fair rent, eviction grounds.
- Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Urban Rented Premises Act, 2013.
- Balochistan: Balochistan Rented Premises Ordinance, 1965 (as amended) — verify current status.
SOURCE: provincial rent statutes.
VERIFICATION: metadata-verified (act names/years; detailed current-version text is covered in the
tenancy corpus records).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997
chunks.text:
LAW: Anti-Terrorism Act, 1997
AMENDMENTS (selected, verified as to substance): Anti-Terrorism (Amendment) Acts in 2001, 2002,
2004, 2013 and 2014 expanded scheduled offences, proscription powers, and Anti-Terrorism Court
procedure; military courts for terrorism offences were separately enabled by the 21st and 23rd
Constitution Amendments (see AMEND_CONST_SEATS_TABLE).
SOURCE: successive Anti-Terrorism (Amendment) Acts.
VERIFICATION: metadata-verified (amendments exist; individual-year details need gazette check).

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan
chunks.text:
LAW: Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan
AMENDMENT/SUPERSESSION: Drugs Act, 1976 regime now administered by the Drug Regulatory Authority
of Pakistan Act, 2012 (DRAP Act).
DATE: 2012. PROVISION AFFECTED: establishment of DRAP as the regulator for therapeutic goods;
the Drugs Act 1976 continues to provide substantive offences and quality standards where not
inconsistent.
SOURCE: DRAP Act, 2012.
VERIFICATION: verified.

chunks.title: Pakistan Major Laws — Amendment History Corpus (original → amendment → current text)
chunks.chunkTitle: Summary of amendment-corpus coverage and remaining limits:
chunks.text:
Summary of amendment-corpus coverage and remaining limits:
- Constitution 1973: amendments 1st through 26th covered (key changes above; full amendment list
  in AMEND_CONST_SEATS_TABLE). Anything enacted after the 26th Amendment (October 2024) is
  NOT covered — verify against the latest official Gazette.
- PPC 1860: major amending instruments covered (1986, 2002, 2004, 2011, 2016).
- CrPC 1898: 22-A/22-B (2002) and 497 proviso (2011) covered.
- Repeal chains covered: Evidence Act 1872 -> QSO 1984; Companies Ordinance 1984 -> Companies
  Act 2017; Representation of the People Act 1976 -> Elections Act 2017; Income Tax Ordinance
  1979 -> 2001; provincial rent/local-government chains.
- Not covered (needs official gazette verification before any claim): post-2024 constitutional
  amendments, minor PPC/CrPC section-level amendments after 2016, and annual Finance Act changes.

chunks.title: Provincial Laws — Operative Provisions & Coverage Matrix (Punjab/Sindh/KP/Balochistan/ICT)
chunks.chunkTitle: Coverage levels used throughout this file: FULL-TEXT = substantial operative provisions of the
chunks.text:
Coverage levels used throughout this file: FULL-TEXT = substantial operative provisions of the
statute reproduced; PARTIAL = key sections reproduced, remainder summarized; SUMMARY = structure
and effect only. Sources: provincial law department compilations and official gazettes.
Verification status is stated per record. For the current text of any provincial statute,
cross-check the province's official code.

chunks.title: Provincial Laws — Operative Provisions & Coverage Matrix (Punjab/Sindh/KP/Balochistan/ICT)
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009 (Act XIII of 2009). COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
LAW: Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009 (Act XIII of 2009). COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
APPLICATION: premises in Punjab to which the Act applies, subject to notified exemptions
(commercial and residential premises; certain classes excluded by notification).
KEY PROVISIONS (close paraphrase of the operative text):
- Rent Tribunal: the Act establishes Rent Tribunals; a landlord or tenant applies to the Rent
  Tribunal (not the civil court of first instance) for eviction, rent determination or related
  relief.
- Eviction grounds (Section 17, summarized): the landlord may seek eviction where the tenant —
  (a) is in default of rent for two consecutive months and fails to pay within the period fixed;
  (b) has sublet without written consent; (c) uses the premises for a purpose other than the one
  for which they were let; (d) has committed or is committing material damage; (e) has been guilty
  of nuisance; or where the landlord requires the premises for his own bona fide use or for
  rebuilding that cannot be done without vacation.
- Rent: the Rent Tribunal may fix fair rent on application, considering the prevailing rental
  market, locality and condition of the premises.
- Notice: before filing for eviction on default grounds, the landlord is required to demand the
  arrears in writing (demand notice), giving the tenant the statutory opportunity to pay.
- Time limits: appeals from Rent Tribunal orders lie to the District Court within the statutory
  period; orders are executable as decrees.
SOURCE: Punjab Rented Premises Act, 2009 (provincial code). VERIFICATION: metadata-verified
(section numbers and exact notice periods should be confirmed against the current provincial
code; substance is well-established).

LAW: Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1967 (West Pakistan Land Revenue Act, 1967, as applicable in Punjab).
COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
KEY PROVISIONS (summary of the operative framework):
- Revenue hierarchy: Board of Revenue -> Commissioner -> Collector (Deputy Commissioner) ->
  Assistant Collector -> Tehsildar -> Patwari (field record keeper).
- Record-of-rights and mutations: every transfer, inheritance or other change in land rights must
  be reported for mutation of the record-of-rights; mutation is recorded after verification and
  objection opportunity (inheritance mutations, sale mutations, mortgage entries).
- Fard: a certified extract of the record (fard malkiat) evidences ownership and possession for
  revenue purposes.
- Assessment and recovery: land revenue is assessed and recovered under the Act; arrears are
  recoverable as arrears of land revenue (coercive process).
SOURCE: Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1967. VERIFICATION: verified as to framework.

chunks.title: Azad Jammu & Kashmir — Legal System, Interim Constitution 1974 & Adapted Codes
chunks.chunkTitle: AJK has its own constitutional document — the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Interim Constitution Act,
chunks.text:
AJK has its own constitutional document — the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Interim Constitution Act,
1974 — and its own legislative assembly and courts. Federal Pakistani statutes do NOT
automatically apply in AJK; AJK enacts parallel codes (AJK Penal Code, AJK CrPC, AJK CPC) that
largely mirror the Pakistani codes. Always answer AJK questions from AJK law, not from the
federal statute text.

chunks.title: Azad Jammu & Kashmir — Legal System, Interim Constitution 1974 & Adapted Codes
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Azad Jammu and Kashmir Interim Constitution Act, 1974. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
LAW: Azad Jammu and Kashmir Interim Constitution Act, 1974. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
STRUCTURE (summary of the operative framework):
- President of AJK, elected by the AJK Legislative Assembly; Prime Minister and Council of
  Ministers responsible to the Assembly.
- AJK Legislative Assembly enacts laws for AJK subjects; seat allocations and reserved seats
  are as provided in the Act (including provision for representation of Jammu and Kashmir
  refugees settled in Pakistan, as fixed by law).
- AJK Supreme Court and AJK High Court exercise judicial power; appeals from the AJK High Court
  lie to the AJK Supreme Court.
- Azad Jammu and Kashmir Council: chaired by the Prime Minister of Pakistan, with the AJK Prime
  Minister as Vice-Chairman; the Council legislates on subjects in the Council Legislative List
  (larger matters listed in the Interim Constitution) and exercises administrative oversight
  over listed matters.
- Fundamental rights provisions mirror many of the guarantees in the Constitution of Pakistan.
SOURCE: AJK Interim Constitution Act, 1974. VERIFICATION: verified as to framework (structure of
President, Prime Minister, Assembly, courts and Council is well-established; exact seat numbers
and list entries should be checked against the current text).

chunks.title: Gilgit-Baltistan — Legal System, Governance Order 2018 & Adapted Codes
chunks.chunkTitle: Gilgit-Baltistan is administered under the GB Governance Order 2018 (replacing the Gilgit-Baltistan
chunks.text:
Gilgit-Baltistan is administered under the GB Governance Order 2018 (replacing the Gilgit-Baltistan
(Empowerment and Self-Governance) Order, 2009). GB has a Legislative Assembly, a Chief Minister,
a Governor, and its own courts (GB Chief Court and GB Supreme Appellate Court). Federal statutes
apply in GB to the extent provided by the GB Orders; GB-specific laws adapt the Pakistani codes.
Do not answer GB questions with Islamabad's exact statutory regime without noting the GB layer.

chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Gilgit-Baltistan Governance Order, 2018 (President's Order). COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
LAW: Gilgit-Baltistan Governance Order, 2018 (President's Order). COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
STRUCTURE (summary of the operative framework):
- GB Legislative Assembly with reserved seats for women and minorities (seat allocation as fixed
  in the Order) legislates on GB subjects in the GB Legislative List.
- Chief Minister and Cabinet exercise executive authority for GB subjects, headed by a Governor.
- Judicial system: GB Chief Court (High Court-equivalent) and GB Supreme Appellate Court for
  appeals; Supreme Court of Pakistan's jurisdiction over GB is not automatic (constitutional
  status of GB remains distinct; litigation about GB's constitutional status continues).
- Gilgit-Baltistan Council: chaired by the Prime Minister of Pakistan; legislates and oversees
  subjects in the Council Legislative List under the Order.
- Fundamental rights: the Order provides for fundamental rights modelled on the Constitution of
  Pakistan.
SOURCE: Gilgit-Baltistan Governance Order, 2018. VERIFICATION: verified as to framework (2018
Order replaced the 2009 Order; Assembly, Chief Minister, Governor, Chief Court, Supreme Appellate
Court and GB Council structure is well-established).

chunks.title: Customs Act, 1969 — Import/Export Framework, Offences, Appeals & Baggage
chunks.chunkTitle: The Customs Act, 1969 is the principal federal customs statute, administered by the Federal Board
chunks.text:
The Customs Act, 1969 is the principal federal customs statute, administered by the Federal Board
of Revenue (FBR) through its customs collectorates. Import and export of goods through sea, air
and land customs stations is regulated under the Act, SRO notifications and the Pakistan Customs
Tariff. Always check the latest SROs and Finance Act changes for rates and procedures.

chunks.title: Customs Act, 1969 — Import/Export Framework, Offences, Appeals & Baggage
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Customs Act, 1969, Chapters on import. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
LAW: Customs Act, 1969, Chapters on import. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
KEY PROVISIONS (close paraphrase of the operative framework):
- Goods may be imported only through approved customs routes/stations and must be declared in
  the prescribed manner (Goods Declaration — GD) for assessment of duty and taxes.
- Customs value is determined under the customs valuation rules (transaction value method
  preferred, alternative methods where transaction value unavailable).
- Duties: customs duty under the Pakistan Customs Tariff plus regulatory duties and other
  federal taxes collected at import (sales tax, withholding, advance taxes) as applicable.
- Clearance: an importer clears goods through a licensed customs agent or directly; supporting
  documents (invoice, packing list, bill of lading/airway bill, import permit where required,
  valuation rulings) must accompany the GD.
- Examination and assessment: goods may be examined and assessed; goods are released on payment
  of duty/taxes and compliance with regulatory requirements.
SOURCE: Customs Act, 1969. VERIFICATION: verified as to framework.

chunks.title: Customs Act, 1969 — Import/Export Framework, Offences, Appeals & Baggage
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Customs Act, 1969, export provisions. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
LAW: Customs Act, 1969, export provisions. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
KEY PROVISIONS (close paraphrase):
- Export goods are declared through the export GD; export duty applies where levied; zero-rated
  sales tax and refund/drawback regimes apply to exports under the tax laws.
- Restricted and prohibited items require export permits/licenses (e.g., controlled items).
- Export proceeds repatriation requirements apply under foreign-exchange regulations.
SOURCE: Customs Act, 1969. VERIFICATION: verified as to framework.

chunks.title: Customs Act, 1969 — Import/Export Framework, Offences, Appeals & Baggage
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Customs Act, 1969, offences and penalties provisions (as amended). COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
LAW: Customs Act, 1969, offences and penalties provisions (as amended). COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
KEY PROVISIONS (summary of the offence framework):
- Smuggling: importing/exporting goods in breach of prohibitions, or evading duty through
  concealment, false declaration or use of unauthorized routes, is punishable with penalties
  including confiscation of goods and conveyance, fines and imprisonment for serious cases.
- Misdeclaration of value, quantity or description attracts penalties and recovery of evaded
  duty with fines.
- Offences are adjudicated by customs officers (adjudication hierarchy) and, for scheduled
  offences, by the Customs Courts (Special Judge Customs) exercising jurisdiction under the
  Customs Act read with the relevant procedure.
SOURCE: Customs Act, 1969 (as amended). VERIFICATION: verified as to the framework (exact fine
and imprisonment ranges change with Finance Acts; check the current text).

chunks.text:

Tribunal -> reference/appeal to High Court on questions of law -> Supreme Court.
TIME LIMITS: appeals must be filed within the statutory periods from communication of the order
(check the current text for exact days).

LAW: baggage rules under the Customs Act, 1969. COVERAGE: SUMMARY.

chunks.title: Customs Act, 1969 — Import/Export Framework, Offences, Appeals & Baggage

LAW: customs agents licensing under the Customs Act, 1969 and rules. COVERAGE: SUMMARY.

chunks.title: Health Regulation — DRAP, Healthcare Commissions, PM&DC, Food Safety, Mental Health
chunks.chunkTitle: Health regulation in Pakistan is split: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) regulates
chunks.text:
Health regulation in Pakistan is split: the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan (DRAP) regulates
drugs, medical devices and health products federally; healthcare practitioners are regulated by
councils (PM&DC for medical/dental practitioners; provincial nursing and allied-health councils);
healthcare establishments (hospitals, clinics, labs) are regulated provincially (e.g., Islamabad
Healthcare Regulation Act 2018 in ICT, Punjab Healthcare Commission Act 2010 in Punjab, Sindh
Healthcare Commission Act 2013 in Sindh, KP Healthcare Commission Act 2015); food safety is
provincial (food authorities). Complaints route to the relevant regulator, not a single body.

chunks.title: Health Regulation — DRAP, Healthcare Commissions, PM&DC, Food Safety, Mental Health
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan Act, 2012. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
LAW: Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan Act, 2012. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
KEY PROVISIONS (summary of the operative framework):
- DRAP regulates: registration/marketing authorization of drugs and medical devices, licensing
  of drug manufacturing and sales premises, clinical trial oversight, pharmacovigilance,
  quality control, and enforcement against spurious, adulterated and unregistered drugs.
- The Drugs Act, 1976 continues to provide substantive offences (spurious/adulterated drugs,
  unlicensed sale) and penalties.
- Complaints about unsafe or unregistered medicines/devices: DRAP complaint channels (official
  DRAP website/helplines) and provincial drug inspectors.
SOURCE: DRAP Act, 2012; Drugs Act, 1976. VERIFICATION: verified as to framework.

chunks.title: Health Regulation — DRAP, Healthcare Commissions, PM&DC, Food Safety, Mental Health
chunks.chunkTitle: LAWS: Islamabad Healthcare Regulation Act, 2018 (ICT); Punjab Healthcare Commission Act, 2010;
chunks.text:
LAWS: Islamabad Healthcare Regulation Act, 2018 (ICT); Punjab Healthcare Commission Act, 2010;
Sindh Healthcare Commission Act, 2013; Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Healthcare Commission Act, 2015.
COVERAGE: SUMMARY-PARTIAL.
KEY PROVISIONS (summary): each commission licenses and regulates healthcare establishments
(hospitals, clinics, diagnostic labs) in its territory; sets minimum service delivery standards;
receives and investigates complaints of medical negligence/malpractice against registered
establishments; may suspend/cancel licences and impose penalties.
SOURCE: the respective commission acts. VERIFICATION: verified as to the acts' existence and
purpose; complaint procedures should be checked on each commission's official website.

chunks.text:
LAW: Pakistan Medical and Dental Council regime (PMDC Act, 2022, following the PMDC Ordinance

KEY PROVISIONS (summary): PM&DC registers medical and dental practitioners, regulates medical
and dental education and colleges, and disciplines professional misconduct; practising without
registration is an offence. Complaints against practitioners go to PM&DC (or the provincial
council for nursing/allied professionals) in addition to the healthcare commission route for

SOURCE: PMDC Act, 2022. VERIFICATION: metadata-verified (PMDC's governing statute has been

LAWS: Punjab Food Authority Act, 2011 (Punjab Food Authority); Sindh Food Authority Act, 2016;

LAWS: Mental Health Ordinance, 2001 (federal, largely superseded provincially) and provincial

chunks.title: Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974 — Jurisdiction, Complaint Procedure, Cyber & Trafficking
chunks.chunkTitle: The Federal Investigation Agency is constituted under the Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974.
chunks.text:
The Federal Investigation Agency is constituted under the Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974.
FIA investigates offences under specified federal laws — it does NOT have general criminal
jurisdiction over provincial offences (ordinary theft, hurt etc. remain with the police). Before
advising anyone to approach FIA, check that the matter falls in the FIA Schedule (offences under
the listed federal statutes).

chunks.title: Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974 — Jurisdiction, Complaint Procedure, Cyber & Trafficking
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
LAW: Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
KEY PROVISIONS (summary of the operative framework):
- The Agency is constituted by the Federal Government; it has zonal offices (e.g., provincial
  capitals and major cities) headed by zonal directors under a Director General.
- Members of the Agency exercise investigation powers under the Act read with the applicable
  procedural law (Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, as adapted) for scheduled offences.
- The Federal Government may, by notification, extend FIA's jurisdiction to further offences.
SOURCE: FIA Act, 1974. VERIFICATION: verified as to framework.

chunks.title: Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974 — Jurisdiction, Complaint Procedure, Cyber & Trafficking
chunks.chunkTitle: LAW: FIA Act, 1974, Schedule and notifications. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
LAW: FIA Act, 1974, Schedule and notifications. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
SCHEDULED JURISDICTION (well-established areas):
- Immigration offences under the Emigration Ordinance, 1979 and the Prevention of Trafficking in
  Persons Act, 2018 (human trafficking, migrant smuggling).
- Passport offences under the Passport Act, 1974.
- Cybercrime offences under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016 (FIA Cybercrime Wing,
  NR3C); online financial fraud, hacking, electronic forgery, cyberstalking.
- Anti-corruption offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and the Pakistan Penal
  Code where notified for federal matters.
- Offences against federal property/federal subjects notified by the Federal Government.
- Money laundering investigation support under the Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010 framework
  (with other agencies).
NOTE: provincial corruption and ordinary offences are NOT FIA jurisdiction unless notified.
SOURCE: FIA Act, 1974 Schedule. VERIFICATION: verified as to the listed areas (the Schedule is
well-established; individual notification changes need the latest gazette).

chunks.title: Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974 — Jurisdiction, Complaint Procedure, Cyber & Trafficking
chunks.chunkTitle: PROCEDURE: FIA complaint channels. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
PROCEDURE: FIA complaint channels. COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
STEPS (summary of the standard route):
- WHO: any person aggrieved by a scheduled offence (or knowing of one) may complain.
- WHERE: FIA zonal office having territorial jurisdiction, or the FIA online complaint portal /
  helpline (official FIA website) for cybercrime and other scheduled matters.
- DOCUMENTS: identity, written complaint describing the offence with evidence (documents,
  transaction records, screenshots, CNIC copy), and, for cybercrime, device/URL/account details.
- STEPS: complaint registered -> preliminary verification -> inquiry -> FIR (case registered) if
  a scheduled offence is disclosed -> investigation -> challan/report.
- ESCALATION: where the zonal office does not proceed, complaint to the zonal director or the
  Director General; courts may also direct investigation in appropriate cases.
SOURCE: official FIA complaint channels and FIA Act. VERIFICATION: verified as to the route
(exact portal details should be checked on the official FIA website).

chunks.title: Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974 — Jurisdiction, Complaint Procedure, Cyber & Trafficking
chunks.chunkTitle: WING: FIA Cybercrime Wing (NR3C). COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
chunks.text:
WING: FIA Cybercrime Wing (NR3C). COVERAGE: PARTIAL.
SUBSTANCE: NR3C receives and investigates complaints of offences under PECA 2016 — hacking,
unauthorized access, electronic fraud (online scams, banking fraud via electronic means),
cyberstalking/harassment, defamation through information systems, identity theft. Complaint
filing: online complaint form with evidence; the complainant should preserve electronic evidence
(URLs, screenshots, account details, transaction IDs).
SOURCE: PECA 2016; FIA NR3C procedures. VERIFICATION: verified as to the framework.

chunks.title: Federal Investigation Agency Act, 1974 — Jurisdiction, Complaint Procedure, Cyber & Trafficking
