G . Department al AI Stewardship Committee As an aspirational and alerting body to act against academic abuse of Generative AI Tools, the Departmental AI Stewardship Committee (DSC), Unfair - Means Control Committee ( UMCC ) or any equivalent statutory body is crucial in fighting to prevent the misuse of Generative AI Tools in tertiary educational institutions. These responsibilities consist of oversight, policy formulation , and the implementation of measures that prevent ethical use of Generative AI technologies .
H . Review and Develop Ins titutional Guidelines HEIs must develop detailed guidelines for AI use in specific contexts (undergraduate teaching, graduate research, assessment, etc.). Guidelines should provide examples of appropriate and inappropriate uses and be made available to all community members.
I . Educational Initiatives HEIs must r aise awareness among the faculty, staff, and students about the capabilities of Generative AI Tools including capabilities, limitations, ethical considerations, and proper disclosure practices through educational programs. Such workshops, seminars , and training sessions Should address both misuse detection and appropriate use encouragement.
J. Review and Approval Mechanism Institutions should establish clear mechanisms for review and approval of AI tools before deployment. Assessment tools relying on AI should be reviewed by relevant academic committees.
Major deployments should be approved by appropriate institutional bodies.
K. Monitoring and Enforcement It is important to monitor the use of Generative AI Tools on a regular basis, as well as auditing to make sure that the tools are being used in an ethically compliant manner. There is learning from reviewing projects, assignments , and assessments to discov er any academic dishonesty and unethical practices.

M. Reporting Mechanisms
Institutions must p ut in place reporting mechanism to the HEC on implementation of this framework, including number of violations processed on undergraduate and graduate level, institutional guidelines developed, and trainings conducted. This data will enable HEC identify and mitigate emerging issues in t he framework.
N. Framework Review and Continuous Improvement HEIs should review the AI policies and practices adapted by Universities/DAIs at least six monthly intervals to assess effectiveness, identify emerging issues, and incorporate institutional experience. Institutions should submit an annual AI Integration Report to the HEC documenting:
(i) number and nature of AI - related academic integrity cases; (ii) institutional guidelines and
policies developed; (iii) training and awareness programs conduct ed; (iv) technology infrastructure deployed; (v) emerging issues or challenges identified; and (vi) recommendations for framework updates. Given the fact that GenAI technology is dynamic, the committee should reexamine the existing policies on the appropri ate usage of GenAI tools periodically . Annual AI use reports and phased rollout can be integrated with the HEI’s internal policy for the use of Gen - AI tools aligned with the HEC ’s framework .
N - A. Assessment Resilience Institutions should establish a comprehensive assessment review plan to ensure that all major assessments (examinations, major assignments, projects) are resilient to AI use — meaning they reliably measure student learning even when students have access to g enerative AI. This review should be completed within 12 months of framework adoption and should consider: (i) assessment design that emphasizes critical thinking, analysis, and application rather than content generation;
(ii) in - class and supervised assess ments for foundational skills; (iii) oral examinations or
presentations in key courses; (iv) authentic tasks requiring local knowledge or realtime problem solving; and (v) portfolio assessment capturing development over time.
N - B. AI Literacy in Curricula Institutions should integrate AI literacy into curricula, ensuring graduates understand AI capabilities, limitations, ethical implications, and appropriate workplace use. This integration should be completed within two years of framework adoption and shou ld include: (i) foundational AI literacy for all students covering concepts, capabilities, and responsible use; (ii) discipline specific applications and implications; (iii) ethical frameworks for AI decision - making; and (iv) technical literacy for relevan t programs.
O. Ethics Training Offer ongoing ethics training and seminars for those in the faculty and students who are engaged in Generative AI tool projects. Responsible use, academic integrity , and the consequences of misuse are key points that should be focused on in this training.
P. Coordination with Higher Authorities Additionally, HEC’s policies shall be reflected in the departmental policies for fighting academic misuse of generative AI tools coherently .
Q. Ethically Promoting Research Be an advocate and advocate for ethical research practices in the department. It includes a focus on building an academic integrity and responsible innovation culture, not only in faculty, but also in students.
Therefore, the Departmental AI Stewardship Committee acts as an important avenue for legal protection against the inappropriate use of Generative AI tools in academic contexts t hrough the policies formulated with clear measures of accountability, an awareness mechanism, and constant checking of any Generative AI technologies within the academic domain.

# 8. Constructive and Encouraged Uses
Title: HEC Framework for Generation AI use in Higher Education Institutions
Authority: Higher Education Commission (HEC) of Pakistan
Section: 8. Constructive and Encouraged Uses
Official page: https://www.hec.gov.pk/english/policies/Pages/Framework-GenAI.aspx
Source file: https://www.hec.gov.pk/english/policies/Documents/Framework-Gene-AI.pdf

8. Constructive and Encouraged Uses
This section identifies uses of generative AI that should be encouraged and supported as they enhance teaching, learning, and research. Institutions should actively promote these uses through professional development, infrastructure support, and policy clarity.
8 A . Teaching a nd Learning Applications
Faculty are encouraged to use generative AI in teaching contexts such as: (i) possibility engine — generating multiple examples, case studies, or problem variations to illustrate concepts; (ii) Socratic opponent — providing counterarguments or alternative pers pectives to deepen student thinking; (iii) collaboration coach — offering feedback on group dynamics, presentation skills, or project management; (iv) personal tutor — explaining concepts in different ways tailored to individual student needs; (v) co - designer — assisting in course design, learning objectives, and assessment alignment; (vi) study buddy — generating practice problems, study guides, or quiz questions for student self - study; (vii) motivator — providing encouragement and learning strategies during challen ging coursework; (viii) writing coach — offering feedback on clarity, organization, and argumentation in student drafts; and (ix) research assistant — supporting literature review, data synthesis, and research methodology planning .
Faculty should share pract ices and lessons learned through faculty development programs and departmental colloquia to build institutional knowledge and help colleagues implement these tools effectively 8B . Research Applications Researchers are encouraged to use generative AI to s upport research processes including: (i) literature review — identifying relevant studies, synthesizing findings, and mapping research landscapes; (ii) hypothesis generation — brainstorming research questions and theoretical frameworks; (iii) data analysis — ex ploring patterns, generating initial interpretations, and suggesting statistical approaches (subject to verification); (iv) writing improvement — enhancing clarity and coherence of research manuscripts; (v) translation — making research accessible across langu ages; (vi) citation verification — checking accuracy of citations and references; and (vii) replication checking — identifying potential methodological issues or alternative explanations.
Generative AI should never be listed as a research author. The researche r bears full responsibility for all content and claims in publications regardless of AI assistance used. AI use in research should be disclosed in appropriate sections (methods, acknowledgments) of published work and should comply with journal guidelines.
8 C . Administrative Applications
Administrative staff and managers are encouraged to use generative AI for: (i) translation — providing multilingual support for communications; (ii) document processing — organizing, summarizing, and categorizing administrativ e documents; (iii) communication drafting — preparing routine correspondence, announcements, and reports; and (iv) data management — assisting with data organization and basic analysis. Administrative use should comply with data privacy requirements and instit utional information security policies .

# 9. Data Sovereignty and Protection
Title: HEC Framework for Generation AI use in Higher Education Institutions
Authority: Higher Education Commission (HEC) of Pakistan
Section: 9. Data Sovereignty and Protection
Official page: https://www.hec.gov.pk/english/policies/Pages/Framework-GenAI.aspx
Source file: https://www.hec.gov.pk/english/policies/Documents/Framework-Gene-AI.pdf

9. Data Sovereignty and Protection
Data sovereignty — the right of institutions to maintain control over institutional and student data — is a critical consideration in AI tool selection and deployment. Many cloud - based AI services process data on servers outside Pakistan or within jurisdictions with different data protection standards. Institutions should be aware of data flows and make informed choices about tools and data types. Sensitive institutional data (including student records, financial information, research data from government projects) should be processed using enterprise - grade AI tools with data residency guarantees or local hosting options. Publicly available or anonymized data may be processed using commer cial AI services, subject to explicit consent and compliance policies.
Institutions should consider deployment of local AI solutions where feasible, including open source language models and institutional AI services with on - premises hosting. These soluti ons provide greater data control and align with national data sovereignty objectives. Anonymization techniques — removing identifying information before processing — should be employed where sensitive data use cannot be avoided with commercial services.
The HEC will conduct a feasibility study within 12 months of framework adoption examining: (i) national AI infrastructure capacity; (ii) options for institutional or sectoral AI platforms with data residency in Pakistan; (iii) open - source AI model deployment i n HEIs; and (iv) procurement guidance for enterprise AI tools with appropriate data sovereignty provisions.

# 10. Rules and Penalties of Plagiarism
Title: HEC Framework for Generation AI use in Higher Education Institutions
Authority: Higher Education Commission (HEC) of Pakistan
Section: 10. Rules and Penalties of Plagiarism
Official page: https://www.hec.gov.pk/english/policies/Pages/Framework-GenAI.aspx
Source file: https://www.hec.gov.pk/english/policies/Documents/Framework-Gene-AI.pdf
Version: Framework-Gene-AI as published; HEC GenAI notification attached in the register
Notification / publication date: 2026-10-10
Effective date: 2026-10-10
Legal status: Current
Extracted verbatim from the official HEC source on 2026-10-10; only layout was repaired (line wraps, page markup) — no wording was changed.

10. Rules and Penalties of Plagiarism
Academic integrity is something students really need to be aware of , and how their institution stands about it . When in doubt, make sure they know what is going on , but also contact teachers or have a meeting with their academic advisor. The use of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT helps enhance learning, particularly outside the academic setting (e.g. brainstor ming ideas, exploring concepts, etc.) while its use to complete assignments and Thesis will have very serious consequences. However, the information that these tools produce was originally written and published , and it may be incorrect or out of date . Plag iarism occurs when students use text generators without proper citation. The information supplied by these tools may be deficient as well as mistaken , which necessitates students to verify their work . The University expects students to present original wor k that they produced independently in all graded assignments and theses.
Academic misconduct , together with a zero grade , follows both plagiarism detection and unauthorized tool usage of Generative AI in student work.
The following rules shall be incorporated at the institutional level:
i. Author credit must not go to generative AI tools in any writing project. The usage of these
tools should remain limited to make texts more readable but safety precautions should always be deployed. O ne must include a declaration statement regarding all AI - assisted technologies or generative AI tool use before references in the final manuscript section.
Declaration of G enerative AI tools and AI - assisted technologies in the writing process:
“During the preparation of this work , the author(s) used [NAME TOOL / SERVICE] in order to [REASON]. After using this tool/service, the author(s) reviewed and edited the content as needed and take(s) full responsibility (legal, moral, etc.) for the content of the publication.”
ii. Universities need to create internal protocols that establish how students should acknowledge
the integration of Generative AI tools when preparing academic papers. Any content produced by AI systems needs to receive appropriate acknowledgment in addition to proper recognition of the original authors who provided referenced material.
iii. Generative AI tools have specific conditions where their academic implementation meets
approval according to Section 6. Educational researchers should not rely on Generative AI tools for collecting data because they yield inadequate information that includ es outmoded facts as well as spurious references and artificial research findings. Students must avoid all activities of data generation and fabrication , including data manipulation that utilizes Generative AI tools. The student will face responsibility fo r misconduct when this situation occurs.
iv. Plagiarism detection software, including tools capable of identifying AI - generated text, may
be used to assess content originality when available. The evaluation of similarity and acceptable use of AI - assisted cont ent shall be guided by the prevailing policies and guidelines issued by the HEC, with final determinations made by the DSC and the relevant statutory bodies of the respective HEIs. HEC periodically updates these guidelines in line with global best practice s and feedback from the academic community. Detection as a single indicator is insufficient for disciplinary action; detection must be accompanied by additional corroborating evidence of intent to misrepresent.
v. Aligned with the recent plagiarism policy of HEC
, the student of UG as well as PG must add the updated plagiarism undertaking statement stating:
“ I, [Name of Student] , declare on oath that the research work presented in my UG/MS/PhD project/thesis, where applicable, entitled “[Project/Thesis Title]” is my own research work and is not substantially contributed by any other person or Generative AI Tools. Any small contribution/assistance wherever received has been duly acknowledged/cited , and the whole project/thesis has been written by me under the latest plagiarism policy declared by HEC and [Name of University] , as per the policy on use of Generative AI Tools.
Where Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have been used during the preparation of this project/thesis, such use has been limited to purposes permitted under the applicable HEC and University policies and guidelines. Any use of GenAI that has materially contributed to th e content, analysis, or presentation of this work has been appropriately acknowledged or disclosed, where required.
I further declare that GenAI tools have not been used to fabricate or falsify research data, results, references, citations, or sources, no r to generate work that is presented as my own in violation of applicable academic integrity requirements.
I understand that the use of GenAI does not relieve me of responsibility for the accuracy, originality, authenticity, proper citation, and academic integrity of this project/thesis. Any violation identified in this work shall be dealt with in accordance with the applicable policies and procedures of HEC and [Name of University]. ” The above undertaking statement s might be updated by HEC from time to time.
Policy Reference: ANTI - PLAGIARISM POLICY by HEC
vi. Ensure that the use of AI Generative Tools complies with existing copyright and intellectual
property laws. Universities should internally develop /implement guidelines that prevent the generation of content that infringes upon copyright, trademarks, or an y other legal rights (IPO, Ministry of Commerce, is a relevant government body in Pakistan) .
The project / Thesis shall be checked by the supervisor according to the rules mentioned above.
However, in case of any criteria under the rules that are not met , the supervisor may ask the student to revise the project/thesis report and resubmit it to the supervisor. If the revised project/thesis does not meet the criteria set under the rules, the student sha ll be held responsible, and the case sha ll be referred to the UMCC/ DSC or any other relevant committee of the department for awarding a penalty depending upon the level of severity. The participation of an AI - relevant member should also be mandatory in the constitution of these committees to ensure that AI - related concerns are properly addressed. If the departmental committee agrees, the case can be raised to respective university lev el committee and would be dealt with according to the rules and regulation s of the University/DAI .
https:// ipo.gov.pk Flowchart Appendix 1 Applications of Generative AI Tools in Higher Education Some applications of Generative AI Tools in higher education are:
A. Teaching & Learning Generative AI Tools can be used to augment the process and experience of learning for students.
These can be used as standalone tools , or they can be integrated into other platforms used by Universities and DAIs. Although Generative AI tools are evolving and improving at a rapid pace, some possible roles of the tools are described in the table below UNESCO (2023) ChatGPT and Artificial Intelligence in higher education Appendix 1 B. Research Generative AI tools can be employed at different stages of the research process or processes relating to research. Some examples are:
i. Research Design: Generate ideas for research questions or projects.
ii. Writing Up: Improve writing quality, language translation, refo rmat references and citations
iii. Quality Check (language, content, flow of document, etc.)
Some of the famous Gen AI tools include: ChatGPT, Claude, Microsoft Copilot, Researchrabbit, Gemini, etc.

# C. Administration
Title: HEC Framework for Generation AI use in Higher Education Institutions
Authority: Higher Education Commission (HEC) of Pakistan
Section: C. Administration
Official page: https://www.hec.gov.pk/english/policies/Pages/Framework-GenAI.aspx
Source file: https://www.hec.gov.pk/english/policies/Documents/Framework-Gene-AI.pdf
Version: Framework-Gene-AI as published; HEC GenAI notification attached in the register
Notification / publication date: 2026-10-10
Effective date: 2026-10-10
Legal status: Current
Extracted verbatim from the official HEC source on 2026-10-10; only layout was repaired (line wraps, page markup) — no wording was changed.

C. Administration
Employing Generative AI Tools to improve the administrative processes efficiency. Some examples are :
i. Information translation for regional/international students
ii. Finding resources and other information
Appendix 2 Responsibilities of HEIs and Organizations Promoting responsible GenAI Tools use in HEIs involves a combination of proactive measures, policy implementation, and educational initiatives.
i. Ethical Guidelines : Instructors/Supervisors should develop clear and comprehensive
guidelines specifically addressing the use of GenAI Too ls within the academic setting – how and when these tools can be used and when they cannot. These guidelines should outline acceptable use, potential risks, and consequences of misuse and must be referred/mentioned clearly in the course outlines and projec t proposal documents.
ii. Continuous Ethical Review : Create a AI Stewardship committee or ethical review board to
periodically assess GenAI Tools' use and address emerging ethical concerns related to AI technologies. Continuously assess the research manuscripts by field specialists for unethical use of GenAI Tools in light of relevant policies at the national level
iii. Connecting GenAI Tools Use to Learn ing Outcomes : At the outset of course, teachers /
supervisors should connect the use of AI Generative Tools to Outcome - Based Education (OBE)mapping it with learning outcomes (Program Learning Outcomes – PLOs & Course Learning Outcomes - CLOs). This helps students to understand how these tools can support their learning and what the guidelines/expectations are for them.
iv. Transparent Attribution : Encourage students and researchers to transparently attribute the
use of AI - generated content in their work, ensur ing proper acknowledgment and citation.
v. Faculty and Staff Capacity Building : Arrange awareness seminars and workshops to
faculty, staff, and administrators on the responsible and ethical use of GenAI Tools. Educators should understand the capabilities and limitations of GenAI Tools and be equipped to guide students appropriately. Emphasize the importance of academic honesty and integrity through these orientation programs, research seminars, and ongoing awareness campaigns. The universities can include the module related to Gen AI in the courses like “Introduction to ICT” (for BE/BS) or “Research Methodology” for (MS/PhD) , as these subjects are offered in all disciplines.
vi. Incorporate AI Ethics into Curriculum : Integrate discussions on AI ethics, bias, and
r esponsible AI use into relevant courses across various disciplines, including computer science, engineering, management , and social sciences.
vii. Critical Thinking and Information Literacy: Promote critical thinking skills among
students and researchers to hel p them critically evaluate AI - generated content and distinguish it from credible, validated sources.
viii. Originality and Creativity: Encourage and celebrate originality and creativity in student
work, discouraging the overreliance on AI - generated content for a ssignments and research.
ix. Collaboration with AI Developers: Establish collaborations with AI developers and
researchers to explore the ethical implications of AI and work together on responsible AI initiatives.
Appendix 2
x. Support Research on AI Ethics: Support and conduct research on AI ethics and bias, aiming
to develop best practices and guidelines for responsible AI use in academia.
xi. Peer Support & Collaborative Efforts: Faculty and staff share their experiences and best
practices for teaching & ways to use Generative AI Tools in learning, research & administration to increase skill level and bring efficiency in the institution. Foster Collaboration with other educational institutions, industry partners, public sector entities, and AI ethics organizati ons to share knowledge and best practices in promoting responsible and ethical use of AI , as well as in line with other applicable policies.
xii. Adapting Innovative Assessment Methods and Learning Tools: The faculty/advisors are
encouraged to adapt global bes t practices for micro - management of the content at the course/research level. Instructors should provide guidelines regarding acceptable use of Generative AI Tools referred/mentioned clearly in the course outlines and project proposal documents, ensuring t ransparency & ethical considerations. Moreover, a declaration , if asked by the instructor , can also be added. Innovative assessment methods will be developed and put into practice to complement the integration of Generative AI Tools into course learning and evaluation.
In addition to the above , HEIs may ensure compliance with the following agenda through developing DSC / UMCC/ or any equivalent statutory body to practice ethical use of GenAI.

1. OVERVIEW
The aim of this policy is to nurture and enhance academic and publication standards of national journals through financial support and capacity building.

2. OBJECTIVES
The intended objective of the proposed policy for research journals is to bring academic and publication quality of the journals at par with international standards.

3. ACTIVITIES
The activities to be undertaken under this policy include:
a. establishment of minimum and optimal standards, in line with international best practices, for academic review, publication quality, and ethical practices.
b. establishment and strengthening of monitoring systems.
c. capacity building of editorial teams; and
d. provision of financial support and linking such support to performance, i.e., success in meeting
quality criteria.

4. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR REGISTRATION
The following eligibility criteria must be met for purposes of registration at the time of submission of the application:
a. Objectives : The journal must have clearly defined aims, objectives and scope of publication.
b. Transparency : The Journal must have ISSN, title, and URL (verified from the International ISSN register). The journal's website should facilitate online availability and include an archive of previous issues. The submission process, publication fee, and sponsorships / source of funding, must be available publicly, including on the website. The journal must have published at least 5 articles per issue in th e preceding calendar year.
c. Publisher Characteristics : The journal must be owned and published by a registered entity, which
could be university or HEI or a department of faculty of such an entity, or a registered research institution, or registered nonprofit academic society. In all such cases, the publisher should have a formal governing body, which must approve the publication decision. In case of societies and non - HEIs , the term " Registered Entity " means registered with the SECP or ** [Registrar of Societies] .
A pplicable w.e.f 13 th of July, 2025 ** Provincial registration authorities of societies may be considered only if the journal is registered under a unique name and ISSN number, ensuring there is no duplication of the journal’s title or ISSN in any other district across Pakistan.

viii. Adherence to Community Standards (Articles in the journal are consistent with accepted
best practices in their subject area).
ix. Appropriate Citations to Literature

f. All completed applications by eligible journals will be evaluated by a review committee comprised of subject experts.
g. Editors will be informed of the decision, and the final list will be made available on the HEC website.

9. CAPACITY BUILDING
The following steps shall be taken for capacity building of editors and members of the editorial team:
a. HEC will organize capacity building programs for editors and members of editorial teams of eligible journals.
b. An open call will be issued on HEC website for nominations from journal E ditors, who may nominate any members of their editorial team.
c. All eligible journals (regardless of their funding status) may apply.
d. The selected candidates will be invited to participate in the training workshop.
e. HEC will provide remuneration to resource persons and/or trainers.
f. Collaboration with COPE (Committee on Publishing Ethics) and similar national or international organizations will be developed in order to strengthen the accreditation mechanism and mobilize support for training programs.

10. VALIDITY OF RESEARCH JOURNALS AND VERIFICATION OF PUBLICATIONS
a. The Research and Innovation Division of the HEC shall be responsible for the ranking, financing, and capacity building of journals. It will play no role in establishing or monitoring criteria for utilization of journals, validity of research journals, or verification of publications for the purpose of faculty appointments, promotions, appointments as PhD supervisors, or award of PhD degrees.
b. All the Quality Enhancement Cells (QECs) of HEIs are responsible, inter - alia , to facilitate their faculty/students in verification of their research publications as per criteria in vogue. QECs may seek access to required online resources through the digita l library of HEC as per prescribed rules.

How to identify the journals \ organizations using unethical/unlawful practices in research publication & be cautious of Scams Following are some useful tips to identify the scammers:
i. The journal publishes papers that are not academic at all, or the archives of published
articles/ issues are missing.
ii. The Journal/ publisher falsely claims universities or other organizations (such as
authenticate etc.) as partners or sponsors.
iii. Same authors are published several times in the same journal and/or issue.
iv. The publisher/ journal displays prominent statements that promise rapid publication
and/or unusually quick peer review (less than 4 weeks).
v. The journal's website does not have a clearly stated peer review policy or inadequate
peer review.
vi. The Journal publishes an/ the article(s), citing predatory journal(s) and/or predatory
database(s).
vii. There is no geographical diversity of authors, and the journal claims to be International.
viii. The journal uses email option as the medium for entire editorial management
workflow, including. article submission, peer - reviewing invitations to reviewers, multiple rounds of peer - review, decision on articles acceptances/ rejections etc. instead of any recognized editorial manager/ management system (e.g., Scholar One of Clarivate Analytics, EVISE of Elsevier, Open Journal Systems (OJS) of Public Knowledge Project, etc.).
ix. Hijacked journal (defined as a fraudulent website created to look like a legitimate
academic journal for the purpose of offering academics the opportunity to rapidly publish their research for a fee).
x. Information received from the journal does not match the journal's website.
xi. The title of the journal is copied or so like that of a legitimate journal that it could cause
confusion between the two.
xii. No editor or editorial board listed on the journal's website at all, or Editors/ Editorial
board members/ advisory board members do not actually exist or are deceased.
xiii. The founder of the publishing company is the editor of all the journals published by
said company.
xiv. Evident data showing that the editor/review board members do not possess academic
expertise to reasonably qualify them to be publication gatekeepers in the journal's field.
xv. The journal falsely claims indexing in well - known databases (e.g. JCR, indexing data
bases of Clarivate analytics, SCOPUS).
xvi. The journal uses misleading metrics (i.e., metrics with the words "impact factor" that
are not the Thomson Reuters Impact Factor ). The journal is found listed in any fake/ predatory indexing data base.
xvii. The journal offers options for researchers to prepay Article Processing Charges (APCs)
for future articles but does not give information regarding APCs amount or gives conflicting information.
xviii. The author must pay APC or publication fee before submitting the article (specifically
calls the fee, a publication fee, not a submission.
xix. Publisher/ journal states that the journal is completely open access but not all articles
are openly available.
xx. There is no web presence of the publisher or journal.
xxi. There is no web presence of online version of published articles or published issues.
xxii. Seemingly deliberate dead links are present for the online version of published articles
or published issues.
xxiii. PDF/ online version of published articles or published issues are locked.
xxiv. The website(s) of the publisher or journal does not identify a physical address or correct
address for the publisher or gives a fake address.

Revamping the HEC Research Grants Framework 2019 The R&D Division of HEC was established with the goal of providing funding to investigators to pursue ground‐breaking, high‐risk/high‐gain research as well as funding development and innovation projects in key enabling technologies. It is one of the premier research funders in Pakistan. Scientists and scholars of Pakistani nationality and in any discipline can apply to the HEC for a grant to undertake research at the frontiers of knowledge. Researchers at a comparable career stage compete for Starting, Consolidator or Advanced Consortium Grants — the sole criterion for receiving research funding is scientific quality aiming at excellence of both the project and the principal investigator. The evaluation of proposals is conducted by means of a structure of high‐level scientific review panels.
Recently, HEC has been striving to revamp the overall research grant framework in order to meet the national and local needs as well as achieve a much wider societal impact. Error!
Reference source not found. depicts the future landscape of the research grants offered by HEC.
Following are the major components of the R&D research grants portfolio:
 NRPU – National Research Program for Universities  GCF – Grand Challenge Fund  LCF – Local Challenge Fund  TTSF – Technology Transfer Support Fund Figure 1. Landscape of HEC Research Grants.
National Research Program for Universities (NRPU) The objective of the NRPU program is to support university-based researchers for conducting cutting-edge research. The program is open for contributions related to both basic and applied research. NRPU aims to stimulate scientific excellence and the advancement of knowledge by allowing researchers the freedom to formulate by themselves the research concept, method and Revised policy of NRPU approved in the Commission Meeting held in Dec 2021 implementation, and to solve a specific research task within a limited period of time. Demonstration of the strategic relevance and impact of the proposed research to Pakistani industry and/or society will be considere d a merit.
The eligibility criteria for the NRPU grant is as follows:
 The Principal Investigator (PI) has to be a regular faculty member (BPS or TTS) of the HEI or must hold a contract equivalent to the length of duration of the project.
 Each PI can be awarded maximum one research grant under NRPU at the particular time.
 PI must have an advanced academic degree (PhD, MS/MPhil or FCPS/MCPS/FRCS) The budgets for NRPU projects are anticipated upto PKR 20 Million, with a maximum project duration of 3 years. Co-financing – including in kind and cash contributions – by industry partners will be considered a merit and an indicator of industry support.
The NRPU grant awards will be made to the host higher education institution of the lead academic – faculty – associated with the project, and administered through the appropriate ORIC on campus. The budgetary provisions will be covered under Financial Rules for HEC Competitive Research Grants 2021 :
The submitted application is assessed by other active researchers with great expertise within the field. We have clear guidelines for the assessment work, and evaluate the process continuously. The assessment shall be of high quality and be conducted in an objective, impartial and transparent manner.
Nurturing Academic Excellence in Strategic Sectors The World Bank funded Higher Education Development in Pakistan (HEDP) Project will strengthen the research capacity and academic excellence of higher education institutions in Pakistan.
It will promote relevant and cutting-edge research in universities, with a focus on strategic sectors identified for the country’s socioeconomic progress. It will provide funds for peer -reviewed competitive research grants, innovation and commercialization grants, and specialized training and support to potential entrepreneurs identified from among those with a current or recent university affiliation.

1.1. This sub-component is focused on promoting relevant research and
supporting technology transfer through two distinct mechanisms.
1.2. This sub-component is focused on encouraging entrepreneurship and
self-employment through the higher education sector. This will be accomplished through two distinct activities.
1.3. This sub-component is focused on strengthening research capacity at
higher education institutions across Pakistan.
Sub-Component 1.1: Grand Challenge Fund and Technology Transfer Support Fund The Grand Challenge Fund (GCF) The Pakistan Grand Challenge Fund (GCF) will support large, multisectoral/ multidimensional research projects. Each GCF proposal should focus on a specific theme of national interest. The focus under GCF is not on individual researchers, but rather on collaborations necessary to accelerate research progress and make a societal impact. Projects should use a systems-type approach in developing the research agenda, where separate projects come together to achieve concrete results and impact. The project will be implemented under the direction of a Principal Investigator with the support of a research team. The project will include research activities, postgraduate student training, and disseminating knowledge both through traditional academic pathways and those leading to direct societal impact. The priority themes for the GCF include:
 Food security  Water management and sustainability  Sustainable energy, energy efficiency  Identity politics  Export promotion  Urban planning, sustainable urban design, low-cost housing  Climate mitigation and adaptation  IT/Telecom, including but not limited to artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, cloud computing and big data  Innovative governance and reforms  Disaster management GCF proposals will be written by university faculty members from research-intensive institutions. Given the scope of the proposals, a consortia of faculty members from multiple university departments and/or multiple universities may be part of the project team. As appropriate, consortia members may include private sector participants, although grant funding must be used for universitybased team members. International collaborations are encouraged when the international partner brings a unique added value to the project team. Proposals must clearly describe the skills and research strengths that each investigator brings to the systems-type multidisciplinary research agenda.
The budgets for GCF projects are anticipated to range between Rs. 15 million – 225 million (USD 100,000 – USD 1,500,000), with a maximum project duration of 3 years. Co-financing will be sought from relevant Ministries and Departments, and complementary financing for the projects is desirable. The GCF grant awards will be made to the host higher education institution of the lead Principal Investigator. The host institution may make sub awards to partner institutions that host research team members. The project budget can finance the following activities:
a. Salaries for PI and co-PIs based on the amount of time spent on the project b. Stipends for bachelors, masters, doctoral students, and postdoctoral scholars to conduct the research proposed
c. Travel to national and international meetings to present research
results obtained
d. Travel to consortia members’ institutions in support of the
research proposed e. Processing fee for open access journals for disseminating research results f. The purchase and maintenance of appropriate, approved equipment to conduct the research proposed g. The purchase of research supplies necessary to conduct the research proposed h. Grants to attract visiting researchers from outside Pakistan to conduct research that contributes to the grant objectives. These visiting researchers can be either expatriate Pakistani scientists or foreign scientists.
i. A component of the grant will be earmarked for the problem
solving (i.e., it will be released only if there is a demonstrable evidence of success in solving a problem).
The Calls for Proposals for the GCF will be issued by the Higher Education Commission.
Proposals must be submitted by the host higher education institution (public or private) of the lead Principal Investigator. Submission must be made to the Higher Education Commission online portal according to the Guidance provided in the Call for Proposals.
Within the GCF competitions, the Higher Education Commission aims to support a portfolio of projects that, as a whole, address the broad range of development challenges as identified above. It is anticipated that research supported by GCF will be conducted at research-intensive universities around the country. To take full advantage of the national research capacity in Pakistan, the research teams will be comprised of junior and senior academic staff, and a significant proportion of Principal Investigators (team leaders) and team members will be female. Furthermore, GCF consortia should include qualified researchers from institutions with limited research capacity.

The Technology Transfer Support Fund (TTSF) The Technology Transfer Support Fund (TTSF) will support promising university technological research that has previously developed an existing prototype or advanced model. The purpose of the grants is to foster partnerships between academia and industry to facilitate the transfer of technology to industry and the commercial sector. The anticipated result is the development of products or services that are marketable and can generate positive cash flows.
The grant will seek to develop commercializable solutions in a broad range of key areas (e.g., water efficiency, water monitoring, energy efficiency, crop efficiency) implemented through the use of advanced technologies, e.g., a. Telecommunications b. Information Technology and its application in health, textile, agriculture and agribusiness such as dairy and horticulture
c. Engineering sciences, including microelectronics, water, power, energy and fleet
management
d. Biotechnology
e. Materials sciences, for example nano-technology The grant competition will be open to faculty members and students from both public and private universities. Faculty members and students are expected to partner with industry – including industry research and development teams – in project formulation.
The budgets for TTSF projects are anticipated to range between Rs. 7.5 million – 20 million (USD 50,000 – USD 140,000), with a maximum project duration of 2 years. Co-financing – including in kind and cash contributions – by industry partners is mandatory and an indicator of industry support. The TTSF grant awards will be made to the host higher education institution of the lead academic – faculty or student – associated with the project, and administered through the appropriate ORIC on campus. The project budget can finance the following activities:
a. Salaries for PI and co-PIs based on the amount of time spent on the project b. Stipends for bachelors, masters, doctoral students and post-doctoral scholars to help take the prototype or proposed product to market.
c. Travel to national and international meetings to present research results obtained
and in support of the proposed research
d. Processing fee for open access journals for disseminating research results obtained
e. Limited research and development costs f. Patent filing g. Producing licensing agreements h. Legal and financial investment advice
i. Marketing of the prototype or proposed product to appropriate investors or
stakeholders The Calls for Proposals for the TTSF will be issued by HEC. Proposals must be submitted by the host higher education institution (public or private) of the lead academic – faculty or student – associated with the project. Submission must be made to the Higher Education Commission online portal according to the Guidance provided in the Call for Proposals.
Within the TTSF competitions, HEC aims to support a portfolio of projects that, as a whole, address the broad range of sectors as identified above. It is anticipated that research supported by TTSF will be conducted at universities around the country. To take full advantage of the national research capacity in Pakistan, the research teams will be comprised of junior and senior academic staff, students, and female participation will be in line with overall project goals.
Sub-Component 1.2: Business Incubation Centers and Innovator Seed Fund Sub-component 1.2 is focused on encouraging entrepreneurship and selfemployment through the higher education sector. This will be accomplished through two distinct activities.
Remodel Selected Business Incubation Centers (BICs) At Project launch, the Business Incubation Centers (BICs) affiliated with Pakistan higher education institutions do not meet the needs of faculty members and students due to insufficient funds, inadequate facilities and limited services capacity. The first activities planned under Sub-component 1.2 focus on renovation of the infrastructure and facilities associated with selected BICs, and then developing BIC service capacity in line with international good practices.
The HEC is responsible for identifying which BICs will receive support for remodeling and program development. A Consultant will be engaged by HEC to undertake an evaluation of the existing BICs. The Consultant is expected to report on the existing capacity – including physical facilities, resources, and services – at the BICs, and to make recommendations on the investments necessary to achieve a global standard, and to prepare BICs for long-term sustainability. In addition, the Consultant will catalogue previous successes that BICs have had in their incubation activities to provide a baseline of capability.

The renovated BICs are expected to provide a physical infrastructure conducive to the needs of entrepreneurs and startup/early phase companies that launch from the university environment. In particular, the BICs should offer: specific types of laboratory and office space; flexible lease terms; and access to technology. By providing space that brings complementary and synergistic startup companies into close proximity, the BIC may play a role – formal and/or informal – in knowledge transfer.
The renovated BICs are also expected to provide business services – especially focused for entrepreneurs and startup companies – to tenants in the incubator. These services shall include:
management coaching; mentoring; help in preparing business plans; financial management; advice on financing; advice on intellectual property; business networking; and technical assistance focused on marketing, proposal writing, legal support, and human resources. These services should be available via both a formal suite of training programs and ad hoc support by BIC staff. To support the delivery of business services described above, HEC is responsible for coordinating the training of BIC staff by internal and external Experts to ensure that each renovated BIC effectively serves the faculty members and students launching new and startup companies.
The renovated BICs should serve the stakeholders and beneficiaries - including the host universities, entrepreneurs and students – in the following ways:
Higher Education Institutions Entrepreneurs Students  Opportunity to establish university startup linkage  A suite of training and support actions developed to bring tech advances and products to the market, and to create additional resources/income streams for the HEI  Well - equipped common laboratories and facilities, including libraries, computer labs and digital infrastructure  Technological and subject matter expertise through the university faculty members,  A well - educated workfor ce, including recent graduates and current students  Internship and part - time job opportunities  Real world examples as case studies  Opportunity to apply classroom knowledge to novel business problems  Introduction to entrepreneurshi p early in career trajectory The Innovator Seed Fund (ISF) The Innovator Seed Fund (ISF) will be implemented through the remodeled BICs.
Participating BICs are expected to develop a suite of activities that will support the business development of start-ups launched by students, recent graduates and/or faculty from universities.
The package will focus on business mentoring and training activities rather than product development and research activities. Given the nature of ISF, many of the activities supported – especially training programs – will be common amongst all grantees.
The budgets for ISF projects will be Rs. 5 million (USD 35,000). The project budget will finance the following training and mentoring activities:
a. How to develop a business plan b. How to identify potential markets
c. How to successfully market products and services
d. How to manage an enterprise including financial management, and
e. How to put together proposals that could win funds for enterprise development.
The Calls for Proposals for the ISF will be issued by HEC. Proposals must be submitted to the Higher Education Commission online portal according to the Guidance provided in the Call for Proposals.
Within the ISF competitions, the Higher Education Commission aims to support a portfolio of project teams that, as a whole, will lead to successful start-ups emerging from the higher education sector in Pakistan. To take full advantage of the national research and innovation capacity in Pakistan, the portfolio of awards will reflect the diversity of potential entrepreneurs in Pakistan, including current students, recent graduates and faculty members.
Sub-Component 1.3: Locally Relevant Grants Sub-component 1.3 is focused on strengthening research capacity at higher education institutions across Pakistan through research projects focused on local challenges.
The Local Challenge Fund (LCF) The Local Challenge Fund (LCF) will support cross-disciplinary research projects that address any of the 17 SDGs at district levels. The LCF is a competitive research grants competition. A key criteria for proposal evaluation is the relevance and potential impact of the research to the local community – society, governmental, or industry. LCF awards are expected to strengthen the local university research capacity, and to contribute to the research mission of the host institution.
LCF proposals will be written by university faculty members from higher education institutions (as specified by HEC in the Call for Proposals). As appropriate, researchers may form consortia with other universities, and may include private sector participants although grant funding must be used for university-based team members. Proposals must clearly describe the skills and research strengths that each investigator brings to the research, and the benefit to the host institution.

II. Equipment, Consumables, and Service Costs
3. General Conditions : The following general conditions apply to the provision of equipment, consumables and services costs:
a. Equipment and Consumables should be itemized separately. However, the total cost under these heads may not be greater than 70 per cent of the direct cost of the project b. For each item under Equipment , and each item under Consumables , provide the name, description of equipment, specifications, unit cost, quantity, and purpose.
c. For Equipment, Consumables and Services, the university needs to certify in writing
that it does not have access to the said equipment, consumables and service otherwise.
d. 10% additional amount against approved equipment budget for imported items may
be admissible to account for any currency rate fluctuation, subject to provision of justification, and the approval of HEC.
e. LC opening for purchase of permanent equipment is allowed
# Item Details
1. Equipment A few examples are provided here. These, and similar items could be billed to the project if otherwise justified:
 Scientific lab Equipment : tools and equipment used in laboratories for research work relevant to the project. Some examples are DNA sequencers, electrometers, or spectrometer s.
 IT equipment : some examples are servers, network equipment, routers, or communication equipment.
 Office Equipment : some examples are laptops, desktops, scanners, printers.
 Specialized Software/ IT Applications : e.g., LabView, AutoCAD, MATLAB.
2. Consumables A few examples are provided here. These, and similar items could be billed to the project if otherwise justified:
 Lab Chemicals : e.g., chlorates, persulfates, peroxides, oxidizing acids, methanol, ethanol, or reagents.
 Glassware : e.g., beakers, flasks, or test tubes.
 Plastic wares : e.g., pipettes .
 Expendable supplies : e.g., preserving and cleaning material, fuel, medicines, personal protective equipment, i.e., gloves, masks, or surgical caps.
 Accessories : small tools and accessories used routinely in labs, e.g., kits, PCR plates, ladders, sealers, magnetic stands.
3. Services  Access to scientific equipment : cost of access to sophisticated lab or research equipment not available in host institution.
 Service contract for repair/ maintenance of purchased scientific equipment : The service cost should not exceed 25% of the cost of current price of the same/similar model  Subscription to open access journals or publications : provided these are not already covered under HEC's agreement with the HEI.
 Management Cost for organizing national level con ferences, workshops, or seminars : in cases, where such dissemination of research results are outsourced to external professional bodies.
 Limited commercialization and development costs : these will be allowed only for research grants (e.g., TTSF and RTTG) that explicitly include product development and commercialization goals. The admissible expenses are:
o Patent filing Fee o Consultancy Services for product development (limited 10% of the direct cost of the project) o Legal and Financial Services: related to intellectual property rights, research commercialization, or licensing agreements.
o Marketing Services : for marketing of prototype or proposed product to appropriate investors or stakeholders

General Conditions : Travel Cost covers expenses of project team (faculty and students and other project personnel (Research Assistants, Research Associate, Research Fellow) related to research/ field work, participation in project meetings, attending national or international conferences or workshops to present research results from the project.
a. Travel budget must be justified by providing purpose of visit, the city, the country, the number of travelers, and estimated costs per visit.
b. Budget limit for Local travel is Maximum Rs. 150,000/- per year as per actual.
c. Prior approval of HEC must be obtained for each project-related international travel
with proper justification.
d. The international travel expenses are allowed as per following details:
Project Personnel Type Purpose of Expenses Limits Allowed Expenses Faculty, students, other project personnel (maximum one visit per year) Costs of participation in foreign country for fieldwork, research work or meetings under the project Max one visit per year for a v isit duration of not more than
30 days
T ravel expenses of foreign round trip and D aily Allowance including accommodation as per Gov ernment rules Cost of participation in international Conferences, Seminar, Workshops, Symposium to present research results under the project Max 1 visit per year for a visit duration of not more than 6 days Registration fee as per actual, TA, DA including accommodation as per HEC Travel Grant Policy and Government rules .

IV. University Overheads
5. General Conditions : There are three purposes for allowing payment of overhead costs to sponsoring HEIs: first, to compensate HEIs for expenses needed to provide research support in the form of campus facilities, secretarial or administrative services, tuition waivers to research assistants, or project development expenses; second, to enable HEIs to build up a professional research support system in order to enable their faculty members to attract research funding from other sources as well, including, e.g., capacity building activities; and third, to ensure that universities exercise proper quality control over research products.
6. The overhead amount should go directly into the research management budget of universities, which may allocate it for various purposes according to the needs of each project as well as the overall demands of professional research management. In case of multiinstitutional projects, the overhead costs are expected to be shared on the basis of the percentage of funds allocated for each institution.
7. HEC allows three tiers of University overheads or institutional costs, as a percent of the total direct cost of the project: 5%, 10%, and 15%.
a. Basic (5% Overheads): this covers projects that do not require allocation of dedicated office space or dedicated secretarial or support staff. It covers the basic research support services, i.e., accounts management, project reporting, auditing, office supplies (e.g., pens, staplers, or stationery), and monitoring and evaluation.
Researchers are expected to use their own offices and regular university facilities.
b. Extra (10% Overheads): In addition to the services listed in paragraph (a) above, the HEI also provide the following additional facilities: support staff (daily wage clerical or manual labor, secretariat staff), campus expenses (e.g., use of dedicated office, unit, or building), utility costs, cost of access to digital resources (e.g., Digital Library, PERN), maintenance of scientific equipment, and/or access to laboratories.
c. Performance (15% Overheads): In addition to the services listed in paragraph (b), the
HEI may demonstrate superior performance on behalf of the ORICs or other research management institutions.
8. The provision of overheads means that HEIs will not be allowed to include normal administrative expenses (e.g., administrative salaries, TA/DA. honorariums, bonuses, or stipends).

Scientific Review Panels – Assessment Framework – Policy Revision In 2019, HEC adopted the concept of having Scientific Review Panels in order to ensure quality of assessment, transparency, objectivity and efficiency. Under Seven (07) specified broad disciplines, standing panels of experts, comprising of 5-8 members led by a Panel Chair, were constituted to conduct peer review of research grants and publications etc. and to advise HEC about the impact of the overall HEC research grant policies over the scientific community.
Moreover, Program Chairs for various Research Grant Programs (GCF and LCF) have been appointed who are responsible to manage the review process and perform advisory role on strategic direction of research funding in consultation with HEC Scientific Review Panels.
The existing Panels, since their formation in December, 2019, have been under immense work load of reviewing proposals round the year under different calls for research grants applications i.e. GCF, LCF, NRPU, TTSF, ICRG, CPEC etc. In order to eliminate bottlenecks and effectively manage and accelerate the review process, the following revisions reflected in the below table are proposed in the Scientific Review Panels- Assessment Framework 2019.
Sno. Existing Policy Proposed Policy Revisions Remarks
i. HEC Scientific Review Panels: There are
eight (8) Review Panels in following broad disciplines;
i. Agriculture Sciences
ii. Arts and Humanities
iii. Biological and Health Sciences
iv. Management Sciences
v. Education and Human Resource
vi. Engineering and Technology
vii. Mathematical and Physical
Sciences
viii. Social, Behavioral and
Economic Sciences
- Review Panels will be constituted in
Eighteen (18) major disciplines as listed at Annex - I .
- Additional panels in relevant subjects
may be constituted where necessary as per submitted applications in a call for proposals.
- The disciplines are adopted from
the Unit of Assessments/ Panels defined by the REF-UK with some rearrangements.
- The existing panels will merged
with the new ones in relevant disciplines.
- The increase in Panels will
expedite the peer review of proposals and efficiently meet time lines of the process.
ii. Panel Formation
-
- The names of the Panel Chairs & Program
Chairs will be proposed by the DG R&ID and names of Panel members will be proposed by the respective Panel Chairs in consultation with DG (R&ID). The Executive Director, HEC will be the approving Authority for constitution of panels.
-Authority to approve and nominate Panel Chairs, Program Chairs & members
iii. Time Commitment & compensation : the
Chair must dedicate 20% whereas a member 10% of his/her working time to HEC for honorarium of Rs.156,250 (to chair) and Rs.50,000/- (to member).
However external experts serve the panels on voluntarily basis.
The admissible honorarium will be as follow:
- For the Panel Chairs @ Rs. 150,000/ - per
Call for proposals.
- For the Panel Members @ Rs. 2,000/ - per
proposal as a focal point for review after proposals shortlisting.
- For the Panel Members and External
Reviewer @ Rs. 1,000/ - per proposal for shortlisting, @ Rs. 3,000/ - per proposal for Project Outline Review, @ Rs. 8,000/ - per proposal for Full proposal Review The time commitment of Chairs and Panels with monthly honorarium cannot be justified due to heavy work load of evaluation of proposals.
Panels will be responsible for review assignments to relevant subject experts, shortl isting of proposals, discussion on proposals and recommendations for selection .
iv. Panels Applying for HEC Research
Grants:
-
- Panel Chairs or members, willing to apply
as PI or CoPI in any HEC Research grant call, must communicate to HEC before application submission and such Panel Chairs and members will be debarred in the evaluation process of that particular call and substitute arrangements will be made where necessary.
Panel Chairs and members apply ing for HEC grants creates conflict of interest.
v. Evaluation Process - Shortlisting of
Proposals: In full proposals submission, after administrative scrutiny all eligible proposals undergo desk evaluation/ detailed review on the basis of evaluation criteria
- After administrative scrutiny, the eligible
applications/proposals will be shortl isted by the Review Panels if required, keeping in view large pool of submitted applications. O nly shortlisted proposals will be considered for detailed review/ desk evaluation.
- In Full proposal submission stage
in NRPU and other grants, the review of large pool of proposals (more than 3000) is difficult to be managed by the panels in a timely manner.
- Approved by the Chairman, HEC
vi. Assignment of Proposals: The proposals
are assigned to the Panel Chairs of respective HEC Scientific Review panels for further assignment to Panel members and external reviewers for assessment.
- The assignment of proposals to the
respective Panel members and external reviewers wi ll be managed by HEC team and where required consultation with Panel Chairs will b e solicited on subject experts.
- To minimize t ime and work load
of the panels vii Minimum Threshold: The HEC Scientific Review Panels make panel recommendations on proposals after getting 2 - 3 individual reviews. The panel recommendations are followed by a joint multidisciplinary panel decision that seek to recommend portfolio of proposals for award that qualifies minimum threshold decided by the panels, supports the best overall proposals that respond to project goals, diversity of disciplines addressing thematic areas, diversity of senior/ junior, male & female project team.
- Proposals for consideration of award
must receive minimum threshold of average score of 3.5 or above with at least two review scores of 3.5 or above .
- In case one review score is below 3.5 and
another is higher , third review may also be solicited, if necessary.
- Proposals below threshold will be
rejected.
- Proposals qualifying minimum threshold
will be considered by the respective Review Panels that should seek to recommend top ranked proposals and that supports the best overall proposals responding the project goals, diversity of disciplines addressing them atic areas, diversity of senior/ junior, male & female project team .
- Maximum threshold of score will be
based on availability of funds.
- The Competent Authority may approve
proposals for funding based on review scores qualifying minimum threshold and subj ect to availability of funds.
- To set minimum threshold and
screen out proposals having low threshold in order to minimize workload of the panels.
Proposal for the Commission:
The Commission may consider and approve the proposed revisions in HEC Scientific Review Panels- Assessment Framework 2019.

3 8
th Commission Meeting, November 27 - 28 , 2020 HEC Research Awards – Revised Policy Introduction 1. The purpose of HEC Research Awards is to recognize and reward excellence in research, contributions to intellectual development and social welfare, and promote publications with higher impact. The award includes a certificate and a cash prize as described below.
Award Categories and Domains
2. Separate awards shall be given in three broad disciplinary domains:
a. Social Sciences, Arts and Hu manities, Law, Education, Management, or Public Policy b. Physical Sciences, Engineering, Technology, Computer Science, Statistics, or Mathematics
c. Life Sciences, Biological Sciences, Health Sciences, Pharmacy, Agriculture, or
Veterinary Science
3. There are thre e categories of awards in each disciplinary domain:
a. Best Researcher: A cash prize of Rs. 500,000 for research contributions judged to be of the highest quality b. Best Young Researcher: A cash prize of Rs. 500,000, to a researcher under the age of 40, who is judged by the scientific panels to show the most promise of stimulating further research, addressing or resolving social problems, and enhancing the quality of research in Pakistan
c. Best Publication: A cash prize of Rs. 1 million to be awarded to the publication
(i.e., book or journal article) that is judged by the scientific panels as likely to produce the greatest impact on human welfare, either by stimulating and opening up new areas of further research, or by contributing to the resolution of a cri tical problem facing Pakistan and the world at large.
4. In future, depending on the number and quality of the applications, HEC may establish additional awards, increasing the number domains in which the awards are established, or increase the number of awar ds in each domain.
5. In case no suitable candidate is found, the Commission may give fewer awards in any year, or no awards at all.
3 8
th Commission Meeting, November 27 - 28 , 2020 Eligibility and Selection Criteria
6. The following table sets out the eligibility and selection criteria for each
award.
Category Eligibility Criteria Selection Parameters Best Research er To be eligible, a candidate should have been a resident of Pakistan for at least three years prior to the 1st of January of the year of the award, and should not have received the same award earlier.
The objective of the award is to recognize and reward r esearchers who have contributed the most to intellectual and social development through their writings (i.e., not simply through their formal titles or positions). As such, while this is an award for a lifetime of achievement rather than a single publicati on or contribution, it does not preclude recognizing a single publication with a huge impact. On the other hand, the lifetime of achievement should be characterized by outstanding publications with demonstrated major impact.
Best Young Research er A candid ate for this award should have been a resident of Pakistan for at least one year, and should not have reached the age of 40 years on the 1st of January of the year of the award.
The objective of this award is to recognize both the contribution and future p otential of early career researchers in terms of their research and publications. Here, too, selection should place due weight on particular outstanding and impactful discoveries and publications.
Best Publicati on The award is to be given to a scholarly book or journal article published no more than three years before the date of announcement of the aw ard, and written by no more than three authors.
All authors must have been residents of Pakistan for at least three years on the 1st of January of the year of the award.
Publications that have previously been submitted for the same award are not eligible, regardless of The objective of the award is to recognize and reward the book or article tha t has produced a lasting impact on future research as well as socio - economic development in the country.
The focus of the selection committee should be on assessing the impact of the publication, which is to be measured in two dimensions, namely (a) socio - economic, i.e., the resolution of a problem facing society, or the creation of a product that benefits so ciety; and (b) academic, i.e., opening up a new area of research, and stimulating other work that leads towards the resolution of social challenges.
3 8
th Commission Meeting, November 27 - 28 , 2020 Category Eligibility Criteria Selection Parameters whether they were shortlisted. Similarly, extended version of a paper once submitted is not eligible for resubmission.
Only books published by a recognized academic press as defined by HEC are eligible.
Only articles published in a W - category journal in HJRS, and with a minimum citation count of 100, are eligible.
In this regard, the committee may use certain indicators of impact, e.g., associated patents, commercializ ation, conversion of recommendations into policy, and the number of citations.

The committee may also establish standards or indicators of academic merit, e.g., the originality of the idea, the quality of the journals (e.g., HJRS score)/ publishers where the publication was published, the validity of the data analysis, and the quality and clarity of the exposition.
However, the indicators should not be allowed to defeat the main purpose of the award, namely to reward innovative ideas that contribute to so cial welfare and intellectual development.
Application Procedure 7. A call for proposals or nominations shall be issued on the 1st of January every year, and applications shall be due on or before 1st February.
8. Applications or nominations shall be submitted on the online HEC portal on the prescribed form along with the prescribed documents. All applications should upload the CVs of the applicants or authors, as the case might be, on the HEC portal in the prescribed manner. In addition to the standar d personal and professional information, the application requires the following information:
a. Statement of Contribution (500 - 1000 words): the statement should set out a persuasive case for why the applicant (author or publication) is deserving of the award, pointing to the specific contributions that merit the award, and placing these in the context of the contemporary professional developments as well as the careers of the authors/ nominees.
b. Three letters of support : The award applications must include sub stantive letters of support from three prominent individuals, who are broadly representative of the candidate's field or related fields, and who can provide evidence of the lasting impact of the particular publication or candidate, as well as any additiona l insights or evidence that may be relevant. The endorsers should also be registered on HEC's professional portal.
c. Draft Citation : The applications should include a draft citation of up to 300 words,
which describes succinctly the achievements, impact, or potential, for which the award is being granted.
3 8
th Commission Meeting, November 27 - 28 , 2020
d. Copies of Publications : Applications for the publication award should include a
copy of published article or book. In case of journal articles, this should be an electronic copy or link. In case of books, a physical copy will be accepted .
Selection Process 9. Three Scientific Panels will be constituted, one in each broad disciplinary domain, to evaluate the nominations/ applications. Each Panel will comprise three members with subject expertise of the relevant disciplines.
10. Depending on breadth and number of applications, the Panels may engage external reviewers to assess contributions in different disciplines or sub - disciplines.
11. Panel Members and Reviewers shall be compensated for their time in accordance with HEC rules.
12. The Panels shall assess the applications on the basis of the objectives and evaluation criteria of the awards.
13. The Panels shall recommend the awards to the HEC. However, the Commission has the right to reject the recommendations if the work is not considered to be up to the mark.
14. The Panels will review the draft citations submitted by the candidates, and endorse i t, after any editing that may be necessary.
15. Prior to appointment, Panel Members have to submit a Conflict of Interest statement in accordance with the HEC Policy in this regard.

Effective Date: July 1, 2022 Travel Grant for Pakistani Researchers (TGPR) – Revised Policy 2021

1. Overview
Academic events are significant for professional development of researchers and scholars. They serve as a source for guidance, exposure, knowledge sharing, developing linkages, and problem solving. Academic events provide opportunities for academicians to help understand the latest developments in their field and validate research findings, while creating opportunities for future academic collaborations.
Such events are the cornerstone of the academic environment. To cultivate this environment, the Higher Education Commission has set up a special Research Travel Grant Fund for University faculty and scholars at Pakistani Universities. Under this program, an academician and student selected to present research work at a national or international academic event is eligible to get funding from HEC and the expenses will be reimbursed by the HEC after the event.

2. Program Objectives
i. To extend financial assistance to faculty and researchers to present their
research work at national and international events.
ii. To share academic and research experiences and achievements at national
as well as international level.
iii. To share scientific ideas with national/international researchers, get
exposure to latest trends and techniques in research.
iv. To explore opportunities for national and international collaborations.

3. Travel Grant Categories
Travel grant is extended for Presentation of research paper (oral as well as poster) in National or International Conferences/Workshops.

5. Funding Mechanism
i. The Faculty Members/ Scholars will apply to HEC for travel grant duly
endorsed by the University Head and ORIC offices via HEC online portal or in the prescribed manner
ii. HEC will approve the Grant of the applicant on recommendation of Travel
Grant Expert Committee.
iii. The funds will be reimbursed to the concerned University after the event upon
filing duly complete reimbursement claim within the prescribed time limit .
iv. The University will be responsible for timely release of funds to the
Applicant.
v. The Applicant and the University will be responsible for proper utilization of
the Grant after fulfillment of all codal formalities and accounting procedures in accordance with the Government rules/ regulations and HEC relevant policy.
vi. The Grant will be provided for the specified purpose as mentioned in the Award
letter and cannot be utilized for any other purpose.
vii. Any expense made against budget heads/ item(s) not explicitly desired in the
application form or not approved by HEC, will not be reimbursed.
viii. HEC funding support must be acknowledged in any news/ publications
related to the presented paper in electronic or print media and name and/or logo of HEC will be used for the purpose.
ix. In case of postponement or cancellation of the event, HEC must be informed in
writing .
x. No reappropriation under the budget heads is allowed.
6. Funding Allocation to Universities:
i. No more than 20 grants per University will be awarded in a financial year.
ii. Maximum approval of grants will not exceed the budget allocation for a financial
year. The ED HEC, may allow approval of grants greater than budgetary allocation in a financial year, if required .
